units.la: NON patrocinium quæro, non charisticum emendico, non gratiam aucupor vestram, AMPLISSIMI PROCERES. Quorum illud, ab innocuo argumento; istud, à genio & fortunâ etiā meâ, hoc, ab eo quo me tot retro annis complexi estis fa-vore, quodammodo ab-horret. Quod res est dicā, & omnes intelligent. Vobis, non omnino ingratæ meæ erga Vos mentis, aliis, Vestræ erga me beneficen-tiæ rationes, constare pu-blicè volui. Non jam, de manibus loquar, conjunc-tissimi pridem Vobis Pa-rentis nostri. Non de properfisimâ quondam Ve-strâ in eum voluntate, & singulari plane, ac tot illu-stribus probatâ documen-tis. Non de immenso illo, quod apud Vos, Vestros-que optimos Cives, reli-quit sui & relinquit cotti-die, desiderio. Animum tristissima hæc jam exulce-rat, acerbatque nimium recordatio. De me paucis-simis expediam, AMPLISSIMI, & tribus quidem verbis. Agentem apud Vos, quot mactum esse voluistis obæratumq; beneficiis? Quo me affectu, charitatibus penè orbum omnibus, in tutelam vestram recipere? Quâ saepè prosequi, si non juvare, munificentia? Quâ & privatim, atq; etiam in Amplissimo consessu Vestro, exciperehumanitate,cumprimis abiurientem, & gratias agentem? Imò & jungere dextras, ac paternò fere amplexu dimittere. Hæc sanè ita comparata, MAGNIFICI PROCERES, ut non potuerim non aliquid saltè, quantulucunque est, reponere. Faterique ex illâ, quæ in agro prideè Vestro concepta, & à Vobis velut irrigata fuit, semente, quicquid jam est frugis, totum deberi Vobis. Quanquam nec aliis hanc invi-detis,quum domi situber-rima eruditionis omnis ac literaturæ messis. Quum tam ampla & opima inde spolia, cottidie Literatus orbis reportet universus. Hæc tamen,non plane ignobili è loco ad Vos ad-volare cogitate. Sed ex florentissimo pridem, jam etiam reflorescente Athe-næo , non uno autem vinculo, cum Vestro & olim & hodie conjuncto. Atque ita eâdem , quâ tenuiora quondam mea, hanc qualemcunq; etiam disquisitionem, ma nu capessitote. Valete, AM. PLISSIMI VIRI , Vobis, Reipublicæ , Academiæ, Familiisq; Vestris. Dabam Heidelbergæ , Kalend. Septembr. Anno Æræ Christianæ MDCLVIII.
units.tr: I do not seek your patronage, I do not beg for a return favour, and I do not angle for your grace, most distinguished lords. The first would be out of keeping with the harmless character of my argument; the second is somewhat at odds with my disposition and my fortune; the third is somewhat at odds with the favour by which you have embraced me for so many years past. I will say plainly what the matter is, and everyone will understand. I wished to make public to you the reasons for my mind, which is not wholly ungrateful towards you, and to others the reasons for your kindness towards me. I will not now speak of the hands of our father, who was most closely joined to you long ago. I will not speak of your once most ready goodwill towards him, plainly singular and proved by so many illustrious documents, nor of the immense longing he left behind among you and your excellent citizens, and which he leaves every day. Recollection of these sad things already inflames and embitters my mind too much. I shall deal with myself in very few words, most distinguished sirs, indeed in three. How many benefits have you chosen to heap upon me, when I was acting before you and bound to you? With what affection did you take me under your protection, almost bereft of every kind of charity? With what generosity did you often attend me, if not to help me? With what courtesy did you receive me, both privately and even in your most distinguished assembly, especially when I was departing and giving thanks? Indeed, you joined your right hands with mine and dismissed me with an almost paternal embrace. These things are so arranged, most magnificent lords, that I could not but repay something, however small it may be. I confess that whatever fruit there now is, from that seed which was long ago sown in your field and, as it were, watered by you, is wholly owed to you. Although you do not begrudge this harvest to others, since at home there is the most abundant harvest of all learning and letters, and the whole literary world brings home from there such ample and rich spoils every day. Yet think of these works as flying to you from no altogether ignoble place: from the Athenaeum, long flourishing and now also flourishing again, joined to yours both formerly and today by more than one bond. And so, with the same hand with which you once took up my slighter works, take up this inquiry too, whatever sort it is. Farewell, most distinguished men, and to you, your commonwealth, your academy and your families. Given at Heidelberg, on the first day of September, in the year of the Christian era 1658.

units.la: EA est temporum nostrorum ratio, ut quicquid elucubratur, non in lectores, sed censores incidat & Aristarchos. Quo-rum ego, si æqui sunt, nihil est quod censo-riam virgulam reformidem: si iniqui, est quod negligam, & susque deque habeam. Hi quidem, juvenilem prodeundi in publi-cum nobis affingent impetiginem. Aut no-strum admordebunt argumentum, ut vel singulare nimis, vel necessarium minus. Priores autem, ut curtam eruditionis su-pellectilem ætati condonabunt; sic institu-tum probaturos esse confidimus. Intelli-gent non indignam fuisse causam publico patrocinio: nec plane operam lusisse nos, in restituenda Authori suo gravissimâ Epi-stolarum omnium. Non clam erunt, quæ sive frangenda supererant aliorum tela, sive discutienda aliorum dubia. Neque fugiet, per authorem, oblique peti Epistolæ authoritatem. Et quid desiderari po-tuerit in hoc argumento, qui hæc nostra legerit, assequetur. Excusserat dubio pro-cul, celeberrimus & desideratissimus quondam tot nominibus Parens, suis Genevæ ad Epistolam Prolegomenis. Sed no- bis, quod sanctè nec sine animi quadam ægritudine fatemur, non visis, non inter ea, quæ super sunt, spolia & fragmenta ha-ctenus deprehensis. Neque etiam Prolegomenôn illorum ratio & modus, pleniorem rei patitur disquisitionem. Nusquam autem vagamur, aut digredimur, sed hoc agimus, atque intra septa consistimus. Ut autem hæ Exercitationes idem, cum minutiis quibusdam nostris, fatum experiantur, securos nos esse jubet, causæ sive justitia sive innocentia. Vix enim prodierant nostræ, de Articulis pridem in Belgio controversis, pagellæ, quæ ecce in Belgio nonnemo (ater an albus, certè homo Pelagianus) triennio toto, in trivialibus suis mihi reponendis, desudavit. Vix lucem nostra, de Fidei Fundamentalibus, aspexerat dissertatio, quam ecce famosus, idemque ineptissimus in vicinia Irenomachus, infestis passim armis adortus est. Dabit autem utrque, suo tempore, temerarie pœnas incepti. Si enim tantum nobis putant ab re nostra esse otij, ut gravioribus posthabitis, vapulare continuo debeant, næ illi nimium avidens sunt, & nugas profecto suas non intellitelligunt.Primas forte debebamus, mor-dacissimo cuida simulq; mendacissimo A-pologistæ. Quem depexum dedissemus pri-dem, ni hactenus, (quam à nobis san-ctissimi, iidemq; saucy atrocissimis vulne-ribus manes effligatarunt) notis satis de caufis, nonnisi inter amicos Defensio vo-litasset. χρὴ γὰρ αὐτοὺς εἶναι [?]τῆς δὲ πάλαι τὴν δίκην[?]. Interim his fruere, quisquis es Lector, & Vale.
units.tr: Such is the way of our times that whatever is produced by late-night labour falls not into the hands of readers but of censors and Aristarchuses. If the censors are fair, I have no reason to fear their critical rod; if they are unfair, I have reason to disregard them and make light of them. Some will fasten on us the youthful rash of coming forward in public. Others will nibble at our subject, calling it either too singular or insufficiently necessary. The former, however, will pardon the scanty stock of learning in view of our age, and so we trust they will approve our undertaking. They will understand that the cause was not unworthy of public defence, and that we did not wholly trifle in restoring to its author the most weighty of all the Epistles. It will not go unnoticed what remains of others' weapons to be broken, or of others' doubts to be dispelled. Nor will it escape notice that the authority of the Epistle is indirectly attacked through its author. And whoever reads these pages of ours will grasp what could be wanted in this subject. Without doubt our most famous and long-lamented father, once honoured with so many titles, had already dealt with it in his Geneva Prolegomena to the Epistle. But we confess, solemnly and not without some grief of mind, that these have not been seen by us, nor have they been found hitherto among the remaining spoils and fragments. Nor does the plan and manner of those Prolegomena allow a fuller examination of the matter. We nowhere wander or digress, but keep to our task and remain within the hedges. As for these Exercitationes meeting the same fate along with some trifles of ours, the justice and innocence of the cause bid us be unworried. Scarcely had our little pages on the articles long disputed in the Low Countries come out, when lo, someone in Belgium (black or white, certainly a Pelagian) spent a whole three years toiling to answer me with his commonplaces. Hardly had our dissertation on the fundamentals of faith seen the light, when lo, the notorious and equally most inept Irenomachus in the neighbourhood attacked it with hostile arms on every side. Both will in due time pay the penalty for their rash undertaking. For if they think we have so much leisure from our affairs that, with weightier matters set aside, we ought to be beaten continually, then they are too greedy, and truly do not understand their own trifles. Perhaps we owed the first place to a certain most biting and at the same time most lying apologist. We would have given him a thorough combing long ago, had not our Defence, whose holy and wounded shades demanded it from us with the most savage wounds, for reasons well known, hitherto fluttered only among friends. [χρὴ γὰρ αὐτοὺς εἶναι] ... [τῆς δὲ πάλαι τὴν δίκην]. Meanwhile, whoever you are, reader, enjoy these things, and farewell.

Januarij MDCLIIX[?]. confirmato Diplomate habentur.
units.tr: By privilege of CHARLES LUDWIG, by the grace of God Count Palatine of the Rhine, Archtreasurer and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, and likewise its Provisor and Vicar in the parts of the Rhine, Swabia, and in Franconian law, Duke of Bavaria, it is provided that no one shall presume, within the district of the said Vicariate and for a span of thirty years counted from the day of the first edition, to imitate, interpolate, transform or reprint in any way, or to give to others to be reprinted, or even to sell or distribute elsewhere printed copies, openly or in secret, any books which the bookseller and printer of the Academy of Heidelberg, ADRIAN WYNGAERDEN, has printed in Germany, or is yet to print, and in particular the books named here: Burgersdijk's Politics, Casaubon's Distinctions, Clauberg's Introduction to Philosophy, the same author's treatise on the knowledge of God and of ourselves, the same author's paraphrase of Descartes' Meditations, finally Salmasius' Letters, Riolan's Anatomical Handbook, and the Golden Anatomical Harvest, without the special will and consent of the aforesaid ADRIAN WYNGAERDEN, or of his heirs, and of those holding right and cause from him. Whoever does so shall forfeit the books so wrongly reprinted, which the aforenamed ADRIAN WYNGAERDEN, or his heirs, or those holding right and cause from him, may claim for themselves, and in addition shall pay a fine of ten marks of pure gold, to be divided equally between the Imperial Treasury and the petitioner just named, with all hope of pardon cut off. All of these matters are set out more fully in the original diploma, confirmed by the own signature of the most serene Elector and Vicar and by the seal of the Vicariate, given at Heidelberg on the 21st day of January 1658.

units.tr: Reader, you will find typographical errors here and there in this little work as in others. There is neither time nor need to inquire into each one. Nevertheless, we have noticed that these more serious ones have crept in, perhaps while we were absent during the dog-days holiday.

units.la: Controversiæ de variis libris Canonicis. De Epistolâ ad Hebræos. A quibus rejecta & quare. Argumenta pro illius αὐθεντία. Potissimum ab authore [illegible, ~8 letters]. Varius creditus. Paulo vindicatur. Methodus Authoris.
units.tr: Controversies concerning the various canonical books. On the Epistle to the Hebrews. By whom it was rejected, and why. Arguments for its authority. Chiefly from its author [illegible]. Its supposed variable authorship. It is vindicated for Paul. The author's method.

units.la: I. QUi Scripturarum authoritatem aperte ac veluti de plaustro su-gillandam[?] suscepere, in duas semper abiê-re classes. Vel enim ὅλως eam ac secundum se totam, quales Ethnici, Profani, Scepti-ci, & scelerata Celsorum, Iulianorum ac sequacium cohors, vel μερικῶς ad secun-dum varias sui partes rejecerunt. Et Ve-teris quidem Testamenti, Legis & Pro-phetarum adversarios se professi Simo-niani, niani, Basilidiani, Marcionitæ, Manichæi, Artemonitæ, Bogomiles, & generaliori appellatione Antinomi seu Anomæi. Novum explodit hodieque
units.tr: I. Those who have openly attacked the authority of the Scriptures, as it were from the cart-top, have always fallen into two classes. Some have rejected it wholly [ὅλως] and in its entirety, as the heathen, the profane, the sceptics, and the wicked crowd of Celsuses, Julians and their followers did. Others have rejected it in part [μερικῶς], setting aside various of its parts. Among the opponents of the Old Testament, the Law and the Prophets, were the Simonians, Basilidians, Marcionites, Manichaeans, Artemonites, Bogomils, and, under the more general name, Antinomians or Anomeans. The New Testament is still rejected today by the Jew, wandering hither and thither, tossed about by exiles.

units.la: Exilijs vagus huc illuc fluctantibus errans Iudæus.
units.tr: Wandering hither and thither, tossed about by exiles, the errant Jew.

units.la: Libros utriusque Instrumenti singulos, sive Historicos, sive Propheticos, sive Dogmaticos adorti varij, ut vix ullus protervorum hominum tela & scommata declinarit. Ex Paganis, Danielem imprimis Porphyrius; ex Iudæis, Iobum, Ecclesiastem, Proverbia, Talmudistarum quidam; ex hæreticis in Christianâ Ecclesiâ bene multi, alij alios repudiavêre Canonicos; Legem Mosis traduxisse fertur Ptolomæus ille, Valentini Æonum in felicissimi parentis progenies; Prophetas Theodorus Mopsuestenus, post mortem etiam cum Origine Adamantio anathematizatus in Concilio Constantinopolitano II. seu Oecumenico V; Psalmos Gnostici & Nicolaitæ; Salomonis monumenta ex veteribus, imò recentioribus è Socini potissimum schola, varij; Evangelia solo Matthæo theo excepto Ebion, solo Marco Cerinthus, solo Lucâ Marcion, solo Johanne Valentino [?], & Acta Apostolorum Cerinthus, Cerdo, Manes; Paulinas & Catholicas Epistolas, ipsam denique Apocalypsim sacram, è Novi Testamenti Canone expunxêre passim cum iidem tum alii. Quin ne Patrum nonnullos excipimus, non Melitonem, non Origenem, non Athanasium, non Nazianzenum, non Eusebium, non Amphilochium, non paucos alios, quibus controversia fuit aliquando quorundam Canonicorum authoritas, aliâ quamvis ab hæreticis moderatione, alio sane atque instituto. Hinc distinctio Eusebiana in scripta alia ἀντιλεγόμενα, alia ἀναμφίλεκτα, ἐνδιάθηκα [?], καθολικὰ, καὶ ὁμολογούμενα. Notati illi omnes passim Eusebio libris Ἐκκλησιαστικῆς ἱστορίας [?], Irenæo adversus hæreses, Tertulliano adversus Marcionem, Epiphanio in Panario, Philastrio de Hæresibus, Hieronymo in Catalogo script. Eccles. Augustino contrà adversar. Legis & Prophetarum; & ex recentioribus imprimis Bellarmino Tom. I. ConControv. Lib. i. C. v. Quanquam hic invi-diosius Luthero circa Libros Iobi & Ec-clesiastis, imò optimis Albigensibus sce-leratæ cum Antinomis conspirationis at-que consensus noram[?] inusserit.
units.tr: Individual books of both Testaments, whether historical, prophetic or doctrinal, have been assailed by various men, so that hardly any of the shameless men has avoided shooting at them with taunts and jeers. Among the pagans, Porphyry attacked chiefly Daniel; among the Jews, Job, Ecclesiastes and Proverbs were rejected by certain Talmudists. Among the heretics in the Christian Church, very many have rejected different books as canonical, each his own. The Law of Moses is said to have been set aside by that Ptolemy, the offspring of Valentinus's Aeons. The Prophets were rejected by Theodore of Mopsuestia, who after his death was anathematized, together with Origen of Alexandria, at the Second Council of Constantinople, which is counted as the Fifth Ecumenical. The Psalms were rejected by the Gnostics and Nicolaitans. Various books of Solomon have been rejected, some from ancient times and more recently, chiefly from the school of the Socinians. Of the Gospels, Ebion rejected all except Matthew, Cerinthus all except Mark, Marcion all except Luke, and Valentinus all except John [?]. The Acts of the Apostles were rejected by Cerinthus, Cerdo and Manes. The Pauline and Catholic Epistles, and finally the sacred Apocalypse itself, have been struck out of the canon of the New Testament here and there, by these same men and by others. Nor do we except some of the Fathers. Not Melito, not Origen, not Athanasius, not Gregory Nazianzen, not Eusebius, not Amphilochius, nor a few others, have been free of controversy at times about the authority of certain canonical books; though this was by a different and milder moderation than that of the heretics, and certainly from a different purpose and design. Hence Eusebius's distinction between writings that are disputed (ἀντιλεγόμενα), others that are undisputed (ἀναμφίλεκτα), genuine (ἐνδιάθηκα [?]), universal (καθολικὰ), and acknowledged (ὁμολογούμενα). All these men are noted here and there: Eusebius in the books of his Ecclesiastical History, Irenaeus in Against Heresies, Tertullian in Against Marcion, Epiphanius in the Panarion, Philastrius in On Heresies, Jerome in the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, and Augustine against the adversaries of the Law and the Prophets. And among more recent writers, above all Bellarmine in the first volume of his Controversies, book I, chapter 5. Although here he has stigmatized Luther more invidiously concerning the Books of Job and Ecclesiastes, and has even branded the excellent Albigensians with a conspiracy and agreement with the Antinomians in their wicked scheme.

units.la: II. Vix tamen usque adeo disceptatum ac de authoritate nobilissimæ illius Epistolæ quæ inscribitur ad Hebræos. Scilicet ab iis constantissimè damnata, quorum semper dogmatibus adversa fuit. Repudiavit Marcion, cum primis ex odio Ve-to Testamenti, indignatus typos cum antitypis, umbras cum corpore, figuras cum expressiori rerum imagine, vaticinia cum complemento, Vetus Testamentum cum Novo, quàm accuratissimè hanc in Epistolâ conferri. Eadem fuit iniquitate Ebion, Legis & ceremoniarum præpo-stero quàm zelo. Eadem Arrius, Antitrinitarii alii, ob assertam in eâ luculenter ac vindicatam Divinitatem filii Dei, illius τὸ ὁμοούσιον καὶ συναΐδιον. Accesserè Latini nonnulli Veteres, cum Afri, tum imprimis Romani, ad Hieronymi fere usque tempora, maximè quia Novato & NovaNovatianis de lapsis non recipiendis, in gratiam, favere videbatur Epistola, quo de argumento acerrimae Novatum inter ac Novatianum Presbyteros, horumque adversarios Cornelium ac Cyprianum, illum Romae, hunc Carthagini Episcopos, medio tertio saeculo contentiones. Quanquam Baronius id aegre admodum de Romana ferat Ecclesia, quasi unquam Epistolam ad Hebraeos a Paulinis & Canonicis segregarit, & crasse satis calumniam vocet Eusebij, Hieronymo facilius admissa, Annalii Tom. 1. ad A.C. LX. Num. LIII. De quo nos postmodum fusius Capite viii. Hodieque multis modis injurij in hanc Epistolam & contumeliosi Socinianorum quidam, cautius quanquam, suo more, & occultius; eodem nempe cum Marcionitis & Arianis impulsu, & sat criminis authori Epistolae, cum divinitatem Christi, tum eximium Veteris Testamenti sub Novo usum, & essentialem utriusque consensum demonstrasse. Cajetanus Cardinalis, Epistolam pariter dispungendam temere censuit. Lutherus sive Veterum Latinorum authoritate sive alio, ut videtur, motus argumento, secus de hac Epistolâ, ut de Catholicis quibusdam aliis aliquando sensit; adeò vir penè divinus & dotibus supra humanam sortem instructus, hîc, ut in aliis, hu-mani nihil à se alienum ostendit.
units.tr: II. Yet the authority of that most noble Epistle which is inscribed to the Hebrews has scarcely been disputed to the same extent. It has been most firmly condemned by those whose doctrines it has always opposed. Marcion rejected it, chiefly out of hatred of the Old Testament, being indignant at the comparison of types with antitypes, shadows with the body, figures with the fuller image of the realities, prophecies with their fulfilment, and the Old Testament with the New, which this Epistle compares most carefully. Ebion rejected it with the same wrongheadedness, out of a perverse zeal for the Law and ceremonies. Arius did the same, and other Antitrinitarians, on account of its clear assertion and vindication of the divinity of the Son of God, his homoousion and coeternal [τὸ ὁμοούσιον καὶ συναΐδιον]. Some of the older Latins joined them, both the Africans and especially the Romans, almost down to the time of Jerome, chiefly because the Epistle seemed to favour Novatus and the Novatianists in their refusal to receive the lapsed back into grace. On this very question there were most bitter contentions in the middle of the third century between the presbyters Novatus and Novatian and their opponents, the bishops Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage. Although Baronius takes this very badly on behalf of the Roman Church, as though it had never separated the Epistle to the Hebrews from the Pauline and canonical letters, and calls it a rather gross calumny which was too readily accepted from Eusebius by Jerome (Annals, vol. 1, at the year of Christ 60, no. 53). We shall discuss this more fully later, in chapter 8. Even today some Socinians, though more cautiously and more covertly, as is their way, have attacked this Epistle in many ways and disparaged it, moved by the same impulse as the Marcionites and Arians, and not without some offence against its author, since it demonstrates both the divinity of Christ and the remarkable use of the Old Testament under the New, and the essential agreement of the two. Cajetan, the Cardinal, also rashly judged that the Epistle should be struck out. Luther, whether moved by the authority of the older Latins or by some other argument, as it seems, judged otherwise about this Epistle, as he sometimes did about certain other catholic books; so that this man, almost divine and endowed with gifts above the lot of humanity, here showed, as elsewhere, that nothing human was alien to him.

units.la: III. Magnum sanè divinæ & immotæ originis argumentū, quò majores ad subvertendam eam & validiores impetus fecit hostis ille humani generis. Et quem-admodum vix pars ulla Canonis tot ini-qua hominum judicia experta est, ita vix ulla Canonicis notis illustrior, magisque cœlestem spirans originem. Sive atten-dimus doctrinæ genus excelsum, de Chri-sti divinitate, incarnatione, sacerdotio, figuris quæ sive in Aarone, sive Melchise-deco, sive typis legalibus ac ceremoniis præcesserant, quæque sublimius quid sonant humanâ sapientia; sive expendimus sanctissima vitæ instituta, ac morum præ-cepta; sive majorem omni exceptione cum Scripturis utriusque Fœderis con-sensum, in historicis frustrà nonnullis impetitum ; sive dicendi genus arduum & sublime , & humano majus eloquio, in ipso jam limine assurgens; sive efficaciam & ἐνέργειαν[?] in piorum animis, hic ut alibi, sese exerentem, & certissimum loquentis Dei argumentum; sive , ut mittam alia, antiquitatem Epistolæ , jam prima Apostolorum ætate exaratæ, primitus in Ecclesia receptæ, authore etiam viro Apostolico , &, quod demonstrandum suscipimus, Paulo.
units.tr: III. This is indeed a great argument of divine and unshakeable origin, by which that enemy of the human race made greater and stronger assaults to overthrow it. And just as hardly any part of the Canon has undergone so many unjust judgments of men, so hardly any is more conspicuous for the marks of canonicity and breathes more of a heavenly origin. Whether we attend to the lofty character of its teaching, on the divinity of Christ, the incarnation, the priesthood, and the figures which had gone before, whether in Aaron or in Melchizedek, or in the legal types and ceremonies, teachings which sound higher than human wisdom; or whether we weigh its most holy rules of life and precepts of morality; or whether we weigh its agreement with the Scriptures of both covenants, which is greater than any exception, though in some historical matters it has been vainly assailed; or whether we consider the lofty and sublime style of speaking, greater than human eloquence, rising up already at the threshold; or the efficacy and energy which it displays in the souls of the godly, here as elsewhere, and which is the most certain proof of the God who speaks; or, to pass over other matters, the antiquity of the Epistle, written already in the first age of the Apostles, received at the outset in the Church, with an apostolic man as its author, and, what we undertake to demonstrate, Paul.

units.la: IV. Prioribus ergo κεφαλαίοις[?] alibi expensis, posterius subjicimus disquisitioni, & si de Authore convenerit, de authoritate vix scrupulus reliquus esse poterit. Sic enim esto argumentum. Quæ Epistola virum θεόπνευστον[?], certe Paulum, habet authorem, sacram illam ac Canonicam esse necesse fuerit: sed talis est hæc ad Hebræos Epistola. De nexu antecedentis non laboramus. Fateor viros θεοπνεύστας[?] scribere alia potuisse reduplicative quatenus & in quantum tales, alia etiam quà homines. Huc facit protrita distinctio Augustini de Civit. Dei L.xviii. C. xxxviu[?], ubi de ve-
units.tr: IV. Therefore, having examined the earlier heads elsewhere, we add the latter to our inquiry; and if agreement is reached about the author, there can hardly remain any scruple about the authority. For the argument may run thus. An epistle which has as its author a man inspired by God, certainly Paul, must of necessity be sacred and canonical. But this Epistle to the Hebrews is such. We are not troubled about the connection of the antecedent. I grant that men inspired by God could write some things as such, in so far as they were such, and other things also as men. Here the well-worn distinction of Augustine in The City of God, book 18, chapter 38, is relevant, where, speaking of the writings of the ancients not received into the Canon, he says that those very men, to whom the things that ought to be of authority in religion were revealed by the Holy Spirit, wrote some things as men and others as prophets; some with historical diligence, others with divine inspiration; some things which were to be attributed to themselves, others to God speaking through them; some things which pertained to the abundance of knowledge, but others to the authority of religion.

units.la: { } terum scriptis agens non receptis in Ca-nonem, inquit,illos ipsos , quibus ea quæ in authoritate religionis esse deberent, Spi-ritus S. revelavit, scripsisse alia, sicut homines alia sicut Prophetæ ; alia historicâ diligentiâ , alia inspiratione divinâ ; quæ ipsis tribuenda, alia Deo per ipsos loquenti;alia quæ pertinerent ad ubertatem cognitionis , alia verò ad authoritatem religionis. Istius modi esse potuêre libri Historici in Vetero Instrumento aliquoties memorati, neque tamen Canoni inserti, authoribus licet viris Propheticis , nec tam ad institutionem Ecclesiæ, quàm ad civilem usum consignati, neque ut divini essent & Canonici, sed fasti potiùs & annales politici. Huc referenda quæ adscribuntur Salomoni viro Ἰωαντύσῳ[?] I. Reg. iv. 32,33, neque illico Canonica, i.e. eum in finem sive scripta sive enunciata,ut in Canonem referrentur,& usui essent Ecclesiæ Universali omnium temporum. At longè aliter comparatum est cum Epistolâ Novi Testamenti , quæ ad Ecclesiam directa, quæ in illius usum consignata , quæ facit ad authoritatem religionis; quæ ejusdem cum Canonicis aliis Epistolis argumenti, quæ eodem cum aliis tempore & fine scripto mandata; quæque ἀπὸ χρόνων ἀρχαίων [?] Canone donata: si præterea constet, viro Apostolico, imò Paulo authore, exaratam, de Canonicâ illius authoritate nemo cordatus litem intenderit.
units.tr: Of this kind could have been the historical books mentioned several times in the Old Testament, which were nevertheless not inserted into the Canon, though written by prophetic authors, and composed not so much for the instruction of the Church as for civil use, and not as divine and canonical, but rather as political annals and records. To this class belong the things ascribed to Solomon, a man of wide learning (1 Kings 4:32, 33); these were not at once canonical, that is, they were not written or uttered with the aim of being placed in the Canon and being of use to the universal Church of all times. But it is far otherwise with the Epistle of the New Testament, which is addressed to the Church, which is written for its use, which serves the authority of religion; which is of the same subject as the other canonical Epistles, which was committed to writing at the same time and for the same purpose as they; and which has been given a place in the Canon from ancient times [ἀπὸ χρόνων ἀρχαίων]. If, moreover, it is established that it was written by an apostolic man, indeed by Paul as its author, no sensible person will bring a dispute about its canonical authority.

units.la: V. Estque hæc de Authore Epistolæ ad Hebræos controversia illustris, olim hodieque Theologis agitata, etiamnum indecisa, & dignus, quanquam alio vindice, nodus. Sic autem discutiendum venit atque expendendum hoc argumentum, ut ad ornatum & elegantiam orationis plurimùm, ad causæ momentum ac methodi ἀκρίβειαν vix quicquam desiderari possit. Sententias omnes ad duas classes revocamus, ut alij Paulo Apostolo vendicarint Epistolam, derogarint alij. Posteriores denuò abiêre in diversa, & transcripsêre alij authori sacro & debitâ ad scribendum authoritate instructo, sive Barnabas fuerit, sive Lucas, sive Apollo, sive Marcus, sive quisquis alius Apostololorum[?] socius : alij authori Ecclesiastico, puta Clementi Romano, cujus jam olim celebris ad Corinthiorū Ecclesiam schismate laborantem Epistola; vel juxta quosdam ipsi Tertulliano, si vera refert Sixtus Senensis Biblioth. L. vii. C. viii: alij denique, qui erroris & νοθεύσεως[?] hanc postularunt Epistolam, homini hæretico & malo feriato, puta Novato, aut alij ejusdem furfuris.
units.tr: V. This question about the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews is a famous one. Theologians have debated it both in the past and today, it is still undecided, and it is a knot worth untying, though it needs another champion. The matter must be examined and weighed so that very little could be wanted for the ornament and elegance of the discourse, for the weight of the cause, or for exactness of method [ἀκρίβεια]. We reduce all opinions to two classes. Some have claimed the Epistle for the Apostle Paul, while others have denied it to him. The latter have again split into different views. Some have ascribed it to a sacred author with due authority to write, whether Barnabas, Lucas, Apollo, Marcus, or some other companion of the Apostles. Others have ascribed it to an ecclesiastical author, namely Clement of Rome, whose famous letter to the Church of Corinth, troubled by schism, has been known for a long time. Or, according to some, it is by Tertullian himself, if Sixtus of Siena reports the truth (Bibl. lib. vii, cap. viii). Finally, others who have called this Epistle a work of error and forgery have assigned it to a heretical and wicked man, namely Novatus, or to another man of the same chaff.

units.la: VI. Nos, salvis magnorum hodieque virorum judiciis, illis accedimus, & cum iis facimus, qui Paulum authore pronunciarunt. Quod pluribus demonstrandum aggredimur, & quàm factum hactenus fusiùs & accuratiùs, cùm sententiam nostram varió tibicine fulciendo, tum argumenta, atque instantias omnium quotquot aliter hoc senserunt in argumento diluendo. Tribus partibus rem totam complexuri, quarum prima authoritates; altera rationes pro Paulo militantes; tertia objectiones vestiget & expendat. Authoritates aliae ferint[?] testimonij divini, aliae humani, sive publici, sive pri-vati, vati, sive veterum, sive recentiorum, sive Græcorum sive Latinorum. Prius quidem testimonij genus, αὐτόπιστον & δεικτικόν, posterius [illegible, ~7 letters], ἢ[?] συλλογιζόμενον ὡς ἐξ ἐνδόξων, utrumq; in hac controversia potissimum expendendum.
units.tr: VI. We, with due respect for the judgments of great men still living, come over to those who have declared Paul the author, and we side with them. We undertake to demonstrate this at greater length than has been done so far, and more fully and accurately. We will support our opinion with a variety of props, and we will refute the arguments and instances of all who have thought otherwise. We shall take the whole matter in three parts. The first will survey and weigh the authorities; the second the reasons fighting on Paul's side; the third the objections. Some authorities are of divine testimony, others of human testimony, whether public or private, whether of the ancients or of more recent writers, whether Greek or Latin. The former kind of testimony is self-credible and demonstrative [αὐτόπιστον καὶ δεικτικόν]. The latter, [illegible], is syllogistic, reasoning from reputable opinions [συλλογιζόμενον ὡς ἐξ ἐνδόξων]. Both must be weighed especially in this controversy.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Primum Argumentum ἄτεχνον. Locus II. Petri III. 15. Scribit Petrus Hebræis. Demonstratur. Ad eosdem Paulus. Occurritur VIII. Exceptionibus. Loci varij passim illustrati. Occasionaliter de Paulinis Epistolis vulgò interversis.
units.tr: First argument, ἄτεχνον. Place: 2 Pet. 3:15. Peter writes to the Hebrews. Demonstrated. Paul writes to the same. Eight objections are met. Various passages illustrated here and there. Incidentally, on the Pauline Epistles, commonly misplaced.

units.la: I. Primum argumentum ἄτεχνον testimonij divini suppeditant ilicò hæc Petri verba, II. Pet. III. 15. Καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς Παύλῳ ἔγραψεν[?] ὑμῖν. Nempe sermonem dirigit suum Petrus ad Hebræos, ad quos juxtà cum priori transmissa hæc posterior Epistola. His ipsis Hebræis Paulum scripsisse dicit, juxta datam illi sapientiam divinam sanè ac humanum omne fastigium supergressam. Quare vel excciderit Paulina illa ad Hebræos & interversa fuerit, quod affirmare proclive, probare operosum; vel hanc ipsam, de cujus authore controvertitur, innuerit Petrus ac designarit.
units.tr: The first argument, ἄτεχνον, drawn from the testimony of Scripture, is supplied at once by these words of Peter, 2 Pet. 3:15: "as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you" [Καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς Παύλῳ ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν]. Peter, of course, directs his discourse to the Hebrews, to whom this second letter is sent along with the first. He says that Paul wrote to these same Hebrews, according to the divine wisdom given to him, which far surpassed all human attainment. Therefore either that Pauline letter to the Hebrews has perished and been lost (which is easy to assert but laborious to prove), or Peter is hinting at and pointing to this very letter whose authorship is in question.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Itaque in eo imprimis vis tota probationis consistit, compellari à Petro Hebræos, iisque posteriorem hanc inscriptâ. Patet id vel ex Capite ejusdem tertio, sub initium. Ταύτην ἤδη, ἀγαπητοὶ, δευτέραν ὑμῖν γράφω ἐπιστολὴν, ἐν αἷς διεγείρω &c. Iisdem ergò data hæc Epistola cum priori. Hinc δευτέρα, hinc pariter Catholica, ut ex titulo & inscriptione, hinc paris etiam argumenti, ut ex collatione liquet. Quare assurgendum ad Παυλείαν Epistolæ prioris, quæ habet ἐκλεκτοῖς, παροικήμασις, διασπορᾶς Ποντ, Γαλατίας, Καππαδοκίας, Ἀσίας & Bιθυνίας. Iudæos sive Hebræos intelligi constat sanè. 1. quod παροίκους illos dicit, seu παροίκους, ξένους, ἀλλοεθνεῖς, ἀλλοφύλας, advenas, peregrinos inter gentes: quod in Iudæos patriis sedibus motos & extrà Iudææ pomœria alibi terrarum vicitantes, per belle quadrat. 11. Dispersos eosdem, diaδιασπορᾶς Πόντου[?], Γαλατίας &c. Quod intelligi de διασπορᾷ sive Assyriacâ decem tribuum, sive Babylonicâ reliquarum, sive Antiochenâ, furente Epiphane ac saeviente in Iudaeorum gentem; sive, ut alii, Claudianâ Act. xviii. 1. dum Iudaeos assiduè tumultuantes Româ Claudius expulit; quanquam verius de generaliori dispersione tribuum, non novissimâ illa ac quorundam Romae agentium. Cl. Salmasius dispersionem intelligit non coactam, sed voluntariam, non exulum sed colonorum partem generalis illius dispersionis quâ Iudaei per totum orbem dispersi inter gentes agitabant, de Hellenist. Quaest. v. III. Ex Iacobo idem intelligimus, cujus inscriptio gemina: τοῖς ἐντὸς διασπορᾶς, i.e. ut ipse addit exegeticè, τοῖς δώδεκα φυλαῖς, Iudaeorum nempe tribubus, pervariis Orientis partes, utique minoris Asiae provincias dispersis. IV. Lucem hic accenditur Historia Act. 11. ubi ex illis ipsis locis, Cappadociâ, Ponto, Asiâ &c. recensentur Iudaei conversi ad Christianam fidem, & Petri imprimis oratione affecti, ad quos in Prouinciis jam agentes suis fir-mandos & erigendos, iterato scripsisse videtur omnino Apostolus. V. Accedit Petro commissam fuisse Iudaeorum curam seu Apostolatum circumcisionis, Gal. II. 8.9. Et quidem, si fides Chrysostomo ad locum, non tam ultroneâ Petri optione quam prouincias distribuente Christo, τὰς μὲν Ἰουδαίους ἐπιτρέψε τῷ Πέτρῳ, τὰς δὲ Ἕλληνας τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίστησεν ὁ Χριστός. Adeoque juxta demandati rationem muneris, Petri fuit Iudaeos imprimis quà voce quà scripto e-rudire, erigere, hortari. Nec moramur Baronium, Petrum, Christi exemplo, non minus Gentium quàm Iudaeorum Apo-stolum fuisse, gratis, suo sane more, con-tendentem. VI. Iudaeos Petro compellari liquet, variorum inductione locorum utriusque Epistolæ. Sane dum redemptos illos dicit ἐκ τῆς ματαίας ἀναστροφῆς πατρο-[?]παραδότου, à variis traditionibus maiorum, 1. Pet. 1. 18. dum vocat eosdem βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, ἔθνος ἅγιον, 1. Pet. II. 9. plane ut Exod. XIX. 6. ואתם תהיו לי ממלכת כהנים וגוי קדוש; dum etiam alludit passim ad ty-pos, pos, vaticinia, historias, exempla Veteris Testamenti, ut quæ familiaria Iudæis, & efficacissima longè iis in Christiana fide[?] obfirmandis.
units.tr: The whole force of the proof therefore rests, above all, on this: that Peter addresses the Hebrews, and that this later letter is addressed to them. This is clear even from the beginning of the third chapter of the same letter: "Beloved, this is now the second letter I write to you, in which I stir up your minds," etc. The letter was therefore given to the same people as the first. Hence it is called "second," and likewise "Catholic," as is clear from the title and address, and it has the same subject, as the comparison shows. We must therefore turn to Peter's first letter, which is addressed to "the elect sojourners of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia." It is quite certain that Jews, or Hebrews, are meant. First, because he calls them paroikoi, that is, παροίκους, ξένους, ἀλλοεθνεῖς, ἀλλοφύλας: aliens, strangers, foreigners among the nations, which fits Jews who were moved from their ancestral homes and lived elsewhere outside the borders of Judea. Second, they are called dispersed, dia διασπορᾶς Πόντου, Γαλατίας, etc. This can be understood of the Assyrian dispersion of the ten tribes, or the Babylonian dispersion of the rest, or the Antiochene dispersion under Epiphanes, who raged against the Jewish nation; or, as others think, the Claudian dispersion (Acts 18:1), when Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews who kept up constant tumult. Yet it is more truly understood of the general dispersion of the tribes, not of that very recent one of some who were living in Rome. Salmasius understands the dispersion not as forced but as voluntary, not of exiles but of colonists, a part of that general dispersion by which the Jews, scattered throughout the whole world, lived among the nations (de Hellenist. Quaest. v, III). We understand the same from James, whose double address is: "to those in the dispersion," i.e., as he adds in explanation, "to the twelve tribes," namely the tribes of the Jews, scattered through very many parts of the East, and especially the provinces of Asia Minor. Fourth, the history in Acts 11 sheds light here, where Jews converted to the Christian faith are listed from those very places, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, etc., and affected especially by Peter's speech. It seems that the Apostle wrote to them again, to strengthen and raise up those already living in the provinces. Fifth, Peter was entrusted with the care of the Jews, or the apostleship of the circumcision (Gal. 2:8, 9). And indeed, if we trust Chrysostom on this passage, it was not so much by Peter's own free choice as by Christ's distribution of the provinces: "Christ assigned the Jews to Peter and the Greeks to Paul." Therefore, according to the nature of his commission, it was Peter's task to instruct, raise up and exhort the Jews, by voice and by writing. We do not linger over Baronius, who, in his own way, contends that Peter, following Christ's example, was no less an apostle of the Gentiles than of the Jews. Sixth, it is clear that the Jews are addressed by Peter, from the citation of various passages in both letters. Indeed, when he says that they were redeemed "from the empty manner of life handed down from their fathers" (1 Pet. 1:18), from "the various traditions of their ancestors"; when he calls them "a royal priesthood, a holy nation" (1 Pet. 2:9), plainly as in Exod. 19:6, "you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" [ואתם תהיו לי ממלכת כהנים וגוי קדוש]; and when he alludes throughout to types, figures, prophecies, histories and examples of the Old Testament, which were familiar to Jews and most effective for confirming them in the Christian faith.

units.la: III. Atque hactenus docent tot ratio-num momenta luce meridiana clarius, scripsisse Petrum Hebræis gente, Iudæis antea religione. Quod si concessum fuerit, reliquum est, si vera Petri verba, idem de Paulo affirmemus. Multa tamen ad primum hoc & validissimum quidem argumentum excipi posse videntur, nec uno illud modo enervari. Primò ἀρνήσεως negando Petrum Hebræis scripsisse, & rationibus rationes, opponendo. Secundò ὑπο-χωρητικῶς & per concessionem, scripsisse, non sequi Paulinam ad eosdem datam Epistolam 2.Pet.iiij. hanc ipsam necessariò designari quæ in controversiam venit.
units.tr: III. So far, so many considerations show more clearly than the noonday sun that Peter wrote to the Hebrews by nation, and to the Jews formerly by religion. If this is granted, it remains that, if Peter's words are true, we affirm the same about Paul. Yet many objections seem to be raised against this first and most powerful argument, and it cannot be weakened in only one way. First, by denying (ἀρνήσεως) that Peter wrote to the Hebrews, and by opposing reasons to reasons. Second, by concession (ὑποχωρητικῶς), granting that he wrote, but not following that the Pauline letter addressed to the same people, mentioned in 2 Pet. 3, is necessarily the one now in controversy.

units.la: IV. Exceptiones primæ classes sunt: Primò, non Iudæos tantum sed & electos ex Gentibus pariter variè dispersos fuisse sæviente persecutione, & pristinis sedibus pulsos, sive etiam facile pellendos, verè [illegible, ~9 letters] quosque Petrus hoc soleter Epistolio; adeóque frustra dispersorum & peregrinorum nomine Iudæos solos hoc loco intelligi. Respondemus 1. Probationem esse in sufficientem, potiores longè rationes superiùs expositas quæ pro Iudæis militant, ut pleniori demonstratione opus non sit. Cumprimis id intelligitur ex parallelo Iacobi loco. Et ad eosdem scripsisse Apostolum utrumque, cum ex inscriptione, tum ex affinitate sive argumenti sive muneris, utrique Iudæorum Apostolatu commisso, liquidò constat. Διασπορὰ etiam sic Iudæorum propria, ut Ioh. vii. 35. διασπορὰ Ἑλλήνων, non de Græcorum & Gentium dispersione, sed Iudæorum inter Græcos, sit accipienda. Ἑλλήνων verò nomine etiam Asiani venêre & Galatæ, & Pontici & quotquot græca illis temporibus supabant. Quin dum vocatur διασπορὰ Ποντου, Γαλατίας &c. hæc ipsa dispersio per minoris Asiæ tractum, χώρων dicit ad dispersiones alias per varias orbis partes, Syriam, Babyloniam, Persidom, Ægyptum, & remotissima etiam Orienorientis loca, in quæ Iudæos inde à tem-poribus Assyriacis avectos ac translatos in confessò est. II. Supponitur gratis fide-les ex Gentibus, vel παρεπιδήμους[?] potuisse dici, vel dispersione quâdam huc illuc per omnes illas Ponti, Galatiæ, Cappado-ciæ, Asiæ Provincias, Evangelij causâ fuisse disjectos. At qui παρεπίδημοι[?], qui agebant inter gentes, & patrias sedes oc-cupabant? Qui dispersionem passi, qui nonnisi recens admodum Christianæ fidei initiati esse poterant, qui gravissimâ cer-te in Christianos persecutione, ex aliis se-dibus huc delati esse debuissent? Qualis ante decimum Neronis annum, Petro jam sanè fini proximo, Christianis tum etiam suppliciis magis quàm exilio affli-ctis, nulla memoratur. παρεπιδήμους[?] alias pios omnes dixeris, sed metaphoricè & improprie, in ordine ad mundum in quo hospites, Hebr. xi.13. 1.Pet. ii.11. Tales verò hic dicti Petro proprie, certè in ordine ad Pontum, Galatiam, & regiones circumja-centes, adeoque soli Iudæi. Qui & exulum ac παροικων[?] nomen ut peculium quod-dam dam suum adoptare solent. Illi vero Gentilium qui sive Iudaicæ, sive Christianæ Ecclesiæ inserti, ἐπήλυτοι[?] vocati, non παρεπίδημοι, affini quanquā vocis significatu.
units.tr: IV. The first objections are of this kind. First, not only Jews but also believers chosen from among the Gentiles were scattered in various ways, when persecution raged and they were driven from their former homes, or could easily be driven out; and it is in fact to such that Peter writes this letter. Therefore it is in vain to understand only Jews in this place under the name of "dispersed and sojourners." We reply: 1. The proof is not sufficient. The stronger reasons set out above, which favour the Jews, are far better, so that a fuller demonstration is not needed. This is especially understood from the parallel passage in James. And that the Apostle wrote to the same people in both cases is clear, both from the address and from the affinity of subject and office, since both letters were entrusted with the apostleship of the Jews. Moreover, dispersion is so much a proper term of the Jews that in John 7:35, the dispersion of the Greeks must be taken not of the dispersion of Greeks and Gentiles, but of Jews among the Greeks. Under the name of Greeks there also came the Asians and the Galatians, and the Pontians, and all who used the Greek language in those times. Indeed, when it is called "the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia," etc., this very dispersion throughout the region of Asia Minor refers to other dispersions through various parts of the world, Syria, Babylon, Persia, Egypt, and even the most remote regions of the East, to which it is admitted that the Jews were carried and transported from the times of the Assyrians. 2. It is assumed without reason that believers from the Gentiles could be called parepidemoi, or were scattered here and there through all those provinces of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia and Asia for the sake of the gospel. But who were the parepidemoi, who lived among the nations and occupied their homes? Who suffered dispersion, who could have been initiated into the Christian faith only very recently, who must have been driven from other homes by a most grievous persecution of Christians? No such thing is recorded before the tenth year of Nero, when Peter was surely near his end, and Christians were then afflicted with punishments rather than exile. You may call all the pious parepidemoi, but metaphorically and improperly, in relation to the world in which they are strangers (Heb. 11:13; 1 Pet. 2:11). But those spoken of here by Peter are such properly, certainly in relation to Pontus, Galatia, and the neighbouring regions, and so only the Jews. They, too, are accustomed to adopt the name of exiles and paroikoi as a kind of proper title. Those of the Gentiles, however, who were grafted into either the Jewish or the Christian Church are called epelytoi (proselytes), not parepidemoi, though the meanings of the words are related.

units.la: V. Altera exceptio esto: aperte satis vocatos ex gentibus designari, prioris Epistolæ C. 11.10. Dum dicit antea fuisse illos non populum, jam vero Dei populum factos; quod Hosea de Gentium vocatione oraculum Os. 11.23. pariter ad Gentes traducitur Paulo Rom. 1x.25. Respondemus I. συγχωρητικῶς[?], hoc Hosea vaticinium ad Gentes etiam trahi, docente Apostolo ad Romanos, quatenus & illæ revera fuerant aliquando לא רחמה, ולא עמי, jam vero luce Evangelij collustratæ, sunt ὁ λαὸς θεοῦ, καὶ οἱ ἠλεημένοι. II. Ἀφηλικῶς[?] de illis vel solis vel ex primariâ intentione loqui Prophetam, quod falsum. Imò verò directè & primariò de Judæis agit, dispergendis per orbem terrarum, ob perfidiam & ignaviam rejiciendis, castigandis, postmodùm verò in gratiam recipiendis, & denuò cooptandis in fœdus. Patet ex ἀλληλουχία[?] contextus & Cap. 1.10. Factum id autem eorundem vocatione ad Christi fidem. Rectè itaque Petrus cum Judæis agens, ex tenebris Pharizaicorum dogma-tum, in admirabilem illam lucem transla-tis, hujusce oraculi complementum in il-lis ostendit. Paulus verò nonnisi indirectè & per accommodationem quandam hoc trahit ad vocationem Gentium. , & ali-quoties illo ipso Capite ix.Rom. usu venit Apostolo, ut præter literalem etiam my-sticum eruat sensum ex prophetarum vati-ciniis : quæ in Scholis oracula composita, geminâ impletione illustria, quale & apud Hoseam illud, Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum C.xi.1. in Christo & Israëlitis, ἐν τῷ τυπωθέντα adimpletum. iii. Imò verò per retorsionem κατὰ τὸ βίωσιν, eo ipso Petrus scribit Judæis dispersis, τῷ λείμματι κατ' ἐκλογὴν χάριτος, Rom. xi.5. quando de illis primò vaticinatus Hoseas, con-vertendis scilicet & in populum Dei alle-gendis, & hinc pro nobis exurgit argu-mentum. iv. Damus Judæos suam an-te conversionem, Dei fuisse populum, nempe secundum carnem, non secundum spiritum, ut ipse distinguit Apostolus; quoad externam aggregationem & cooptationem in fœdus, non quoad insitionem internam, & spiritualem adoptionem; æstimatione & opinione etiam propriâ, non ex mente & æstimatione Dei, adeòque secundum dici non secundum esse. Posteriori hoc sensu erant revera non populus, & quadrat illud Pauli, Rom. ix.6. ἀ γὰρ οὐ πάντες οἱ ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ, οὗτοι[?] Ἰσραήλ. ubi triplicem facit Israëlem seu populum, vel secundum carnem tantùm, vel secundum spiritum tantùm, vel secundum carnem & spiritum simul, quales conversi Judæorum.
units.tr: V. Let the second objection be this: it is clear enough that those called from the Gentiles are designated in the earlier letter, chapter 2:10, where he says that they were once "not a people," but are now the "people" of God. Paul applies this to the Gentiles in Rom. 9:25, where Hosea's oracle about the calling of the Gentiles is quoted (Hos. 2:23). We reply: I. by concession (συγχωρητικῶς), that this prophecy of Hosea is indeed applied to the Gentiles too, as the Apostle teaches the Romans, inasmuch as they too had once been not pitied and not my people [לא רחמה, ולא עמי], but now, illuminated by the light of the gospel, are the people of God and those who have obtained mercy [ὁ λαὸς θεοῦ, καὶ οἱ ἠλεημένοι]. II. It is false to say that the Prophet speaks of them alone, or chiefly in his primary intention (ἀφηλικῶς). On the contrary, he deals directly and primarily with the Jews, to be scattered throughout the world, rejected and punished for their faithlessness and sloth, but afterwards to be received again into favour and once more gathered into the covenant. This is evident from the connection of the context and from chapter 1:10. That this happened by their calling to faith in Christ is also true. Rightly, therefore, Peter, dealing with the Jews who had been brought out of the darkness of Pharisaic doctrines into that wonderful light, shows the fulfilment of this oracle in them. Paul, however, draws it to the calling of the Gentiles only indirectly and by a certain accommodation. And it happens to the Apostle in Rom. 9 itself, and at other times, that he brings out from the prophetic oracles a mystical sense as well as the literal one; such oracles, which the schools call composite, are illustrated by a double fulfilment. Such is also that in Hosea, "Out of Egypt I have called my son" (Hos. 11:1), fulfilled in Christ and in the Israelites, ἐν τῷ τυπωθέντα. III. Indeed, by a retorsion (κατὰ τὸ βίωσιν), Peter in this very way writes to the Jews scattered, "to the remnant according to the election of grace" (Rom. 11:5), when Hosea first prophesied about them, namely about their conversion and their being gathered into the people of God; and from this an argument arises for us. IV. We grant that the Jews, before their conversion, were the people of God, namely according to the flesh, not according to the spirit, as the Apostle himself distinguishes; as to external aggregation and admission into the covenant, not as to internal ingrafting and spiritual adoption; and by their own estimation and opinion, not by the mind and estimation of God; and so they were a people according to what was said, not according to what they were. In the latter sense they were indeed "not a people," and Paul's words fit, Rom. 9:6: "For they are not all Israel who are of Israel" [οὐ γὰρ πάντες οἱ ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ, οὗτοι Ἰσραήλ], where he makes a threefold Israel or people: either according to the flesh only, or according to the spirit only, or according to the flesh and the spirit together, such as the converted Jews were.

units.la: VI. Tertiò instant nonnulli ex loco 1. Pet. 1.10. Ibi de gratiâ in Gentes effusâ, & à Prophetis prænunciata, sermocinari Petrum, adeòque & scribere ad Gentes; περὶ ἧς σωτηρίας ἐξεζήτησαν, καὶ ἐξηρεύνησαν προφῆται, οἱ περὶ τῆς εἰς ὑμᾶς χάριτος προφητεύσαντες. Atqui 1. falsum loqui Apostolum de gratiâ speciali in Gentes, aut eorundem vocatione, quod ab ejus scopo antecedentium ac consequentium nexu est alienum. 11. Loquitur itaque de gratia fidei & salutis in Christo exhibita, & per Christum collata, adeoque commune conversis omnibus tum Gentilium, tum Judaeorum. 111. Falsa hypothesis hanc gratiam non fuisse verè in Judaeos effusam, nec ad Judaeos conversos posse dirigi sermonem Petri ; quod est ipsum [?]ἐν ἀρχῇ. iv. Vaticinia etiam ad quae respicit Apostolus, non sunt alia quàm de Christi in carne exhibitione, de manifestatione ejusdem conspicuâ, de adimplenda promissione erga fideles posteriorum temporum, quo privilegio gaudere illos ostendit, ut ἐξ ἀλληλουχίας patet, versibus 11.12.
units.tr: VI. Thirdly, some press the passage 1 Pet. 1.10. There Peter speaks of the grace poured out upon the Gentiles and foretold by the prophets, and so writes to the Gentiles: "Concerning which salvation the prophets have sought and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that would come to you" [περὶ ἧς σωτηρίας ἐξεζήτησαν, καὶ ἐξηρεύνησαν προφῆται, οἱ περὶ τῆς εἰς ὑμᾶς χάριτος προφητεύσαντες]. But, first, it is false that the Apostle speaks of a special grace toward the Gentiles, or of their calling, which does not fit the connection of what comes before and after, given his purpose. Second, he therefore speaks of the grace of faith and salvation offered in Christ and bestowed through Christ, and so a grace common to all converts, both Gentile and Jewish. Third, it is a false hypothesis that this grace was not truly poured out upon the Jews, or that Peter's words could not be directed to Jewish converts; this is itself the error at the outset [ἐν ἀρχῇ]. Fourth, the prophecies to which the Apostle refers concern only the exhibition of Christ in the flesh, his visible manifestation, and the fulfilment of the promise to the faithful of later times, a privilege which he shows they enjoy, as is clear from the chain of connection in verses 11 and 12.

units.la: VII. Quarto excipitur, competere Gentibus non Hebraeis, quae habet Petrus 1.Pet.iv.3. de praeterito vitae tempore in lascivijs, cupiditatibus, vinolentijs, com-messationibus, compotationibus, nefarijs simulachrorum cultibus, ad libidiné Gen-tium exacto. Hinc non ad Hebraeos sed conversos ex Gentibus scriptitasse Petrum. Speciosè satis, solidè nequaquam. Neque enim 1. οἱ καταρρᾳζόμενοι τὸ θέλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν[?], seu iisdem se cum Gentibus flagitiis & sceleribus polluentes, eorum imitantes affectus & propudiosas libidines, illicò gentes sunt. Tales certè ingenio & moribus, non genere illicò & sanguine, tales vitâ, non nomine & professione; tales imitativè, non originaliter; practicè non theoreticè. De prioribus sermo tantum Apostolo. Ita flagitiosam illam Israëlitarum Davidem insectantium turbam, vocat ipse Gentes Pf. LIX. 6. Alibi eosdem dicit peregrinos, exteros. Pf. LIV. §[?]. Hoc sensu Iudæi, Ductores Sodomæ & populus Gomorræ. Esai. 1. 10. Ita profanis authoribus ἀσωτιάζειν[?], Κορινθιάζεσθαι, Συβαρίζειν &c. Massiliensem esse, aut Cyprium, aut Lydium &c. est mollitiem illarum Gentium ac luxuriem æmulari. 11. Retorqueri locus non uno modo potest, Eo ipso Petrus hic Iudæos distinguit à Gentibus, quando ad harum se vixisse mores, ad harum ingenium & libidinem, instar Gentium, diserte satis affirmat. Quin se Petrus illis accensetº ἀρκετὸς[?] γὰρ ἡμῖν, sufficiet nobis. &c. saltè juxta plerorumq; codicum fidè, aliter quàvis Syrus & Vulgatus Interpres. Itaque vel pariter Gentilis fuerit Petrus, vel omninò etiam Judæis quadrant, quæ de anteacto vitæ tempore recenset. Nisi forte excipias per ἀναχοίνωσιν[?], rhetorum sæpè more, (sed duriorem, si de Gentibus sermo) sese illis adjunxisse Petrum.
units.tr: VII. Fourthly, it is objected that what Peter says in 1 Pet. 4.3 about the past time of life, spent in lasciviousness, lusts, drunkenness, revelries, carousings, and abominable worship of idols, fits Gentiles who had lived by the desires of the Gentiles. Hence, it is argued, Peter wrote not to Hebrews but to converts from the Gentiles. This is plausible enough, but not solid at all. For, first, those who walk in the will of the Gentiles [οἱ καταρρᾳζόμενοι τὸ θέλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν], that is, who defile themselves with the same vices and crimes as the Gentiles, imitating their passions and shameless lusts, are not on that account Gentiles. Such men are Gentiles in disposition and manners, not at once by birth and blood; in their life, not in name and profession; by imitation, not by origin; in practice, not in theory. Peter speaks only of the former. Thus the Apostle himself calls that shameful crowd of Israelites who pursued David "Gentiles" (Ps. 59.6), and elsewhere calls them strangers and foreigners (Ps. 54). In this sense the Jews are called "rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah" (Isa. 1.10). So too among profane authors, to play the wanton [ἀσωτιάζειν], to live like a Corinthian [Κορινθιάζεσθαι], to act like a Sybarite [Συβαρίζειν], etc., and to be a Massilian, or a Cypriot, or a Lydian, is to emulate the softness and luxury of those nations. Second, the passage can be turned back in more than one way. By this very fact Peter distinguishes Jews from Gentiles, when he plainly affirms that he himself lived in accordance with their manners, their disposition and lust, as the Gentiles did. Indeed Peter counts himself among them: "for the time past is sufficient for us" [ἀρκετὸς γὰρ ἡμῖν], at least according to the faithful reading of most manuscripts, and otherwise according to the Syriac and the Vulgate translator. So either Peter was equally a Gentile, or what he recounts of the past time of life fits Jews entirely as well. Unless perhaps you make the exception that Peter joined himself to them by anacoenosis, as rhetoricians often do (though this is harsher if the talk is of Gentiles).

units.la: iii. Peccatur etiam falsâ hypothesi, quasi flagitia illa omnia & inquinamenta, ἀσέλγειαι, ἐπιθυμίαι, οἰνοφλυγίαι, κῶ-μοι, πότοι, καὶ ἀθέμιτοι εἰδωλολατρείαι, nonnisi Ethnicorum esse potuerint. Quidni & Judæos, flagitiosissimos aliquando mortalium, permixtos Gentibus, ad varium jam superstitionum genus prolapsos, contagio quodam, inquinarint? Nec quempiam moveat vox εἰδωλολατρείας, à quo flagitij genere Judæi posteriores vehementer semper abhorruêre.
units.tr: iii. There is also a fault in a false hypothesis, as if all those shameful deeds and pollutions, debaucheries, lusts, drunkenness, revels, drinking-bouts, and unlawful idolatries [ἀσέλγειαι, ἐπιθυμίαι, οἰνοφλυγίαι, κῶμοι, πότοι, καὶ ἀθέμιτοι εἰδωλολατρείαι] could only have been the work of Gentiles. Why should the Jews not also have defiled themselves by a certain contagion, since they, at one time the most flagrant of mortals, mixed with the Gentiles and fell into the various kinds of superstition? Nor should anyone be moved by the word "idolatry" [εἰδωλολατρείας], since the later Jews have always vehemently abhorred that kind of vice.

units.la: Quid si generalius notet superstitionem quamvis, & inanem omnem cultum, in quem Judæi tum variè prolapsi? Quid si participatam Idololatriam intelligat, ut Judæorum multi, agentes medios inter Idololatras, illis vel connivérent conni-verent sæpè, vel conviverent, vel arctiùs adhærerent. Quid si ad defectiones & apo-stasias Judæorum reflectat, quales præte-ritis temporibus, sæviente Antiochorum, Ptolomæorum &c. in Judæos persecutio-ne, longe plurimæ? Quid si metaphoricè vitia alia notet & scelera, quibus vel dæ-monem vel creaturas colimus impensiùs, quomodo vox alibi usurpatur; Syrus ובפולחנא דשאר [?] Et in cultu dæmo-nis.
units.tr: What if it denotes more generally any superstition and any empty worship, into which the Jews then fell in various ways? What if it means participated idolatry, as many Jews, living in the midst of idolaters, often either connived with them, or lived alongside them, or clung to them more closely? What if it refers to the defections and apostasies of the Jews, which were very numerous in past times, when persecution raged against the Jews under Antiochus, the Ptolemies, and others? What if it metaphorically denotes other vices and crimes, by which we worship demons or creatures more intensely, as the word is used elsewhere; the Syriac has "and in the worship of demons."

units.la: VIII. Exceptiones secundæ classes palmariæ esse possunt: primò, concessò Petrum dedisse ad Judæos literas, per minoris Asiæ Provincias dispersos, omninò etiam Paulum ad eosdem scriptitasse, non in hac ipsâ quæ inscribitur ad Hebræos, sed in suis ad Galatas, Ephesios, Colossenses Asiæ minoris incolas, Epistolis. Adeoque nihil necesse esse priorem denotari. Frustrà tamen vocari hasce in subsidium ostendimus. 1. quia Epistola ad Galatas data ad solam Galatarum Ecclesiam; Petrus vero meminit Paulinæ Epistolæ etiã ad Cappadociæ, Ponti, Bithyniæ, Asiæ spectantis Ecclesias Καθῶς ἐγραψεν ὑμῖν, non ἐστὶν[?] ἐξ ὑμῶν. II. Quia Galatæ ad quos Paulus, Gentiles erant sanguine & origine, quondam nescientes Deum & servientes τοῖς[?] μὴ φύσει οὖσι θεοῖς. Gal.iv.8. Cum Hebræis vero rem esse Petro & concessum, & in antecessis demonstratum. III. Quia diversum longè argumentum Petrinæ Epistolæ & Epistolæ ad Galatas, & quæ Petrus de fiducia, perseverentia, judicio ultimo, apostatarum interitu &c. certè divus ille Gentium Apostolus alibi longè fusius & luculentius; imò verò in Epistolâ ad Hebræos maximè, cujus affinitatem argumenti cum Petrinâ, offendemus infrà. iv. Eadem ratione patet non Epistolam ad Ephesios, non ad Colossenses, Petro designari; partim quod ad eos datæ, qui ex Gentilismo, non Judaismo, ad fidem Christianam adducti, ut ex utriusque contextu intelligimus; partim quod nonnisi duabus scriptæ sint Ecclesijs, Ephesinæ & Colossensi, Petrus verò de Epistolâ ad omnes minoris Asiæ cœtus, & quidem ex Hebræis collectos agit; partim quod de his ipsis, de quibus Petrus, Paulus aliàs disertius longè ac prolixius disseruerit.
units.tr: VIII. The second group of exceptions may be the most notable. First, granted that Peter wrote letters to the Jews scattered through the provinces of Asia Minor, Paul certainly also wrote to the same people, not in this letter which is inscribed to the Hebrews, but in his letters to the Galatians, Ephesians, and Colossians, inhabitants of Asia Minor. And so there is no need for the earlier to be meant. We have shown, however, that these are called in support in vain. 1. Because the letter to the Galatians was addressed only to the church of the Galatians; but Peter mentions a Pauline letter addressed also to the churches of Cappadocia, Pontus, Bithynia, and Asia: "as he wrote to you" [Καθῶς ἐγραψεν ὑμῖν], not "is" [ἐστὶν] "from you." II. Because the Galatians to whom Paul wrote were Gentiles by blood and origin, who once did not know God and served those that by nature are not gods (Gal. 4.8). But with Peter the matter concerns Hebrews, as both is granted and was shown above. III. Because the argument of Peter's letter is very different from that of the letter to the Galatians, and what Peter says of confidence, perseverance, the last judgement, the destruction of apostates, etc., that divine Apostle of the Gentiles treats elsewhere far more fully and clearly; indeed, chiefly in the letter to the Hebrews, whose affinity of argument with Peter's we shall meet below. IV. By the same reasoning it is clear that Peter does not designate the letter to the Ephesians or the letter to the Colossians; partly because they were addressed to those brought to the Christian faith from Gentilism, not Judaism, as we understand from the context of each; partly because they were written to only two churches, the Ephesian and the Colossian, whereas Peter speaks of a letter to all the assemblies of Asia Minor, and indeed of those gathered from Hebrews; partly because Paul discussed these very matters, of which Peter speaks, elsewhere far more clearly and at much greater length.

units.la: IX. Secundò, urgeri potest, Petrũ loco memorato reflectere ad Epistolã quandã Ecclesijs minoris Asiæ transmissam; Illam verò, de cujus authore instituta quæstio, videri datâ ad illos Hebræorum, qui Hierosolymis, qui inpalæstinâ, quos sæpe Paulus τὰς Ἐκκλησίας τῆς Ἰουδαίας, τὰς ἔνους[?] ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ, Gal. i. 22. i. Thess. ii. 14. &c. Hos proprie Hebræos, priores Hellenistas nūcupatos, & in hac sententiâ esse doctissimos Interpretes. Quin dū author Epistolæ ad eos se venturū pollicetur Hebr. xiii. 23. verosimillimū esse, eodē illos egisse in loco nec per tot provincias fuisse divisos. Atqui primò, peccatur falsâ hypothesi, Epistolam ad Hebræos, illos spectasse tantùm, qui Hierosolymis, aut certè in Palæstinâ. Imò verò & ad Palæstinas & ad alias extrà Palæstinam Ecclesias directam esse colligimus. 1. Ex inscriptione, πρὸς Ἑβραίους, indefinitè, nec limitato loco, adeoque communis illa fuerit, Hebræorum genti
units.tr: IX. Secondly, it may be urged that Peter, in the passage mentioned, refers to a certain letter sent to the churches of Asia Minor; but that letter whose author is in question seems to have been given to those Hebrews who were at Jerusalem and in Palestine, whom Paul often calls "the churches of Judea" [τὰς Ἐκκλησίας τῆς Ἰουδαίας, τὰς ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ] (Gal. 1.22; 1 Thess. 2.14), etc. These, properly called Hebrews, the former being called Hellenists, are the view of the most learned interpreters. Indeed, since the author of the letter promises to come to them (Heb. 13.23), it is very likely that they were in one place and not divided through so many provinces. But, first, it is at fault through a false hypothesis to think that the letter to the Hebrews looked only to those at Jerusalem, or certainly only to those in Palestine. Indeed, we gather that it was addressed both to the churches of Palestine and to others outside Palestine. 1. From the inscription, "to the Hebrews" [πρὸς Ἑβραίους], stated indefinitely and not limited to any place; and so it would be common to the Hebrew nation.

units.la: n. Ex Hebræorū appellatione, quales erāt quotquot siveHeberi, sive Abrahæ posteri, etiā extrà Judeæ fines alibi terrarum agères. Nec hac se nomēclatione excidere ullā ratione passi essent. Nec minus dicti Hebræi, quæ hodieque procul à Palæstinæ finibus, quique vix aliā se appellatione insignire solent. Ipse Paulus patriā quanquā Cilix, civitate Romanus, nihilominus se Hebræum dicit aliquoties, Hebræum ex Hebræis 1.Cor.xi.22. Phil.iii.5. Adeóque solos Palæstinos distinctè à Judæis aliis per provincias dispersos, Hebræos dictos, gratis viri magni, affirmarunt. Quare verò Paulus Hebræis potius quā Iudæis inscripserit, ratio gemina, 1. quia cōmune nomē fuit totius gentis 11. quia Iudæi dicebantur qui tales nō tantùm gente sed & religione, unde Ἰουδαΐζειν, Ἰουδαϊσμὸς, ut pluribus Illustris Salmasius de Hellenist. Quæst. v. At Epistola fidelibus & Christianis ex illā gente inscripta. 111. Idé colligimus ex occasione Epistolæ, quæ communis Judæis omnibus conversis adChristi fidé, scripta nempe iis partim in doctrinā de Messiā & adimplectione legis confirmandis, partim afflictis ter- ris Asiæ cœtus, & quidem ex Hebræis collectos agit; partim quod de his ipsis, de quibus Petrus, Paulus aliàs disertiùs longè ac prolixius disseruerit.
units.tr: 2. From the appellation "Hebrews": all were such who were either Hebrews or descendants of Abraham, even those living elsewhere in the world beyond the borders of Judea. Nor would they have suffered themselves to be excluded from this name on any ground. Nor are Hebrews any less so called today, far from the borders of Palestine, who hardly ever are wont to distinguish themselves by any other appellation. Paul himself, though a Cilician by country and a Roman by citizenship, nevertheless calls himself a Hebrew several times, "a Hebrew of Hebrews" (1 Cor. 11.22; Phil. 3.5). And so great men have affirmed, without reason, that only the Palestinians, as distinct from the other Jews scattered through the provinces, were called Hebrews. As to why Paul inscribed the letter to Hebrews rather than Jews, there is a twofold reason: first, because it was the common name of the whole nation; second, because those were called "Jews" who were such not only by nation but by religion, whence "to Judaize" [Ἰουδαΐζειν] and "Judaism" [Ἰουδαϊσμὸς], as the illustrious Salmasius shows at length in his work on the Hellenists, question v. But the letter is inscribed to the faithful and Christians of that nation. 3. We gather the same from the occasion of the letter, which was common to all Jews converted to faith in Christ, written to them partly to confirm them in doctrine concerning the Messiah and the fulfilment of the law, and partly to those afflicted in the lands of Asia; the assemblies gathered from Hebrews are treated, and indeed the things about which Peter spoke, Paul discussed elsewhere far more clearly and at much greater length.

units.la: IX. Secundò, urgeri potest, Petrũ loco memorato reflectere ad Epistolã quandã Ecclesijs minoris Asiæ transmissam; Illam verò, de cujus authore instituta quæstio, videri data ad illos Hebræorum, qui Hie-rosolymis, qui inpalæstinâ, quos sæpe Paulus τὰς Ἐκκλησίας τῆς Ἰουδαίας, τὰς ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ, Gal. 1.22.1. Thess. ii.14. &c. Hos proprie Hebræos, priores Hellenistas nūcupatos, & in hac sententiâ esse doctissimos Interpretes. Quin dū author Epistolæ ad eos se venturū pollicetur Hebr. xiii.23. verosimillimū esse, eodē illos egisse in loco nec per tot provincias fuisse divisos. Atqui primò, peccatur falsâ hypothesi, Epistolam ad Hebræos, illos spectasse tantùm, qui Hierosolymis, aut certè in Palæstinâ. Imò verò & ad Palæstinas & ad alias extrà Palæstinam Ecclesias directam esse colligimus. 1. Ex inscriptione, πρὸς Ἑβραίους, indefinitè, nec limitato loco, adeoque communis illa fuerit, Hebræorum genti.
units.tr: IX. Secondly, it may be urged that Peter in the passage mentioned refers to a certain letter sent to the churches of Asia Minor, and that the letter whose author is in question seems to have been addressed to those Hebrews who were at Jerusalem and in Palestine, whom Paul often calls the churches of Judea, those in Judea (Gal. 1.22; 1 Thess. 2.14, etc.) [τὰς Ἐκκλησίας τῆς Ἰουδαίας, τὰς ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ]. These are properly called Hebrews, while the others were called Hellenists, and the most learned interpreters hold this view. Indeed, since the author of the Epistle promises to come to them (Heb. 13.23), it is very likely that they were in one place and not scattered through many provinces. But first, this argument proceeds from a false hypothesis, that the Epistle to the Hebrews looked only to those at Jerusalem, or at least in Palestine. Rather, we gather that it was directed both to the churches in Palestine and to churches outside Palestine. 1. From the inscription, To the Hebrews, which is indefinite and names no particular place, and so it was a letter for the whole Hebrew nation.

units.la: ¶[?]. Ex Hebræorum appellatione, quales erāt quotquot sive Heberi[?], sive Abrahæ posteri, etiā extrà Judeæ fines alibi terrarum agéres. Nec hac se nomenclatione excidere ullā ratione passi essent. Nec minus dicti Hebræi, quæ hodieque procul à Palæstinæ finibus, quique vix aliâ se appellatione insignire solent. Ipse Paulus patriâ quanquam Cilix, civitate Romanus, nihilominus se Hebræum dicit aliquoties, Hebræum ex Hebræis 1.Cor.xi.22. Phil.iii.5. Adeòque solos Palæstinos distinctè à Judæis aliis per provincias dispersos, Hebræos dictos, gratis viri magni, affirmarunt. Quare verò Paulus Hebræis potius quàm Iudæis inscripserit, ratio gemina, 1. quia cómune nomen fuit totius gentis 11. quia Iudæi dicebantur qui tales non tantùm gente sed & religione, unde Ἰουδαΐζειν, Ἰουδαϊσμὸς, ut pluribus Illustris Salmasius de Hellenist. Quæst. v. At Epistola fidelibus & Christianis ex illâ gente inscripta. iii. Idé colligimus ex occasione Epistolæ, quæ communis Judæis omnibus conversis ad Christi fidé, scripta nempe iis partim in doctrinâ de Messiâ & adimplectione legis confirmandis, partim afflictis temtemporibus ac sæviente gentilium furorum rabie, erigendis solandisque, cui non in Judæa tantùm, ut supponitur, sed alibi etiam locorum obnoxij. iv. Ex subjecto Epistolæ Iacobi & Petri, & verisimile il-los ipsos esse Hebræos ad quos Iacobus, & Petrus ex parte scripsère, & ad quos Epistolam aliam à Paulo transmissam, hic in posteriori suâ monet: Nihil jam ego de Chrysostomo, Hebræos Hispanos interpretante, Homil. in Matt. LXXVI. quod postmodum Paulum eosdem visendi gratiâ in Hispanias, juxtà cum quibusdam Veterum, profectum putet, atque ita quadrare illud Heb. xiii. 23. Quanquam & idè alibi Palæstinos intelligit, Præfat. in Epist. τῶν δὲ οὕτω ἐπιστέλλει· ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ ἐν [?]Ἱεροσολύμοις [?]ἢ Παλαιστίνῃ. v. Quia nihil obstant rationes allatæ. Non, quod alibi memo-rentur aliquoties Ecclesiæ in Palæstina collectæ, quum non minùs frequens sit in Actis & paulinis mentio Ecclesiarum collectarum ex Judæis, per Syriæ, aut minoris Asiæ tractum; Non etiam, quod Helle-nistæ nuncuparentur qui extrà palæstijam dispersi Judæi; quasi vero hoc fuerit διασπορὰ[?] illorum nomen, quod nomen verius dialecti, omniúq; adeò ἑλληνιζόντων[?] quasi nec iidem Hebræi ratione originis qui alias Hellenistæ ratione idiomatis, & Græci quo utebantur sermonis; quasi etiam Hebræorum nomen nonnisi Palæstinis inditum fuerit, quod falsum esse demon-stravimus; imò vero Hellenistas apud Lu-cam nec Judæos esse, nec Hebræos, sed proselytos, gente extraneos, religione Ju-dæos, idem Salmasius de Hellenist. p. 233.
units.tr: ¶[?]. 2. From the name Hebrews, which applied to all who were descendants of Eber or of Abraham, even those living elsewhere in the world outside the borders of Judea. Nor would they have allowed themselves to be deprived of this name in any way. The Hebrews are still called so today, far from the borders of Palestine, and they hardly ever use any other name to distinguish themselves. Paul himself, though a Cilician by birth and a Roman by citizenship, nonetheless calls himself a Hebrew several times, a Hebrew of Hebrews (1 Cor. 11.22; Phil. 3.5). Therefore, the great men have asserted, not without reason, that only the inhabitants of Palestine, as distinct from the Jews scattered through other provinces, were called Hebrews. Why Paul addressed the Hebrews rather than the Jews has a twofold reason: 1. because Hebrew was the common name of the whole nation; 2. because Jews were those who were such not only by nation but also by religion, whence Judaizing and Judaism, as the illustrious Salmasius shows at length in his De Hellenistis, question 5. But the Epistle is addressed to the faithful and Christians of that nation. 3. We gather the same from the occasion of the Epistle, which was common to all Jews converted to the faith of Christ; it was written to them partly to confirm them in the doctrine concerning the Messiah and the fulfilment of the law, partly to raise up and comfort them when afflicted and when the rage of the Gentiles raged against them, a danger to which they were exposed not only in Judea, as is supposed, but also elsewhere. 4. From the subject matter of the Epistles of James and Peter, and it is likely that those very people were the Hebrews to whom James and Peter in part wrote, and to whom Paul sent another letter, as he notes in his later one. I say nothing yet of Chrysostom, who, interpreting the Hebrews of Spain (Homily 76 on Matthew), thinks that Paul went to Spain to see them, together with some of the ancients, and so the words of Heb. 13.23 would agree. Yet elsewhere he understands the Palestinians, in the preface to the Epistle, where he says: It seems to me that he writes these things in Jerusalem or in Palestine [ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ἢ Παλαιστίνῃ]. 5. Because the reasons alleged do not stand in the way. Nor is it an objection that churches gathered in Palestine are mentioned elsewhere, since the mention in Acts and the Pauline letters of churches gathered from Jews in the region of Syria or Asia Minor is no less frequent. Nor is it an objection that Jews dispersed outside Palestine were called Hellenists, as if this were the name of the dispersion, which is rather the name of a dialect, and of all who speak Greek. As if the same Hebrews by origin were not also Hellenists by language and by the Greek tongue they used. As if also the name Hebrews had been given only to the Palestinians, which we have shown to be false. Indeed, the Hellenists in Luke are neither Jews nor Hebrews but proselytes, foreign by nation and Jews by religion, as the same Salmasius shows in De Hellenistis, p. 233.

units.la: Non denique, quod author Epistolæ, He-bræos illos erigit spe sui conspectus & alloquii, quando indefinitè loquitur, non universaliter, visurum se illos seu illorum quosdam, non visurum omnes, & illos forte ad quos primò & immediatè trans-missa Epistola, cum aliis deinceps He-bræis communicanda. Respondemus se-cundò per συγχώρησιν[?], dato Hebræos illos Hierosolymitanos fuisse & Palæstinos (ut ex Veteribus Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Ambrosius, Theophylactus, initio Com-mentariorū in Epistolā) nihil obstat quo minùs Petrus eandem illam Epistolam invenerit.
