Sic directè & primò ad illos datas ut secundariò ad Hebræos alios spectarit & cum iis communicanda fuerit à fratribus Palæstinis, quando communia illis omnia, nomen, genus, causa, fides, afflictiones. Atque utrumque statuerunt doc-tissimi Interpretes, nec minùs stat sen-tentia.
units.tr: Finally, it is not an objection that the author of the Epistle encourages those Hebrews with hope of seeing and speaking with him, when he speaks indefinitely, not universally, saying that he will see them, or some of them, not all of them, and perhaps those to whom the Epistle was first and directly sent, with the others to share it afterwards among the Hebrews. Secondly, we reply by concession: granted that those Hebrews were Jerusalemites and Palestinians (as the ancients Chrysostom, Theodoret, Ambrose and Theophylact say at the beginning of their commentaries on the Epistle), nothing prevents Peter from having found that same Epistle. Thus it was sent directly and first to them, so that it might also concern the other Hebrews secondarily, and be shared with them by the brothers in Palestine, since all things were common to them: name, race, cause, faith, afflictions. The most learned interpreters have affirmed both points, and the opinion is no less well founded.

units.la: X. Tertiò excipiet aliquis, posse istiusmodi Epistolam, de quâ Petrus, idem cum multis aliis subjisse fatum; qualis credita Pauli ad Laodicenses, & ad Corinthios tertia, & quales intercidisse complures disertè Calvinus, Beza, aliique viri magni affirmarunt ad locum 1.Cor. v.9. Nos vero 1. eadem id facilitate negamus, quâ affirmatur, & talem excidisse Epistolam dici potest, non probari, meminit nemo Veterum, nullo vel conjicere licet indicio, τῷ δὲ καταφανεῖ ὁ ἔλεγχος[?]. 11. Imò verò Ca-nonicarum ullam sive injuriâ temporum, sive quovis alio fato interversam, inficiamur. Non nescimus ita sentire de quibusdam Canonicis sublatis, Orthodoxorum Theologos Calvinum, Bezam, Musculum, Witakerum, Willetum, Pareum, Maccovium, alios; ut nihil de Socinianis & Pontificijs, Stapletonem certè, & quosdam alios si excipias. Frustrà tamen illos esse, nos alibi ex professo & fusiùs. iii. Dato tamen, at à jactură quarundam Epistolarum, ad jacturam Paulinae ad Hebraeos, nulla consequentia, si non alia praesto sint argumenta. Imprimis quando supersunt quae ad eosdem Hebraeos aliae, à viris θεοπνεύστοις exaratae. iv. Quae verò in specie de Epistolâ ad Laodicenses, & ad Corinthios tertiâ, ut obiter huic occurramus instantiae, nihilo certiora. priori sententiae occasionem praebuit locus Col. iv. 16. καὶ τὴν [?]ἐκ Λαοδικείας ἵνα ὑμεῖς ἀναγνῶτε[?]. Vulgatus, Et eam quae Laodicensium est; hinc existimarunt alij missam à Paulo Epistolam ad Laodicenos; hinc jam olim talis Epistola circumlata, teste Hieronymo in Cat. Script. Eccles. & Philastrio haer. xc. quamvis non recepta in Canone; hinc Sixtus Senensis Bibl. L. ii. in Paulo, & Faber Stapulensis illius exhibet Epistolę argumentū; hinc BellarBellarminus, nondum edito Recognitionum Libro, L.iv. de Verbo Dei C. iv. à Canone excidisse illam censet; hinc à nonnullis, Novi Testamenti codicibus eadem aliquando inserta. Atqui I. [illegible, ~12 letters] dato Epistolam illam memoratam Sixto & Stapulensi, & quæ habetur hodieque ad Laodicenses, eandem esse cum veteri illa Paulo tributa, ergo extat etiamnum, ergo neutiquam interversa, ergo illius hodieq; saltè non vestigia & rudera, qualia alterius illius Paulinæ ad Hebræos, quæ intercepta dicitur, sunt nulla. II. Vel eadem fuerit cum antiqua illa, de qua Hieronymus, Philastrius, Epiphanius, vel diversa. Si prius, suppositicia jam pridem habita, & ab omnibus explosa, eodem Hieronymo teste, & ejusdem cum Epistolis Pauli ad Senecam, & Christi ad Abgarum, & Epistolâ Barnabæ, & aliis id genus quisquiliis, quibus secundo jam sæculo refertus Christianus orbis, commatis. Si posterius, ut rectius affirmat Baronius ad A.C.LX, inconsultò verò nec re pensitata, negat quidā Morus de Causâ Dei part.II.
units.tr: X. Thirdly, someone will object that an Epistle of this kind, of which Peter speaks, may have suffered the same fate as many others, such as the supposed letter of Paul to the Laodiceans, and the third letter to the Corinthians, and several others which Calvin, Beza and other great men expressly assert to have perished, on the passage 1 Cor. 5.9. But we, first, deny this with the same ease with which it is affirmed. That such a letter has perished can be said, but not proved; no one of the ancients mentions it, and one cannot even conjecture it from any clue, and what is manifest needs no refutation. Second, indeed, we deny that any canonical letter has perished, whether through the injury of time or by any other fate. We are not unaware that the theologians of the orthodox, Calvin, Beza, Musculus, Whitaker, Willet, Pareus, Maccovius and others, think otherwise about certain lost canonical letters; to say nothing of the Socinians and the Papists, Stapleton certainly, and some others, if you except them. Yet they are mistaken, as we have shown elsewhere at length and expressly. Third, granting nevertheless the loss of some letters, there is no consequence that Paul's letter to the Hebrews was lost too, if no other arguments are at hand. Above all, when there are still other letters to these same Hebrews, written by men inspired of God. Fourth, as for the specific case of the letter to the Laodiceans and the third letter to the Corinthians, to meet this objection in passing, they are no more certain. The former opinion arose from the passage Col. 4.16: "and the letter from Laodicea, that you also read" [καὶ τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας ἵνα ὑμεῖς ἀναγνῶτε]. The Vulgate has and that which is of the Laodiceans. Hence some thought that Paul had sent a letter to the Laodiceans. Hence such a letter was already long circulating, as Jerome in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers testifies, and Philastrius (heresy 90), although it was not received into the canon. Hence Sixtus of Siena (Bibliotheca, book 2, on Paul), and Faber Stapulensis gives an account of its contents. Hence Bellarmine, before the publication of his book Recognitions (book 4, On the Word of God, ch. 4), thinks it dropped out of the canon. Hence in some manuscripts of the New Testament the same letter was at some time inserted. But: I. Granting that the letter mentioned by Sixtus and Faber Stapulensis, and the one still extant today to the Laodiceans, is the same as that ancient letter ascribed to Paul, it still exists, and so it has by no means perished; and therefore there are today at least no traces or remains of it, unlike that other Pauline letter to the Hebrews, which is said to have been lost. II. Either it is the same as the ancient letter of which Jerome, Philastrius and Epiphanius speak, or it is different. If the former, it was long ago held to be spurious and rejected by all, as Jerome testifies, and it is of the same kind as the letters of Paul to Seneca, of Christ to Abgar, the Epistle of Barnabas, and other such trifles with which the Christian world was crowded already in the second century. If the latter, as Baronius rightly maintains at the year 60, but Morus, in his Cause of God, part 2, denies, rashly and without weighing the matter, then that letter is more recent, and no less in need of proof [illegible].

units.la: Quæst. 1. recentior illa fuerit, nec minus postulanda [illegible, ~8 letters].iii. Sed peccatum evidentissimâ [illegible, ~8 letters] loci Coloss.iv.16. & hinc origo fraudis. Legerunt in Græco contextu τὴν Λαοδικέων. Hinc Vulgatus, eam quæ Laodicensium est, quod secus interpretati, quæ ad Laodicenses scripta. Nescij dici Epistolam Laodicensium, quæ ab iis profecta, ab iis consignata, prout dicimus Epistolas Pauli, Petri, Epistolas Tullij, Plinij &c. Adeóque designatur Epistola non εἰς Λαοδικείαν, vel πρὸς Λαοδικέας quomodo legerunt nulli codices, sed ἐκ Λαοδικείας, ut plerique habent; scripta Laodicea, istic loci, ab ipsis Laodicenis, ut videtur ad Paulum, quamque legi voluerit à Colossensibus vicinis, & in quâ erant forte quæ Colossenses ipsos concernerent. Atque ita legit vetustissimus interpres [illegible, ~5 letters]; & hæc fuit sententia Chrysostomi, aliorumque ex Veteribus in Epistolâ ad Coloss.iv. Placeret Theophylacti sententia, per τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας, interpretantis primam ad Timotheum, ab ipso Paulo Laodicea Phrygiæ Pacatianæ perscriptam, scriptam, ut habet subscriptio, quæquè[?] illa ipsa Laodicea vicina Colossis Phrygiæ majoris oppido; in quà quidem Epistolà nonnulla affinis cum hac ad Colossenses argumenti: Nisi nutaret sæpe subscriptionum illarum fides; nisi etiam hoc loco emphaticè & aperte innueret Epistolæ Laodicenorum Ecclesiam, quoquo modo spectantem; nisi denique, cum hæc scriberet Paulus ad Colossenses, de facie se & his & Laodicenis ignotum profiteretur Cap.ii.i. v. Dato, non concesso agi de Epistolâ, non subjectivè & originaliter scripta à Laodicensibus, sed objectivè & terminativè ad Laodicenos, ne sic quidè evincitur fuisse Pauli, nec constat ex textu, & vel Lucæ Evangelistæ, ut monet Philastrius, libro de Hæresibus, vel alius cujuspiam esse potuit. vi. Dato etiā Paulinam illā fuisse ad Laodicenses, suppònitur denuò eandē hodiè interceptam, & è Canone sublatam. Sanè Marcion dici voluit Epistolam ad Laodicenses, quæ nobis ad Ephesios, ut Tertullianus contrà Marcion. L. v. C. xvii. Hic contrà ad Ephesios, quę perperam existimabatur Laodicensium, & hoc ipsum occasione forte fortè præbuit ex parte novam ad Laodicenos parturiendi. Sed de his alibi, suo loco. Quod attinet tertiam ad Corinthios, huic sententiæ locum fecêre verba 1. Cor. v. 9. ἐγραψα ὑμῖν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι πόρ-νοις, quæ de priori quâdam Epistolâ interpretati, imprimis recentiorum longè plurimi. Gratis tamen, neque aliam ab hac ipsâ primâ Epistolâ denotari constat.
units.tr: Question 1: whether that letter was more recent, and no less to be demanded [illegible]. iii. But the mistake lies in the very evident [illegible] of Colossians 4:16, and hence the origin of the fraud. They read in the Greek text τὴν Λαοδικέων [the Laodicean one]. Hence the Vulgate renders it eam quae Laodicensium est [that which is of the Laodiceans], while others, translating differently, render it quae ad Laodicenses scripta [written to the Laodiceans]. One cannot say it is called the Epistle of the Laodiceans in the sense that it came from them and was sealed by them, as we say the Epistles of Paul or Peter, or the letters of Tully or Pliny. Rather, the letter meant is not εἰς Λαοδικείαν or πρὸς Λαοδικέας [to Laodicea or to the Laodiceans], as no manuscripts read, but ἐκ Λαοδικείας [from Laodicea], as most have it: written from Laodicea, in that place, by the Laodiceans themselves, apparently to Paul, and which he wished to be read by the neighbouring Colossians, and in which there were perhaps things that concerned the Colossians themselves. So the most ancient translator reads, and this was the view of Chrysostom and other Fathers on Colossians 4. Theophylact's opinion would also please, who, interpreting τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας as the First Epistle to Timothy, holds that it was written by Paul himself from Laodicea in Pacatian Phrygia, as the subscription says. That Laodicea lay near Colossae, a town of Greater Phrygia, and in that letter there is some similarity of subject with this one to the Colossians. Yet the credit of those subscriptions often wavers; and unless this place emphatically and plainly pointed to a church of the Laodiceans in some way, unless finally Paul, writing this to the Colossians, professed that he was unknown in person to them and to the Laodiceans (Col. 2:1), the view stands on weak ground. v. Granting, though not conceding, that the matter concerns a letter not written subjectively and originally by the Laodiceans, but objectively and terminatively addressed to the Laodiceans, even so it is not proved thereby to be Paul's, nor does it appear from the text. It could have been by the Evangelist Luke, as Philastrius advises in his book on heresies, or by someone else altogether. vi. Granting also that the Pauline letter was addressed to the Laodiceans, it is again assumed that it has since been lost and removed from the canon. Marcion, indeed, wanted the letter that we have as "to the Ephesians" to be called "to the Laodiceans", as Tertullian reports against Marcion, book 5, chapter 17. Here, on the contrary, the letter "to the Ephesians", which was wrongly thought to be of the Laodiceans, perhaps gave some occasion for partly giving birth to a new letter to the Laodiceans. But of these matters elsewhere, in their proper place. As for the third letter to the Corinthians, the words of 1 Corinthians 5:9 gave room to this opinion, and most of the recent writers, above all, have interpreted them of an earlier letter. Yet this is a gratuitous claim, and it is not established that any letter other than this very first one is meant.

units.la: 1.Ex phrasi Apostoli, ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ, i.e. αὐτῇ τῇ ἐπιστολῇ, prout Coloss. iv.16. ἡ ἐπιστολή, i.e. αὕτη ἡ ἐπιστολή, Syrus אגרתא הדא, ii. Ex serie contextus & antecedentium nexu. Corinthios se monuisse dicit μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι πόρνοις. Scilicet jamjam proscribi & communione arceri jusserat hominem incestis pollutum nuptiis, quem πόρνον seu πορνείας reum dixerat vers.1. ejusdem Capitis, prout vox generaliùs etiâ μοιχείαν, Matt. v.32. & quamvis ἀνόσιον συνουσίαν, ac illicitos adeoq; etiâ incestos concubitus notat. iii. Ex versu 11. hujusce Capitis, νυνὶ δὲ ἐγραψα μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι, ergò hoc ipsum jamjam scripserat, eodem hoc Epistolio. iv. Ex cofensu[?] veterum, imprimis Græcorum Patrum, Chrysostomi, Theodoreti, Oecumenij, Theophylacti, alioaliorum, v.Exfilentio etiam antiquitatis de tertiâ hac ad Corinthiorum Ecclesiam Epistolâ, de quâ ne apex in antiquissimis monimentis, de qua etiam ne ἔγε[?], quantum nobis constat, Baronius. Ergo, frustrà harum Epistolarum exemplo, Paulinam etiam ad Hebraeos perire potuisse dicebatur, ὅπερ ἐδὴ δεῖξαι[?].
units.tr: 1. From the phrase of the Apostle, ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ [in the letter], that is, αὐτῇ τῇ ἐπιστολῇ [in this same letter], as in Colossians 4:16 ἡ ἐπιστολή [the letter], that is, αὕτη ἡ ἐπιστολή [this letter]; the Syriac has agarta hada. ii. From the sequence of the context and the connection of what precedes. He says he had admonished the Corinthians μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι πόρνοις [not to associate with fornicators]. Clearly he had already ordered that the man polluted by an incestuous marriage be cast out and debarred from communion, the man he had called guilty of fornication (πορνεία) in verse 1 of the same chapter; the word is used more generally also of adultery (Matt. 5:32), and it denotes an unlawful union, and so also incestuous intercourse. iii. From verse 11 of this chapter, νυνὶ δὲ ἐγραψα μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι [but now I have written not to associate], therefore he had just written this very thing in the same letter. iv. From the agreement of the ancients, above all the Greek Fathers, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, Theophylact and others. v. From the silence of antiquity about a third letter to the Corinthian church: no trace of it survives in the most ancient records, and, so far as we know, Baronius too says nothing of it. Therefore it is vain to argue from the example of these letters that the Pauline letter to the Hebrews could also have perished.

units.la: XI. Denique, si urgeant posse indi-rectè ad Ecclesias Hebraeorum, per minoris Asiæ regiones distributas, spectare Paulinas alias, hodieque ab interitu vindicatas, toti sanè dicatas Ecclesiæ, neque Petrum necessitate quâdam Epistolam aliquam innuere, speciatim Hebraeis illis inscriptam; quam verò hoc sit elumbe & ficulneum docebunt totidem Petri verba.
units.tr: XI. Finally, if they press that other Pauline letters, which have been preserved to this day from perishing, could refer indirectly to the churches of the Hebrews scattered through the regions of Asia Minor, these letters are entirely devoted to the Church at large, and Peter does not by any necessity hint at any letter specifically addressed to those Hebrews. How feeble and fig-leaf-like this claim is, the very words of Peter will show.

units.la: 1. Quia dixisset alias, ut scripsit Paulus, indefinitè, non, ut scripsit vobis, δεικτικῶς[?] & cum emphasi. 11. quia eandem Epistolam omninò distinguit ab aliis omnibus, ὡς ἡ[?] ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς[?] &c. iii. quia respicit ad Paulinarum aliquam, ubi specialiùs hoc ipsum argumentum, & diserte Paulus exequitur, quod fieri cumprimis in Epistolâ ad Hebræos, sequens docebit ar-gumentum. IV. Quia confunditur finis scriptionis cum objecto, & aliud scripsisse in usum totius Ecclesiæ, adeoque & particularium omnium Ecclesiarum, aliud scripsisse illis ipsis Ecclesiis; aliud scripsisse alicui immediatè & directè, ut sonant verba Apostoli, aliud vero mediatè tantùm & indirectè. prout Epistolæ ad Romanos, Corinthios, &c. in Hebræorum illorum, ut Christianorum omnium usum scriptæ dici poterant, nō vero scriptæ illis, à Paulo ad illos date, immediatè scilicet & directè. Atque hactenus primum argumentum ἄτεχνον [?], pressum idcirco à nobis fusiùs & accuratiùs excussum, quod vim illius longè maximam, eruditi vel neglexerint, vel nondum satis in aprico collocarint. Unum adhuc & alterum forte argumentum suppeditabunt quæ porrò Petrus subjun-git; futuri tamen sumus in urgendis iis minùs operosi, & ad alias exinde argu-mentorum classes progressuri.
units.tr: 1. Because he had said elsewhere as Paul wrote, indefinitely, not as he wrote to you, pointedly and with emphasis. 2. Because he distinguishes that letter entirely from all the others, ὡς ἡ ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς [as in all the letters], and so on. 3. Because he refers to one of the Pauline letters in which this very subject is treated more specifically, and Paul expounds it expressly, which the following argument will show was done above all in the Epistle to the Hebrews. 4. Because the purpose of writing is confused with the object: to write for the use of the whole Church, and therefore of all the particular churches, is one thing; to write to those churches themselves is another; to write to someone immediately and directly, as the Apostle's words sound, is another still, and to write only mediately and indirectly is another. Thus the letters to the Romans, Corinthians and so on could be said to have been written for the use of those Hebrews, as of all Christians, but not written to them, given by Paul to them, that is, immediately and directly. So far, then, the first argument, which I have pursued more fully and carefully because scholars have either neglected its very great force or not yet set it sufficiently in clear view. The further words that Peter adds will supply one or perhaps another argument; I shall not labour much over pressing them, and shall pass on from there to other classes of arguments.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Secundum argumentum à testimonio Petri. Affinitas argumenti inter Petri posteriorem & Epistolam ad Hebræos. Sigillatim expenditur. Occurritur Exceptionibus. Conferuntur & illustrantur nonnulla quædam loca utriusque Epistolæ.
units.tr: The second argument, from the testimony of Peter. The affinity between the second Epistle of Peter and the Epistle to the Hebrews. This is examined in detail. The objections are met. Some passages of both Epistles are compared and illustrated.

units.la: I. Hactenus primum argumentum in-artificiale, ex loco 2. Pet. iii. 15. quo Petrus cum Hebræis agens, testabatur Epistolam ad eosdem à Paulo fuisse perscriptam. Hoc argumento fusiùs excusso, & ab omnibus undequaquè exceptionibus vindicato, protinus alterum succedit, ex eodem quidem loco: dum Petrus affirmat, in illâ suâ Pauli Epistolâ, eodem, quo ipse, scrip-sisse de argumento. Καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς Παῦλος κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ σοφίαν ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν &c. λαλῶν ὡς ἐν πάσαις ἐπιστολαῖς περὶ τέτων. Sumimus autem pro confessis, quæ in superioribus tantùm non demonstrata, & Petro rem esse cum Hebræis, & meminisse Paulinæ ad eosdem Hebræos datæ, & vix aliam esse posse quàm quæ dubia hodie & controversa. Quo jacto veluti fundamento & totius causæ fulcro, anquirendum porrò an eidem Epistolæ quadrent quæ Petrus subjunxit. Et quidem primò an aliqua intercedat affinitas argumenti inter Petri posteriorem, & nostram ad Hebræos, hæcque de iisdem cum Petrina præscripserit? Quod si probatum fuerit, & evidenter atque aperte demonstratum, res sanè confecta, & nodus omnis solutus esse videbitur.
units.tr: I. So far the first argument, the inartificial one, has been drawn from 2 Peter 3:15, where Peter, writing to the Hebrews, testifies that Paul had written an Epistle to the same people. That argument has been examined at length and defended against every objection. A second argument follows at once from the same passage, in which Peter affirms that in that Epistle of Paul's he wrote on the same subject, as he himself did: "Even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, speaking of these things as in all his epistles" [Καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς Παῦλος κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ σοφίαν ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν &c. λαλῶν ὡς ἐν πάσαις ἐπιστολαῖς περὶ τούτων]. We take as granted what the earlier discussion has shown, if not fully demonstrated: that Peter had to do with the Hebrews, that he remembered Paul's Epistle written to those same Hebrews, and that this can hardly be any other than the one that is doubtful and disputed today. With this laid as the foundation and the prop of the whole cause, we must next inquire whether what Peter adds fits the same Epistle. And first, whether there is some affinity of argument between Peter's later Epistle and ours to the Hebrews, and whether the latter deals with the same matters as Peter's. If this is proved and clearly and openly demonstrated, the matter will seem finished and every knot untied.

units.la: II. Verba sunt Petri, Καθὼς, sicut Paulus scripsit vobis, λαλῶν περὶ τούτων, de iis agens, quemadmodum & in Epistolarum reliquis. Ergò respicit primò ad hortationem immediatè præcedentem, superiorum summam quandam & ἀναγκαῖα [?] Φαλαίωσιν hisce verbis expressam; Διὸ, ἀγαπητοὶ, ταῦτα προσδοκῶντες, σπουδάσατε ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἀμώμητοι αὐτῷ εὑρεθῆναι ἐν εἰρήνῃ. Καὶ τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν μακροθυμίαν, σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε, καθὼς &c. Ubi geminum potissimùm ὑπομνήσεως [?] membrum, 1. studeant sanctimoniæ, servent quantùm potè vitæ modum inculpatæ. 11. constanter expectent diè illū Domini, patientiam Dei in illo prorogando sibi salutarem arbitrentur. Quae quidem παραί-νεσις in Epistolâ Paulinâ duplici ratione expressa esse potuit, vel ῥητῶς vel ἀναλόγως, vel κατὰ τὴν λέξιν vel κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν, vel ἐξ τὸ χρῆμα[?] vel κατὰ τὸ πρᾶγμα. Posteriori saltem sensu exhiberi docebit σύγκρισις[?] & αὐτοψία.
units.tr: II. Peter's words are: "as Paul wrote to you, speaking of these things" [Καθὼς ... λαλῶν περὶ τούτων], "as also in his other Epistles." So he refers first to the exhortation immediately preceding, a kind of summary of what has gone before, expressed in these words: "Therefore, beloved, seeing that you look for these things, be diligent that you may be found by him without spot and blameless, in peace. And account the longsuffering of our Lord as salvation, even as &c." [Διὸ, ἀγαπητοὶ, ταῦτα προσδοκῶντες, σπουδάσατε ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἀμώμητοι αὐτῷ εὑρεθῆναι ἐν εἰρήνῃ. Καὶ τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν μακροθυμίαν, σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε, καθὼς &c.] Here there are two main parts of the admonition: first, that they should strive for holiness and keep, as far as possible, a blameless manner of life; second, that they should wait steadily for the day of the Lord, and consider God's patience in deferring that day to be salutary for them. This exhortation could have been expressed in Paul's Epistle in two ways: either explicitly or by analogy, either according to the wording or according to the sense, either in words or in substance. The latter sense, at least, will be shown by comparison and by direct observation.

units.la: III. Prius membrum hortationis, dent scil: fideles operam vitae sanctae & defaecatae, interea dum adventat extrema illa dies, persequitur author Epistolae ad Hebraeos Cap. x. jam inde à versu 19. & sequentibus. Ubi i. eadem hortatio, & quos Petrus vult esse ἀσπίλους ἢ ἀμεμπτους, Paulus eosdem Hebraeos esse ἀληθινὺς seu καθαρὰς τῇ καρδίᾳ, praeterea ῥεραντισμένους τὰς καρδίας ἀπὸ συνειδήσεως πονηρᾶς, i. e. ἀμωμήτους, ἀσπίλους, ab omni labe & maculâ defaecatos; meminisse tandem se λελουμένους τὸ σῶμα ὕδατι καθαρῷ, seu καθαρίζοντι, atque adeo ad puritatem & innocentiam obstringi, vers. 22. 23. Quae ipsa cum alibi passim, tum Cap. xii. & xiii. specialius & prolixius exequitur. ii. idem utriusque scopus, p[?]us, Hebræos roborare in fide & pietate, à seductione, lapsu & mundi inquinamentis præstare immunes. iii. Eadem motiva, non tardaturum Dominum, appropinquare illius adventum, nec aliter quàm pro ipsorum salute prorogari. Hebr. x. 25.37. 2.Pet. iii. 9.10.11.12.13. Posterius vero membrum Petrinæ hortationis, scil. constanter novissimam illam diem expectent, nec morari Deum sed ipsorum & electorum omnium bono patientia nonnihil uti arbitrentur, exponit idem author Epist. ad Hebræos Cap. x. v. 36. 37. & Cap. vi. 12. &c. Utrobique i. eadem commonefactio ad εὐδοκίαν[?], sive ὑπομονὴν[?], sive μακροθυμίαν[?], & quidem circa adventum Domini non ita protrahendum. ii. Idem etiam scopus, Hebræos erigere spe retributionis & beati illius adventus, eorumque animos contra diffidentiam defectionemque præmunire. Quæ si ita habeant, nostra stabit assertio.
units.tr: III. The first part of the exhortation, that the faithful should devote their effort to a holy and purified life while that final day approaches, the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews pursues in chapter 10 from verse 19 onwards. Here (i) it is the same exhortation. Where Peter wants them to be "spotless and blameless," Paul calls the same Hebrews "true" or "pure in heart," and also "sprinkled in their hearts from an evil conscience," that is, "unblemished and spotless, cleansed from every stain and defilement"; and finally he reminds them that their bodies have been "washed with pure water," or "cleansing" water, and so are bound to purity and innocence (vv. 22, 23). He works this out more fully and at length, both here and elsewhere, especially in chapters 12 and 13. (ii) The aim of both is the same: to strengthen the Hebrews in faith and piety, and to keep them free from seduction, falling away and the pollutions of the world. (iii) The same motives are given: the Lord will not delay, his coming is near, and it is deferred only for their salvation. Heb. 10:25, 37; 2 Pet. 3:9, 10, 11, 12, 13. The second part of Peter's exhortation, namely that they should wait steadfastly for the last day, and should consider that God is not delaying but using patience for the good of themselves and of all the elect, is set out by the same author of the Epistle to the Hebrews in chapter 10, verses 36, 37, and chapter 6, verse 12, etc. In both places (i) there is the same reminder to endurance, or patience, or longsuffering [εὐδοκίαν, ὑπομονὴν, μακροθυμίαν], and that not to be drawn out with regard to the coming of the Lord. (ii) The same aim also: to raise the Hebrews up with hope of reward and of that blessed coming, and to fortify their minds against distrust and defection. If these things stand as stated, our assertion stands.

units.la: IV. Nonnulla tamen excipi posse videntur[?]. Alia plane esse utriusque scriptoris verba, phrasim aliam. Scopum etiam quaquadantenus diversum ; Petri quidem suos obfirmare contra πλάνας, ἐμπαίκτας, &c contemptores novissimorum temporum, nostrae vero Authoris Epistolae, Hebraeos erigere & solari medios inter afflictionum ignes, & componere impatientes & diffi-dentes animos. II. Luculentius Paulum & expressius alibi urgere utrumque hor-tationis membrum, imprimis εἶναι ἀσπίλ-λους, ἀμωμήτους, ἀνεγκλήτους, ἀνεπιλήπ-τους, ἀμέμ-πτους, ἁγίους, καθαρὰς τῇ καρδίᾳ, τῇ συνειδήσει &c. III. Illa etiam Petri verba τὴν μακροθυμίαν τῶν [?] σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε, & quae habet v.9. hu-jusce capitis, respicere ad locum Rom. 11. 4. ubi pariter [?]τῆς τῆς μακροθυμίας, & hanc ἄγειν εἰς μετάνοιαν.
units.tr: IV. Yet some objections may seem to arise. The words of the two writers are plainly different, and so is the phrasing. The aim, too, is somewhat different: Peter's is to confirm his readers against deceivers, scoffers, and those who despise the last times, whereas the aim of our author's Epistle is to raise up and console the Hebrews in the midst of the fires of affliction, and to calm their impatient and distrustful minds. (ii) Paul, elsewhere, presses both parts of the exhortation more clearly and more expressly, above all to be spotless, unblemished, irreproachable, blameless, faultless, holy, pure in heart, in conscience, etc. (iii) Peter's words "account the longsuffering of our Lord as salvation", and what he says in verse 9 of this chapter, should be referred to Romans 2:4, where likewise there is the riches of his longsuffering, and it is said to lead to repentance.

units.la: V. Ad primam respondemus instan-tiam, 1. peccari falsâ hypothesi, quasi haec totidem verbis à Paulo perscripta esse debuerint. Quod nec intendit Petrus nec affirmat. Agit de identitate rei non verborum, de convenientia argumenti non phraseos, materia adeo non forma. Constat 1. ex verbis καθὼς ἔγραψεν. Atqui sexcentis in locis Novi Testamenti, κατὰ τὰς [illegible, ~3 letters] [?]φη, καθὼς γέγραπται, respicit id quod scrip-ptū alibi dianoëticè & quoad sensum tan-tùm. ii.ex verbis λαλῶν περὶ τότων i.e. eodē de argumento, quod non idè ac si dixisset λαλῶν οὕτως, vel λαλῶν τύπος. iii. ex eo, quod hæc ipsa in omnibus Paulinis scripta esse memorat; Atqui frustra totidem verbis in iisdem reperiri arbitreris. iv. Quia de convenientia scriptionis, ex identitate mate-riæ & scopi, nó verborum dijudicandum. v. quia Petrus id scriptū dicit simpliciter, non quomodo scriptū, & quibus verbis, ré affirmat nó modum rei. Diversimode autē rem eandem exprimi quid vetat? Respon-demus ii. peccari elencho oppositorū & divisionis, dū opponitur & dividitur scopus utriusq; scriptoris, qui reverà non disjun-gi sed conjungi, subordinari debet nó co-ordinari, ut ex ante dictis liquet. Et mu-niuntur Hebræi ab utroque adversus seductionem, impatientiam, diffidentiā.
units.tr: V. To the first objection we reply: (1) it errs by a false hypothesis, as if these things had to have been written by Paul in exactly these words. Peter neither intends nor asserts this. He speaks of the identity of the matter, not of the words; of the agreement of the argument, not of the phrasing; of the material and not the form. This is clear (i) from the words "as he wrote" [καθὼς ἔγραψεν]. But in countless places of the New Testament, "as it is written" [καθὼς γέγραπται] refers to what was written elsewhere in sense and only as to meaning. (ii) From the words "speaking of these things," that is, on the same subject, which is not the same as saying "speaking thus" or "speaking in this manner." (iii) From the fact that he says these very things are written in all Paul's Epistles; but it would be vain to expect them to be found in the same words in all of them. (iv) Because the agreement of the writing is to be judged from the identity of matter and aim, not of words. (v) Because Peter says simply that it was written, not how it was written or in what words; he affirms the fact, not the manner of it. And what prevents the same thing from being expressed in different ways? We reply also: (2) it errs by an elenchus of opposites and division, in that the aim of the one writer is set over against and divided from the aim of the other, whereas in truth they should not be disjoined but joined, subordinated and not co-ordinated, as is clear from what was said before. And the Hebrews are fortified by both against seduction, impatience and distrust.

units.la: VI. Secundam, quod attinet, instantiā, 1. peccatur paralogismo ἀγνοίας ἐλέγχου; nec negamus, eadem in aliis Pauli Epistolis, & si verba spectamus, forte expressius repeti-imò affirmat Petrus, ὡς [?]ἐν πάσαις ἐπιστολαῖς. Sufficit itaque nihil horum in altera illa ad Hebræos prætermissum, eademque clarè & distinctè, ἐμφύτως[?] non παρεισάκτως[?] contineri. II. supponitur falsò in aliis epistolis contineri luculentius, quia fortè major, verborum quorundam affinitas; at non certè disertius, non evidentius, ut ex collatione superius instituta. III. Falsa etiam est hypothesis alibi non tantùm idem affirmari, sed ad eosdem Hebræos, eodem fine & scopo, quod hic imprimis attendendum. IV. Quin nonnulla à Petro in hac suâ posteriori inserta, muniendis itidem contra defectionem Hebræis, ut jamjam demonstrandum fuerit, quæ nullibi Paulus præterquàm in Epistolâ ad Hebræos.
units.tr: VI. As to the second objection: (1) it errs by the paralogism of ignoratio elenchi (missing the point). Nor do we deny that the same things are repeated more expressly in Paul's other Epistles, if we look only at the words; indeed Peter affirms it, "as in all his epistles." It is enough that nothing of these is omitted in that other Epistle to the Hebrews, and that they are contained there clearly and distinctly, inherently and not incidentally. (II) It is falsely supposed that these are contained more clearly in the other Epistles, because perhaps there is a greater affinity of certain words; but certainly not more eloquently or more evidently, as the comparison made above shows. (III) The hypothesis is also false that the same is affirmed elsewhere not only as the same thing, but as addressed to the same Hebrews, with the same end and aim, which is especially to be noted here. (IV) Indeed, some things that Peter inserts in this later passage, for fortifying the Hebrews likewise against defection, as will be shown presently, are found nowhere in Paul except in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: VII. Tertia exceptio petit ipsum τὸ ὃν[?] ἀρχῆ[?]: nempe hisce Petrum verbis, τὴν μακροθυμίαν[?] τοῦ Ἰησοῦ σωτηρίαν[?] ἡγεῖσθε[?], & v.9. μακροθυμεῖ[?] εἰς ἡμᾶς, μὴ βουλόμενός[?] τινας ἀπολέσθαι, ἀλλὰ πάντας εἰς μετάνοιαν[?] χωρῆσαι[?], reflectere ad locum Rom.11.4. Non nescimus sentire ita Interpretes varios, cumprimis Veteres. Frustrà tamen illos esse demonstramus, I. Quia Petrus respicit ad Epistolo-
units.tr: VII. The third objection calls into question the very point at issue: namely, that by the words "account the longsuffering of our Lord as salvation," and in verse 9, "he is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance," Peter refers back to Romans 11:4. We are not unaware that various interpreters, especially the ancient ones, think so. Yet we show that they are wrong in this, first, because Peter is referring to the Epistle addressed by Paul to the Hebrews; but the Epistle to the Romans was written to a Church made up for the most part of Gentiles, and although some Jews were in it, others were among those whom Peter addresses. (II) Because in that very passage, Romans 2:4, the Gentiles are addressed as such, formally, as men...

units.la: sium à Paulo Hebræis inscriptum; Episto-la verò ad Romanos scripta Ecclesiæ ma-xima parte ex Gentilibus constitutæ, & si quidam in illâ Judæi, alij fuêre ab iis qui Petro compellantur. ii. Quia illo ipso lo-co Rom.ii.4. conveniuntur Gentiles for-maliter tales, homines impij & flagitiosi, quos ad spretæ illius providentiæ tribu-nal citat Apostolus. Constat ex nexu se-cundi & primi capitis, ac serie orationis.
units.tr: …sium written by Paul and addressed to the Hebrews. The Epistle to the Romans, however, was written to a Church made up for the most part of Gentiles, and if some Jews were in it, others were among those whom Peter addresses. (ii) Because in that same passage, Rom. ii.4, the Gentiles addressed are, in form, such people: impious and shameless men, whom the Apostle summons before the tribunal of the providence they had despised. This is clear from the connection of the second and first chapters and from the sequence of the argument.

units.la: Cum Judæis verò demùm infrà Paulus congressurus. At Petro res cum Christia-nis, cum fidelibus, quos vocat ἀγαπη-τὰς postremo hoc capite versu i.& 8. qui-busque tribuit ἐιλικρινῆ [?] διάνοιαν, ut jam antè observatum Theologis. iii. Paulus agit de μακροθυμίᾳ seu longanimitate Dei erga reprobos, in eorum flagitiis & scele-ribus tolerandis; Petrus de μακροθυμίᾳ Dei seu patientiâ circa Ecclesiam, circa electos (εἰς ἡμᾶς, vel ὑμᾶς ut Vulgatus) in differendo nonnihil suo adventu, & pro-missionibus adimplendis, usque dum resi-puerint omnes. iv. Illius scopus argue-re Gentiles αὐτοκατακρισίας & ἀναπολογησίας; Hujus fideles ad patientem ex-pectapoenitentiam ultimorum temporum excitare. v. Ille, Gentiles Dei longanimitate & tolerantia, invitari, provocari ad sanio-rem mentem & resipiscentiam; Hic, fideles qualemcunque Dei moram ac dilatio-nem adventus, debere [σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθαι?]: in electorum bonum salutemq; interpreta-ri, dum iis omnibus resipiscentiæ spatium tempusque concedit. vi. Ille vocem [μετα-νοίας?] latius (vel ringente nupero quodâ, sed lævo, & mordaci, & cujus inanem factum alibi retundimus, Apologistâ) pro resipiscentiâ externâ & morali, per abruptum scelerum ac facinorum filum, qualis in Ethnicis, ex solo divinæ longanimitatis sensu, in statu destituto, exoriri potuit; Hic strictius, pro resipiscentiâ interna & salutari, in electis omnibus, Dominicum ante adventum, promovenda. Adeoque nemo non intelligit, diversissimam hactenus esse loci utriusque rationem, affinitatem longè maximam Petrum inter & Authorem Epistolæ ad Hebræos, ubi identitas & argumenti & scopi & personarum quas uterque compellat.
units.tr: Paul will engage with the Jews only later on. But Peter's business is with Christians, with the faithful, whom in the last chapter, verses 1 and 8, he calls beloved [ἀγαπητοί], and to whom he attributes a sincere disposition [ἐιλικρινῆ διάνοιαν], as the theologians have already observed. (iii) Paul deals with the longanimity [μακροθυμία] or long-suffering of God towards the reprobate, in tolerating their wickedness and crimes; Peter deals with the longanimity, that is, the patience, of God towards the Church and the elect (εἰς ἡμᾶς, or ὑμᾶς in the Vulgate), in somewhat delaying his coming and the fulfilment of his promises, until all have come to repentance. (iv) The aim of the former is to convict the Gentiles of self-condemnation [αὐτοκατακρισίας] and want of excuse [ἀναπολογησίας]; the aim of the latter is to rouse the faithful to await patiently the repentance of the last times. (v) The one invites and provokes the Gentiles, through the longanimity and tolerance of God, to a saner mind and to repentance; the other tells the faithful that whatever delay and postponement of his coming God makes must be taken as salvation [σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθαι?], that is, interpreted for the good and salvation of the elect, since he grants all of them a space and time for repentance. (vi) The former uses the word [μετάνοια?] more broadly, for an external and moral repentance, arising in the Gentiles from the mere sense of divine longanimity while they were in a destitute state, as the thread of their crimes and wickedness is broken off; this is the sense of the word in the mouth of that rather unlearned, but bitter and biting, apologist (whose empty effort I refute elsewhere). The latter uses it more strictly, for an internal and saving repentance, to be promoted in all the elect before the Lord's coming. Hence no one fails to see that the two passages are treated in quite different ways, and that Peter and the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews have the closest affinity, where there is identity of argument, aim and persons addressed by each.

units.la: VIII. Sed Petrus ita primò hortatio-nem immediatè antecedentem respicit, ut secundò etiam alia quæ hac in Epistola præcesserant, quæque itidem à Paulo Hebræos accepisse refert. Intelligimus ex verbis, λαλῶν περὶ τούτων [?], indefinitè de hisce agens, de hac meâ doctrinâ, de causâ hac totâ vobis jam à me expositâ. Et sanè gemina non pauca & similis argumenti notare licet in utraque Epistolâ. Et quæ Petrus jam inde ab exordio, de beneficiis Dei in Christo, de fructibus hinc oriun-dis, speciatim de constantiâ & perseveran-tiâ in fide & vocatione, Paulus ex professo tradit Hebræis Capitibus iii. vi. x. xi. xii. xiii. & toto passim epistolio. Verùm enim verò ne in ipso limine fastidiû pro-lixitate excitemus, unum instar omnium fuerit, quod habet uterq; de periculo ma-néte lapsos & deficientes ab agnita semel veritate, 2. Pet. Cap. ii. v. 20. 21. 22. Heb. vi. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. Cap. x. 26. 27. 28. 29. 30. 31. Summa hic sanè & singularis quædâ doctrinæ conformitas, imò tanta in argumento difficili & intricato, ut nuspiam major, utq; dubium controversiq; esse non possit, quin Petrus hæc ipsa' loca in memoriam revocare He-bræis, suamque hoc firmare doctrinam auctoramento, constitutum habuerit.
units.tr: VIII. But Peter, first, looks back to the exhortation immediately preceding, and, second, also to the other things that had gone before in this Epistle, which he likewise says Paul had delivered to the Hebrews. We understand from the words, λαλῶν περὶ τούτων [speaking about these things], that he speaks indefinitely about these matters, about this my teaching, about this whole cause already set out before you by me. And indeed one may note not a few parallel points of a similar kind in both Epistles. What Peter from the very beginning sets out, about God's benefits in Christ, and the fruits arising from them, and specifically about constancy and perseverance in faith and calling, Paul expressly delivers to the Hebrews in chapters iii, vi, x, xi, xii and xiii, and throughout the Epistle. But, to avoid wearying the reader with prolixity right at the threshold, let one example stand for all: the danger both writers state for those who have fallen away and who fail after having once known the truth: 2 Pet. ii.20, 21, 22; Heb. vi.4–8; x.26–31. Here there is surely a considerable and singular conformity of doctrine, indeed so great in such a difficult and intricate matter, and nowhere greater, that there can be no doubt, nor any dispute, that Peter had it in mind to recall these very passages to the Hebrews and to confirm his teaching by their authority.

units.la: IX. Utrobique 1. idem ferè verborum nexus. Paulus Hebr.x. in antecessis egerat de quibusdam Apostatis qui sensim se subducendo à publicis Christianorum coetibus, à Christo deficiebant, fidemque Christianam ejurabant. Petrus itidem, de Apostatis qui inescari se ac seducì temerè & incautè patiebantur. 11. Idem utrobique subjectum, & quibus Petrus tribuit ἐπίγνωσιν τῶ Κυρίου, ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ὁδῶ τῆς δικαιοσύνης, Paulus ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ἀληθείας, Hebr.x. & φωτισμὸν Hebr.vi. cognitionem saltem theoreticam, convictivam; illumi-nationem partialem, inchoatam, secun-dùm alios sacramentalem, seu baptisma-lem. Quos Petrus dicit etiá ἀποφυγόντας τὰ μιάσματα τοῦ κόσμου, si non ex affectu inter-no, saltem externâ professione, si non ve-râ conversione, putativâ saltem & apparenti; Paulo Hebr.x. dicuntur ἡγιασθῆναι ἐν τῷ αἵματι τῆς διαθήκης, sanctificati pariter externè & comparatè, seu segregati ab in-fidefidelibus, & à mundi inquinamentis, sanctificati sacramentaliter, per aquam baptismi, repræsentativam sanguinis Novi Fœderis, extrinsecùs abluti; sanctificati etiam inchoatè, quoad aliqualem cordis motum & communia charismata spiritus S. Eidem Hebr. vi. dicuntur γευσαμένους τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπουρανίου [?], gustu sanè oris magis quàm cordis, labiorum quàm animi, theoretico magis quàm practico; καὶ μέτοχοι γενηθέντες πνεύματος ἁγίου [?], participatione quâdam communi, temporariâ, initiali, qualis & in Saule, Juda, Simone Mago; καλὸν γευσαμένους θεοῦ ῥῆμα, δυνάμεις τε μέλλον-τος αἰῶνος [?], scilicet cognitione quâdam theoreticâ assecuti, & quàm salutaris sit E-vangelij doctrina, & quàm eminens gloria-futuri seculi. III. Utrobique ejusdem criminis, sceleratæ defectionis, & totalis apostasiæ rei supponuntur: Petrus, si iidem illi qui effugerunt mundi inquinamenta, τίνες πάλιν ἐμπλακέντες ἡττῶνται [?], iisdem se rursus implicari, & à maleseriatis hominibus perverti sinant ac superari; Paulus Hebr. x. Si post acceptam cognitionem veriveritatis &c. [illegible, ~12 letters] facto nos defectionis voluntaria crimine obstrin-gamus, Filium DEI conculcemus &c. idem Hebr. vi. Illi qui semel illuminati &c. τοὺς παραπίπτοντας[?] si prolabantur, si in peccata sua & apostasiam totalem & voluntariam recidant. IV. Utrobique eadem illis poena, idem exitium denunciatur, Petrus γεγονέναι αὐτοῖς τὸ ἔσχατον χείρονα τῶν πρώτων[?], κρεῖττον αὐτοῖς μὴ ἐπεγνωκέναι[?] &c. illis fuisse satius nunquàm nosse viam veritatis, dum isti ignorantiae accessit defectio, contumacia, rebellio: similiter Paulus Heb. x. οὐκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία[?], non hostiam, non sacrificium esse reliquum, nec in Christo, quae hostia nihil contumacibus, nihil incredulis, nihil impoenitentibus prosit, nec extra Christum; adeo-que ubi non hostia, ibi nec expiatio, ubi non expiatio, ibi reatus, ubi reatus, ibi ira, ubi ira, ibi horrenda expectatio judicij, &c. Idem Heb. vi. ἀδύνατον πάλιν ἀνακαινί-ζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν, impossibile esse & ipsismet renovare sese per poenitentiam, & Do-ctoribus eosdem renovare, imo impossi-bile [?]bile DEO, per justitiam tantæ ultricem contumaciæ, quâ Christum ἑαυτοῖς ἀναστανρ-ζοῦντες[?], denuò velut cruci & ignominiæ sibi seu in perniciem suam exponunt; adeoque ut Petrus, conditionem eorum ultimam priori esse deteriorem. V. Utrobique hæc doctrina, subjecto simili, per ὑπόδειγμα[?] τῆς παροιμίας illustratur; Petro, simili canis ad vomitum, & suis lotæ ad volutabrum redeuntis; Paulo, terræ quæ post effusos imbres nihil nisi spinas profert & tribulos, & exustioni tandem destinatur. VI. Utrobique scopus idem, & uterque intendit Apostolus, Hebræorum præcavere apostasiam, gliscentem jam & multorum animos occupantem. 2.
units.tr: IX. In both (1) almost the same connection of words. Paul in Heb. x had earlier spoken of certain apostates who, by gradually withdrawing from the public assemblies of Christians, were falling away from Christ and renouncing the Christian faith. Peter likewise speaks of apostates who allowed themselves to be enticed and led astray rashly and carelessly. (2) In both the subject is the same. Peter attributes to them knowledge of the Lord [ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ Κυρίου] and knowledge of the way of righteousness [ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ὁδοῦ τῆς δικαιοσύνης]; Paul, knowledge of the truth [ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ἀληθείας], Heb. x, and illumination [φωτισμόν], Heb. vi: at least a theoretical, convincing knowledge; a partial, inchoate illumination, according to others sacramental, or baptismal. Peter says of them also that they have escaped the pollutions of the world [ἀποφυγόντας τὰ μιάσματα τοῦ κόσμου], if not from inner affection, at least by outward profession, and if not by true conversion, at least by a supposed and apparent one. In Paul, Heb. x, they are said to have been sanctified in the blood of the covenant [ἡγιασθῆναι ἐν τῷ αἵματι τῆς διαθήκης], sanctified equally outwardly and comparatively, that is, set apart from unbelievers and from the defilements of the world, sanctified sacramentally, by the water of baptism, which represents the blood of the New Covenant, and washed externally; sanctified also inchoately, as to a certain movement of the heart and the common gifts of the Holy Spirit. In the same Heb. vi they are said to have tasted the heavenly gift [γευσαμένους τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπουρανίου], surely a taste of the mouth rather than of the heart, of the lips rather than the soul, theoretical rather than practical; and to have become partakers of the Holy Spirit [μέτοχοι γενηθέντες πνεύματος ἁγίου], by a certain common, temporary, initial participation, such as was also in Saul, Judas and Simon Magus; and to have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come [καλὸν γευσαμένους θεοῦ ῥῆμα, δυνάμεις τε μέλλοντος αἰῶνος], that is, to have attained by a certain theoretical knowledge both how salutary the doctrine of the Gospel is and how eminent is the glory of the coming age. (3) In both they are held guilty of the same crime, of wicked defection and total apostasy: Peter, if those same persons who have escaped the pollutions of the world are again entangled and overcome [τίνες πάλιν ἐμπλακέντες ἡττῶνται], if they let themselves be entangled again and be perverted and overcome by ill-bred men; Paul, Heb. x: If, after receiving the knowledge of the truth etc. [illegible in the scan], we bind ourselves by the voluntary crime of defection, we trample underfoot the Son of God, etc. Likewise Heb. vi: those who were once illuminated etc., [τοὺς παραπίπτοντας], if they fall away, if they relapse into their sins and total and voluntary apostasy. (4) In both the same punishment and the same ruin is announced to them. Peter: the last state has become worse for them than the first [γεγονέναι αὐτοῖς τὸ ἔσχατον χείρονα τῶν πρώτων], it would have been better for them not to have known [κρεῖττον αὐτοῖς μὴ ἐπεγνωκέναι] etc., that it would have been more fitting for them never to have known the way of truth, since to that ignorance there has been added defection, obstinacy and rebellion. Similarly Paul, Heb. x: there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins [οὐκέτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία]: no victim, no sacrifice remains, neither in Christ, a victim which profits nothing to the obstinate, nothing to the unbelieving, nothing to the impenitent, nor outside Christ; so that where there is no victim, there is no expiation; where there is no expiation, there is guilt; where there is guilt, there is wrath; where there is wrath, there is a dreadful expectation of judgement, etc. The same in Heb. vi: it is impossible to renew them again to repentance [ἀδύνατον πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν]: it is impossible for them to renew themselves by repentance, and for teachers to renew them; indeed it is impossible even for God, by justice that avenges such obstinacy, since by crucifying Christ again for themselves [ἑαυτοῖς ἀνασταυροῦντες] they expose him afresh, as it were, to the cross and to shame, that is, to their own destruction; so that, as Peter says, their last condition is worse than the first. (5) In both this teaching is illustrated, with a similar subject, by an example from a proverb [ὑπόδειγμα τῆς παροιμίας]: in Peter, by the likeness of a dog returning to its vomit, and of a sow washed and returning to the wallow; in Paul, by the earth which, after heavy rains, produces nothing but thorns and thistles, and is at last destined for burning. (6) In both the aim is the same, and each Apostle intends to guard the Hebrews against apostasy, which was already spreading and taking hold of the minds of many. 2 Pet. ii.14; Heb. x.25, 26; Heb. vi.6.

units.la: Pet. II. 14. Hebr. x. 25. 26. Hebr. vi. 6.
units.tr: 2 Pet. ii.14; Heb. x.25, 26; Heb. vi.6.

units.la: X. Hæc pressiùs, ut intelligatur non sinè causâ Petrum ad testem Paulum, in eodem & singulari quidem argumento, & ad ejusdem tenoris loca provocasse. Nec quis excipiat Petrum adea reflectere, de quibus in omnibus reliquis Paulinis, ὡς ἐν πάσαις ἐπιστολαῖς λαλῶν περὶ τούτων[?]; nusquam tamen in illis extare gemina cum locis suprà discussis, quare aliò respexisse. Atqui I. loquitur ἀορίστως[?] & indefinitè, Paulum de hisce, aliquibus nempè aut plerisque hujusce Epistolæ capitibus, etiam in omnibus sparsim ac distributim Epistolis, tradere ac disputare. II. τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ non exponi in Paulinis aliis hanc de apostatarum exitio atque interitu doctrinam, implicitè sanè, materialiter, & quoad doctrinæ fundamentum. Quanquam etiam in Epistola ad Hebræos explicite, formaliter, & quoad eundem cum Petro doctrinæ modum, iisdem etiam Hebræis, eádemque scopi affinitate & methodi.
units.tr: X. I press these points more closely so that it may be understood that Peter did not without reason appeal to Paul as witness, in this same and singular argument, and to passages of the same tenor. Nor should anyone object that Peter refers to matters found in all the remaining Pauline letters, as ὡς ἐν πάσαις ἐπιστολαῖς λαλῶν περὶ τούτων [speaking of these things in all his letters]; yet nowhere in those do we find twin passages to those discussed above, so he must have had something else in view. But (I) he speaks ἀορίστως, indefinitely, of Paul's delivering and disputing these matters, that is, some or most of the chapters of this Epistle, and also of what is scattered and distributed throughout all his Epistles. (II) The phrase τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ [what is in the beginning] does not mean that this doctrine of the destruction and ruin of apostates is set out in Paul's other letters, implicitly indeed, materially, and as to the foundation of the doctrine. Though it is also set out in the Epistle to the Hebrews explicitly, formally, and in the same manner of teaching as Peter's, to the same Hebrews, with the same affinity of aim and method.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Tertium argumentum ex eodem Petro. Sapientia Paulina. Maxime conspicua in Epistolâ ad Hebræos. Demonstratur. Diluuntur exceptiones. Non notari Petro Epistolam ad Galatas.
units.tr: The third argument, from the same Peter. Paul's wisdom, most conspicuous in the Epistle to the Hebrews. This is demonstrated. The exceptions are answered. Peter is not taken to refer to the Epistle to the Galatians.

units.la: 1. Tertium succedit argumentum, expediendum paucis. Ex Petri itidem verbis, scripsisse Hebræis Paulum, non illo tantùm de argumento, sed [illegible, ~9 letters]σὺν[?] αὐτῷ σοφίαν. Quid planius? Vult Pauli-nam illam ad Hebræos spirare ubique sapientiam, cœlestem certè ac reconditam. Quod si & hoc quoque nostra se probet indicio, si in illâ undique effulgeant divinæ sapientiæ radij, si referat Paulinum illum ac sublimem genium, si non repugnet scriptam dici juxta concessas Paulo eximiæ sapientiæ dotes, sat causæ fuerit cur hanc ipsam innui Petro arbitremur. Imprimis ex hypothesibus superius assertis, & post tot alia de hac Petri mente documenta, eademque clarissima. Imò verò Petrus emphaticè, de singulari quadam sapientiâ, de eximio quodam gradu cognitionis, in hac speciatim Epistola elucescente.
units.tr: 1. The third argument follows, and it can be dealt with briefly. From Peter's own words, Paul wrote to the Hebrews not only on that subject but [illegible] with wisdom [σὺν αὐτῷ σοφίαν]. What could be plainer? He means that the Pauline Epistle to the Hebrews breathes wisdom everywhere, heavenly and certainly profound. If our reading is also confirmed by this evidence, if divine rays of wisdom shine out on every side in that Epistle, if it reflects that Pauline and lofty genius, and if it is not inconsistent to say it was written in keeping with the extraordinary gifts of wisdom granted to Paul, there is sufficient reason for thinking Peter alludes to this very thing. This holds especially on the basis of the hypotheses asserted above, and after so many other proofs of Peter's mind on this point, which are equally clear. Indeed Peter emphatically speaks of a singular wisdom and an outstanding degree of knowledge, shining out in this Epistle in particular.

units.la: II. Nihil sanè detractum volumus E-pistolarum reliquis, nihil sapientiæ per immortalia illa diffusæ monimenta. Ubique Paulus altum sapit, ubique sublimis fertur, ubique se Paulum prodit. Merito ὁ σοφώτατος, ὁ πάνσοφος, ὁ θεόπνευστος, communiori elogio, Græcis Patribus. Hic verò ἐξόχως ἢ ἐξαιρέτως[?], & eminenti quodā ratione, constatque I. ex sententiarum expressionumque conspicua ubique majestate. II. ex sublimitate rerum mysteriorumque fastigio, quo jam penetrat εἰς τὸ ἐσώτερον τῆς κατα-πετάσματος Hebr. vi. 19. & in tertium quasi cœlum raptus, testis est functionum Christi, illiusque æterni sacerdotii. III. ex stupenda illa vi ratiociniorum, in conferendis typis & rebus typis illis expressis, Lege & Evangelio, Christo & Mose, sacerdotio Melchisedeciano & Aaronitico, Fœdere veteri & novo, sanctuario mundano & cœlesti, sacrificiis legalibus & Christi sacrificio; in omnibus hisce explicandis, diffundendis, illustrandis, applicandis ad usus theoreticos & practicos. IV. Ex Interpretum omnium ore, ac unanimi veterum recentiorumque consensu, de sublimi Epistolæ argumento.
units.tr: II. We do not at all wish to detract anything from the remaining Epistles, nor from the monuments of wisdom diffused through those immortal writings. Everywhere Paul thinks deeply, everywhere he is carried aloft, everywhere he reveals himself as Paul. The Greek Fathers rightly call him, in the more common praise, "the most wise" [ὁ σοφώτατος], "the all-wise" [ὁ πάνσοφος], "God-inspired" [ὁ θεόπνευστος]. But here he is wise eminently or exceptionally [ἐξόχως ἢ ἐξαιρέτως], and in a certain outstanding manner, and this is evident: I. from the conspicuous majesty of the thoughts and expressions found everywhere; II. from the sublimity of the subjects and the height of the mysteries, by which he now penetrates "within the veil" [εἰς τὸ ἐσώτερον τῆς καταπετάσματος] (Heb. 6:19), and, as if caught up to the third heaven, bears witness to the functions of Christ and his eternal priesthood; III. from the astonishing force of his reasoning, in comparing the types and the things typified by them: Law and Gospel, Christ and Moses, the Melchizedekian and the Aaronic priesthood, the old and the new covenant, the earthly and the heavenly sanctuary, the legal sacrifices and the sacrifice of Christ; in explaining, expounding, illustrating and applying all these to theoretical and practical uses; IV. from the testimony of all the interpreters and the unanimous agreement of the ancients and moderns concerning the sublime subject of the Epistle.

units.la: III. Excipiat aliquis, hæc Petri verba notare Epistolam ad Galatas, in qua Paulus diserte profitetur, scribere se secundum datam sibi cœlitus sapientiam διὰ ἀπο-καλύψεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ Gal. i. 12. Petro hæc vero etiam rem ex parte esse cum Galatis. Respondemus I. τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ [?] hanc designari Epistolam, & quia, ut antè ostensum, scripta uni Galatarum Ecclesiae, & scripta Gentibus non Hebræis, & alius plane argumenti, de modo nempè nostrae justificationis coràm DEO. II. Illatio omninò inconsequens. Paulus juxta Petrum scripsit Hebræis sapientissimâ omninò ratione; Paulus in sua ad Galatas monet se edoctum divinitus, non ordinariè & mediatè ab hominibus, sed extraordinariè ac immediatè à Christo; Ergo Epistola illa ad Hebræos non alia fuerit ab eâ, quae est ad Galatas? Quasi verò Petrus non tam sublimitatem rerum, quàm verba illa de modo revelationis, attendat? Quasi sola ad Galatas, hoc nomine scripta dici debeat κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ σοφίαν [?]? Quasi Paulus in hac tantùm, non in aliis etiam ad Romanos, Corinthios, Thessalonicenses &c. Epistolis, à divinâ illâ & immediatâ origine doctrinam derivet suam? III. Est elenchus à dicto secundùm quid. Nec Paulus simpliciter scripsisse dicitur Petro secundùm datam sibi sapientiam, sed scri-psisse pisse Hebræis, neque Galatis tantùm sed Cappadocibus, sed Bythyniis, sed Ponti-cis, sed Asiaticis, & quidem de tali argu-mento, quale Petrus exequitur, non quale Paulus ad Galatas. Secundò excipi possent, quæ contrà Epistolæ authoritatem motæ partim ἀντιλογίᾳ, partim ἐνισταμέναι, partim ἀπόρως, tantùm abest ut Paulinam illa sapientiam redoleat; Nisi res nobis cum iis qui authorem, non verò authoritatem Epistolæ in dubium vocant, nisi etiam inanissima hæc tela olim hodieque in contorquentium capita Theologi retorsissent, de quibus aliquid in parte ἀνασκευαστικῶς.
units.tr: III. Someone may object that these words of Peter refer to the Epistle to the Galatians, in which Paul plainly declares that he writes according to the wisdom given him from heaven, "through the revelation of Jesus Christ" (Gal. 1:12), and that for Peter these words also apply in part to the Galatians. We reply: I. First, that this Epistle is designated by the phrase about the beginning [τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ]; and because, as shown before, it was written to one congregation of the Galatians, and to Gentiles rather than Hebrews, and is of a plainly different subject, namely the manner of our justification before God. II. The inference is altogether inconsequent. Paul, according to Peter, wrote to the Hebrews in a most wise manner; Paul in his letter to the Galatians says that he was taught by God, not ordinarily and mediately by men, but extraordinarily and immediately by Christ. Therefore that Epistle to the Hebrews would not be different from the one to the Galatians? As if Peter were attending not so much to the sublimity of the matters as to those words about the manner of revelation! As if only the Epistle to the Galatians could rightly be said to be written "according to the wisdom given to him" [κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ σοφίαν] for this reason! As if Paul derived his doctrine from this divine and immediate origin only in this Epistle, and not also in the others, to the Romans, Corinthians, Thessalonians and so on! III. This is the fallacy of the qualified statement [elenchus à dicto secundum quid]. Nor is it said that Paul simply wrote according to the wisdom given him, but that he wrote to the Hebrews, not only to the Galatians but to the Cappadocians, the Bithynians, the Pontics, the Asians; and indeed on such a subject as Peter treats, not the kind Paul treats in the Epistle to the Galatians. Secondly, objections could be raised against the authority of the Epistle, some by contradiction [ἀντιλογίᾳ], some by opposition [ἐνισταμέναι], some by doubt [ἀπόρως], which are so far from breathing the Pauline wisdom. Unless our dispute is with those who call into question the author, not the authority, of the Epistle, and unless the Theologians had already turned back on the heads of those who hurl them these most empty weapons, both formerly and today; of which something will be said in the refutative part [ἀνασκευαστικῶς].

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quartum argumentum à testimonio divino. Paulinarum τὰ δυσνόητα. Respicit Petrus Epistolam ad Hebræos. Probatur. Difficultates illius sigillatim excussa. De interitu Apostatarum. De Melchisedeco. Non expediunt se Interpretes. Sententiarum omnium nodi. De Christi sacerdotio &c. De ἀναλογοφανίαι quibusdam. Centor
units.tr: The fourth argument, from the divine testimony. Paul's hard sayings (τὰ δυσνόητα). Peter has in view the Epistle to the Hebrews. This is proved. Its difficulties are examined one by one. On the perishing of apostates. On Melchizedek. The interpreters do not extricate themselves. The knots of all opinions. On Christ's priesthood, etc. On certain analogies. Concluding.

units.la: Fere omnia ἀπαθῆ[?]ς ἢ ἀσυμφωνίαι[?]. Occurritur exceptioni. Ratio producta ex Petrino loco disputationis.
units.tr: Almost all things are [unclear: impassive or inconsistent]. The objection is met. The argument drawn from the passage of Peter under discussion.

units.la: I. Ultimum tandem exurgit argumentum, & à quo plurimùm mutuatur sententia nostra roboris, ex verbis ejusdem Petri C. III. 16. ἐν οἷς ἐστι δυσνόητά τινα, ἃ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσι. Quibus indigitari ex parte nostra ad Hebraeos ostendimus. I. quia dicit ἐν ᾗς[?], non ἐν αἷς, & respicit non ad Paulinas Epistolas, sed ad Paulina dogmata, nec omnia sed quaedam, & quidem illa ipsa de quibus Hebraeis tradidisse refert. II. quia illa arguit difficultatis, mysterij, esse δυσνόητα[?], δυσπαρακολούθητα[?], δυσερμήνευτα[?]: atqui caetera omnia prae Epistola ad Hebraeos, lux mera. III. quia obnoxia illa dicit strophis, cavillis, falsisque interpretamentis, qualia haec omni aevo cumprimis, nec Petrus historicè tantùm quid tum fieret, sed & prophetice, quid post modum etiam contingeret. IV. quia congruunt authoris verba Hebr. v. 11. multa sibi esse δυσερμήνευτα, & narratu difficilia, talia cùm ex parte rerum, tum ex parte Hebraeorum, ex parte cum objecti tum etiam subjecti.
units.tr: I. At last there arises the final argument, and the one from which our view draws most of its strength: the words of Peter himself, 3:16, "in which there are some things hard to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort" [ἐν οἷς ἐστι δυσνόητά τινα, ἃ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσι]. We have shown that these words point to the Epistle to the Hebrews on our side. (1) Because he says ἐν ᾗς, not ἐν αἷς, and he refers not to Paul's Epistles, but to Paul's dogmas, and not to all of them but to some, and indeed to those very matters about which he says he had written to the Hebrews. (2) Because he calls those things hard to understand, difficult to follow, and hard to interpret [δυσνόητα, δυσπαρακολούθητα, δυσερμήνευτα], whereas everything else in comparison with the Epistle to the Hebrews is pure light. (3) Because he says these things are open to twisting, quibbling and false interpretations, the sort of thing that has always happened, and Peter speaks not only historically, of what was then happening, but also prophetically, of what would later come to pass. (4) Because the author's own words in Hebrews 5:11, that he had many things to say which were hard to interpret and hard to tell, agree with this, and these difficulties arise both from the side of the matters and from the side of the Hebrews, both from the side of the object and also of the subject.

units.la: II. Sed constabit vis argumenti inductione exemplorum in actu exercito; & ad oculum demonstrandum quaenam sint, illa δυσνόητα[?], quae crucem figant, quaeque imperiti & male sani contorqueant. Et, quidem primo notari possunt illa de apostatarum interitu, Hebr. vi. & x. Quae quidem adeo perplexa ut I. Latini veteres Epistolam hoc fere nomine expungendam è Canonicarum censu, & nodum hunc secandum hac ratione censuerint.
units.tr: II. But the force of the argument will be clear if we set out examples of it in actual use, and to show plainly which are those hard sayings that twist the mind and which the unlearned and ill-balanced distort. And first, there may be noted those things about the perishing of apostates, Hebrews 6 and 10. These are so perplexing that the early Latins, for this reason chiefly, judged that the Epistle should be struck from the list of canonical books and that this knot should be cut in that way.

units.la: II. Ut Novatus & Novatiani spem omnem, si non salutis, saltem veniæ in foro externo Ecclesiæ, post Baptismum in peccata prolapsis interdixerint.
units.tr: II. Thus Novatus and the Novatianists denied all hope, if not of salvation then at least of pardon in the external forum of the Church, to those who had fallen into sin after baptism.

units.la: III. Ut Clinici Baptismum nonnisi ἐπὶ κλίνης[?] & animam agentes susciperent, quibus dum se Patres opponunt, urgent necessitatem Sacramenti absolutam & medij.
units.tr: III. Thus the Clinics administered baptism only to those on their sick-bed and at the point of death, and while the Fathers opposed them, they insisted on the absolute and necessary necessity of the sacrament.

units.la: IV. Ut Pelagij nepotes, apostasiam sanctorum to-talem finalemque propugnarint.
units.tr: IV. Thus the followers of Pelagius defended the total and final apostasy of the saints.

units.la: V. Ut iidem Christi mortem universalem etiam pro impiis & apostatis ex utroque loco defenderint.
units.tr: V. Thus the same people defended the universal death of Christ, even for the impious and apostates, from both passages.

units.la: VI. ut Romanenses hinc etiam suum pœnitentiæ Sacramentum & satisf[?] satisfactiones, plusquam Chrysippeo acumine, eruerint, probarintque. VII. Ut quotquot fuêre Interpretes, mirum in modum desudarint in geminihujusce loci cùm ἐξηγήσεις[?], tum ἀνδικώτερα[?].
units.tr: VI. Thus the Romanists have drawn out, and proved, from these passages their sacrament of repentance and their satisfactions with more than Chrysippean subtlety. VII. Thus all who have been interpreters have sweated wonderfully over this twofold passage, both in its explanations and in its more subtle points.

units.la: III. Secundò inter illa reponimus quae habet author de Melchisedeco, ejusque persona & sacerdotio. Nec sanè toto Veteri aut Novo Testamento perplexius quicquam & intricatius. Et benè in hanc rem Hieronymus ad Euagr. Epistol. cxxvi. quae extat Operum Tomo III: Si vas electionis stupet ad mysterium & de quo disputat ineffabile confitetur, quanto magis nos vermiculi & culices, solam debemus scientiam inscientiae confiteri. In quam vis enim partem sese vertant interpretes, vix sese expediunt, δοκὸς δὲ ἐπὶ πᾶσι τέτυκται[?].
units.tr: III. Secondly, we place among those hard things what the author says about Melchizedek, his person and his priesthood. Indeed nothing in the whole of the Old or New Testament is more perplexing and intricate. And Jerome rightly, in his letter to Evagrius, Epistle 126, which is found in Volume III of his Works: "If the vessel of election is astonished at the mystery, and confesses the ineffable thing he is discussing, how much more should we little worms and gnats confess only our ignorance." For whichever way the interpreters turn, they hardly extricate themselves, and "a beam is set across all of them."

units.la: I. Nec solvebant nodum qui olim Mel-chisedeciani, nugantes Melchisedecum θεὸν[?] fuisse δύναμιν[?], Christo majorem, si fides Epiphanio Haeresi LV. Lib. II. Tom. I: Mirifica sanè Virtus, quae & alia à Deo, & Deo major, & humana forma, dignitate regiâ, sacerdotali officio, personalibus aliis insignis. II. Nec rem expedicbant, si-ve Hierax apud eundem Epiphanium Hær. LV. & LXVII. sive ἀνωνύμῳ[?] ille apud Hieronymum Ep. ad Euagr. Melchisede-cum in Spiritum sanctum transforman-tes. Atqui repugnabat Spiritum S. vel fuisse incarnatum, vel egisse sacerdotem, vel imperasse Salemi, vel ditatum mune-ribus, vel Christum expressisse ordine sa-cerdotij, nec fas erat in re tam ardua ex-tra Scripturas sapere. III. Nec felicius Origenes Homil. I. in Genes. & post eum Didymus, Angelum fecere ex Melchisedeco. Quod erat ἄγραφον[?] & ἀντίγραφον[?], quando illi tribuit Moses & humanam dignitatem, & humanum officium, & huma-nas actiones, & sacerdos omnis esse debuit ex hominibus Hebr. v. 1. IV. Non etiam rem satis acu tetigere, qui putarunt fuisse ipsissimum Filium Dei, Abrahamo visum habitu regio & sacerdotali, decimas accipientem, illi benedicentem, benedictione non tam optativâ quàm collativâ, incarnationi praeludentem, Regem Zedek & Salem nominibus appellativis, non propriis, in quem adeò apprimè quadret tota illa oratio Hebr. vii. Hæc quidem sententia latuisse videtur Hieronymum Epistolâ illâ ad Euagrium. Sed respondit novissimè & in eâ multus prolixusque est, Doctiss. Cuneus Lib. iii. de Republ. Hebr. c. iii: imò tacitus in eam propendet, illud Theologorum decus Petrus Molinæus de præcogn. Futur. L. iv. C. xi. xiv. xv. Sed quantis illa urgetur incommodis? Obsecro!an idem fuerit τύπος [?] & τυπωθεὶς [?], figura & figuratus, & quidem secundùm idem, puta sacerdotium? An Christus dicatur sacerdos secundùm ordinem Christi, & Davidi Psal. cx. Tu es sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, i. e. ordinem tuum? Involvisset ne hoc mysterium Apostolus alto silentio? Quî etiam non legitur Abrahamo Dei Filius adoratus, ut Angelus Gen. xviii. Quî non Jehovah, ut ille, dictus? Quî ut Rex peregrinus, ut Sacerdos Dei altissimi historicè descriptus? Quî etiam Christus suam ante ἀνθρώπων [?] fuerit Sacerdos Dei altissimi, & verus quidem Sacerdos, fine quo concidit & his-toria & ratio typi? Qui fuerit Rex Salem, seu τῆς[?] Σολύμα πόλεως? ut Josephus L.1. Anti-tiq. C. xi. Si etiam appellativa hæc nomi-na, cur non dictus מלך צדק & מלך שלום, imò vero Melchizedek, vt Adonizedek, Adonibezek? Cur Rex Salem, vt Rex Se-dom, vocibus ad nominum propriorum formam inflexis? An vero quia Aposto-lus ostendit in his nominibus aliquid ty-pici & significativi, nec sine omine illis fuisse insignitum, eo minus propria sunt? Vt taceam laborare falsa hypothesi, quasi non alia ratione cum Mose conciliari possit Apostolus, quod vt molestum neu-tiquam sanè desperatum. V. Neque diffi-cultatem exhauriunt, qui Melchisedecum eundem cum Semo fuisse contendunt, quales olim Samaritæ[?], Epiphanio teste Hær[?]. LV, quales Hebræi, Hieronymi tem-pore, Ep. ad Euagr; quales Talmudistæ passim, Targum Hierof. & Rabbinorum hodieque doctissimi; quales etiam ex Theologis sive Orthodoxis sive Pontifi-ciis longe plurimi. Risit olim sententiam, & vexavit Epiphanius. Et quanquam in firma sit illius ratio, & vitiosus calculus, à nato Semo ad occursum Melchisedeci, modò annos MCXXX, modò MCXXVII. praeter Codicum Hebraeorum fidem, ingenti μεταχρονισμῷ, supputantis, aliis illi difficultatibus implicantur. Tum quia hæc sententia ex Hebraeorum lacunis hausta, qui & alia incerta de Melchisedeco; tum quia ut alium à Semo sistunt eum nobis sagacissimi Judæorum Josephus ac Philo, tum quia nec reticuisset Moses, nec Apostolus fusior aliâs in describendo Melchisedeco; imò verò quia hic negat Melchisedecum idem cum Levitis duxisse à majoribus genus, Hebr.vii.6. quia cum nominibus plane aliis anteponit Abrahamo, quàm ratione juris illius paterni, & avitæ potestatis; quia facit ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, cùm Semus nulla ratione fuerit talis, nec κατὰ τὸ ἄναρχ[?], nec κατὰ τὴν Φαιν[?], ipse γενεαλογούμενος; quia etiam Cananæa cujus Melchisedek regulus, non Semo, sed Chamo ejusque posteris cessit, ex Historicorum omnium fide; nec in Semo sed demùm in nepotibus adimpleri debuit oraculum Gen. ix. 27. Erit Canaan servus ejus, quia etiam Abraham Cananæam petiit, ut regionem exteram, remotam ab omni cognatione suâ & patriis sedibus, cessuram demùm posteris, minimè sanè pro avo ex parte subjectam; ne referam illud Suidæ aliorumque ex Veteribus, de Melchisedeco cœlibe, nec conjugato, quod alienum est à Semo. VI. Neque fidem merentur Arabes, Elmacinus, & Patricides, ἰσοφινῶς[?] citati ταλαίοις[?] nostro Hottingero, Collegæ Celeberrimo, & in novissimo Smegmate Orientali, Melchisedecum statuentes Pelegi filium. Quum & iisdem cum Semitis urgeantur incommodis; & commentum prodant annexæ fabulæ de Noachi Testamento, in quo declàm condendo Adami corpore, de ratione sacerdotij à Melchisedeco obeundi, de sacrificiis ex solo pane & vino &c. Omnia Siculis vaniora gerris. VII. Adeoque id unum supererit ut Melchisedek statuatur Salemensium Regulus (sive urbs illa Hierosolyma, ut Josephus, sive alia illa Job. Job. iii.[?] 2 ✕ ut Hieronymus) & quidem iustus, pius, cultor Numinis; ad Abime-lechi, Jobi, aliorumque inter Gentes ex-emplum; ipse sacrorum minister, hocque nomine benedicens & decimans; imago quin etiam & typus æterni illius, ἀΐδια δέ-ξων, ἢ μὴ ἀγεννήτου, sacerdotij. Sed necdum sublata omnis difficultas, & jam demum constant Paulina illa δυσνόητα. Hoc de-mum opus, hic labor, docere, qui idem ille Regulus, obviam factus Abrahamo, dicatur Hebr. vii. 2,3, &c. βασιλεὺς δικαιο-σύνης, ἡ εἰρήνης? qui ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλο-γητος? qui μήτε ἀρχὴν ἡμερῶν ἔχων μήτε τέλος? qui ἀφωμοιωμένος τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ? qui μένει εἰς τὸ διηνεκές? qui [illegible, ~3 letters] & major Abraham credentium Patre? qui μαρτυρούμενος ὅτι ζῇ? qui in eo aut in Messiâ poni videatur δύνα-μις ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου, &c? Et quanquam dici possit, efferri de Melchisedeco alia historicè, alia mysticè; quædam affirmari de typo, quæ conveniant antitypo; dici quæ-dam non absolutè, sed limitatè, non po-sitivè, sed negativè, & κατὰ λόγον ἀληθείας, ἀλλὰ κατὰ λόγον ἰσότητος, Διὰ τὸ μὴ γεγράφ-θαι, μὴ γενεαλογῆσθαι, μὴ [illegible, ~3 letters]σθαι, non facta mentione vel patris, vel matris, vel genealogiæ, vel mortis, prout moris aliàs scriptori Genesèos: quanquam hæc appositè, nec sine vel ratione, vel authoritate, vel exemplo, tutiùs sanè tenuitatem nostram profiteri, & agnoscere quàm sit nobis curta supellex, quàmque ínibi latent etiamnum reconditi sapientiæ & cognitionis thesauri. Optimè Josephus Scaliger, imitandam in talibus Judæorum modestiam, qui ubi in nodum vindice dignum inciderunt, hoc modo defunguntur, Elias solvet.
units.tr: I. Nor did those solve the knot who once were called Melchizedekians, who foolishly made Melchizedek a power that was God, greater than Christ, if we trust Epiphanius, Heresy 55, Book II, Vol. I: "A wondrous power indeed, which is other than God and greater than God, and has a human form, and is distinguished by royal dignity, priestly office, and other personal attributes." II. Nor did they settle the matter, whether Hierax, in the same Epiphanius, Heresies 55 and 67, or that anonymous writer in Jerome's letter to Evagrius, who transformed Melchizedek into the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit could not be incarnate, or act as priest, or rule Salem, or be enriched with offices, or express Christ in the order of priesthood, and it was not permitted in so difficult a matter to be wise beyond the Scriptures. III. Nor did Origen, Homily 1 on Genesis, and after him Didymus, do better when they made Melchizedek an angel. This was unwritten and contrary to what is written, since Moses assigns to him both human dignity, human office and human actions, and every priest must be taken from among men, Hebrews 5:1. IV. Nor have those hit the matter quite right who thought he was the very Son of God himself, seen by Abraham in royal and priestly guise, receiving tithes, blessing him with a blessing not so much optative as conferring, foreshadowing the incarnation, the king of Zedek and Salem named by appellative names, not proper ones, into whom the whole of that discourse in Hebrews 7 fits so exactly. This opinion seems to have escaped Jerome in his letter to Evagrius. But it has been answered most recently, and at length, by the very learned Cuneus, Book III, On the Hebrew Commonwealth, ch. 3; indeed the glory of the theologians, Peter Molinaeus, On Future Foreknowledge, Book IV, chs. 11, 14, 15, tacitly leans towards it. But by how many inconveniences is it burdened? I ask you! Could the type and the thing typified, figure and figured, be the same, and indeed the same thing, namely the priesthood? Is Christ called a priest "after the order of Christ," and to David, Psalm 110: "You are a priest after the order of Melchizedek," that is, after your order? Would the Apostle have passed over such a mystery in deep silence? Why is it not read that the Son of God was worshipped by Abraham, like the Angel in Genesis 18? Why is he not called Jehovah, as that one was? Why is he described historically as a foreign king and as a priest of the Most High God? Why too would Christ, before his incarnation, have been a priest of the Most High God, and indeed a true priest, which would destroy both the history and the reasoning of the type? Who was the king of Salem, or of the city of Solyma, as Josephus says in Antiquities, Book I, ch. 11? If these are appellative names, why is he not called melek-tsedek and melek-shalom, indeed Melchizedek, like Adonizedek and Adonibezek? Why is he the king of Salem, like the king of Sodom, with words inflected into the form of proper names? Or is it because the Apostle shows that these names carry something typical and significant, and that he was not named without some omen, that they are therefore less proper? To say nothing of the fact that this labours under a false hypothesis, as if the Apostle could not be reconciled with Moses in some other way, which, though troublesome, is by no means hopeless. V.
