Nor do those exhaust the difficulty who contend that Melchizedek was the same as Shem, as the Samaritans once did, according to Epiphanius, Heresy 55; as the Hebrews did in Jerome's time, in his letter to Evagrius; as the Talmudists commonly do, and the Targum of Jerusalem, and the most learned of the rabbis even today; and as by far the greater number of theologians, both Orthodox and Papists, also do. Epiphanius once mocked this opinion and harassed it. And although the reasoning behind it is firm, and the calculation of the years from the birth of Shem to the meeting with Melchizedek, sometimes 1130 and sometimes 1127, is faulty, by a huge error of chronology, and contrary to the testimony of the Hebrew manuscripts, yet it is entangled in other difficulties. First, because this opinion is drawn from the gaps in the Hebrew sources, which also contain other uncertain statements about Melchizedek. Second, because the most acute Jews, Josephus and Philo, make him a different person from Shem. Third, because Moses would not have kept silent, nor would the Apostle, otherwise so full in describing Melchizedek. Indeed, because here he denies that Melchizedek derived his descent from the Levites by his ancestors, Hebrews 7:6; because he places him above Abraham with names entirely different, by reason of that paternal right and ancestral authority; because he makes him without father, without mother, without genealogy, whereas Shem was in no way such, but was himself genealogically listed; neither in respect of the beginning nor in respect of the end of life. Also, because Melchizedek was king of the Canaanites, and according to the faith of all historians the Canaanites yielded to Ham and his posterity, not to Shem; and the oracle of Genesis 9:27, "Canaan shall be his servant," had to be fulfilled not in Shem but at last in his descendants. Also because Abraham sought Canaan as a foreign region, remote from all his kin and ancestral seats, which would at last pass to his posterity, and was by no means subject to his ancestor. Not to mention that story of Suidas and others among the ancients, that Melchizedek was unmarried and celibate, which is foreign to Shem. VI. Nor do the Arabs, Elmacinus and Patricides, cited superficially by our Hottinger, a most distinguished colleague, and in his recent Smegma Orientale, who make Melchizedek a son of Peleg, deserve any credit. Since they are pressed by the same inconveniences as the Shemites, and they put forward a fable attached to it about Noah's testament, in which, while founding a new testament, he speaks of the body of Adam, of the manner of the priesthood to be carried out by Melchizedek, of sacrifices made only of bread and wine, and so on. All of which are emptier than Sicilian gerrae. VII. So there remains only that Melchizedek be made a petty king of the Salemites (whether that city be Jerusalem, as Josephus says, or that other place Salem mentioned in John 3:23, as Jerome says), and indeed a just, pious worshipper of the Deity; an example among the Gentiles like Abimelech and Job; himself a minister of sacred rites, and under that name blessing and receiving tithes; indeed an image and type of that eternal priesthood, which lasts forever, or is unbegotten. But even so the whole difficulty is not removed, and those Pauline hard sayings still stand. This is the real task and labour: to show who that same king was, who met Abraham and is described in Hebrews 7:2, 3 as king of righteousness and of peace; who is without father, without mother, without genealogy; who has neither beginning of days nor end of life; who is made like the Son of God; who remains for ever; who is greater than Abraham, the father of believers; who is witnessed to as living; in whom, or in the Messiah, a power of indissoluble life seems to be placed, and so on. And although it may be said that some things are stated about Melchizedek historically and others mystically, that some things are affirmed of the type which agree with the antitype, and that some things are said not absolutely but in a limited way, not positively but negatively, and not according to the reasoning of truth but according to the reasoning of likeness, because it is not written, not genealogically recorded, and so on, with no mention of father, mother, genealogy or death, as is otherwise the custom of the writer of Genesis: although these things are appropriately said, and not without reason, authority or example, it is surely safer to confess our own slenderness and to acknowledge how meagre our resources are, and how the treasures of wisdom and knowledge still lie hidden there. Well did Joseph Scaliger say that the modesty of the Jews should be imitated in such matters, who, when they fall into a knot worthy of an avenger, get out of it in this way: "Elijah will solve it."

units.la: IV. Tertio inter illa δυσνόητα καὶ ψευδώνυμα observare licet, quæ scriptor exinde tradit de Christi Pontificatu & sacerdotio; de functione ejusdem in cœlesti sacrario; de multiplici legis defectu; de veteris antiquatione Fœderis; de oppositione inter Veteris & Novi εὐαγγελίας, λειτουργίας, σκηνὰς, πεπρᾶσθαι; de nondum patefacta sub illo ad sacrarium via &c. Capitibus potissimùm VII. VIII. IX. X. Hæc sanè istius modi, sive res spectemus, sive verba, sive doctrinæ, sive orationis genus excelexcelsum & arduum, ut cum ex se, tum ex accidenti, haereticorum nempe protervia, difficultatem pepererint semper maxi-mam. Hinc [illegible, ~9 letters] Petri dubio pro-cul tempore indignari, & dicam scribere Paulo, nec ferre legis in speciem contemptum; Hinc Anomaeorum illa colluvies legem arguere, criminari, usum omnem proscribere; Hinc saepe Patres in Episto-la enarranda vel parciores, vel certe minus felices; Hinc hodieque Sociniani va-riis ex locis propugnare discrimen essen-tiale utriusque foederis; de Christi dispu-tare Sacerdotio, ut mere figurato, analo-gia quadam cum Levitico, ut in coelis de-mum obeundo, ut vix a Regno distinc-to, nisi in quantum ibi principium imperans, hic exequens &c. Hinc Pontificij latebras hincinde, sacrificio suo missatico, aliisque id genus hypothesibus salvandis, sectari anxie, ne refricem aliorum ulcera.
units.tr: IV. Third, among those things that are hard to understand and falsely named [δυσνόητα καὶ ψευδώνυμα], one may observe what the writer teaches about Christ's priesthood and the office of that priesthood; about his ministry in the heavenly sanctuary; about the many defects of the law; about the abolition of the old covenant; about the opposition between the Old and New [covenants], [εὐαγγελίας, λειτουργίας, σκηνὰς, πεπρᾶσθαι], that is, the gospel, ministries, tabernacles and sold; and about the way into the sanctuary, not yet revealed under the old order, and so on. This is chiefly found in chapters 7, 8, 9 and 10. Whether we look at the matters, the words, the doctrines or the style of expression, these passages are so lofty and hard that, both in themselves and through the stubbornness of heretics, they have always caused the greatest difficulty. Hence, doubtless already in Peter's time, some were indignant and said that Paul was writing and not bearing the appearance of contempt for the law. Hence the Anomoeans' rabble argued against the law, accused it, and rejected all its use. Hence the Fathers, when expounding this Epistle, were often more sparing, or at any rate less successful. Hence even today the Socinians, from various passages, contend that there is an essential difference between the two covenants; they dispute Christ's priesthood as purely figurative, with some analogy to Leviticus, to be exercised only in heaven, and hardly distinct from his kingly office, except that there the principle is commanding and here executing, and so on. Hence the Papists anxiously seek out hiding places here and there, to save their sacrifice of the Mass and other hypotheses of that kind, lest I should reopen the sores of others.

units.la: V. Quartò accenseri iisdem possunt, quae [illegible, ~9 letters], & in speciem aliena à Veteri Testamento, passim exhibentur. V.g. ubi Cap. 1. ad generationem Christi trahit. locum Psal. II. 7. qui tamen vel de adoptio-ne Davidis ipsius, vel certe de resurrectio-ne Christi, teste Paulo Act. xiii. 33. aut constitutione in Pontificem Hebr. v. 5. videatur intelligendus. Ubi hoc ipso capite & sequenti loca quædam alia è vete-ri Instrumento, Psalmis imprimis, cum citantur, tũ applicantur, quæ videri possent non usq; adeò cum verbis aut mente scriptoris consona. Ubi Cap. ix. 4. præter fidem historiæ, urnam & virgam Aharonis in arca Fœderis repositam, quemadmodum v. 19. præter Moisis verba Exod. xxiv. 8. non populū tantùm, sed & librum, & quidem cum aqua, lana coccina & hyssopo conspersum memorat: Ut præterea quæ istius generis & Iudæis fidem Epistolæ derogandi, & Samosatenianis oggannien-di, & profanis cavillandi, & multis, ipsi Cajetano, Epistolæ authoritate vertendi in controversiam, [?] sane omnibus, Petro teste, [?] occasionem præbuêre.
units.tr: V. Fourthly, there can be counted among these the passages which, though they seem foreign to the Old Testament, are displayed everywhere. For example, where in chapter 1 he brings in Psalm 2:7 to prove Christ's generation; yet this verse must be understood either of the adoption of David himself, or certainly of the resurrection of Christ, as Paul testifies in Acts 13:33, or of his appointment as high priest, Hebrews 5:5. Here, in this same chapter and the following, certain other passages from the Old Testament, especially from the Psalms, are both cited and applied, and these may seem not altogether consonant with the words or the mind of the writer. Where in chapter 9:4 he mentions, beyond the testimony of history, the urn and the rod of Aaron laid up in the ark of the covenant; and likewise in verse 19, beyond the words of Moses in Exodus 24:8, he records that not only the people but also the book was sprinkled, indeed with water, scarlet wool and hyssop. Besides these, there are passages of this kind which have given occasion, to the Jews for denying the Epistle's credit, to the Samosatenians for sneering, to profane men for mocking, and to many, even to Cajetan himself, for calling the authority of the Epistle into question; and these, as Peter testifies, have given occasion to all [?].

units.la: VI. Sed de his plus satis conciliandæ argumento nostro fidei. Nec excipiat aliquis, non minus [?] in Paulinis aliis, de prædestinatione, de Antichristo, de novissimis temporibus &c. contineri, quare in firmam esse vim argumenti. Fateor Veteres de obscuritate Epistolę ad Roma-mos[?] aliquando conquestos. Fusius Orige-nes initio Commentariorum in Epistolā. Alij de perplexitate Epistolæ ad Ephe-sios. Unde Epistola illa Ambrosÿ ad Ire-næum, quæ est xxxvii. Lib.v.Epist. At verò 1. non negamus esse etiam alibi quædam obscura & perplexa, ad quæ Petrus pariter respexerit; sed negamus eò respexisse exclusivè ad Epistolam ad Hebræos, vel respexisse principaliter, quod falsum esse probavimus suprà. II. Supponitur gratis, imò pernegatur eundem esse difficultatis gradum & modum in Paulinarum ullá, qui in Epistolá ad Hebræos; imò verò hujus nonnulla, comparatè præ cæteris, sunt quædam quasi Sibyllæ folia, & sacræ Sphyngis ænigmata, eminenter [illegible, ~6 letters], quanquàm nec simpliciter, nec suâ naturâ talia, nec æqualiter omnibus, pro gradu luminis & mensurâ gratiæ. Deniq; si quis nolit necessaria esse & apodictica hæc argumenta, per nos sane licuerit. Hactenus metam nostram fuerimus assecuti, si da-tum ea pressius quàm factum antè urgere, liberare ab exceptionibus variis & instan-tiis, fœnerare subinde lucem dubiis quibusdam & obscuris, demonstrare suum illis inesse pondus idquè maximum, explere forte animum lectoris æqui & attenti, & viam sternere ad pleniorem sufioremque, & quâ his ipsis lux major affulgeat, ἀπόδειξιν[?] deinceps instituendam.
units.tr: VI. But of these things there is more than enough for the purpose of establishing our argument. Nor let anyone object that the same kind of difficulty is found in the other Pauline letters, on predestination, on Antichrist, on the last times, and so on, and that for this reason the force of the argument is weak. I admit that the ancients at times complained of the obscurity of the Epistle to the Romans. Origen complains more fully at the beginning of his commentaries on the Epistle; others of the perplexity of the Epistle to the Ephesians, whence Ambrose's letter to Irenaeus, which is number 37 in book 5 of the Epistles. But, first, we do not deny that there are some obscure and perplexing passages elsewhere too, to which Peter likewise may have referred; but we deny that he referred to them exclusively with respect to the Epistle to the Hebrews, or referred to them chiefly, which we have proved above to be false. Second, it is assumed without warrant, indeed stoutly denied, that any Pauline epistle has the same degree and kind of difficulty as the Epistle to the Hebrews; indeed, some parts of this one, compared with the rest, are like the leaves of the Sibyl and the riddles of the sacred Sphinx, eminently [?], though not simply or by their nature such, nor equally to all, according to the degree of light and the measure of grace. Finally, if anyone does not wish these arguments to be necessary and apodictic, we may allow that. So far we shall have reached our goal, if we have pressed the given matter more closely than before: freed it from various objections and difficulties, lent light from time to time to certain doubtful and obscure points, shown that it has its own weight and that a very great one, perhaps satisfied the mind of a fair and attentive reader, and paved the way to a fuller and more solid treatment, in which greater light may shine upon these very matters, to be undertaken afterwards by demonstration.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Transitur ad testimonium Veterum. Et primò Græcæ Antiquitatis. Universa Paulo Epistolam adscribit. Triginta & amplius Græcorū testimonia. Singula juxtà seriem temporum & ætatum. Varia expenduntur, illustrantur. Hieronymi de Græcorum omnium consensu assertio. Exceptiones I. Cameronis discussæ, & enervatæ.
units.tr: We turn to the testimony of the Ancients, beginning with the Greek antiquity. Universally they ascribe the Epistle to Paul. Thirty and more Greek testimonies. Each is set out in order of time and age. Various points are weighed and clarified. Jerome's assertion of the agreement of all the Greeks. The objections of I. Cameron examined and refuted.

units.la: I. A testimonio divino, ad humanum ex methodi nostrae instituto progredimur. Nosseque operæ pretium quid in hac causâ, historicâ sanè & facti, vel om-nes[?] nes, vel plerique, vel potiores authoritate ac fide tradiderint. Imprimis convenit πάντας πολλαχῶς λόγοις[?], ἐξ τῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων διαδοχὴν[?] καταληφθῶσι[?]. Adeoque replicanda Veterum monumenta, & explorandum, Paulone Epistolam acceptam tulerint, eumne Authorem praedicarint, qui omninò, qui secus, quae cùm Graecae, tum Latinae Ecclesiae, juxtà temporum ac saeculorum seriem, sententia fuerit. Praivère[?] ex parte Baronius ad A.C.LX. Bellarminus L.1. de Verbo Dei C. XVII. ex nostris Commentatoribus varij. Neque tamen actum agimus, dum & authoritates innumerae praetermissae, aliae vel non expressae satis, vel non excussae, vel non eo, quo debuit, ordine digestae. Haec igitur molestia superanda, & dispiciendum quid Graeci senserint, quid Latini, quid denique recentiores; quae privata singulorum, quae aliquando publica synodorum sententia, observata scriptorum aetate & serie. Ex ipsismet verò fontibus, ipsis Patrum verbis mens illorum indaganda,ne tam testimonijs credamus. ut olim Hadrianus ad Rufum Proconsulem, quam ipsis testibus auditis & examinatis.
units.tr: I. We now move from the divine testimony to the human, as our plan requires. It is worth knowing what the writers of antiquity have handed down in this matter, which is wholly historical and concerns a fact: whether all of them, or most, or the most weighty in authority and trustworthiness. Above all it is agreed that [the Epistle was received and recognised through the succession of the Apostles]. So we must go back over the ancient records and examine whether they received the Epistle as Paul's, and whether they named him its author, or the reverse; and what the opinion of the Greek and of the Latin Church was, in order of times and centuries. Some of this has already been handled in part by Baronius at the year of Christ 60 and by Bellarmine, On the Word of God, Book 1, chapter 17, and by various of our own commentators. Yet we are not wasting effort here, since countless authorities have been passed over, others have not been stated clearly enough, not examined, or not arranged in the proper order. This difficulty must therefore be overcome, and we must see what the Greeks thought, what the Latins thought, and finally what the more recent writers thought, both the private opinion of individuals and, at times, the public opinion of synods, observed by the age and succession of the writers. The mind of these men must be sought from the sources themselves, in their own words, and not simply believed on testimony, as Hadrian once did with Rufus the proconsul, but only after the witnesses themselves have been heard and examined.

units.la: II. In prima ergo acie Graecos collocamus, qui communi suffragio Paulo adscripsere Epistolam. Justinus Philosophus qui & Martyr, celebratus sub Antonino Pio, A.C. cL. nusquam sane aperte Epistolam citat expresso Pauli nomine. At citat aliquoties eadem cum Paulinis aliis serie, ut ejusdem sane authoris, V.g. Libro Eἀpistolōn ... Ἀ[?]poriῖn ad Quaest. LXXI, tria citat loca conjunctim ex Paulo, tacito nomine Hebr. 1.2. ἐπτ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τύτων ἐλάλησεν &c. 1.Cor. x.11. εἰς ἐν τῆ συντελεία τῶν αὶωνων κατήντησεν. Gal. iv.4. ὅτε δὲ ἦλθε τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου. Quod si ipse hic libor controversus sit multis atque irreptitius, alibi etiam a Justino ex eadem Epistola citantur, quanquam implicitè, nec nominato authore, sed quod Justino familiare.
units.tr: II. In the front rank, then, we place the Greeks, who with common agreement ascribed the Epistle to Paul. Justin the Philosopher, also called Martyr, famous under Antoninus Pius, around the year 150, nowhere indeed cites the Epistle openly under Paul's name. But he cites it several times in the same sequence as the other Pauline writings, as is characteristic of the same author. For example, in his book Quaestiones et Responsiones, question 71, he cites three passages from Paul together, without naming him: Heb. 1.2. [in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son], 1 Cor. 10.11 [εἰς ἐν τῆ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων κατήντησεν], Gal. 4.4 [ὅτε δὲ ἦλθε τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου]. But if this book itself is disputed by many and is thought spurious, he is also cited elsewhere from the same Epistle, though implicitly, and without naming the author, which was customary for Justin.

units.la: III. Irenaeus, proximus aetati Apostolorum, Lugdunensis Episcopus, Polycarpi discipulus, Justino fere aequalis, certe huic citatus Libro illo Quaest. & Resp.
units.tr: III. Irenaeus, nearest in age to the Apostles, Bishop of Lyons, a disciple of Polycarp and nearly a contemporary of Justin, is certainly cited in the book of Questions and Answers.

units.la: Quaest.cxv. passim Epistolam ad Hebraeos ut Canonicam in subsidium vocat, autho-re quanquam, suo sane more, tacito. Ita Libro II. adversus Haer. C.xv. citat verba Hebr.1.3. faciens omnia verbo virtutis suae. L. IV. C.xxi. adducit locum, Hebr. VIII.8,9. Ecce disponam Testamentum novum &c. L.v. C.v. ex loco Hebr.xi.5. Quoniam quidem Enoch placens Deo, in quo placuit corpore translatus est. Praeterea Eusebius, Hist.Eccles. L.v. C.xxv. ubi de scriptis Irenaei, meminisse dicit exer-tim, in scripto quodam variarum disquisitionum, [illegible, ~20 letters] Excipi tamen potest illud Stephani Tritheitae, apud Photium in Bibliotheca Cod.CCXXXII [illegible, ~30 letters] Hippolytus & Irenaeus, Epistolam Pauli ad Hebraeos, illius esse ne-gant. Qua vero fide id de Irenaeo asserat Tritheita, docent alia ejusdem plura fa-bulosa, inepta, falsa; ut Photius illum etiam [illegible, ~12 letters] insimulet. Forte quia Hippolytus (de quo infrà) fertur Irenæi discipulus, apud Photium Cod. cxxxi. Hinc à Magistro putavit hausisse Hippolytum suam, de alio quodam à Paulo Epistolæ scriptore, sententiam.
units.tr: Question 115 repeatedly calls on the Epistle to the Hebrews as canonical in support of his argument, though without naming the author, in his own manner. Thus in Book II, chapter 15 of Against Heresies he cites the words of Hebrews 1.3, "upholding all things by the word of his power." In Book IV, chapter 21 he adduces the passage Hebrews 8.8, 9, "Behold, I will make a new covenant," etc. In Book V, chapter 5, from Hebrews 11.5, "For before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God," Moreover Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History Book V, chapter 25, where he speaks of the writings of Irenaeus, says that he recalled, in a certain work of various inquiries, [illegible]. Yet that statement of Stephen the Trithaeite, reported by Photius in the Bibliotheca, codex 232, may be excepted, that [illegible], Hippolytus and Irenaeus deny that the Epistle to the Hebrews is Paul's. But the reliability of the Trithaeite on this point regarding Irenaeus is shown by many other fabulous, foolish, and false things he says about him, so that Photius even accuses him [illegible]. Perhaps because Hippolytus (of whom more below) is said to have been a disciple of Irenaeus, according to Photius, codex 131, the Trithaeite thought that Hippolytus had drawn his opinion, that the Epistle was written by some other person than Paul, from his master.

units.la: IV. Clemens Alexandrinus, στρωματεὺς dictus, clarus secundo adhuc sæculo, in Stromatum potissimùm libris, utitur aliquoties Epistolæ testimonijs, sub nomine Pauli, & divini Apostoli. In libris ὑποτυπώσεων, apud Eusebium Hist. Eccles. L. vi. C. xiv. τὴν μὲν πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἐπιστολὴν Παύλου μὲν εἶναι φασι, γεγράφθαι δὲ Ἑβραΐδι φωνῇ, Λουκᾶν δὲ φιλοτίμως αὐτὴν μεταγραμμάτισαντα ἐκδοῦναι τοῖς Ἕλλησιν. Epistolam verò ad Hebræos, Pauli esse dixit, scriptam verò Hebræis patrio sermone, & à Luca summo studio translatam, ut traderet Græcis.
units.tr: IV. Clement of Alexandria, called the Stromateus, famous already in the second century, in the books of the Stromata especially, uses testimonies from the Epistle several times, under the name of Paul and the divine Apostle. In the books Outlines, as Eusebius reports in Ecclesiastical History Book VI, chapter 14, [the Epistle to the Hebrews is said to be Paul's, but written in the Hebrew tongue, and Luke, having translated it with great care, published it for the Greeks] He said that the Epistle to the Hebrews is Paul's, but that it was written in the Hebrew language, and that Luke translated it with great care and published it for the Greeks.

units.la: Addit Clemens, eodem loco, causas suppressi à Paulo nominis atque Apostolicæ dignitatis. Atque id jam antiquitùs traditum refert, & creditum decessoribus.
units.tr: Clement adds in the same place the reasons why Paul suppressed his name and apostolic dignity. He reports that this had been handed down from of old and was believed by their predecessors.

units.la: Citatur etiam ipse hic Clementis locus apud Theodoretum & Oecumenium in Argumento Epistolæ ad Hebræos, Τίνι δὲ τρόπῳ[?] ὡς ἔφησεν τὴν ἰδίαν ὀνομασίαν ἐν Ἑβραίοις γράφων[?], Κλήμης ἐν ταῖς ὑποτυπώσεσι[?], λέγων ὅτως[?], &c. Quâ verò ratione non apposuit nomen, ad Hebraeos scribens, optime Clemens Alexandrinus in libris ὑποτυπώσεων. Sive verò Graecè, sive Hebraicè Paulum scripsisse dixerit, Clemens (de quo nos infrà problemate) hactenus sanè de authore consentit.
units.tr: This very passage of Clement is also cited by Theodoret and Oecumenius in the Argument to the Epistle to the Hebrews, where, in the manner in which he (Paul) did not put his own name when writing to the Hebrews, Clement, in the Outlines, says as follows, etc. For the reason why he did not put his name when writing to the Hebrews, Clement of Alexandria has excellently explained in the books of the Outlines. Whether he said that Paul wrote in Greek or in Hebrew, Clement (on whom we will say more below, in the problem section) at least agrees so far about the author.

units.la: V. Origenes, Clementis discipulus & successor in Cathedrâ Catechetica, secundus post Apostolos Magister habitus, Homil. ix. in Exod. ex recensione Genebrardi. Praecipuè tamen Apostolus Paulus de intelligentiâ tabernaculi, quædam nobis prodit scientiæ excelsioris indicia; dicit namque ad Hebraeos scribens, citatq; locum Hebr.ix.2. Sic passim in Commentariis, & περὶ ἀρχῶν L.1.C.11. ex eádem Epistolâ quædam profert sub nomine Apostoli Pauli. In Fragmento Origenis περὶ ἀρχῶν, apud Ruffinum, Tom.ix. Operum Hieronymi. Unde sufficere existimo unò hoc Pauli testimonio debere nos uti, ex Epistolâ quæ ad Hebraeos scribit, in quâ ita ait &c. Sed idem fusius apud Eusebium Hist. Eccles. L. VI. C. XIX. vel XX. Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπο-φαινόμεθα [?] ἐστιν, ὅτι τὰ μὲν νοήματα τῆς Ἀ-ποστόλου ἐστὶν, ἡ δὲ Φέρεσις καὶ ἡ σύνθεσις, ὀνομάμησι-νέματος πν [?] τὰ Ἀ[?]ποστολικὰ, καὶ ὥσπερ σχολιο-γραφήσουτ [?] τὰ ἑρμηνέα ὑπὸ τῆς Διδασκάλ. Ego vero constanter dixero, sensus esse Pauli, phrasim vero & constructionem verborum alterius cujusdam, concio-nes Apostoli in commentarios redigen-tis, & dictata Magistri describen-tis. Subjungit, Εἴπις οὖν Ἐκκλησία ἔχει αὐτὴν τὴν Ἐπιστολὴν, ὡς Παῦλος αὐτὴ εὐδοκι-μεῖτω, καὶ ἀπὶ τοῦτο. Οὐ γὰρ εἰκῇ οἱ ἐξ ἀρχαῖοι ἄν-δρες Παῦλος αὐτὴν ἀποδεδώκασι, si quae ve-ro Ecclesia eam habet Epistolam, pro-bet eam, ut Pauli, vel hac ratione: Non enim temere Veteres eam Pauli esse tradiderunt. Addit tandem, Ὡς δὲ ὁ χρῆσας τὴν Ἐπιστολὴν, τὸ μὲν ἀληθὴς θεὸς αἶδν. Ἡ δὲ εἰς ἡμᾶς Φιλόσοφος [?] ἐστιν, ὑπὸ τινῶν μὲν λέγονται ὅτι Κλήμης ὁ γενόμενος Ἐπίσκοπος Ῥωμαίων, ἐχάψε τὴν Ἐπιστολὴν, ὑπὸ τινῶν δὲ ὅλως ἀρνᾶς &c. At quis scripserit Epistolam, certè Deus novit. Nos vero accepimus à quibusdam, Clementem Romanorum Episcopum scripsisse Epistolam, ad alijs Lucam &c. Ex quibus intelligimus Origenem, tum quidem materialiter & quoad res scriptas, Paulo transscripsisse Epistolam, formaliter & quoad scriptionem, uni ex Apostolorum discipulis. Interim tamen citat ubique ut Paulinam, pro Paulina haberi jubet, idque [illegible, ~6 letters], adeoque jam[?] prima Apostolorum aetate, traditum memorat.
units.tr: V. Origen, the disciple and successor of Clement in the catechetical chair, regarded as the second master after the Apostles, in Homily 9 on Exodus, in the edition of Genebrard. Yet the Apostle Paul in particular, writing to the Hebrews, gives us certain signs of a loftier knowledge concerning the understanding of the tabernacle, and he cites Hebrews 9.2. Thus throughout his Commentaries, and in De principiis Book 1, chapter 11, he brings forward certain passages from the same Epistle under the name of the Apostle Paul. In the fragment of Origen's De principiis, as preserved by Rufinus, in volume 9 of Jerome's works, I think it is enough to use this one testimony of Paul, from the Epistle which he writes to the Hebrews, in which he says, etc. But the same is set out more fully in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History Book VI, chapter 19 or 20: [I declare that the thoughts are the Apostle's, but the style and the composition belong to someone who recorded the Apostle's discourses as commentaries, and wrote down what the Master said.] I, however, state constantly that the thoughts are Paul's, but the style and composition are another's, one who took down the Apostle's sermons as notes, and as it were recorded the teaching of his Master. He adds: [If any Church holds this Epistle as Paul's, let it be commended for this; for the ancient men did not hand it down as Paul's without reason.] If any Church has this Epistle, let it approve it as Paul's, and it deserves that for this reason: the Ancients did not hand it down as Paul's without cause. He adds at last: [But who wrote the Epistle, God indeed knows. But what has reached us is that some say Clement, Bishop of the Romans, wrote the Epistle, and others say Luke.] Who wrote the Epistle, God indeed knows. But what has come down to us is that some say Clement, who became Bishop of the Romans, wrote the Epistle, and others that it was Luke, etc. From these words we understand that Origen held that the Epistle was transcribed by Paul in respect of its matter and the things written, materially, but in respect of its writing, formally, by one of the Apostles' disciples. Yet he everywhere cites it as Pauline and bids it be held as Pauline, and he records that this was handed down from the earliest age of the Apostles.

units.la: VI. Patres Concilij Laodiceni (celebrati Laodiceae Phrygiae Pacatianae, quodque decennio fit anterius Concilio Nicaeno Oecumenico.) nobilissimo illo canone Liv. sive ultimo, inter τὰ Κανονικὰ τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης[?], imò inter Paulinas recensent Epistolam ad Hebraeos. Ἐπιστολαὶ Παύλου δεκατέσσαρες[?], πρὸς Ῥωμαίους μία, πρὸς Κορινθίους δύο &c. πρὸς Ἑβραίους μία. Epistolae Pauli quatuordecim, ad Romanos una, ad Corinthios duae &c. ad Hebraeos una. Cujus quidem Concilij Canones sanciti ae confirmati, in Concilio Oecumenico vi. sive Constantinopolitano III. sub Constantino Pogonato,, ut patet ex e-jusdem Concilij Canone secundo.
units.tr: VI. The Fathers of the Council of Laodicea, held at Laodicea in Pacatiana Phrygia, which took place a decade before the Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, in their famous canon 59, or the last, among the canonical books of the New Testament, indeed among the Pauline Epistles, list the Epistle to the Hebrews: [The Epistles of Paul are fourteen: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, etc., one to the Hebrews.] The Epistles of Paul, fourteen in number: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, etc., one to the Hebrews. The canons of this Council were indeed sanctioned and confirmed at the sixth Ecumenical Council, or the third of Constantinople, under Constantine Pogonatus, as is clear from the second canon of that same Council.

units.la: VII. Eusebius Cæsariensis Episcopus, Pamphili cognomento, Constantini Magni temporibus illustris, quid de scriptore Epistolæ ad Hebræos censuerit, prodit Hist. Ecclesiast. L.iii.C.iii. Τῷ δὲ Παύλῳ ἀπόδηλοι καὶ οὐχ[?] αἱ δεκατέσσαρες (Ἐπιστολαί). Pauli vero testatæ & notæ Epistolæ sunt quatuordecim. Eodem libro C.xxxii. Ubi agens de Epistolâ Clementis Romani ad Corinthiorum Ecclesiam, ἐν ᾗ, inquit τῆς πρὸς Ἑβραίους πολλὰ νοήματα[?] ἀπ[?]ωδέξατο, ἡ δὲ ἐν αὐτῷ λέξει ῥητῶς πῶν ἐξ αὐτῆς χρησάμενον, ἐπὶ μὴ νέον ὑπάρχειν τὸ συγγεγραμμένον. Inquâ (sc. Clementis Epistola) dum sensus plurimos ex Epistola ad Hebræos interserit, aliquando etiam ijsdem omnino verbis utitur, apertissime declarat antiquitatem scripti. Pergit, ὅθεν ἀκότως ἐδοξεν αὐτὸ, τῆς λοιπῆς ἐγκαταλεχθῆναι γράμμασι τῷ Ἀ-ποστόλῳ. Unde merito reliquis Apostoli scriptis annumerata videtur. Tandem,
units.tr: VII. Eusebius of Caesarea, bishop, surnamed Pamphilus, distinguished in the time of Constantine the Great, reports what he thought about the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, in Ecclesiastical History book 3, chapter 3: "The fourteen epistles of Paul are clear and well known" [Τῷ δὲ Παύλῳ ἀπόδηλοι καὶ οὐχ αἱ δεκατέσσαρες]. Ecclesiastical History book 3, chapter 38, where he is discussing the Epistle of Clement of Rome to the Church of the Corinthians. He says that in it Clement "takes over many thoughts from the Epistle to the Hebrews, and sometimes uses its very words, which clearly shows that the writing is ancient." Since Clement's epistle draws many meanings from the Epistle to the Hebrews, and sometimes uses the very same words, it declares most plainly the antiquity of the writing. He goes on: "For this reason it seems reasonable that it should be numbered among the rest of the Apostle's writings." Hence it is rightly reckoned among the other writings of the Apostle. Finally,

units.la: Ἑβραίοις γὰρ διὰ τῆς πατρίου γλώττης ἐγγεγραμμένῃ[?] ὁμιλητὴν[?] τῷ Παύλῳ, οἱ μὲν τὸν Εὐαγγελιστὴν[?] Λουκᾶν, οἱ δὲ τὸν Κλήμεντα τῆσδε αὐτὸν, ἐμμηνεύσαντα[?] λέγουσι τὴν γραφὴν, ὃ ἢ μᾶλλον εἴη ἂν ἀληθὲς &c. Cum enim Paulus scripsisset Hebraeis patrio sermone, alii quidem Lucam Evangelistam, alii Clementem illum ipsum, Epistolae Interpretem dicunt. Quod etiam omnino est verisimilius &c. Atque constantissimam hanc fuisse Eusebij, Arrianorum aliàs partibus addictioris, sententiam, monet Theodoretus, Praefat. Comment. in Ep. ad Hebr. Nam etiam Eusebius divinissimi Pauli hanc esse Epistolam confessus est, & veteres omnes hanc de ea sententiam habuisse asseruit. Idem, Gobarus apud Photium Cod. ccxxxii. Εὐσέβιος[?] ... ἄλλος[?] τῶν ἀσεβῶν[?] ... ἐπιστολὴν[?] ... τοῦ Παύλου[?]. Eusebius & multa Veterum Patrum turba, hanc Epistolam Paulinis alijs accensent.
units.tr: "For since Paul wrote to the Hebrews in their native tongue, some say that Luke the Evangelist, and others that Clement himself, translated the letter, which is more likely to be true" [Ἑβραίοις γὰρ διὰ τῆς πατρίου γλώττης ἐγγεγραμμένῃ]. For when Paul had written to the Hebrews in their native language, some say that Luke the Evangelist, others that Clement, was the interpreter of the Epistle. This is also altogether more probable, etc. And that this was Eusebius's most settled opinion, though he was otherwise inclined to the Arian side, Theodoret notes in his preface to the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews. For Eusebius too acknowledged this epistle to be that of the most divine Paul, and asserted that all the ancients held this opinion of it. The same is found in Gobarus, quoted by Photius, Codex 232: "Eusebius and a large crowd of the ancient Fathers reckon this Epistle among those of Paul." Eusebius and a great throng of the ancient Fathers count this Epistle among the Pauline ones.

units.la: VIII. Alexander Episcopus Alexandriae, quiq; primus Arrium presbyterum exauctoravit; Epistola ad συλλογισμὸν[?], paulo[?] paulò ante Nicænam Synodum, datâ quæ extat apud Socratem Histor. Eccles. L.1.C.iii. citat Epistolâ ad Hebræos, sub nomine Pauli Apostoli. Ἀλλὰ ὡς Ἀ̔ποστόλος [?] Χριστὸς χθὲς καὶ σήμερον ὁ αὐτὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας [?]. Sed sicut Apostolus, Iesus Christus heri, hodie idem ipse, qui locus est ad Hebr. C.xiii.v.8.
units.tr: VIII. Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, who was the first to depose the presbyter Arius, in a letter written shortly before the Nicene Synod, which is extant in Socrates, Ecclesiastical History book 1, chapter 3, quotes the Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of the Apostle Paul: "But as the Apostle says, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever" [Ἀλλὰ ὡς Ἀπόστολος]. But as the Apostle says, Jesus Christ is yesterday and today the same, and forever. This is the passage at Hebrews 13:8.

units.la: XI. Patres Concilij Niceni Oecumenici I. coacti anno Christiano cccxxv. dicuntur Hieronymo, Præfat.cxi. in Judith, Tomo iii. Scripturarum Canonicarum numerum computasse. Quod si verum est extrà omnem controversiam fuerit, Epistolam ad Hebræos Paulinis annumeratam. Quando ea tum communis Orientalium sententia, & ex Nicænis Patribus Athanasius, publicâ Constantis authoritate, Scripturæ synopsim texens, Paulinarum Catalogo Epist. ad Hebræos inseruit. Non recessurus sanè à Nicænorum mente atque decreto. Quando etiam horum fuit tueri eandem ac vindicare adversus Arrianorum insultus, Paulo Epistolam derogantium. Ita etiam Baronius ad Annum Christi ix[?], Num. xlix. Sic Author Commentariorum in Damascenum, L. iv. C. xviii. Quum in sacrosancta Nicaena Synodo Ecclesia universa eam recepit, tanquam ab Apostolo Paulo scriptam, ipsamque talem haberi debere sanxit ac decrevit.
units.tr: XI. The Fathers of the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, assembled in the year of Christ 325, are said by Jerome, in the preface to Judith, volume 3, to have drawn up the number of the canonical Scriptures. If that is true, beyond all controversy the Epistle to the Hebrews was counted among the Pauline epistles. This was then the common opinion of the Easterns, and among the Nicene Fathers Athanasius, under the public authority of Constans, when he drew up a synopsis of Scripture, included the Epistle to the Hebrews in his catalogue of the Pauline epistles. He would certainly not have departed from the mind and decree of the Nicene Fathers. It also fell to them to defend and vindicate this same view against the assaults of the Arians, who disparaged the Pauline authorship. So also Baronius, at the year of Christ 9 [sic], number 49. So too the author of the commentaries on Damascene, book 4, chapter 18: When in the most holy Nicene Synod the whole Church received it as written by the Apostle Paul, it also decreed and ordained that it should be held as such.

units.la: X. Athanasius Archiepiscopus Alexandrinus, tot Arianorum telis sub Constantino & successoribus impetitus, in synopsi script. S. Lib. viii. Tom. ii. Epistolam ad Hebraeos ex Paulinis decimam facit, ibidemque statuit causam exaratae Epistolae; χρείας πρὸς τὰς ἐθνῶν[?], χάριν λοιπὸν καὶ αὐτῶν[?] τῆς ἐκ περιτομῆς πιστευόντων[?] ἐ Ἑβραίοις[?] &c. postquam scripsisset Gentibus omnibus, tandem ex omnibus iis scribit ex circumcisione Hebraeis, qui crediderant &c. Alibi Dialogo i. de S. Trinitate, ad instantiam Anonymi, urgentis Pauli Epistolam ad Hebraeos τὸν ἐκκλησίαν[?] ζήσαν[?] (i.e. [illegible, ~6 letters], de quibus vocibus erudite Scaliger Anim. ad verf. Euseb. ad A. MDLXXXIV.) in haec verba respondet, Α᾽Φ᾽ ἐξαγγέλλη τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον Χριστοῦ [illegible, ~8 letters] ἡ ἐ[?]Ηολῆ, ἐμοὶ αὐτῆς ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ, τῷ Παύλου. [?]
units.tr: X. Athanasius, archbishop of Alexandria, assailed by so many Arian weapons under Constantine and his successors, in the synopsis of the Holy Scriptures, book 8, volume 2, counts the Epistle to the Hebrews as the tenth of the Pauline letters, and in the same place states the occasion for writing it: "after he had written to all the Gentiles, at last he wrote to those of the circumcision who believed, the Hebrews" [χρείας πρὸς τὰς ἐθνῶν]. Elsewhere, in the first dialogue on the Holy Trinity, answering an anonymous opponent who pressed the Epistle to the Hebrews [τὸν ἐκκλησίαν ζήσαν] (on which words see Scaliger's notes on Eusebius's chronicle, at the year 1584), he replies in these words: "Since the Gospel of Christ was announced [...] by Paul, this epistle was believed to be his, together with which there are fourteen Pauline epistles in all" [Α᾽Φ᾽ ἐξαγγέλλη τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον Χριστοῦ].

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] A quo annunciari coeptum Evangelium Christi, Pauli credita fuit haec Epistola, cum quâ sunt Pauli Epistolae in universum quatuordecim. Ibidem, ὅτι δὲ αὐτῆς ἡ ἐπιστολή, Φαμεν ἐν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς Ἐπιστολῆς, μέμνηται γὰρ ἡ Τιμοθέου, λέγων &c.
units.tr: [illegible, ~12 letters] By whom the preaching of the Gospel of Christ was first announced, this epistle was believed to be Paul's, together with which there are fourteen Pauline epistles in all. In the same place: "That this is the epistle of Paul we say at the beginning of the Epistle, for it mentions Timothy, saying etc." [ὅτι δὲ αὐτῆς ἡ ἐπιστολή].

units.la: Quod verò Pauli sit haec Epistola, vel ex sive ejusdem liquet; meminit enim Timothei, dicens &c. Ita causam reddit ibidem Athanasius praetermissi nominis Paulini, à praeconcepto Iudaeorum odio. Ita frequentissimè ex eâdem, tanquam Pauli, petit argumenta adversus Arianos, imprimis in orationibus Tomo 1. Operum.
units.tr: That this epistle is Paul's is clear from the epistle itself, for it mentions Timothy, saying etc. Athanasius there gives this reason for the omission of Paul's name: the prior hatred of the Jews. Thus, very often, from the same epistle, as being Paul's, he draws arguments against the Arians, especially in the orations in volume 1 of his works.

units.la: XI. Ephraem, natus Edessae Syrorum, Ecclesiae ejusdem Diaconus, alius ab illo de quo Photius, Biblioth. p. 774. dictus Nysseno, [?]ὁ ἐν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας Εὐφράτης, ἢ πολύφορος τῷ Θεῷ ἀμφιτελής, ὁ καλὸς νῦν μετὰ τῶν [?]χάριτος, φύγγ[?] τῆς βίας, καὶ τῆς ἡμέρας εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν [?]ἐπιλεγόμενος &c: clarus sub Iuliano, Epistolam Paulo perpetuò tribuit, & citat frequentius tribus, quos habehabeamus[?], operum Tomis. Modo Paulum, modò Apostolum ἐξόχως[?] vocat, v.g. ci-caturus[?] locum Hebr. 1 v.12. Idémque alio in loco Paulus. Vivus sermo Dei.
units.tr: XI. Ephraem, born at Edessa among the Syrians, deacon of the Church there, not to be confused with the one Photius mentions, called the Nisibene, [...] famous under Julian, always ascribes the Epistle to Paul and quotes it more often than three times in the volumes of his works. He sometimes calls him Paul, and sometimes the Apostle par excellence, as when he cites Hebrews 1:12, and in another place: Paul, the living word of God.

units.la: XII. Didymus Alexandrinus, praeceptor Hieronymi, familiaris Athanasio, captus oculis, sed oculum habens sponsae de Cantico Canticorum; inquit Hieronymus; Libro de Spir. S. in fine Tomi vi. Operum Hieronymi; Paulus in Epistola quam ad Hebraeos scribit &c. Unde & Apostolus in Epistola quam ad Hebraeos scripsit, &c.
units.tr: XII. Didymus of Alexandria, teacher of Jerome, close friend of Athanasius, blind, yet "having the eye of the bride in the Song of Songs," as Jerome says, at the end of the sixth volume of Jerome's works, in the book on the Holy Spirit: Paul, in the epistle which he writes to the Hebrews, etc. Whence also the Apostle, in the epistle which he wrote to the Hebrews, etc.

units.la: XIII. Cyrillus Hierosolymorum Episcopus, Præses Constantinopolitani I. Oecumenici, mortuus sub Theodosio: Catechesi 1 v. Catalogum contexens Gano-nicorum utriusque Testamenti, specia-tim τῆς Καινῆς διαθήκης Παύλῳ; inquit, Ἐπιστολὰς δεκατέσσαρας; Pauli Epistolae quatuor-decim.
units.tr: XIII. Cyril of Jerusalem, bishop, president of the First Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, who died under Theodosius. In his first Catechesis, drawing up a catalogue of the canonical books of both Testaments, he says specifically of the New Testament: "to Paul, fourteen epistles" [Τῆς Καινῆς διαθήκης Παύλῳ]; the fourteen epistles of Paul.

units.la: XIV. Gregorius Nyssae in Cappadocia E-piscopus, Basilij frater natu maximus, sub Valente Ariano civitate pulsus, Eunomij adversarius; pro Paulo authore similiter pronunciat, Epistolam sub hoc nomine [?] frequentissimè citat, ὁ πάνυ φος [?] Παῦλος [?] ; ὁ Παῦλος ἐν ἐπιστολῇ ἐπιστέλλων [?] ; ὁ Ἀπόστολος &c.
units.tr: XIV. Gregory of Nyssa in Cappadocia, bishop, elder brother of Basil, driven from his city under the Arian Valens, an opponent of Eunomius. He likewise pronounces Paul to be the author, quotes the epistle under this name very often, calling him "the most illustrious Paul," "Paul writing in his epistle," "the Apostle," etc.

units.la: XV. Basilius Cæsariensis Cappadociæ Episcopus vir ἀλογισμώτατος [?], coævus Athanasio, florens sub Valente, Epistolâ ad Gregorium fratrem, Episcopum Nyssenum, quæ est XLIII. Tom. III. agens περὶ διαφορᾶς ὀνόματος καὶ ὑποστάσεως, & de sensu loci Hebr.1.3. quo Christus dicitur ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ &c. vocat hoc ipsum τὴν τῶν ἀποστόλων γραφὴν, scripturam Apostolicam, & ἀποστολικὸν λόγον, dictum Apostolicum; citatque ut alias ejusdem Apostoli voces, locum Colos. C.II.v.15. Sic alibi varia ex Epistolâ ad Hebræos, ut Paulina, in medium profert, imprimis operum Tomo I.& II.
units.tr: XV. Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia, bishop, a man of the greatest reasonableness, contemporary with Athanasius, flourishing under Valens. In his letter to his brother Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, which is the 43rd in volume 3, dealing with the difference between the words ousia and hypostasis, and with the sense of Hebrews 1:3, where Christ is called the brightness of the glory and the express image, etc., he calls this itself the writing of the Apostles, and the apostolic saying, and he cites, as another utterance of the same Apostle, Colossians 2:15. So too elsewhere he brings forward various passages from the Epistle to the Hebrews as Pauline, especially in volumes 1 and 2 of his works.

units.la: XVI. Gregorius Episcopus Nazianzenus, proximus Basilio ob arctiorem cum eo necessitudinem, clarus sub Valentiniano & Theodosio; Carminibus περὶ τῶν γνησίων βιβλίων τῆς θεοπνεύστου γραφῆς, post enumeratos Evangeliorum libros, & Actus Apostolicos, subjungit, Δίχα δὲ Παύλου, πα[illegible, ~4 letters] τ' Ἐπιστολαί, Pauli verò Epistolæ quatuor decim. Multus etiam est in citandâ E-pistolâ, implicitè quanquam, & suppresso plerumque, oratorum & poëtarum sæpe more, scripserit nomine.
units.tr: XVI. Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, closest to Basil because of his closer intimacy with him, famous under Valentinian and Theodosius. In his verses on the genuine books of divinely inspired Scripture, after listing the books of the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, he adds: "Apart from these, Paul's fourteen epistles" [Δίχα δὲ Παύλου]. Paul's fourteen epistles. He is also very much given to quoting the epistle, though often implicitly and without naming the author, after the manner of orators and poets.

units.la: XVII. Amphilochius, Iconij Lycaoniæ Episcopus, prioribus [illegible, ~6 letters] & pari cum iis loco habitus Hieronymo; carminibus ad Seleucum de legendis scriptu-ræ libris, post enumeratas Paulinas alias:
units.tr: XVII. Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium in Lycaonia, held in the same esteem as the earlier writers and on a par with them by Jerome, in his verses to Seleucus on reading the books of Scripture, after listing the other Pauline epistles:

units.la: Duæ ad Timotheum, ad Titum & Phi-lemona
units.tr: Two to Timothy, to Titus and Philemon

units.la: Ad singulos una, & ad Hebræos itidem.
units.tr: One to each individual, and likewise one to the Hebrews.

units.la: Quæ verò ad Hebræos, notha esse dicitur Plerisque, sed male; nam germana gratia est.
units.tr: Some say that the one to the Hebrews is spurious, but wrongly, for it is genuine.

units.la: XVIII. Epiphanius Constantiæ Cypri Episcopus, itidem sub Valentiniano, Valente, & Gratiano Principibus clarus, magnis Chrysostomü inimicitiis, Origenis verò manes implacabili odio prosecutus, in Panario Hær. xlii. contrà Marcionitas ubi de ordine Epistolæ Pauli ad Philemonem. Apud ipsum (nempe Marcionem) nem) habetur nona, apud Apostolum vero ultima est. Verùm in quibusdam exemplaribus decimatertia est, ante eam quæ ad Hebræos scripta est, locata. Alia verò exemplaria, habent eam quæ ad Hebræos scripta est, decimam, ante duas ad Timotheum, & ad Titum, & ad Philemonem. Hæres. LV. contrà Melchisedecianos, Cæterùm de ipso Melchizedec dicunt, quod sit sine Patre, sine matre, sine prosapia, ex Epistolâ Pauli ad Hebræos id ipsum comprobare volentes. Ibidem, Spiritualiter non intelligentes ea quæ à sancto Apostolo in Epistolâ ad Hebræos dicta sunt.
units.tr: XVIII. Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, likewise famous under the emperors Valentinian, Valens and Gratian. He pursued Chrysostom with great enmity, and the memory of Origen with implacable hatred. In his Panarion, heresy 42, against the Marcionites, where he discusses the order of Paul's Epistles, he says: Among them (namely Marcion's) it is ninth, but in the Apostle's it is last. But in some copies it is placed thirteenth, before the one written to the Hebrews. Other copies have the one written to the Hebrews tenth, before the two to Timothy, and to Titus, and to Philemon. Heresy 55, against the Melchizedekians: Moreover they say of Melchizedek himself that he is without father, without mother, without genealogy, wishing to prove this very point from Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews. Likewise, in the same place: Not understanding spiritually the things said by the holy Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: Eundem Paulum Epistolæ authorem facit Hæres LXVII. Hieracitarum, & Hæres. LXIX. contrà Ἀλογιστῶν, asserentes ipsam Pauli non esse; & alibi passim. Imò verò talem creditum jam olim ab ipsis hæreticis, profligatissimâ sanè Ebionitarum familiâ, haud obscurè notat Hær. XXX. contrà Ebionæos; Paulum enim hi traducebant, quasi ex quodam in Hebræos odio, ob negatam sibi filiam sacerdotis, scripsisset contrà Legem & ceremonias, quod etiam
units.tr: He makes the same Paul the author of the Epistle in heresy 67 of the Hieracites, and in heresy 69 against the Alogi, asserting that it is not Paul's; and he does so throughout elsewhere. Indeed, that such a belief was held long ago by the heretics themselves, namely the most profligate family of the Ebionites, is clearly indicated in heresy 30 against the Ebionites. For these men slandered Paul, as if, out of a certain hatred of the Hebrews because a priest's daughter had been denied to him, he had written against the Law and the ceremonies, which also

units.la: ctiam etiam de Epistolâ ad Hebræos videtur accipiendum. Imo ne ipse Marcion, si fides Epiphanio Haer. xlii. Epistolâ rejecit, ut non Pauli, sed ut cum Paulinis quibusdam aliis adulteratam: Item primæ & secundæ ad Timotheum, & ad Titum, & ejus quæ est ad Hebræos, quæ feruntur apud ipsum, velut quæ non plenæ sint, sed adulteratæ.
units.tr: seems to be understood also of the Epistle to the Hebrews. Indeed, not even Marcion himself, according to Epiphanius, heresy 42, rejected the Epistle as Paul's; he thought it had been corrupted with certain other Pauline writings: Likewise the first and second to Timothy, and to Titus, and that which is to the Hebrews, which are carried among them as if they were not complete but corrupted.

units.la: XIX. Theophilus, Alexandrinæ Ecclesiæ Episcopus, socius Epiphanij in causâ Origenis contrà Chrysostomum, quique cum Hieronymo, commutavit literas; Epistolâ Paschali prima, Paulo eadem nobiscum prædicante, Iesus Christus heri, & hodie &c. Hebr. xiii. 8. Epistolâ tertiâ, sub nomine Pauli Apostoli citat locum Hebr. xiii, 7. ὧν[?] ἀναθεωροῦντες τὴν ἔκβασιν τῆς ἀνα-στροφῆς.
units.tr: XIX. Theophilus, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, a partner of Epiphanius in the cause of Origen against Chrysostom, who also exchanged letters with Jerome. In his first Paschal letter: Paul preaching the same to us: Jesus Christ yesterday, and today, etc. Heb. 13.8. In his third letter, under the name of the Apostle Paul, he cites Heb. 13.7: [ὧν ἀναθεωροῦντες τὴν ἔκβασιν τῆς ἀνα-στροφῆς], considering the outcome of their conduct.

units.la: XX. Johannes Episcopus Constantinopolitanus, Chrysostomi elogio insignitus, Eudoxiæ impotentiâ, Epiphanij & Theophili injuriis ad extremum lacessitus, commentatus est in Epistolam ad Hebræos ut Paulinam, Paulo perpetuò vendicet, & in praefatione fusius disquirit, qui Gentium quum esset Apostolus, ad Hebraeos scripserit, Commentariorum in N T. Tomo vi. inter alia, πῶς οὖν ἡ ἐπι-στολὴ τύπος, ὅτε ἐν καὶ ἀνάθεμα γενέσθαι ἤθελε, διὰ τῶν ἐλεγε, γνώσεσθε τὸν ἀδελφὸν Τιμόθεον &c. Quomodo non ad eos scripsisset pro quibus & anathema fieri aliquando voluit; idcirco dixit, Cognoscite fratrem Timotheum &c.
units.tr: XX. John, bishop of Constantinople, marked by Chrysostom's praise, was at last harassed by the violence of Eudoxia and by the injuries of Epiphanius and Theophilus. He wrote a commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, treating it as Pauline, and constantly vindicated it for Paul. In its preface he discusses at length how Paul, being Apostle of the Gentiles, could have written to the Hebrews. In his Commentaries on the New Testament, volume vi, among other things: [πῶς οὖν ἡ ἐπιστολὴ τύπος, ὅτε ἐν καὶ ἀνάθεμα γενέσθαι ἤθελε, διὰ τῶν ἐλεγε, γνώσεσθε τὸν ἀδελφὸν Τιμόθεον &c.] How then did he not write to those for whom he once wished even to become an anathema? Therefore he said, Know the brother Timothy, etc.

units.la: XXI. In Actis Concilij Ephesini, instituti Anno Domini cccc xxxi, sub auspiciis Theodosij Junioris; Parte, quae est Tom. ii. Concil. General. Inter Paulinas recensetur Epistola ad Hebraeos, ex qua eadem cum Epistolis aliis serie confirmantur articuli, 1. ὅτι θεὸς ὁ χριστὸς, ἐνώσει &c. 2. ὅτι ζωὴ ἡ ζωοποιὸς ὁ χριστὸς, ἡ ὅτι ὁ χριστὸς θάνατ[?] τῷ κόσμῳ Σωτήριος &c.
units.tr: XXI. In the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, held in the year of the Lord 431 under the auspices of Theodosius the Younger, in the part which is volume ii of the General Councils, the Epistle to the Hebrews is counted among the Pauline letters. From it, in the same sequence as the other epistles, the articles are confirmed: 1. [ὅτι θεὸς ὁ χριστὸς, ἐνώσει &c.], that Christ is God by union, etc. 2. [ὅτι ζωὴ ἡ ζωοποιὸς ὁ χριστὸς, ἡ ὅτι ὁ χριστὸς θάνατ[?] τῷ κόσμῳ Σωτήριος &c.], that the life-giving life is Christ, or that Christ, death [?] to the world, is the Saviour, etc.

units.la: XXII. Proclus Episcopus Cyriae, Homilia εἰς τὴν εὐαγγελισμὸν τῷ Κυρίῳ, habita contrà Nestorium, ante Concilium Ephesinum; πῶς αὐτὸς ἀπάτωρ ἢ ἀμήτωρ ἐκ τοῦ Παῦλου, Quomodo ipse sine patre, sine matre, secundum Paulum ? innuens locum ad Hebraeos C. vii.3.
units.tr: XXII. Proclus, bishop of Cyzicus, in his homily on the Annunciation of the Lord, delivered against Nestorius before the Council of Ephesus: [πῶς αὐτὸς ἀπάτωρ ἢ ἀμήτωρ ἐκ τοῦ Παῦλου], How is he himself without father or mother according to Paul? He is alluding to Heb. 7.3.

units.la: XXIII. Isidorus Pelusiota, Chrysostomi discipulus, clarus temporibus Concilij Ephesini, sub Theodosio juniore, Libro 1. Epistolarum, Epist. xciv. in locum Hebr iv. 13. Τὰ γυμνὰ καὶ πεπραχηλισμένα τῷ πολυφρονι γεγραπται Παύλῳ ut scriptum est sapientissimo Paulo. Libro ii. Epist. Lviii [?] citaturus locum Hebr.1,3. de Christo effulgentia gloriae &c. charactere Personae Patris, Ταῦτα ἐννοήσας ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος, καὶ ὥσπερ ἐνθὺς γενόμενος, Haec animadvertens divinus ille Paulus, & quasi numine afflatus &c. Sic alibi passim.
units.tr: XXIII. Isidore of Pelusium, a disciple of Chrysostom, famous in the time of the Council of Ephesus under Theodosius the Younger. In Book 1 of his Epistles, Ep. 94, on Heb. 4.13: [Τὰ γυμνὰ καὶ πεπραχηλισμένα τῷ πολυφρονι γεγραπται Παύλῳ], as written by the most wise Paul. In Book ii, Ep. 58, citing Heb. 1.3 on Christ, the brightness of glory and the express image of the person of the Father: [Ταῦτα ἐννοήσας ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος, καὶ ὥσπερ ἐνθὺς γενόμενος], Considering these things, that divine Paul, as if inspired by a god, etc. So elsewhere throughout.

units.la: XXIV. Cyrillus, Episcopus Alexandrinus, Praeses Concilij Ephesini; Epistolam ad Hebraeos utique Paulo transcribit; ita Thesauro de sancta Trinit. λόγῳ [?], citat locum Hebr.ix.24. his verbis, ὁ Παῦλος ἐπιστέλλων, φησίν, Paulus in Epistola scribens dicit; sic locum adducturus Hebr. i.1,2,3. Παῦλος Ἐβραίοις διαλεγόμενος, καὶ μετὰ πολλῆς παρρησίας, &c. Paulus ad Hebraeos differens, & multa quidem cum dicendi libertate. Alibi [illegible, ~12 letters] λέγοντα, Paulum dicentem audiamus, & subjungit locum Hebr. 11 v.1. Ita assertione xxxv. ὁ Παῦλος, ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ ἐνεργὴς[?] &c. Paulus, Vivens enim est sermo Dei & efficax Hebr. iv. 12. Plura passim in Dialogis.
units.tr: XXIV. Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, president of the Council of Ephesus, certainly ascribes the Epistle to the Hebrews to Paul. Thus in his Thesaurus on the holy Trinity he cites Heb. 9.24 with these words: [ὁ Παῦλος ἐπιστέλλων, φησίν], Paul, writing in the Epistle, says. So, about to quote Heb. 1.1-3: [Παῦλος Ἐβραίοις διαλεγόμενος, καὶ μετὰ πολλῆς παρρησίας], Paul, discoursing to the Hebrews, and with much freedom of speech. Elsewhere [illegible], let us hear Paul saying, and he adds Heb. 11.1. Likewise in assertion 35: [ὁ Παῦλος, ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ ἐνεργὴς] Paul: For the word of God is living and effective, Heb. 4.12. Many more instances occur throughout his Dialogues.

units.la: XXV. Theodoretus, Episcopus Cyri-[?] cum Cyrillo aliquando commissus, præ-sens in utroque Oecumenico Ephesino & Chalcedonensi; in argumento Episto-læ ad Hebræos, quod Commentario in eandem Epistolam præfixit, ex Latinâ recensione Coloniensi: taxatis primùm Arianis ob Epistolæ contemptum hæc subjungit; Ex quo literarum Apostolicarum fuerunt Ecclesiæ participes, ex illa etiam Epistolæ ad Hebræos utilitatem percipiunt. Addit causas, tum rejectæ ab hæ-reticis Epistolæ; tum taciti à Paulo nomi-nis & Apostolatus, ut qui Gentium non Hebræorum esset Apostolus. Idem Theodoretus alio argumento, si modò Theodoreti est, quod extat apud Oecumenium Comment. in hanc Epistolam, solvit pluribus quæstionem τὴν ἔνεκεν Ἀπόστολος ὑ-πάρχων ὁ Παῦλος πρὸς τὰ ἔθνη, Ἑβραίους πιστέλ-λει; Unde Paulus, Gentium sanè Apostolus, ad Hebræos scribat?
units.tr: XXV. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, at one time at odds with Cyril, present at both the ecumenical councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon. In the argument to the Epistle to the Hebrews, which he prefixed to his commentary on that epistle, from the Latin Cologne edition: after first censuring the Arians for despising the epistle, he adds these words: Since the churches have shared in the Apostolic letters, they also gain profit from that Epistle to the Hebrews. He gives reasons both why the epistle was rejected by heretics and why Paul passed over his name and apostleship in silence, as one who was Apostle of the Gentiles, not of the Hebrews. The same Theodoret, in another argument, if it is indeed his, which survives in Oecumenius's commentary on this epistle, resolves at length the question: [τὴν ἔνεκεν Ἀπόστολος ὑπάρχων ὁ Παῦλος πρὸς τὰ ἔθνη, Ἑβραίους πιστέλλει], Why, though Paul is Apostle of the Gentiles, does he write to the Hebrews?

units.la: XXVI. Eulogius Archiepiscopus Alexandrinus, florens sub Martiano Imperatore, medio quinto sæculo, ut ex Photij Bibliothecâ, in excerptis Eulogianis Cod. ccxxx; L. ii. Contrà Novatianos, apud eundem Photium Cod. cccxxx. respondens objectioni Novatianorum ex loco Hebr. vi.4. x. 24. τοὺς Φέρωσιν οἱ ἀπὸ Νοvατ-ιανοῦ τὴν Ἀποστολικὴν ῥῆσιν, τὸ Φάσκον. τῆς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας &c. Proferunt Novatiani di-ctum Apostoli, docens, Impossibile &c. De eodem loco; φησὶν ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος, dicit divus Paulus; οὕτως οὖν ἀφέντες τὴν τῆς Χριστοῦ διδασκαλίαν ὁ Παῦλος, ἐπὶ τὴν τε-λειότητα ἔρχεται. Sic ergo omittit elementa-lem illam doctrinam Paulus, & ad perfe-ctionem venit. Sic alia citaturus loca ex eodem Epistolio, λέγει ὁ Ἀπόστολος; ὡς αὐτὸς ὁ Ἀπόστολος φησί.
units.tr: XXVI. Eulogius, archbishop of Alexandria, flourishing under the emperor Marcian, in the middle of the fifth century, as shown by Photius's Bibliotheca, in the excerpts from Eulogius, Cod. ccxxx. In Book ii against the Novatians, in the same Photius, Cod. cccxxx, he answers the objection of the Novatians from Heb. 6.4 and 10.24: [τοὺς Φέρωσιν οἱ ἀπὸ Νοvατ-ιανοῦ τὴν Ἀποστολικὴν ῥῆσιν, τὸ Φάσκον. τῆς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας &c.], The Novatians bring forward the saying of the Apostle, which says: those once enlightened, etc. Latin: The Novatians bring forward the saying of the Apostle, teaching that it is impossible, etc. On the same passage: [φησὶν ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος], says the divine Paul; [οὕτως οὖν ἀφέντες τὴν τῆς Χριστοῦ διδασκαλίαν ὁ Παῦλος, ἐπὶ τὴν τελειότητα ἔρχεται], Thus Paul, leaving aside the teaching of Christ, comes to perfection. So Paul therefore sets aside that elementary doctrine and comes to perfection. So too, about to cite other passages from the same epistle: [λέγει ὁ Ἀπόστολος], the Apostle says; [ὡς αὐτὸς ὁ Ἀπόστολος φησί], as the Apostle himself says.

units.la: XXVII. Iobius Monachus Primasio, Cassiodoro, aliisque Latinae Ecclesiae scriptoribus συγγραμμα[?], Commentario cui titulum fecit, οἰκονομικῆς πραγματείας[?], sive de Redemptionis mysterio, Libro ix, Καὶ τὸν θεῖον Παῦλον, ἐνκαίνιον ἡμῖν ὁδὸν τὴν [illegible, ~6 letters] ἐφανερὰν ἐκ ζωῶν[?], ἐξ ἐκ ... χειροποιήτου ἁγια[?] ... &c. Nam secundum Beatum Paulum, adducitque loca Hebr.x.24. ix,24.vi.20. Videatur Photij Biblioth. Cod. ccxxii. p.651, editionis Pauli Stephani.
units.tr: XXVII. Iobius, a monk, who wrote for Primasius, Cassiodorus and other writers of the Latin Church. In his commentary, entitled on the economy of the ... or on the mystery of redemption, Book ix: [Καὶ τὸν θεῖον Παῦλον, ἐνκαίνιον ἡμῖν ὁδὸν τὴν [illegible] ἐφανερὰν ἐκ ζωῶν[?], ἐξ ἐκ ... χειροποιήτου ἁγια[?] ... &c.], and the divine Paul, a new and living way for us ... For according to the blessed Paul, and he adduces Heb. 10.24, 9.24, 6.20. See Photius's Bibliotheca, Cod. ccxxii, p. 651, in the edition of Paul Stephanus.

units.la: XXVIII. Johannes Damascenus, Monachus & Presbyter, juxta quosdam Theodosio Magister Epistolarum, revera aliquot saeculis junior, & Leonis demum Isauri temporibus clarus, octavo saeculo: αὐτῆς ἐφόδου ζῆς πίστεως[?] L. iv. C. xviii. recensens Novi Testamenti Libros, Epistolam hanc reliquis Paulinis accenseт; Παύλου Ἀποστόλου Ἐπιστολαὶ δεκατέσσαρες[?], Pauli Apostoli Epistolae quatuordecim. Passim citat sub nomine Pauli, & Apostoli.
units.tr: XXVIII. John Damascene, a monk and presbyter, according to some the master of the Epistles under Theodosius, though in fact several centuries later, and famous under Leo the Isaurian in the eighth century. In Book iv, chapter xviii of his Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, reviewing the books of the New Testament, he counts this epistle among the other Pauline ones: [Παύλου Ἀποστόλου Ἐπιστολαὶ δεκατέσσαρες], The Epistles of the Apostle Paul, fourteen. He cites it throughout under the name of Paul the Apostle.

units.la: XXIX. Theodorus, cognomento Studites, clarus sub Constantino Copronymo & successoribus, sub finem octavi, & initia noni seculi familiaris Nicephoro Patriarchae: in sermonibus Catecheticis, aliquoties profert loca Epistolae, sub nomine Apostoli.
units.tr: XXIX. Theodorus, surnamed Studites, famous under Constantine Copronymus and his successors, at the end of the eighth and the beginning of the ninth century, a close friend of Patriarch Nicephorus. In his catechetical sermons he several times cites passages of the Epistle under the name of the Apostle.

units.la: XXX. Nicephorus, Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus, author τῆς χρονογρα-φίας; idem aliis cum Nicephoro illo Iconolatrâ sede Patriarchali pulso sub Leone Armenio, scriptore ἱστορικῶν συντόμων[?], aliis merito nonnihil junior: in illâ suâ Chronographiâ, à Scaligero insertâ chronico Eusebiano, refert inter scripta N.T. τὰ ἐκκλησιαζόμενα[?], ἢ κεκανονισμένα[?], παύλου ἐπιστολὰς ιδ[?]. Pauli Epistolas quatuordecim.
units.tr: XXX. Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople, author of the Chronography. He is not the same as the other Nicephorus, the image-worshipper, who was driven from the patriarchal see under Leo the Armenian, and who wrote the Brief Histories; he was rightly somewhat later than the others. In his Chronography, which Scaliger inserted into the Eusebian chronicle, he lists among the writings of the New Testament the books read in the churches or accepted as canonical, namely the fourteen Epistles of Paul [τὰ ἐκκλησιαζόμενα, ἢ κεκανονισμένα, Παύλου ἐπιστολὰς ιδ'].

units.la: XXXI. Photius, Patriarcha itidem Constantinop.clarus medio nono seculo, sub Michaële III. & Basilio Imperatoribus, cum Nicolao Papa mutua vibrans anathemata; quid de authore Epistolae ad Hebraeos sentiat, prodit aliquoties in Μυριοβίβλῳ[?]. Imprimis Codice XLVIII. & cxxi, ubi de Caio & Hippolyto Epistolam Paulo negantibus; quod ut novum & à veritate alienum memorat, refertque id inter alia τὰ ἀκριβείας λεγόμενα[?].
units.tr: XXXI. Photius, likewise Patriarch of Constantinople, famous in the middle of the ninth century under the emperors Michael III and Basil, who hurled anathemas back and forth with Pope Nicholas. What he thinks of the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews he reveals several times in the Myriobiblon, especially in Codices 48 and 121, where he says that Caius and Hippolytus denied the Epistle to Paul. He reports this as something new and alien to the truth, and counts it among what are called the "accuracies" [τὰ ἀκριβείας λεγόμενα].

units.la: XXXII. Oecumenius, posteriori quidem, sed nec adeo certæ ætatis; Commentario in Epist. ad Hebræos, passim eam Paulo adscribit. Imprimis in triplici ὑποθέσει[?] seu argumento Epistolæ in limine præfixo. Quorum primum depromptum ex Athanasio in synopsi, alterum inscriptum Theodoreto, de quo suprà; tertium pluribus & urgentissimis rationibus evinci esse Paulinam. Et quidem primò, respondet objectionibus quæ petuntur à diversitate styli, aut à nomine non præfixo: secundò [illegible, ~6 letters] Pauli esse Epistolam probat μαρτυρεῖται δὲ καὶ ἐν τῇ ἐξῆς ἡ Ἐπιστολὴ ὑπάρχουσα Παύλου. 1. τῷ γεγράφθαι, ὅτι ἡ τῆς δεσμοῖς μου συνεπαθήσατε[?], 2. καὶ ἐν τῷ λέγειν, περισσότερον εὔχεσθε, ἵνα τάχιον ἀποκατασταθῶ ὑμῖν; 3. καὶ ἐν τῷ λέγειν, γινώσκετε τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν Τιμόθεον ἀπολελυμένον &c. Ubi triplici argumento ex ipsâ Epistolâ mutuato probari dicit, quod sit Pauli, 1. dum scribit, Nam & de vinculis meis condoluistis; dum dicit, Orate am-plius; pius, ut ab citius restituar[?] vobis; dum dicit, scitote Fratrem nostrum Timotheum solutum esse &c. Ibidem, μὲν δὲ ἡ γνωρίζων ὑμῖν αὐτῷ πρὸ Πα-ολὴν, ὡς ἡ ἀνάγκη αὐτῷ πολλὰ διδάσκει[?]. Multa etiam alia palàm faciunt illius esse Epistolam, ut & lectio ipsa sequens docebit.
units.tr: XXXII. Oecumenius, indeed of a later date, but not of a very certain age, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews ascribes it to Paul throughout. Especially in the threefold hypothesis, or argument of the Epistle, prefixed at the beginning. The first of these is taken from Athanasius in his synopsis, the second is ascribed to Theodoret, of whom we spoke above, and the third proves by several very forceful arguments that the Epistle is Pauline. First, he answers the objections drawn from the difference of style or from the absence of the name at the head. Second, [illegible] he proves that the Epistle is Paul's: "it is also witnessed in what follows that the Epistle is Paul's" [μαρτυρεῖται δὲ καὶ ἐν τῇ ἐξῆς ἡ Ἐπιστολὴ ὑπάρχουσα Παύλου]. (1) By the words "for you also sympathized with my bonds"; (2) by the words "pray more earnestly, that I may be restored to you the sooner"; (3) by the words "know that our brother Timothy has been released," and so on. Here he says that the Epistle is shown to be Paul's by a threefold argument drawn from the Epistle itself. Likewise, "I make known to you, as necessity teaches him many things" is said there. Many other things also make it plain that the Epistle is his, as the reading that follows will show.

units.la: XXXIII. Theophylactus, Archiepiscopus Bulgariæ, undecimo jam sæculo, Græcorum Patrum novissimus, Commentario in Epistolam, acerrimum se receptæ sententiæ defensorem profitetur. In Præfatione, postquam Paulum Hebræis invisum fuisse monuit, imò nec quidem gratiâ valuisse apud conversos Hebræorum, annectit rationes quas ipsum nihilominus ad scribendum impulerunt; easdem sanè cum rationibus Chrysostomi, & aliorum. ὥσπερ οὖν ἐπιχειρεῖν βαπτίζειν, ἀλλ' ὅμως, οὕτω καὶ Ἑβραίοις ἐκ περιουσίας (alij ἐκ περιτομῆς) ἐπιστέλλει. Σφόδρα αὐτῶν σκάνδαλον, ὑπὲρ ὧν ἀναγκαῖα ἢ γενέσθαι ἤυχετο. Quemadmodum non incommodè illi ma-nus baptizandi, baptizabat tamen, sic & Hebraeis ex abundanti charitate scribit. Summopere sanè de illis sollicitus, pro quibus & anathema fieri exoptavit. Subjungit tempus exaratæ Epistolæ, facitq; salvo vetustiorem posteriori ad Timotheum.
units.tr: XXXIII. Theophylact, Archbishop of Bulgaria, already in the eleventh century, the last of the Greek Fathers, professes in his Commentary on the Epistle to be a most fierce defender of the accepted opinion. In the Preface, after noting that Paul was disliked by the Hebrews, and not even held in favour among the Hebrew converts, he adds the reasons which nevertheless moved him to write, certainly the same reasons as those of Chrysostom and others. "Just as, though his hands were not well suited to baptizing, he nevertheless baptized, so he also writes to the Hebrews out of abundant love" [ὥσπερ οὖν ἐπιχειρεῖν βαπτίζειν, ἀλλ' ὅμως, οὕτω καὶ Ἑβραίοις ἐκ περιουσίας (others read ἐκ περιτομῆς) ἐπιστέλλει]. "Certainly he was deeply concerned for them, for whom he even wished to become an anathema" [Σφόδρα αὐτῶν σκάνδαλον, ὑπὲρ ὧν ἀναγκαῖα ἢ γενέσθαι ἤυχετο]. He adds the time when the Epistle was written, and makes the older one agree with the later letter to Timothy.

units.la: XXXIV. Tandem subnectimus Græcorum Codicum, plerorumque & antiquissimorum fidem. Quorum constans inscriptio est, τὰ ἁγίας πύλας [?], vel πρὸς τὰς [illegible, ~6 letters] Ἀποστόλας, ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίους Ἐπιστολή. Beza sub initium annotationum, Ita scriptum invenimus in omnibus nostris Codicibus, uno tantum excepto, in quo duntaxat scriptum erat, πρὸς Ἑβραίους. Idem codices R. Stephano in recensione suâ N. T. usurpati. Cujus quanquam inscriptionis originem non ab ipso Paulo derivemus, & antiqua fuerit, & Græcorum in eo consensus argumentum. Syrus simpliciter, אגרת [?] עברית [?] Epistola ad Hebraeos. Sed inscriptionis illa ratio communis aliis Epistolis, quoad Syrum Interpretem, neque Pauli nomen hic tacitum magis quam in inscriptione Epistolæ ad Galatas, Ephesios, &c.
units.tr: XXXIV. Finally, we add the testimony of the Greek manuscripts, most of them and the oldest. Their constant title is "The Epistle to the Hebrews" [ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίους Ἐπιστολή]. Beza, at the beginning of his notes: "We found it written thus in all our manuscripts, with one exception only, in which it was written merely 'to the Hebrews' [πρὸς Ἑβραίους]." The same manuscripts were used by Robert Estienne in his edition of the New Testament. Although we do not derive the origin of this inscription from Paul himself, it is old, and the agreement of the Greeks on it is an argument. The Syriac simply has "Epistle to the Hebrews" [ʼeggrta dʻebrayē]. But this manner of inscription is common to the other Epistles, so far as the Syriac translator is concerned, and the name of Paul is no more omitted here than in the inscription of the Epistles to the Galatians, the Ephesians, and so on.

units.la: XXXV. Atque ita perpetuâ serie intelligimus, quanti Orientalis Ecclesia, jam inde à primis temporibus, Epistolam [?]secerit; ut Paulo transcripserit; ut eidem constantissimè vindicârit; ut controversias de illius sive Authore, sive Authoritate in Hæreticorum rejecerit pertinaciam; ut traditionem de scriptore Paulo [?]inde ab Apostolorum filiis derivârit; ut denique nullus ex magna illa turba Patrum, secùs vel scripserit vel senserit, quantùm ex illorum scriptis assequimur.
units.tr: XXXV. And so we understand in unbroken sequence how greatly the Eastern Church, from the earliest times onwards, esteemed the Epistle: that it attributed it to Paul; that it most constantly vindicated it for him; that it rejected controversies about its author or its authority as the obstinacy of heretics; that it derived the tradition of Paul as author from the sons of the Apostles; and finally that none of that great crowd of Fathers, so far as we can learn from their writings, either wrote or thought otherwise.

units.la: Unde Hieronymus Epist.cxxix. ad Dardanum. Illud nostris dicendum est, hanc Epistolam quæ inscribitur ad Hebræos, non solum ab Ecclesiis Orientis, sed ab omnibus retrò Ecclesiis, & Græci sermonis scriptoribus, quasi Pauli Apostoli suscipi. Ad quem locum Erasmus, pertinacissimus alias oppositæ sententiæ vindex, ne ausus quidem hiscere.
units.tr: Hence Jerome, Epistle 129 to Dardanus: "This must be said by us: that this Epistle, which is inscribed to the Hebrews, is received as the Apostle Paul's not only by the Churches of the East, but by all the Churches and writers of the Greek language, from of old." At this place Erasmus, otherwise the most stubborn champion of the opposite opinion, did not even dare to open his mouth.

units.la: XXXVI. Ausus id tamen I.Camero, qui Græcorum in eo consensum, gemina exceptione solicitandum censuit. Prima est, consensum illum non esse universum dubitâsse enim Eusebium, an sit Pauli, & in eam rem citare Clementem Alexandrinum. Sic ille Quæst ii. in Epist. ad Hebræos: Quæ sanè miramur excidisse Cameroni, Dubitâsse ipsum Eusebium, nec licuit quidem suspicari. Nec sinunt, quæ ex Eusebio suprà §. vi. adduximus in medium, quæ item ex Theodoreto, & Gobarro. ii. Citâsse in eam rem Clementem Alexandrinum somniavit Vir eruditus. Sanè de Clementis τῶν στρωματικῶν scriptisargens, sistit eum pro Paulo authore sententem. Hujusque eum sententiæ vindicem atque assertorem facit eximium. Neque tamen ut sibi, aut Clementis decessoribus, aut Græco ulli scriptori dubiæ & controversæ. iii. Forte ad locum illum Eusebij respexit Vir cætera Doctissimus, quo Epistolam ad Hebræos refert inter ἀντιλεγομένας γραφάς, Hist. Eccles. Lib. vi. C. xi. Attendens sanè non suam, non ullius Græci, sed Latinorum quorundam, ac Romanæ præxim Ecclesiæ, notatam illi ante L. iii. C. iii.
units.tr: XXXVI. Yet I. Camerarius ventured to challenge that agreement of the Greeks with a twofold exception. The first is that the consensus was not universal, since Eusebius doubted whether it was Paul's, and to prove this he cites Clement of Alexandria. So he writes in his Questions on the Epistle to the Hebrews. It is indeed surprising that this slipped from Cameron, that Eusebius himself doubted; there was no reason even to suspect it. Nor do the passages from Eusebius that we cited above in §vi, and likewise those from Theodoret and Gobarus, allow it. A learned man has dreamed that Clement of Alexandria was cited for this. Certainly, when he wrote the Stromata, Clement set Paul forth as the author of the view, and he makes him its outstanding defender and champion. Yet he did not treat it as doubtful and disputed, either for himself, for Clement's predecessors, or for any Greek writer. iii. Perhaps the otherwise very learned man had in mind that passage of Eusebius where he counts the Epistle to the Hebrews among the disputed Scriptures (Church History, book vi, chapter xi). Yet he plainly failed to notice that this mark was not put on it by himself, nor by any Greek, but by certain Latins and by the Roman church, which had marked it as such before book iii, chapter iii.

units.la: XXXVII. Altera Cameronis exceptio est: Primum omnium qui Epistolam Paulo Apostolo adscribit, fuisse Clementem Alexandrinum. Sed rationes quibus impulsus fuit, ut eam Paulo attribueret vanas esse & frivolas, ejúsq; testimonium non debere esse magni momenti. Imò verò va[?]nas & frivola, nullius adeò momenti Cameronis assertio. Neq; hæc tam ex tripode, quin potiùs ex plaustro. 1. Clemente antiquiores Irenæus, Justinus, quorum jā ante exploravimus mentem, ut nihil jā de Areopagitā. Antiquior toto sæculo Clemens Romanus, quem mox adstipulantē intelligemus. 11. Nec dubium quin si plura ad seram hanc posteritatē vel Dionysij, Polycarpi, vel Ignatij, vel Justini, vel primorum Orientalis Ecclesiæ antistitū promanâsset monimenta, his solis testibus ac Judicibus, hoc quicquid est controversiæ decisum foret. 111. Quin ipse Clemens apud Eusebiū, L. vi. c. xi. vel xiv. à majoribus hęc sua arcessit. ἤδη δὲ ὡς ὁ μακάριος ἔλεγε πρεσβύτ[?]-ρος &c. Jā verò sicut beatus quidam presbyter dicebat. nēpe quā de causā non sePaulus Hebræorū inscripserit Apostolū. Sic
units.tr: XXXVII. Cameron's second exception is this: Clement of Alexandria was the first of all who ascribed the Epistle to the Apostle Paul. But the reasons that moved him to attribute it to Paul are vain and trifling, and his testimony ought not to carry great weight. On the contrary, Cameron's assertion is vain and trifling and of no weight at all, and it is no more solid than a cart-load of sand. First, Irenaeus and Justin are older than Clement; we have already examined their judgement, and nothing has been said of Dionysius the Areopagite. Clement of Rome is older than him by a whole century, and we shall see him presently lending his support. Second, there is no doubt that if more records had come down to this late posterity from Dionysius, Polycarp, Ignatius, Justin, or the first bishops of the Eastern Church, this whole controversy would have been settled by these witnesses and judges alone. Third, Clement himself, in Eusebius (book vi, chapter xi, or xiv), draws these views from his elders: And so, as the blessed presbyter used to say [ἤδη δὲ ὡς ὁ μακάριος ἔλεγε πρεσβύτερος], that is, for what reason the Hebrews did not inscribe the Apostle Paul's name. So too

units.la: Origenes Clementi proximus, Paulum authorem traditum, ἀπὸ τῶν ἁγίων ἀνδρῶν [?] sic Athanasius, ἀφ' ὧν Εὐαγγέλιον κατηγγελ-[?]μένοις [?]. Sic Hieronymus, ab omnibus Græci sermonis scriptoribus. iv. Rationes quibus impulsus, ut eam Paulo attribueret, Clemens nullas profert. Tantùm abest ut varia sint & frivola. Habet sanè quasdam nec contemnendas; cur Epistolam Hebraicè scriptam credat; cur etiam Pauli Apostoli nomen prætermissum. At Paulum ipsum esse authorem, quocunque tandem idiomate scripserit, non tam probat quàm supponit. v. Clementis testimonium non debere esse magni momenti, in quibusdam fateor. Quando, aut Legem per se Judæis, aut Philosophiam Ethnicis salutarem facit; quando Paulum ad Sybillarum & Hydaspis provocantem oracula suóq; calculo comprobantem introducit; quando nimia quadam facilitate ἀποκρύφα & ψευδεπίγραφα varia, verè ἀπὸ θεϊκὰς ἀντὶ ἡμῶν [?] nobis obtrusit; quando magno ipsi in pretio Evangelia Ægyptiorum & Hebræorum, Conciones Petri Pauli, Traditiones Matthiæ, Epistola Barnabæ, &c. At nullius esse momenti in aliis, v.g. quando de Epistolâ ad Hebræos cū Græca omni antiquitate, quando de Catholicâ Judæ, &c. benè sentit, gratis & frustrà Camero. vi. Denique,quâ hic asseruit fide, ante Hieronymum Latinorum neminem affirmâsse eam esse Pauli Apostoli, eâdem, neminem Græcorum ante Clementem. Prius enim, quod ex E-rasmo & paucis aliis Camero didicerat, jam jam imus destructum.
units.tr: Origen, next after Clement, records that Paul is the author, from holy men [ἀπὸ τῶν ἁγίων ἀνδρῶν]; so Athanasius, from those by whom the Gospel was proclaimed [ἀφ' ὧν Εὐαγγέλιον κατηγγελμένοις]. So Jerome, from all the writers of the Greek tongue. iv. The reasons that moved Clement to attribute it to Paul he sets out nowhere; far from being varied and trifling, they are in fact not to be despised: why he believed the Epistle was written in Hebrew, and why the name of Paul the Apostle was omitted. But that Paul himself is the author, in whatever language he wrote, he does not so much prove as presuppose. v. That Clement's testimony ought not to carry great weight, I admit in some matters: when he makes the Law saving for the Jews, or philosophy for the Gentiles; when he introduces Paul appealing to the oracles of the Sibyls and of Hydaspes and confirming them with his own authority; when with too great ease he has thrust upon us various apocryphal and pseudonymous writings, truly "divinely inspired" [ἀπὸ θεϊκὰς] in place of ours; when he holds in high esteem the Gospels of the Egyptians and the Hebrews, the Preaching of Peter and Paul, the Traditions of Matthias, the Epistle of Barnabas, and so on. But that his testimony is of no weight in other matters, for example when he judges rightly about the Epistle to the Hebrews along with all antiquity, and about the Catholic Epistle of Jude, is a claim Cameron makes groundlessly and in vain. vi. Finally, the claim by which he asserted that before Jerome no Latin had affirmed that it is the work of the Apostle Paul, is equally true of no Greek before Clement. For the former, which Cameron had learned from Erasmus and a few others, has already been overturned.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.
