units.la: Latinorum testimonia. Causa accura-tioris indaginis. Qui Paulo Epistolam tribuêre. Citantur inde à Clemente Romano, ad ætatem Scholasticorum. Sexaginta ferè scriptores pro Paulo adducti. Series temporum in citatione observata. Subinde quædam vel notata vel illu-strata.
units.tr: The testimonies of the Latins. The reason for a more careful inquiry. Who ascribed the Epistle to Paul. Citations from Clement of Rome down to the scholastic age. Some sixty writers cited for Paul. The order of time observed in the citations. Certain points noted or illustrated along the way.

units.la: I. De Græcis hactenus. Super est La-tinorum Patrum de hac lite sententia. Eò accuratiùs, sepositò partium studio, exploranda, quod diversum sentire visi ab Ecclesiis Orientis. De Romanâ Ecclesia Eusebius, Hist. Libr. III. C. III. Οἳ γε μὴν ἴδιῶ- τὴν ...
units.tr: I. So much for the Greeks. What remains is the opinion of the Latin Fathers on this controversy, which must be examined all the more carefully, with partisan feeling set aside, because they seem to have thought differently from the Churches of the East. On the Roman Church, Eusebius, Hist. Book III, ch. III, says: "Those private individuals who rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is contradicted by the Church of Rome as not Paul's [Οἳ γε μὴν ἰδιῶται...]."

units.la: {Greek passage, transcribed:} Οἳ γε μὴν ἰδιῶτες ηὐτήκασι τὴν πρὸς Ἑβραίους, πρὸς τῆς Ῥωμαίων Ἐκκλησίας, ὡς μὴ Παύλου ἔσαν αὐτὴν, ἀντιλέγοντας φήσαντες οὐ δίκαιον ἀγνοεῖν
units.tr: Those private individuals, however, have rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is contradicted by the Church of the Romans as not being Paul's; it is not right to be ignorant of this [Οἳ γε μὴν ἰδιῶτες ηὐτήκασι τὴν πρὸς Ἑβραίους, πρὸς τῆς Ῥωμαίων Ἐκκλησίας, ὡς μὴ Παύλου ἔσαν αὐτὴν, ἀντιλέγοντας φήσαντες οὐ δίκαιον ἀγνοεῖν].

units.la: Quòd vero quidam Epistolæ ad Hebræos derogârint, dicentes eidem ab Ecclesiâ Romana, tanquam quæ Pauli non sit, contradici, in obscuro relinquere minimè consentaneum est. Hieronymus Catalogo script. Ecclesiast. in Caio, Romanæ urbis Episcopo, Epistolas quoque Pauli tredecim tantùm enumerans, decimam quartam, quæ fertur ad Hebræos, dicit non esse: Sed & apud Romanos usque hodie, quasi Pauli Apostoli non habetur. Simile quid habet Epist. cxxix. ad Dardanum; Quòd si eam Latinorum consuetudo non recipit inter scripturas Canonicas, nec Græcorum quidem Ecclesiæ Apocalypsim Johannis &c. Idem de Latinis alij, ut videbitur infrà, tradidêre. Agedùm ergò, primò per singulas Latinorum Patrum ætates, mentem illorum indagemus. Citatis [?]is perpetua serie inde à Clemente Romano, ad ætatem Scholasticorum, qui Paulinam credidêre. Deinceps motæ ex Eusebio & Hieronymo instantiæ, alia quamvis à Baronio fide, occursuri.
units.tr: That some have detracted from the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is contradicted by the Roman Church, as not being Paul's, is not at all fitting to leave in obscurity. Jerome, in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, under Caius, Bishop of the city of Rome, when listing only thirteen Epistles of Paul, says that the fourteenth, which is ascribed to the Hebrews, is not his: but even among the Romans to this day it is not regarded as the Apostle Paul's. He has something similar in Epistle 129 to Dardanus: If the custom of the Latins does not receive it among the Canonical Scriptures, neither does the Church of the Greeks receive the Apocalypse of John, etc. Others among the Latins have handed down the same, as will be seen below. Let us now, then, first examine their mind through each age of the Latin Fathers. Citations follow in an unbroken series from Clement of Rome down to the age of the Schoolmen, who believed it to be Paul's. Afterwards the objections raised from Eusebius and Jerome will be met, along with the other opinion of Baronius.

units.la: II. Clemens Romanus, Apostolis coævus, de quo secundùm Hieronymum, Paulus ad Philippenses. C. iv. [?]3, in Epistolâ, quam ad Corinthios ex personâ Romanæ Ecclesiæ, scripsisse fertur; quámque Eusebius [illegible, ~18 letters] πᾶσιν, Hist. L. iii. C. xxxii. Epistolam ad Hebræos aliquoties citat, & quoad sensum, & quoad verba. Ita Eusebius, loco superiori capite allegato §. vii. Ita Hieronymus in Clemente: Sed & multis de eadem Epistolâ non solùm sensibus, sed juxtà verborum quoque ordinem abutitur. Iam sanè, si Epistola Clemente anterior, si Clementi citata, si in Canonicis eidem habita, cui nisi Paulo ex Apostolorum choro tribuenda? de Clemente idem affirmat Gobarus apud Photium Cod. ccxxii. Κλήμης μέν τοι [?]ἐ[?] εὐφορίῳ &c. τῆς ἄλλαις (Παύλῳ) συνα- [?]ριθμοῦσι πάντῃ Ἐπιστολαῖς. De Clemente Romano sermonem esse, constat ex verbis annexis; ὃ φασὶν αὐτὴν ἐκ τῆς Ἑβραΐδος μεταφερέσθαι τὸν ἐρμηνευτὴν Κλήμεντα; & dicunt ab eodem Clemente ex Hebræo sermone in Græcum fuisse translatam. Quod Clementi Romano à Veteribus tributum. Huc faciunt omnia illa Clementis Alexandrini, Origenis, Eusebÿ, aliorum testimonia, de Clemente Epistolæ non scriptore, sed Interprete. Quo ipso inter Paulinas à Clemente innuunt fuisse exceptam. Ex quâ etiam translationis famâ, nata opinio de Clemente ipso authore Epistolæ. Quod si illorum obtineret sententia, qui LXXXV. Canones Apostolicos à Clemente collectos arbitrantur, (Gelasio pridem, Gratiano, & Trullanâ Synodo reluctantibus,) sanè Canone LXXXIV, inter libros N.T. recensentur Παῦλο ἐπιστολαὶ δεκατέσσαρες, Pauli Epistolæ quatuordecim. Quanquam nec hic canon genuinus est cordatioribus ex Pontificiis; ob expunctam Apocalypsim, admissas verò Clementis Epistolas, & VIII. Constitutionum Libros.
units.tr: II. Clement of Rome, a contemporary of the Apostles, of whom, according to Jerome, Paul writes to the Philippians ch. iv. [verse 3], in the Epistle which is said to have been written to the Corinthians in the person of the Roman Church, and which Eusebius [illegible] to all, Hist. Book III, ch. xxxii, cites the Epistle to the Hebrews several times, both in sense and in words. So Eusebius in the passage above, cited in the previous chapter §. vii. So Jerome on Clement: But he also abuses the same Epistle, not only in its meanings but also in the very order of the words. Now indeed, if the Epistle is earlier than Clement, if it is cited by Clement, if it was held by him among the canonical books, to whom else should it be ascribed but to Paul, of the choir of Apostles? Gobarus, quoted by Photius, Cod. ccxxii, affirms the same of Clement: Clement indeed ... the others [Paul's] numbered together in all Epistles. That the discussion concerns Clement of Rome is clear from the words annexed: which they say was translated from the Hebrew tongue by the interpreter Clement; and they say it was translated from Hebrew into Greek by this same Clement. This was attributed by the Ancients to Clement of Rome. To this point belong all those testimonies of Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius and others, about Clement not as the writer but as the translator of the Epistle. By this very fact they imply that he admitted it among the Pauline Epistles. From this same report of the translation arose the opinion that Clement himself was the author of the Epistle. But if the opinion prevailed of those who think the eighty-five Apostolic Canons were collected by Clement (Gelasius, Gratian and the Trullan Synod having long ago objected), then indeed in Canon LXXXIV the books of the New Testament are enumerated as Paul's Epistles, fourteen [Παῦλου ἐπιστολαὶ δεκατέσσαρες]. Yet not even this canon is genuine in the judgment of the more discerning among the Papists, on account of the Apocalypse being struck out, while the Epistles of Clement and the eight Books of the Constitutions are admitted.

units.la: III. Quæ secundo sæculo fuerit sententia Latinorum, haud sanè ex illius ævi scriptis intelligimus. Vix enim eorum genuini quicquam & synceri ad nos transmissum. Si forte Minucium unum excipias, quem tamen Tertulliano postponit Hieronymus, & ex eo Trithemius de script. Eccles. Cujusque nec argumentum, nec genus dicendi, de Epistolâ nos certiores reddere patiebatur. Non magis quàm de illius mente circa Universalitatem misericordiæ, redemptionis, & vocationis, quam ex Minucio, ineptissimus Rhapsodus, probare nuper lepidè satagebat. Certum tamen hoc sæculo moveri inter Latinos quosdam cœptâ, ipsam hanc de Authore Epistolæ controversiam. De quo dicendum infrà fuerit fusiùs & distinctiùs.
units.tr: III. What the opinion of the Latins was in the second century we cannot at all learn from the writings of that age, for scarcely anything genuine and pure from them has come down to us. If perhaps you except Minucius alone, whom Jerome nevertheless places below Tertullian, and after him Trithemius in De script. Eccles., his subject and style of writing do not allow us to be informed about the Epistle, any more than about his mind concerning the universality of mercy, redemption and calling, which the most inept rhapsodist recently tried so wittily to prove from Minucius. It is certain, however, that in this century the very controversy about the author of the Epistle began to be stirred among some Latins. This shall be discussed more fully and distinctly below.

units.la: IV. Nihil obstat tamen, quò minùs sanctissimi Latinæ Patres Ecclesiæ, paucissimis demptis, perpetua serie ab antiquissimis temporibus Paulo Epistolam transcriptum iverint. Cyprianus, Episcopus Carthaginensis, secundus Latinorum rum Patrum, magnus Tertullianei nominis æstimator, martyrio sublatus tertio nonnihil inclinante sæculo, Epistolam ad Hebræos ut Paulinam citat, Libro de Cardinal. Operibus Christi ad Cornelium. Quod licet opus, Possevinus, & Erasmus Cypriano affectum censent, refert sane in plurimis genium Cypriani, & pervetustum esse in confesso est. Pariter inter opera Cypriani, & sub ejus nomine, habetur Expositio in symbolum Apostolorum (Ruffino aliàs adscripta) cujus articul.36. inter Novi Testamenti Libros recensentur Pauli Apostoli Epistolæ quatuordecim. Quod excipitur, nusquam usurpari Epistolam Cypriano in scriptis confessis & ἀδιάθετος[?], infrà notamus.
units.tr: IV. Nothing stands in the way, however, of the most holy Latin Fathers of the Church, with very few exceptions, having carried the Epistle over to Paul in an unbroken series from the most ancient times. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, the second of the Latin Fathers, a great admirer of the name of Tertullian, taken away by martyrdom while the third century was somewhat declining, cites the Epistle to the Hebrews as Paul's, in the book On the Cardinal Works of Christ, to Cornelius. Although Possevinus and Erasmus judge this work to be affected by Cyprian, it certainly bears in most respects the genius of Cyprian and is admittedly very old. Likewise among the works of Cyprian, and under his name, is found an Exposition of the Apostles' Creed (elsewhere ascribed to Rufinus), in whose article 36 the fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul are listed among the books of the New Testament. As for the exception, that nowhere does Cyprian use the Epistle in writings confessedly his, we note below.

units.la: V. Arnobius Presbyter, Philosophus & Rhetor, quarto ineunte sæculo in Africa celebratus, Commentario in Psalmum civ. (si modo Arnobij est, ex Trithemij, Erasmi aliorumque etiam mente) citaturus Caput vi. Epistolæ ad Hebræos, Paulus clamat Hebræus ex Hebræis. Libris vero vii. adversus Gentes EpiEpistolæ nullus meminit. Nec mirum rationibus pugnans non authoritate; Platonem verius, quàm Paulum objectans; proprio Gentiles gladio, rarius alieno scripturarum jugulans; Iustinum, Minucium, Tertullianum, Cyprianum, antecessores in simili imitatus argumento. Ut non procedat negativa illa quorundam ab Epistolâ non citatâ ad rejectam, argumentatio.
units.tr: V. Arnobius, a presbyter, philosopher and rhetorician, celebrated in Africa at the beginning of the fourth century, in his Commentary on Psalm civ (if indeed it is Arnobius's, in the opinion of Trithemius, Erasmus and others), when about to cite ch. vi of the Epistle to the Hebrews, says: Paul, a Hebrew of the Hebrews, cries out. Yet in the seven Books against the Gentiles he mentions the Epistle nowhere. Nor is this surprising: he fights with reasons rather than with authority, objecting more to Plato than to Paul, slaying the Gentiles with their own sword and more rarely with another's Scriptures, having imitated Justin, Minucius, Tertullian and Cyprian, his predecessors, in a similar line of argument. So that negative argument of some, from an Epistle not cited to a rejected one, does not hold.

units.la: VI. Lactantius Firmianus, discipulus Arnobij; florens sub Diocletiano & Constantino, & de quo Trithemius, de script. Eccles. in arte dicendi post Ciceronem facile obtinuisse principatum, pari cum cæteris incedit passu. Paulum Epistolæ authorem nec affirmat, nec negat. Totus in Gentilibus confutandis, & principiis ipsis Christianę religionis vindicandis, occupatus. Ratione ergo usus, & argumentis, & poëtarum, philosophorum, Sibyllarum, Trismegisti, authoritate, Pauli nequaquam. Hinc ipse Lactantius divinarum Inst. Lib. v. C. iv. Gentiles non scripturæ testimonijs, quam illi illiutique[?] vanam, fictam, commentitiam putant, sed argumentis & ratione esse re-fellendos. Hinc ob eam in profanarum religionum errore subvertendo dexteritatem, Apollinaris Ep. III.[?] ad Claudian. In-struit ut Hieronymus, adstruit ut Augustinus, destruit ut Lactantius. Prophetas tamen nonnunquam, ob eventum vaticiniorum adhibet in causæ subsidium. Interim Epistolam ad Hebræos adscripsisse Paulo, vel ex omnium ferè Latinorum, quotquot etiam ex Afris, post Lactantium scripsere consensu colligimus.
units.tr: VI. Lactantius Firmianus, a disciple of Arnobius, flourishing under Diocletian and Constantine, and of whom Trithemius, in De script. Eccles., says that "after Cicero he easily obtained the leading place in the art of speaking", goes along with the others at the same pace. He neither affirms nor denies that Paul is the author of the Epistle. Wholly occupied in refuting the Gentiles and defending the very principles of the Christian religion, he used reason and arguments, and the authority of poets, philosophers, Sibyls and Trismegistus, but by no means Paul's. Hence Lactantius himself, in the Divine Institutes, Book v, ch. iv, says that the Gentiles, who think Scripture's testimonies vain, fictitious and made up, are to be refuted by arguments and reason. Hence, because of his skill in overthrowing the error of the profane religions, Apollinaris, Ep. III, to Claudian, says: He instructs as Jerome, he establishes as Augustine, he destroys as Lactantius. He does, however, sometimes adduce the prophets, because of the fulfilment of their prophecies, as support for his cause. Meanwhile, from the agreement of almost all the Latins who wrote after Lactantius, including those from Africa, we gather that they ascribed the Epistle to the Hebrews to Paul.

units.la: VII. Certè Marius Victorinus Afer, clarus sub Constantio & Constantino, etiam Juliano Principibus, de quo Hieronymus in script. Eccles. adversus Arrium Libro I. Idcirco adjecit Paulus, quousque ponat omnes inimicos, scabellum pedum qui locus extat Hebr.x.13. Alibi Libro II. Ipsum substantiam dicit Paulus ad Hebræos, Hebr.1.3.
units.tr: VII. Certainly Marius Victorinus, an African, famous under Constantius and Constantine, even under the Emperor Julian, of whom Jerome, in De script. Eccles., says: in his first book against Arius: For this reason Paul added, "until he puts all his enemies as a footstool for his feet", which passage stands in Hebrews 10:13. Elsewhere, in Book II: Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews that he is the substance, Heb. 1:3.

units.la: VIII. Optatus itidem Afer, Milevitanus, in Numidiâ Episcopus æqualis Victorino: Libro VI. adversus Parmenianum DonaDonatistam : citat pariter locum Paulinum ad Hebr. viii. 10. de novo Fœdere pangendo post illos dies, &c. Non quidem expresso Pauli Apostoli nomine, ut affirmat Baronius, sed eo haud obscurè notato.
units.tr: VIII. Optatus, likewise an African, of Milevis, a bishop in Numidia contemporary with Victorinus, in Book VI against Parmenianus the Donatist, likewise cites the Pauline passage Heb. 8:10, on making the new covenant after those days, etc. Not, indeed, with the express name of the Apostle Paul, as Baronius asserts, but with it clearly indicated.

units.la: IX. Hilarius, Episcopus Pictaviensis, Latinæ Eloquentiæ Rhodanus, clarus sub Constantio, mortuus Valentiniano & Valente regnantibus; Libr. iv. de Trinitate, Facturam autem, per id quod Paulus ad Hebræos dixerit. Tanto melior factus est Angelis &c. Hebr.1.4. Arianæ idem ille hæreseos profligator acerrimus, atque adeò Epistolæ vindex.
units.tr: IX. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, the Rhone of Latin eloquence, famous under Constantius and dead under the reign of Valentinian and Valens. In Book IV of On the Trinity, he says: Moreover, the making is shown by what Paul said to the Hebrews: He was made so much better than the angels, and so on. [Heb. 1.4.] He was also a most fierce opponent of the same Arian heresy and therefore a defender of the Epistle.

units.la: X. Gregorius Baeticus, Hiberi Episcopus, sub Valentiniano & Valente Imperatoribus; Libro de fide, Epistolam inducit ut Paulinam, Alibi docet Apostolus de Filio Dei esse scriptum. Et adorent eum omnes Angeli &c. Hebr.1.6. Quin & ipse à partibus Catholicorum contrà Arianos stetisse fertur, apud Eusebi[?]. Chronicorum Libr. poster. in Valentiniano & Valente. Torserit ergo in Arianos egregia, quæ Epistola suppeditat, argumenta.
units.tr: X. Gregory of Baetica, bishop of Iberia, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens. In his book On Faith, he introduces the Epistle as Paul's, saying: The Apostle teaches elsewhere that it is written of the Son of God: And let all the angels of God worship him, and so on. [Heb. 1.6.] Indeed, he is said to have taken the side of the Catholics against the Arians, according to Eusebius (?) in the later book of the Chronicles, under Valentinian and Valens. So he turned the outstanding arguments that the Epistle supplies against the Arians.

units.la: XI. Synodus Romana, sub Damaso Episcopo Romano, adversus haereses Apollinaris, Timothei, & sectatorum, indicta A.C. CCCLXXIII. Valentiniani, x. (ut Baronius ad eundem annum T. iv. Annal. Eccles.) sancivit numerum Canonicorum, & Paulinis Epistolis accensuit tnam[?] ad Hebraeos. Cujus licet Synodi Acta penitus interciderint, hinc inde ex fragmentis nonnulla restituta. De hoc Canone alibi Baronius ad A.C. LX. num. LIII. item ad A.C. CCCCV. num. LXIII.
units.tr: XI. The Roman Synod, convened under Damasus, bishop of Rome, against the heresies of Apollinaris, Timothy and their followers, in the year of Christ 373, the tenth year of Valentinian (as Baronius reports at that year, vol. IV of the Ecclesiastical Annals), laid down the number of canonical books and counted the Epistle to the Hebrews among the Pauline Epistles. Although the acts of this Synod have entirely perished, some of its contents have been restored from scattered fragments. Baronius discusses this canon elsewhere, at the year of Christ 60, no. LIII, and again at the year of Christ 405, no. LXIII.

units.la: XII. Faustinus, Presbyter Romanus, clarus sub Valentiniano & Theodosio, Libro de fide contra Arianos ad Flaccillam, Cap. iv. adducturus locum Hebr. 1. 5. Ad quem Angelorum dixit &c. utitur his verbis, Paulus Apostolus ait in Epistola sua. Ita locis passim aliis Epistolam sub Pauli Apostoli nomine citat.
units.tr: XII. Faustinus, a Roman presbyter, famous under Valentinian and Theodosius. In his book On Faith against the Arians, addressed to Flaccilla, chapter 4, when he is about to cite Heb. 1.5, To which of the angels did he ever say, and so on, he uses these words: The Apostle Paul says in his Epistle. In this way he cites the Epistle under the name of the Apostle Paul in many other places too.

units.la: XIII. Ambrosius, Mediolanensis Episcopus, magni & excelsi vir animi, natus sub Constantino Magno, denatus sub Theodosio, quarto nondum expirante sæculo ; scripsisse fertur Commentarium in Epistolam ad Hebræos , quam vocat Beati Pauli Apostoli. In Proœmio verò sic loquitur. Qua ratione quóve consilio scripserit Beatus Paulus genti suæ populo Hebræorum, ipsius verbis deprehenditur. Timuit eis, ne superatis tentationibus ad infidelitatem relaberentur. Ibidem exponit causas suppressi nominis, & odij Ju-dæorum in Paulum. Quare autem Aposto-lus morem suum peculiarem scribendi ac phrasim non servaverit, vel nominis sui vel Apostolatus dignitatem subticuerit, conspicuum est &c. Nec clàm nobis est, quid de hoc Commentario, ut additicio plerique eruditorum censent. Inter eos, Clar. Rivetus Crit.Sacr. L. iii [?] C.xix. E-rasmo subscribens, & David Blondellus de Episcopis & presbyt. sect.ii. Testimo-nio xxi. qui ex Chrysostomo & Hieronymo compaginatam farraginem vocat. Quod etiamsi vel maximè largiamur, & Com-mentarios illos vel Remigij, vel Anselmi, vel alius cujusdam esse arbitremur, atqui idem Ambrosius, utique Epistolam usurpat ut Pauli. Imo fere totam sparsim quinque Operum Tomis interpretatur. De Ambrosio ipse Erasmus, in Cap.xiii. Epist. ad Hebr. Ambrosius licet in hanc unam non ediderit Commentarios, tamen ejus testimoniis non infrequenter utitur, & videtur eam Paulo tribuere.
units.tr: XIII. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a man of great and lofty spirit, born under Constantine the Great and dead under Theodosius, while the fourth century was not yet at an end. He is said to have written a commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, which he calls the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul. In its preface he speaks as follows: For what reason and with what purpose the blessed Paul wrote to his own people, the Hebrews, is shown by his own words. He feared that, having been overcome by temptations, they would fall back into unbelief. In the same place he sets out the reasons why he suppressed his name and why the Jews hated Paul. Why the Apostle did not keep his peculiar habit of writing and style, and passed over the dignity of his name or of his apostleship, is evident, and so on. Nor is it unknown to us what most learned men think of this commentary, namely that it is an addition: among them, the distinguished Rivetus, in Critici Sacri book III, chapter 19, agreeing with Erasmus, and David Blondel, in On Bishops and Presbyters, section 2, testimony 21, who calls it a hodgepodge put together from Chrysostom and Jerome. But even if we grant this entirely, and think that those commentaries belong to Remigius, or Anselm, or some other person, nevertheless Ambrose himself plainly uses the Epistle as Paul's. Indeed, he interprets nearly all of it, scattered through five volumes of his works. Erasmus himself, on Hebrews chapter 13, says of Ambrose: Although Ambrose did not publish a commentary on this one Epistle, nevertheless he not infrequently uses its testimonies, and seems to attribute it to Paul.

units.la: XIV. Philastrius, Episcopus Brixiensis, æqualis Ambrosio; Libro de Hæresibus, Hæres.xli. specialem hæresim constituit eorum, qui Epistolam ad Hebræos Pauli esse inficiantur. Sunt alij quoque qui Epistolam Pauli ad Hebræos non asserunt esse ipsius, sed dicunt aut Barnabæ esse Apostoli, aut Clementis de urbe Romæ Episcopi: Rationes tres potissimum adducit, quarum prima est, quia rhetoricè scripsit, sermone plausibili; altera quia Christum factum dicit; tertia quia favere videtur Novatianis.
units.tr: XIV. Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, a contemporary of Ambrose, in his book On Heresies (Heresy 41), set up a distinct heresy of those who deny that the Epistle to the Hebrews is Paul's. There are also others who do not maintain that the Epistle to the Hebrews is Paul's, but say that it is either by the Apostle Barnabas or by Clement, bishop of the city of Rome. He adduces three main reasons. The first is that it is written rhetorically, in a persuasive style; the second that it says Christ was made; the third that it seems to favour the Novatians.

units.la: XV. Hieronymus, Presbyter, natus sub Constantio, florens sub Theodosio, denatus sub Honorio extremâ jam senectute, Paulum Epistolæ authorem non uno loco pronunciat. Libro de Scriptoribus Ecclesiast. in Paulo, reddens causas variantium circa Epistolæ scriptorem sententiarum, Vel certè quia Paulus scribebat ad Hebræos & propter invidiam sui apud eos nominis, titulum in principio salutationis amputaverit. Scripserat autem ut Hebræus, Hebræis Hebraicè, &c. & hanc causam esse, quòd à cæteris Pauli Epistolis discrepare videatur. Alibi Epistolâ cxxix. ad Dardanum, postquam varia ex Epistolâ ad Hebræos protulisset in medium, obiter movet controversiam de Authore & Authoritate Epistolæ; & posthabitâ quorundam Latinorum consuetudine, Comment. ad Galat. C. i. opponit Græcorum omnium & Ecclesiarum Orientis de Paulo scriptore consensum, monet dubia itidem exorta in Græcorum Ecclesiis de Apocalypsi Johannis; mòxque subjungit, Nos tamen utraque suscipimus, nequaquam hujus temporis consuetudinem sed veterum scriptorum authoritatem sequentes, qui
units.tr: XV. Jerome, presbyter, born under Constantius, flourishing under Theodosius, and dying under Honorius in extreme old age, does not pronounce Paul the author of the Epistle in one place only. In his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Paul, he gives reasons for the differing opinions about the writer of the Epistle: Either certainly because Paul was writing to the Hebrews, and on account of the hatred of his name among them, he removed the title at the beginning of the salutation. He had written, moreover, as a Hebrew, to Hebrews in Hebrew, etc., and this is the reason why it seems to differ from his other Epistles. Elsewhere, in Epistle 129 to Dardanus, after bringing forward various things from the Epistle to the Hebrews, he incidentally raises the controversy concerning the author and authority of the Epistle. Setting aside the custom of some Latins, in his Commentary on Galatians ch. 1 he opposes to it the agreement of all the Greeks and the Churches of the East that Paul was the writer. He warns that doubts likewise arose in the Greek Churches about the Apocalypse of John, and he presently adds: Yet we receive both, following not the custom of this time but the authority of the ancient writers, who

units.la: H... p!aplerumque utriusque abutuntur refutan-nijs, &c. Epistolâ cxxvi. ad Euagrium, de-gens de Melchisedeco, Praeterea plurimum esse tractatum in Epistolâ ad Hebræos, quam omnes Græci recipiunt, & nonnulli Latinorum. Ibidem sapiùs, Affirmat Apostolus, Apostolus in Epistolâ suâ ad Hebræos. Alibi Commentar. in Esaiam, L. v. C. VIII. Caeterum beatus Apostolus in epistolâ quae ad Hebræos scribitur &c. Commentariorum Libro IX. in Ezech. C.XXVIII. Et Paulus Apostolus loquitur (si quis tamen ad Hebræos Epistolam scripsit,) Accessistis ad Sion montem &c. Comment. in Matt. ad Caput XVI. Tomo VI. Lib. IV. Nam & Paulus in Epistolâ suâ, licet de eâ multi Latinorum dubitent, quae scribitur ad Hebræos. Comment. in Epist. ad Ephes. Cap. II. Nescio quid mihi & in aliâ Epistolâ (si quis tamen eam recipit) Paulus subjicit dicens &c. Comment. in Epist. ad Titum Cap. II. Relege ad Hebræos Epistolam Pauli Apostoli, sive cujuscunque alterius [?] esse putas. Comment. in Epist. ad Galat. Cap. I. exponit ratiorationes ob quas non se Apostolum hic, ut alias, inscripserit. Libro de Nomin. Hebraicis, Epistolam ad Hebræos ordine inter Paulinas recenset, & præponit Epistolis ad Timotheum &c.
units.tr: ...for the most part abuse both in their refutations, etc. In Epistle 126 to Evagrius, speaking of Melchizedek, he says: Moreover, there is much treated in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which all Greeks receive and some Latins too. In the same place, more often: The Apostle affirms, and the Apostle in his Epistle to the Hebrews. Elsewhere, in his Commentary on Isaiah, book 5 ch. 8: Moreover, the blessed Apostle in the epistle that is written to the Hebrews, etc. In Commentary on Ezekiel, book 9 ch. 28: And the Apostle Paul speaks (if however he wrote the Epistle to the Hebrews): You have come to Mount Sion, etc. In Commentary on Matthew, on ch. 16, Tome VI, book 4: For Paul too, in his Epistle, although many of the Latins doubt about it, which is written to the Hebrews. In Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians ch. 2: I know not what Paul adds in another Epistle (if however anyone receives it), saying, etc. In Commentary on the Epistle to Titus ch. 2: Reread the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews, or of whatever other author you think it is. In Commentary on Galatians ch. 1 he sets out the reasons why he did not inscribe himself "apostle" here, as he did elsewhere. In his book On Hebrew Names he lists the Epistle to the Hebrews in order among the Pauline Epistles, and places it before the Epistles to Timothy, etc.

units.la: XVI. Gaudentius, Episcopus Brixiensis, successor Philastrij, cum Ambrosio [?]fidem florens ; de manducat. agni Pa-schal. sermone II. Lamborum ratio quæ est, significat Apostolus ad Hebræos, Ad-huc (inquit) in lumbis Patris erat Levi. Hebr. VII.10. Sermone XIII. sub initium, Quoniam vetus lex, ut ait Apostolus, um-bra erat futurorum bonorum, Hebr. X.1.
units.tr: XVI. Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia, successor of Philastrius, flourishing in the faith with Ambrose. On the eating of the Passover lamb, sermon II: "The reason of the loins, which the Apostle to the Hebrews signifies: 'Still,' he says, 'Levi was in the loins of his father.'" Heb. 7.10. Sermon XIII, near the beginning: "Since the old law, as the Apostle says, was a shadow of good things to come," Heb. 10.1.

units.la: XVII. Rufinus monachus, & Aquileiensis Ecclesiæ presbyter, qui & in Hieronymum scripsit, Invectivarum libros: in symbolo ad Laurentium Episcopum, Tomo IX. Oper. Hieronymi, Epist. XIX. Credo igitur primò omnium ponitur, sicut Paulus Apostolus ad Hebræos scribens dixit, Credere oportet accedentem &c. Hebr. XI.6. Infra, Idem Apostolus iterum ad Hebræos scribens dicit. Quia per ipsum sæcula instituit &c. Hebr. I.3. Tandem e-
units.tr: XVII. Rufinus, monk and presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, who also wrote the books of Invectives against Jerome, in his treatise on the Creed, addressed to Laurentius the bishop (Tome IX of Jerome's works, Epistle XIX): "I believe, therefore, and this comes first of all, as the Apostle Paul writing to the Hebrews said: it is necessary to believe that he who comes" etc. Heb. 11.6. Below: "The same Apostle again, writing to the Hebrews, says: 'Through him he also made the ages'" etc. Heb. 1.3. At last, the Creed

units.la: numeratur, novi ac Veteris Testamenti volumina, Novi vero quatuor Evangelia, Actus Apostolorum, quos describit Lucas, Pauli Apostoli Epistolae quatuordecim.
units.tr: enumerates the volumes of the Old and New Testament. Of the New, indeed, the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, which Luke describes, and the fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul.

units.la: XVIII. Augustinus Afer, Hipponensis Episcopus, sacrae decus omnis antiquitatis, calculo idem suo comprobavit; De doctrina christiana, L. II. C. VIII. Tom. III. διδασκαλίας, agens de Libris Canonicis eorumque numero, Novi Testamenti terminatur authoritas, quatuor Libris Evangelii &c. quatuordecim Epistolis Pauli Apostoli, ad Romanos &c. ad Hebraeos. De civitate Dei, L. XVI. C. XXII. agens de Melchisedeco, De quo in Epistola quae inscribitur ad Hebraeos, quam plures Apostoli Pauli esse dicunt, quidam vero negant, multa & magna conscripta sunt. Ad quae verba Ludovicus Vives, Hieronymus, Origenes, Augustinus, & alij Veterum de hoc ambigunt. Ante aetatem Hieronymi a Latinis ea Epistola recepta non erat inter sacras. De hac re multis & dubiis verbis disputat Erasmus noster &c.
units.tr: XVIII. Augustine of Africa, Bishop of Hippo, the glory of all sacred antiquity, confirmed the same with his own vote. In On Christian Doctrine, book 2 ch. 8, Tome III, treating of the canonical books and their number: "The authority of the New Testament is completed by the four books of the Gospel," etc., "the fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, to the Romans," etc., "to the Hebrews." In The City of God, book 16 ch. 22, treating of Melchizedek: "Concerning whom, in the Epistle which is inscribed to the Hebrews, which many say is of the Apostle Paul, while some deny it, many great things have been written." On these words, Ludovicus Vives notes that Jerome, Origen, Augustine and other ancients doubt about this. Before Jerome's time that Epistle was not received among the sacred books by the Latins. Our Erasmus disputes this matter at length, with many doubtful words, etc.

units.la: Mira
units.tr: Marvellous

units.la: Mirâ sanè in affirmando temeritate. De Hieronymo, de Origene, de Græcis omnibus videmus. De Latinis ante Hieronymi tempora infrà accuratiùs disquirimus. Quâ etiam fide Erasmus in hac quæstione versatus sit, suo docemus loco. Quod verò ambigisse putet magnum Augustinum, in eo τὸ [?]πάντως [?]ἀναμφισβητήτως ἡ-μάρτηκε. Ambigitne, qui suprà in definiendo Canone, quatuordecim Pauli dicit Epistolas, eam quæ est ad Hebræos complexus? Et quidem in scripto non agoni-stico, non homilico, sed dogmatico, ubi jam docet, instruit & animi sensa sui cautiùs & libratiùs promit? Qui in amplâ illâ operum segete toties Epistolam ut Pauli usurpat Apostoli? Qui illo ipso loco de Civit. Dei plurium testimonio Paulo vindicari docet, & de cætero, ad quorundam Latinorum consuetudinem, minimè sanè suam, respicit?
units.tr: Marvellous indeed in the rashness of his assertion. We see this in Jerome, in Origen, and in all the Greeks. Concerning the Latins before Jerome's time, we inquire more carefully below. We also show in its own place with what good faith Erasmus handled this question. But that he thinks the great Augustine was in doubt, in that he has τὸ πάντως ἀναμφισβητήτως ἡμάρτηκε [by all means, beyond dispute, gone wrong]. Can he be in doubt who, above, in defining the canon, counts the fourteen epistles of Paul and includes the one to the Hebrews? And indeed he does so in a work that is not agonistic or homiletic but dogmatic, where he is teaching and instructing and expresses his views more cautiously and deliberately. Does he, in that vast harvest of his works, so often use the Epistle as the Apostle Paul's? Does he, in that very passage of the City of God, teach that the testimony of several is claimed for Paul, and elsewhere, following the custom of some Latins, which is certainly not his own, pay no attention to it?

units.la: XIX. Synodus Carthaginensis tertia, cui & Augustinus inter fuit, celebrata A. C. cccxcvii, Arcadij & honorij ImpeImperatorum iii. Ejus Capitul. xlvii. inter Canonicas Scripturas, legendas in Ecclesiâ, recensentur Pauli Apostoli Epi-stolæ xiii. ejusdem ad Hebræos una. Quanquam juxtà alios hic Canon fuerit xxiv. Concilij Carthaginensis, habiti consulatu Honorij xii. Theodosij viii. Papâ Zozimo; juxta Baronium alterius Concilij instituti sub Bonifacio Papâ, de quo Annal. Tomo i. ad A. C. ccccxix. num. xcv.
units.tr: XIX. The Third Council of Carthage, at which Augustine was also present, was held in the year 397 of Christ, in the third consulship of the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius. In its forty-seventh canon, among the canonical Scriptures to be read in the Church, are listed the thirteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, with the one to the Hebrews among them. Yet according to others this canon belongs to the twenty-fourth canon of the Council of Carthage, held in the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, under Pope Zosimus; according to Baronius, it belongs to another council instituted under Pope Boniface, on which see Annals, Vol. i, at the year 419 of Christ, number xcv.

units.la: XX. Paulinus Episcopus Nolanus, σύγχρον[?] Augustino & Hieronymo, vir summæ existimationis; in eandem cum cæteris sententiam de Paulo Epistolæ scri-ptore, concessit. Fidem faciunt, quæ il-lius hodieque supersunt, in quibus Epi-stolam aliquoties citat ut Pauli Apostoli Consuli possunt Paulini Nolani Epistolæ, nobis sanè impræsentiarum non ad manus; & Baronius ad A. C. lx. num. l.
units.tr: XX. Paulinus, Bishop of Nola, a contemporary of Augustine and Jerome, a man of the highest reputation, likewise agreed with the others in holding that Paul was the writer of the Epistle. The letters of his that survive to this day give proof of this, in which he several times cites the Epistle as Paul the Apostle's. Those who wish may consult the Letters of Paulinus of Nola, which are not at hand for me at present; and Baronius at the year 60 of Christ, number l.

units.la: XXI. Innocentius, Romanus Episco-pus, quinto ineunte sæculo, de quo meminit Hieronymus; Epistolâ iii ad Exuperium Episcopum Tolosanum, texens Canonicorum Librorum seriem, sub finem Epistolæ recenset Pauli Epistolas quatuordecim. Decretalem quanquam non dixerimus Epistolam cum Baronio ad A.C. ccccv. num. lxiii. Minus habendam in Scripturis Canonicis, ut impiè Gratianus dist. xix. Capit. in Canonicis scripturis.
units.tr: XXI. Innocent, Bishop of Rome, at the beginning of the fifth century, whom Jerome mentions. In his third letter, to Exuperius, Bishop of Toulouse, setting out the series of the canonical books, he counts at the end of the letter fourteen Epistles of Paul. Although we would not call it a Decretal, we do not agree with Baronius, at the year 405 of Christ, number lxiii, that it should be held less than canonical Scripture, as the impious Gratian says, distinction xix, chapter in canonicis scripturis.

units.la: XXII. Idacius Clarus, Lemice Hispaniarum Episcopus, florens sub Theodosio, A.C. cccc. de quo Isidorus, libro de Viris Illustribus, & Sulpitius L. ii. Hist. sacræ: adversus Varimadum Arrianum, Paulus Apostolus ad Hebræos: In eo enim quo passus est ille qui tentatus est &c. Alibi. Paulo Apostolo attestante: Multis partibus & multis modis olim locutus &c. Alia id genus loca sub nomine Pauli Apostoli, habentur apud eundem allegata.
units.tr: XXII. Idacius Clarus, Bishop of Lemica in Spain, flourishing under Theodosius, in the year 400 of Christ, of whom Isidore, in his book on Illustrious Men, and Sulpicius, book ii of the Sacred History, speak. Against Varimadus the Arian, he says: "Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews: For in that wherein he himself suffered, being tempted, etc." Elsewhere: "The Apostle Paul bearing witness: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past, etc." Other passages of this kind are cited under the name of the Apostle Paul by the same author.

units.la: XXIII. Bachiarius, qui tempore Augustini vixisse fertur, de quo Gennadius, Illustrium virorum Catalogo, inserto Tomo ix. Oper. Hieronymi; Epistolâ ad Januarium de recipiendis lapsis, Respondissem Tibi secundum Apostolicam sententiam, qua loquitur ad Hebræos; qui Abrahæ lumbis latens Levi, decimas à Mel-chisedec accepit & dedit.
units.tr: XXIII. Bachiarius, who is said to have lived in Augustine's time, of whom Gennadius, in his Catalogue of Illustrious Men, inserted in volume ix of Jerome's works, speaks. In his letter to Januarius on receiving the fallen, he writes: "I would have answered you according to the Apostolic saying, which speaks to the Hebrews: Levi, who was hidden in the loins of Abraham, received tithes from Melchizedek and gave them."

units.la: XXIV. Sedulius Scotus & Presbyter, clarus sub Theodosio A. C. circiter cccc-xxx, (si fides Trithemio, ) Comment. in Epistolam Pauli ad Hebræos, si modo Sedulij est; Quoniam apud Hebræorum Ecclesias destructæ legis falsâ suspicione habebatur, voluit tacito nomine de figuris Legis, & veritate Christi reddere rationem, ne odio nominis fronte prælati, utilitatem concluderet lectionis. Quæ verba esse reperio quæ occurrunt in Primasio, Præfat. in Epistolas Pauli. Sed idem Sedulius, in Opere Paschali, Epistolam Paulo vindicat aliquoties.
units.tr: XXIV. Sedulius, a Scot and presbyter, famous under Theodosius, about the year 430 of Christ (if we may trust Trithemius), wrote a commentary on the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews, if indeed it is Sedulius's: "Since among the churches of the Hebrews the law which had been abolished was held in false suspicion, he wished, without naming the author, to give an account of the figures of the Law and of the truth of Christ, so that the usefulness of the reading would not be cut off by the hatred of the name that stood at the front." I find these words to be those which occur in Primasius, in his preface to the Epistles of Paul. But the same Sedulius, in his Paschal Work, claims the Epistle for Paul several times.

units.la: XXV. Johannes Cassianus, Chrysostomi auditor, Diaconus, Constantinopolitanus Massiliensis postea Presbyter & Monachus, cum Prospero commissus. de Incarnat. L. vii. Ergò & Paulus mentitur de Christo dicens, sine matre, sine Genealogiâ. Interrogo te, de quo hoc velis dixisse Paulum?
units.tr: XXV. John Cassian, a hearer of Chrysostom, a deacon of Constantinople, afterwards a presbyter and monk of Marseilles, who was at odds with Prosper, in his work on the Incarnation, book vii: "Therefore Paul also lies about Christ when he says, without mother, without genealogy. I ask you, of whom would Paul wish this to be said?"

units.la: XXVI. Cerealis Episcopus Africa-nus, clarus quinto etiam sæculo ; Libro contrà Maximianum Arianum, citat lo-ca Hebr. 1. & ii. de Christo splendore glo-riæ, &c. modicum minore Angelis, hac formula; Apostolus Paulus ad Hebræos de ipso dicit.
units.tr: XXVI. Caesarius, an African bishop, famous also in the fifth century. In his book against the Arian Maximinus, he cites the passages of Hebrews 1 and 2 about Christ, "the brightness of his glory, etc.," and "a little lower than the angels," with this formula: "The Apostle Paul says of him, to the Hebrews."

units.la: XXVII. Faustus ex Abbate, creatus Episcopus Rhegiensis, A.G. (ut quidam) ccccLxxii[?]. Pelagianæ tandem hæreseos notatus: Libro de Gratia Dei, postmodum à Fulgentio & Alcimo Episcopis confutato, Lib. i. C. vii. citat ex. E-pist. ad Hebr. C. xi. 5, 6. sub nomi-ne Pauli Apostoli. Idem etiam a-libi.
units.tr: XXVII. Faustus, from an abbot made Bishop of Riez, around the year 472 of Christ (as some hold). He was at last branded with the Pelagian heresy. In his book on the Grace of God, later refuted by the bishops Fulgentius and Alcimus, book i, chapter vii, he cites Hebrews 11:5, 6 from the Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of the Apostle Paul. He does the same elsewhere.

units.la: XXVIII. Victor, Uticensis Episcopus, συγχρόνος[?] ; in Fidei ratione ad Hunericum Regem Wandalor. Apostolus de eodem filio dicit ; Qui cum sit splendor gloriæ & figura substantiæejus. Hebr. i. 3.
units.tr: XXVIII. Victor, Bishop of Utica, a contemporary; in his account of the faith, addressed to Huneric, King of the Vandals: "The Apostle says of the same Son: Who being the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person," Hebrews 1:3.

units.la: XXIX. Ruricius Episcopus, æqualis Fausto, & Sidonio Apollinari; L.ii. Epi-stolarum, Epist. ad Verum, Ut sicut dicit Apostolus, multifariè multisque modis nos erudiret verbis, instrueret disciplinis, provocaret beneficijs, informaret exem-plis &c.
units.tr: XXIX. Ruricius, Bishop, a contemporary of Faustus and of Sidonius Apollinaris. In book ii of his Letters, in the letter to Verus: "As the Apostle says, he taught us in many parts and in many ways, instructed us with words, trained us with disciplines, moved us with benefits, and formed us with examples," etc.

units.la: XXX. Gelasius, Episcopus Romanus, sub finem v. sæculi, congregato Romæ Concilio, recensuit Canonicos V. & N. Testamenti, ut & libros omnes Ecclesia-sticos. Hic ergò Decreto de libris Canon. Paulinis Epistolis accenset eam quæ est ad Hebræos. Sic, de libris in Ecclesiasticis officiis per anni circulum legi solitis. In parasceve tres lectiones de Apostolo, uti ait in Epistolà ad Hebræos &c. In Sabba-tho sancto tres de Apostolo, ut in Epistolà ad Hebræos, ubi ait, Christus assistens Pontifex &c. De his Gratianus dist. xv. Capit. Sancta Romana Ecclesia, §. Cæte-rùm qui libri.
units.tr: XXX. Gelasius, Bishop of Rome, near the end of the fifth century, having gathered a council at Rome, listed the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments, as well as all the ecclesiastical books. In his Decree on the Books of the Canon, he therefore counts among the Pauline Epistles the one to the Hebrews. So too, concerning the books customarily read in the ecclesiastical offices through the course of the year: "On Good Friday three lessons from the Apostle, as he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews, etc. On holy Saturday three from the Apostle, as in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where he says, Christ, appearing as high priest, etc." Gratian speaks of these in distinction xv, chapter Sancta Romana Ecclesia, section "Moreover, which books."

units.la: XXXI. Alcimus Avitus, Viennensis Galliarum Episcopus, clarus sub Zenone & Anastasio Principibus ; in Catalogo script. Canonicorum, heroico carmine, ubi devenit ad scripta Paulina,
units.tr: XXXI. Alcimus Avitus, Bishop of Vienne in Gaul, famous under the emperors Zeno and Anastasius; in his catalogue of the canonical writers, in heroic verse, when he comes to the Pauline writings:

units.la: Bis septena pij quod spargit Epistola Pauli.
units.tr: Twice seven the Epistle of Paul that the pious man scatters.

units.la: XXXII. Vigilius Episcopus Tridentinus, Gelasio, Fulgentio, Avito contemporaneus, sub Anastasio Imperatore. L. II. Contrà Eutychem, adducit locum Hebr. 11.7. Fecisti eum modicum minorem Angelis, his verbis; Paulo ita ad Hebræos loquente. Alibi Disputat. de Christo & Trinitate, Paulus Apostolus de Filio ad Hebræos scribens Hebr. 1.3. Aliis sæpe locis idem.
units.tr: XXXII. Vigilius, Bishop of Trent, a contemporary of Gelasius, Fulgentius and Avitus, under the Emperor Anastasius. In book ii, Against Eutyches, he adduces the passage of Hebrews 2:7, "You made him a little lower than the angels," in these words: "Paul speaking thus to the Hebrews." Elsewhere, in his Disputation on Christ and the Trinity: "The Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews about the Son," Hebrews 1:3. He does the same in many other places.

units.la: XXXIII. Facundus Afer, Hermianensis Episcopus, clarus sub Iustiniano Imperatore: Pro defens. trium Capitul. ex editione Sirmundi, Lib. xii. C. 1. Et ideò cum audiamus Apostolum, inter alios iustos Samson quoque laudantem, atque dicentem &c. Hebr. xi. 32. Ibidem Cap. iii. sic etiam cum Paulus, Petri coapostolus, Christianis omnibus legitur dicens, Obedite præpositis vestris &c. Hebr. xiii. 17.
units.tr: XXXIII. Facundus of Africa, Bishop of Hermiane, famous under the Emperor Justinian. In his Defence of the Three Chapters, from the edition of Sirmond, book xii, chapter 1: "And therefore, since we hear the Apostle, who, praising among other righteous men Samson also, says etc." Hebrews 11:32. In the same work, chapter iii: "So too, since Paul, fellow apostle of Peter, is read as saying to all Christians, Obey your leaders, etc." Hebrews 13:17.

units.la: XXXIV. Ferrandus, Afer Carthaginen-sis Ecclesiae Diaconus, σύγχρον[?] Ful-gentio; ad quem hodiéque extat Ferran-di Epistolium; Epistolâ ad Severum, De quo Paulus ad Hebræos scribens ita ait, Iesus Christus heri & hodie &c. Hebr. xiii. 6.
units.tr: XXXIV. Ferrandus, African, deacon of the Church of Carthage, a contemporary of Fulgentius, whose little letter still survives; in his letter to Severus: "Of whom Paul, writing to the Hebrews, speaks thus: Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, etc." Hebrews 13:6.

units.la: XXXV. Cæsarius Arelatensis Ar-chiepiscopus prioribus ferè æqualis Tri-themio aliâs collocatus in annum DCLXX; homiliâ xviii. hortatoriâ ad Fratres, Non audisti Apostolum dicentem. Per multas tribulationes oportet &c. Hebr. xiii.
units.tr: XXXV. Caesarius of Arles, archbishop, roughly equal in age to the earlier Trithemius, though elsewhere placed in the year 670; in his eighteenth homily, an exhortation to the brothers: "Have you not heard the Apostle saying: We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations, etc." Hebrews 13.

units.la: XXXV. M. Aurelius Cassiodorus, Vir Senatorij Ordinis, clarus sub initia sexti sæculi, quíque eruditionis omnis suo tempore principatum gessit; Libr. Divinar. Lect. C.xii. de divisione script. secundum Hieronymum. Huic etiam ad-jecti sunt Novi Testamenti libri xxvii. Sc. xiv. Paulinis computatis. Ibid. C.xiii. de divis. script. secundum Augustinum, In Epistolis Apostolorum, i.e. Pauli Apostoli, ad Romanos una, ad Corinthios duæ, & in eadem tandem serie, ad Hebræos una. C. XIV. de divis. S. secundum LXX, Epistolæ Pauli, ad Romanos una, ad Corinthios duæ, ad Galatas una, ad Philippenses una, ad Colossenses una; ad Hebræos una &c. Idem Cassiodorus passim ad Epistolam provocat ut Pauli Apostoli, & sub illius nomine aliquoties citat, Libro de Amicitia & aliis.
units.tr: XXXV. M. Aurelius Cassiodorus, a man of senatorial rank, famous at the beginning of the sixth century, who held the first place of all learning in his time. In his Divine Readings, chapter xii, on the division of the Scriptures according to Jerome: "To these were added the books of the New Testament, twenty-seven in number, the fourteen Pauline ones being counted in." In the same work, chapter xiii, on the division of the Scriptures according to Augustine: "In the Epistles of the Apostles, that is, of the Apostle Paul: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians," and in the same sequence at last, "one to the Hebrews." Chapter xiv, on the division of the Scriptures according to the Seventy: "The Epistles of Paul: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians"; "one to the Hebrews," etc. The same Cassiodorus everywhere appeals to the Epistle as Paul the Apostle's, and in his name cites it several times, in his book On Friendship and elsewhere.

units.la: XXXVII. Primasius Episcopus Africanus, Cassiodoro memoratus, divin. Lect. ix. Augustini non discipulus quidem, ut Sixtus, sed sectator, & junior toto sæculo, Præfat. in Epist. Pauli, Biblioth. Patr. Parte 11. Tomis. Decem sunt (sc. Epistolæ Pauli ad Ecclesias) cum ea quæ dicitur ad Hebræos. Et postmodum illos aggreditur confutandos, qui Epistolam Pauli esse negant; si propterea Pauli non erit, quia ejus nomen non habet, nec alicujus erit, quia nullius nomine titulatur. Quod si absurdum est, ipsius magis credenda est, quæ tanto doctrinæ suæ fulget eloquio &c. Præfat. in hanc ipsam ad Hebræos, causas reddit varias taciti tum nominis, tum Apostolatus, de quibus nos parte ultimâ. Quanquam non Primasij, sed Haimonis hic credatur esse Commentarius.
units.tr: XXXVII. Primasius, Bishop of Africa, mentioned by Cassiodorus (Divine Lections, ch. 9), was not a disciple of Augustine as Sixtus was, but a follower, and a whole generation younger. In his Preface to the Epistles of Paul (Bibliotheca Patrum, Part 11, Tome), he says: There are ten (namely the Epistles of Paul to the churches) together with the one called to the Hebrews. He then goes on to refute those who deny that it is an Epistle of Paul: If it is not Paul's because it does not bear his name, neither will it be anyone's, since it is titled with no one's name. But if that is absurd, it is rather to be believed to be his, since it shines with such eloquence of his teaching, and so on. In his Preface to this same Epistle to the Hebrews he gives various reasons for the omission of the name and of the apostolic office, of which we shall speak in the last part. Although this commentary is thought to be by Haimo rather than by Primasius.

units.la: XXXVIII. Iunilius, Episcopus Africanus, familiaris Primasio, de quo itidem meminit Cassiodorus Libro divin. Lect: De partibus divinæ Legis ad Primasium, L.1.C.vi. inter Paulinas, recenset Epistolam ad Hebræos.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Junilius, Bishop of Africa, a close associate of Primasius, of whom Cassiodorus also makes mention, in his book On the Divine Law (Book 1, ch. 6), addressed to Primasius, lists among the Pauline letters the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: XXXIX. Evodius sive Ennodius Episcopus Ticinensis, clarus sub Anastasio, sexto itidem ineunte sæculo; Opusculo II. Apostolo æquè Paulo proclamante, Obe-dite ductoribus vestris Hebr. xiii.
units.tr: XXXIX. Evodius or Ennodius, Bishop of Pavia, famous under Anastasius, likewise at the beginning of the sixth century, in his Opusculum II: with the Apostle Paul equally proclaiming, Obey your leaders, Heb. xiii.

units.la: XL. Johannes Maurentius, florens itidem sub Anastasio ; responsione ad Hormisdam Papam, citat locum Hebr. XI. de Fide Enochi & Noæ, sub nomine Pauli Apostoli. Idem, in Dialogis varia profert ex Cap. I. & II. Epistolæ, eodem Pauli expresso nomine.
units.tr: XL. John Maurentius, also flourishing under Anastasius, in his reply to Pope Hormisdas cites Heb. xi on the faith of Enoch and Noah under the name of the Apostle Paul. The same writer, in his Dialogues, brings forward various passages from chapters I and II of the Epistle, again with the name Paul expressly given.

units.la: XLI. Gregorius Magnus, Episcopus Romanus, antecessor, (medio Sabiniaño) Bonifacij m. Oecumenici 1. ex Monacho & Diacono Papa factus A. C. DXC suis passim Commentariis & Homiliis, Paulum Epistolae authorem facit. Ut illius tempore, nulla hac de re inter Latinos videatur fuisse controversia.
units.tr: XLI. Gregory the Great, Bishop of Rome, the immediate predecessor of Sabinian and of Boniface III, made pope in AD 590 from being a monk and deacon, in his many commentaries and homilies consistently makes Paul the author of the Epistle. So in his time there seems to have been no controversy about this among the Latins.

units.la: XLII. Isidorus junior, Episcopus Hispalensis, discipulus, ut ipse ait, Gregorij Magni, non uno in loco Epistolam ad Hebraeos Paulo vindicat. Quo etiam nomine citatur Annalium scriptori, ad A. LX. Num. LIV. In hanc etiā Epistolam, ut Paulinam, commentatus est. Quanquam sanè, Libro de Ecclesiasticis officijs, inserto Bibliothecae Patrum, L.1.C.IX. Paulus Apostolus suas scripsit Epistolas, ex quibus novem septem Ecclesijs destinavit, reliquas discipulis. Ad Hebraeos autem Epistola plerisque Latinis ejus fuisse incerta est, propter dissimilitudinem formae. Si modo haec sunt Isidori, quū illo ipso loco plurima superstitionem sapiant posteriorum temporum. Sed fuerint, nihil affirmat, quod non ante ipsum Hieronymus, ac iisdem penè verbis. In eo hallucinatus, quod plerisque Latinis communem hanc facit de incerto scriptore sententiam, quod sal-sum esse infrà demonstrandum.
units.tr: XLII. Isidore the Younger, Bishop of Seville, a disciple, as he himself says, of Gregory the Great, in more than one place claims the Epistle to the Hebrews for Paul. He is also cited under this name by the annalist, at AD 60, no. 54, and he wrote a commentary on it as a Pauline Epistle. Indeed, in his book On Ecclesiastical Offices, included in the Bibliotheca Patrum (Book 1, ch. 9): Paul the Apostle wrote his Epistles, of which he sent nine to churches and the rest to disciples. But the Epistle to the Hebrews was uncertain to most Latins because of the dissimilarity of its style. If indeed these words are Isidore's, since in that same place very many things smack of the superstition of later times. But whether they are his or not, he affirms nothing that was not said before him by Jerome, and in almost the same words. He is mistaken in making this opinion, that the writer is uncertain, common to most Latins, which must be shown below to be false.

units.la: XLIII. Eligius. Noviomensis Episcopus, mortuus A.C. DCLXV, juxta Sigibertum in Chronico, Homil. iv. de cœnæ Domini, Unde Apostolus, nihil dimisit non subjectum ei. Hebr. 11.7. Homil. vi: De his estis, Fratres, sicut ait Apostolus, quibus lac opus sit, non solidus cibus. Idem alibi.
units.tr: XLIII. Eligius, Bishop of Noyon, died in AD 665, according to Sigebert in his Chronicle. In Homily iv on the Lord's Supper: Whence the Apostle: he left nothing unsubjected to him, Heb. 11.7. In Homily vi: Of these you are, brothers, as the Apostle says, those who need milk and not solid food. The same elsewhere.

units.la: XLIV. Beda ille Venerabilis Anglo-saxo, clarus sub initia octavi sæculi, Mo-nachus Benedictinus, magnæ vir autho-ritatis; idem de Epistolâ cum reliquis censuit. Patet ex illius partim operibus, & quos edidit in Paulinas omnes Com-mentariis.
units.tr: XLIV. That venerable Bede, the Anglo-Saxon, famous at the beginning of the eighth century, a Benedictine monk and a man of great authority, judged the Epistle along with the rest in the same way. This is clear from some of his works, and from the commentaries on all the Pauline letters that he published.

units.la: XLV. Bonifacius primus, Archiepiscopus Moguntinus, ὁ μ̃λ̃ξ[?] Joh. Damasceno Martyrio, extinctus A.C. DCCLIV. Epistolâ secundâ, Recordare Apostolicæ sententiæ, & mox adducit locum Hebr. xii. 6.
units.tr: XLV. Boniface the First, Archbishop of Mainz, [illegible], killed in AD 754. In his second Epistle, Remember the apostolic saying, and immediately he adduces Heb. xii. 6.

units.la: XLVI. Paulinus Aquileiensis Episco-pus, [?]uis, clarus sub Carolo Magno, Nestorianæ hæreseos profligator: in Sacrosyllabo, & Libris contrà Felicem, Pauli nomine aliquoties Epistolam citat. Sic lib. i. adducturus locum Hebr. ii.14. Sic Libro ii. itidem locum Hebr. i.4. Apostolus in Epistola ad Hebræos &c.
units.tr: XLVI. Paulinus, Bishop of Aquileia, famous under Charlemagne, a crusher of the Nestorian heresy: in his Sacrosyllabus and in his books against Felix, he cites the Epistle several times under Paul's name. So in book 1, when about to adduce Heb. ii. 14; so also in book 2, Heb. i. 4: The Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews, and so on.

units.la: XLVII. Haymo, ex monacho Halberstadensis in Saxoniâ Episcopus, membrum Synodi Moguntinæ in Gottefchal-chum congregatæ, medio fere nono sæculo: quid de Epistola statuerit, suo prodidit in eam Commentario, ubi Paulinis annumerat, & Paulo vindicat comportatis argumentis, iisdem quæ supra in Pri-masio.
units.tr: XLVII. Haymo, formerly a monk and then Bishop of Halberstadt in Saxony, a member of the Synod of Mainz gathered against Gottschalk about the middle of the ninth century. What he decided about the Epistle he revealed in his commentary on it, where he counts it among the Pauline letters and claims it for Paul, by assembling arguments the same as those above in Primasius.

units.la: XLVIII. Rabanus Maurus, Archiepiscopus Moguntinus, Gottefchalci adversarius, oralis manducationis & corporalis præsentiæ cum Johanne Erigena acerrimus impugnator; de instit. Cleric. L. ii. C. LIV. Hos (sc. Evangeliorum & Actorum libros) quatuordecim Pauli Apostoli Epistolæ sequuntur. Annectuntur tamen illa ipsa verba, quæ supra notavimus in Hispalensi[?], Ad Hebræos Epistolæ risque Latinis ejus esse incerta est, propter dissonantiam sermonis.
units.tr: XLVIII. Rabanus Maurus, Archbishop of Mainz, opponent of Gottschalk, and the bitterest assailant of oral manducation and bodily presence, along with John Scotus Erigena. In his book On the Institution of Clerics, book ii, ch. 54: The fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul follow these (namely the books of the Gospels and Acts). Yet those same words which we noted above from the Hispalensis are appended: To the Hebrews, the Epistle; its author is uncertain to most Latins, on account of the dissimilarity of style.

units.la: XLIX. Hincmarus Archiepiscopus Rhemensis, primùm Monachus S. Dionysij, medio nono sæculo illustris, in Gottescalcum iniquissimus: Opusculo LV.[?] ad Hincmarum Laudunensem Episcopum, sancta quippe Ecclesia, quam beatus Paulus Apostolus, manentem civitatem & ædificationem &c. Sic alibi sæpius eandem Paulo adscribit Epistolam.
units.tr: XLIX. Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, first a monk of St Denis, illustrious in the middle of the ninth century, and most unjust toward Gottschalk. In Opusculum LV, to Hincmar, Bishop of Laon: For the holy Church, which the blessed Apostle Paul calls an abiding city and building, and so on. Likewise he elsewhere often ascribes the same Epistle to Paul.

units.la: L. Remigius Lugdunensis Ecclesiæ Episcopus, prioribus σύγχρονος[?], favens causæ Gottescalci; Commentatus est in hanc Epistolam, ut & reliquas Paulinas, suntque illi ipsi Commentarij Remigio Rhemensi, duobus sæculis vetustiori, perperam adscripti à Bapt. Vilalpando. Hic cum Haymone, reliquisque Commentatoribus, de authore Paulo scribit, & sentit.
units.tr: L. Remigius, Bishop of the Church of Lyon, contemporary [σύγχρονος] with the earlier writers, favoured Gottschalk's cause. He wrote a commentary on this Epistle, as on the other Pauline letters, and those commentaries have been wrongly ascribed by Baptista Villalpando to Remigius of Reims, who lived two centuries earlier. Here, with Haymo and the other commentators, he writes and thinks of Paul as the author.

units.la: LI. Lupus Servatus, Presbyter, itidem coævus, doctrinæ etiam Augustinianæ de particulari gratiâ doctissimus vindex, ex( perpetuam inter Gratiæ Universalis assertores, à Joh.Dallæo relatus )Libro de Tribus Quæst. operâ celeberrimi Riveti paucos ante annos recusó, suppeditante me ex desideratissimi Parentis Bibliothecâ, exemplar ; Quæst.iii. citatis aliis ex Paulo locis, item in Epistolâ quæ inscribitur ad Hebræos. Idem Epistolâ ad Carolum Regem, Johannes Constantinopolitanus Episcopus, cùm exponeret illud Apostoli ; qualiter gratiâ Dei pro omnibus gustaverit mortem, Hebr.11.2o.
units.tr: LI. Lupus Servatus, a presbyter, likewise a contemporary, and a most learned defender of the Augustinian doctrine of particular grace. He is listed by John Dallaeus among the perpetual advocates of universal grace. In his book On Three Questions, which was reprinted some years ago through the work of the most celebrated Rivet, I supplied a copy from the library of my most-missed father. In Question iii, other passages from Paul are cited, likewise in the Epistle which is inscribed to the Hebrews. The same writer, in his Letter to King Charles, John, Bishop of Constantinople, when he expounded that saying of the Apostle: that by the grace of God he tasted death for all, Heb. 2.9.

units.la: LII. Lupus , Abbas Ferrariensis, clarus itidem sub Carolo Calvo , & [illegible, ~7 letters]; Epist.xxxii, Nec experiatur quod ait Apostolus, Horrendum est incidere &c. Hebr.x.31.
units.tr: LII. Lupus, Abbot of Ferrières, likewise famous under Charles the Bald, and [illegible]; Epistle xxxii: and let him not experience what the Apostle says, It is a terrible thing to fall, and so on, Heb. x. 31.

units.la: LIII. Flavaldus , vel Flodoardus, Rhemensis, qui decimo sæculo Rhemensis Ecclesiæ Historiam adornavit ; Ejusdem Historiæ, Libr.iii. Unde terribiliter Paulus admonet, Pacem sectamini cùm omnibus, Hebr.xii.14.
units.tr: LIII. Flavaldus, or Flodoard, of Reims, who in the tenth century composed the history of the Church of Reims. In book iii of that History: Whence Paul warns terribly, Follow peace with all, Heb. xii. 14.

units.la: LIV. Drogo, ex Abbate Ostiensi Episcopus, undecimo jam sæculo, conspicuæ virtutis & eruditionis: Libro de creatione & redempt. primi hominis, citat locum Hebr. xi, 36. de quibus Apostolus loquitur sic &c.
units.tr: LIV. Drogo, from Abbot of Ostia to Bishop, already in the eleventh century, of outstanding virtue and learning. In his book On the Creation and Redemption of the First Man, he cites Heb. xi. 36: of whom the Apostle speaks thus, and so on.

units.la: LV. Sed ad ea jam deventum tem-pora, quæ sibi vendicat sequior Scholasti-corum ætas. Quanquam ex Anselmo, Bernardo, Hugone S. Victoris &c. quæ-dam Latinorum Patrum velut appendi-ce, geminæ pro Paulo Epistolæ scriptore authoritates, proferri possent in medium. Prout hic διαρρήδην[?] in Catalogo Librorum N.T. Cap. VIII[?]. Speculi Ecclesiæ, Epistolis Paulinis annumerat illam ad Hebræos. Sed de recentiorum mente haud ita la-boramus. Adeóque hæc de Veterum, quos usurpare quidem licuit, testimoniis hactenus: Nec de fuissent plura, si forulos omnes excutere, & numero certare animus fuisset. Verum enim vero hoc imprimis superesset, ut de illis constaret, qui Epistolæ sive authorem, sive authoritatem ex Latinis fecere dubiam. Utque motarii[?] su- pra prà ex Eusebio & Hieronymo difficultatem, & instantias quasdam alias, expediamus.
units.tr: LV. But now we have come to those times which the later age of the Schoolmen claims for itself. Although from Anselm, Bernard, Hugh of St Victor, and others, two authorities for Paul as the author could be brought forward from certain Latin Fathers, as an appendix. Thus here [διαρρήδην] in the Catalogue of the New Testament Books, chapter VIII, the Mirror of the Church [Speculum Ecclesiae] counts that Epistle to the Hebrews among the Pauline Epistles. But we are not so concerned about the mind of more recent writers. So far these testimonies of the Ancients, which indeed we were allowed to use, are enough; nor would there have been more, had I wished to search all the shelves and contend by number. But what above all remains is that it be established concerning those who made the Epistle doubtful among the Latins, whether as to its author or as to its authority. And, as above, let us deal with the difficulty raised from Eusebius and Jerome, and certain other objections.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Exceptiones de ancipiti Latinorum mente. Loca ex Eusebio, Hieronymo, Augustino, Philastrio, Isidoro, Rabano. De Caio. de Tertulliano. de Hippolyto. de Cypriano. de Hieronymo. De Commentatoribus in tredecim tantum Epistolas. Cardin. Baronij mala fides. Ejusdem in Eusebium, & Hieronymum iniquitas. Rei accuratius examen. Tempus motae hujus inter Latinos controversiae. Occasiones variae ostensae. Ante Hieronymum Epistola Pauli habita. Assertiones Erasmi, Ludov. Vives, Rhenani, Cameronis, &c. confutatae. Instantiae omnes aliae excussae. Qui ex Latinis in Epistolam commentati.
units.tr: Objections concerning the doubtful mind of the Latins. Passages from Eusebius, Jerome, Augustine, Philastrius, Isidore and Rabanus. On Caius. On Tertullian. On Hippolytus. On Cyprian. On Jerome. On the commentators on only thirteen Epistles. The bad faith of Cardinal Baronius. His unfairness towards Eusebius and Jerome. A more careful examination of the matter. The time when this controversy arose among the Latins. Various occasions given. Before Jerome the Epistle was held as Paul's. The assertions of Erasmus, Ludovicus Vives, Rhenanus, Cameron, etc., refuted. All the other objections examined. Those among the Latins who wrote commentaries on the Epistle.

units.la: I. Esto ergo gravis illa, nec contemnenda exceptio. Frustra ut communem Latinorum sententiam obtrudi, quae diutissime prioribus etiam saeculis, sive in Romana sive Africana Ecclesia contro-versia, versu. Imò verò sententiam eam potiorem, quæ ad Eusebium usque & Hieronymum inter Latinos viguit. Talem autem esse, quæ Paulum Epistolæ authorem negat. Quod cum testimonijs variis, tum exemplis, firmari posse videtur.
units.tr: I. Let that serious objection, which is not to be despised, stand. It is said that the common opinion of the Latins, which prevailed for a very long time even in earlier centuries, whether in the Roman or the African Church, is in vain forced upon us. Indeed, that opinion which held sway among the Latins down to Eusebius and Jerome is the stronger one, and it is held that this opinion denies that Paul is the author of the Epistle. This seems capable of being confirmed both by testimonies of various kinds and by examples.

units.la: II. Testimonijs, primò quidem Eusebij, loco ante citato ex Hist. Eccles. L. iii. C. iii. Quosdam Epistolæ ad Hebræos derogare, dicentes, eidem ab Ecclesiâ Romanâ, tanquam quæ Pauli non sit, contradici. Idem Eusebius Hist. Libr. vi. C. xiv. vel xá. Ἐ'πὶ τῆς δε[?]τέρας [?] Ῥωμαίων [?] οὐ νομίζεται τῆς Ἀποστόλης τυγχάνειν, sc. ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίους. Nam illa, (sc. ad Hebræos,) in hunc usque diem apud quosdam Romanos, non existimatur esse Apostoli. Secundò accedit testimonium Hieronymi, Catal. script. Eccles. in Caio; & Epistola cxxix, ad Dardanum, utrumque superiori Capite positum. Pariter, Catal. script. in Paulo: Epistola autem quæ fertur ad Hebræos, non ejus esse creditur, sed vel Barnabæ. Imò quotiescunque sagacissimus Patrum, Epistolæ meminit, toties ferè [illegible, ~9 letters] interserit, si quis tamen eam suscipit; licet de ea multi Latinorum dubitent; à plerisque extra locum ponitur; licet eam Latinorum consuetudo non recipit. Tertiò etiam testis est Augustinus, de Civit: Dei, L.xvi. Cap.xxii. Plures Apostoli Pauli esse dicunt, quidam verò negant. Etiam Philastrius, Hær.xli. sunt alij quoque qui Epistolam ad Hebræos non asserunt esse ipsius. Etiam Isidorus Hispalensis, de Eccles.Offic. Lib.i.C.xi. plerisque Latinis ejus fuisse incerta est. Eadem Rabanus de Instit. Clericali L.ii. C.liv, & ex his alij.
units.tr: II. As for testimonies, first there is that of Eusebius, cited above from Church History, Book iii, chapter iii: that some reject the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that it is contradicted by the Roman Church, as not being Paul's. The same Eusebius, Church History, Book vi, chapter xiv (or 25), says that among some Romans the Epistle [ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίους] is not thought to belong to the Apostle. For that epistle (namely to the Hebrews) is to this day not considered to be the Apostle's by some Romans. Second comes the testimony of Jerome, in the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers under Caius, and in Epistle cxxix to Dardanus; both have been quoted in the previous chapter. Likewise, in the Catalogue of Writers under Paul: but the epistle which is said to be to the Hebrews is not believed to be his, but either Barnabas's. Indeed, whenever that most shrewd of the Fathers mentions this Epistle, he almost always adds: if anyone nevertheless receives it; though many of the Latins doubt it; it is placed outside its proper place by most; though Latin custom does not receive it. Third, Augustine also bears witness, in City of God, Book xvi, chapter xxii: Some say that there are many Epistles of Paul, while some deny it. Also Philastrius, Heresy xli: there are others also who do not assert that the Epistle to the Hebrews is his. Also Isidore of Seville, On the Offices of the Church, Book i, chapter xi: its authorship is uncertain to most Latins. Rabanus says the same in On Clerical Institution, Book ii, chapter liv, and others besides these.

units.la: III. Atque hinc nata illa quorundam assertio: ante ætatem Hieronymi à Latinis eam Epistolam non receptam fuisse inter sacras. Sic Erasmus, sub finem Annotationum in Epist. ad Hebræos. Sic etiam Ludovicus Vives, ad locum Augustini de Civit. Dei Lib. xvi. Cap. xxii. Sic Cajetanus Cardinalis, aliique horum victi authoritate. Inter quos audacior. Camero, Quæst. 11. in Epist. ad Hebr. Ante tempora Hieronymi, nemo unquam in Ecclesia Romana affirmavit eam esse Pauli Apostoli.
units.tr: III. From this arose that assertion of certain men: that before Jerome's time the Epistle was not received among the sacred books by the Latins. So Erasmus, near the end of his Annotations on the Epistle to the Hebrews. So too Ludovicus Vives, on the passage of Augustine in City of God, Book xvi, chapter xxii. So Cajetan the Cardinal, and others overcome by his authority. Among them the boldest is Cameron, Question 11 on the Epistle to the Hebrews: Before the time of Jerome, no one ever affirmed in the Roman Church that it was the work of the Apostle Paul.

units.la: IV. Accedunt exempla vetustiorum in Latina Ecclesia, magnæque in illa authoritatis, qui de Epistolæ authore secus opinati. Tertullianus Afer, vulgò primus Latinorum Patrum, florens anno à Christo nato cc: Libro v. contrà Marcionem, probaturus nullum aliud Deum ab Apostolo circumlatum, ex ipsis utique Epistolis Pauli, illius quæ est ad Hebræos nullus meminit. Hinc Beatus Rhenanus in ar-gumento Libri. Porrò quod omnibus E-pistolis excussis, (præter eas quæ sunt ad Titum & Timotheum, quas rejiciebat Marcion) illius quæ ad Hebræos inscribitur non est facta mentio, satis declarat eâ ætate Paulo non fuisse tributam. Sed & idem Tertullianus, Libro de Pudic. C.xx, Epistolam tribuit Barnabæ Pauli socio. Unde, B. Hieronymus in Paulo, sed credi-tur, vel Barnabæ juxta Tertullianum &c.
units.tr: IV. To these are added examples from older writers in the Latin Church, men of great authority, who thought otherwise about the author of the Epistle. Tertullian of Africa, commonly the first of the Latin Fathers, flourishing in the year 200 after Christ's birth, in Book v against Marcion, meant to prove that no other God was proclaimed by the Apostle, from the Epistles of Paul themselves, and yet makes no mention of that to the Hebrews. Hence Beatus Rhenanus, in the argument of the book: Moreover, that after all the Epistles have been searched (except those to Titus and Timothy, which Marcion rejected), no mention is made of the one inscribed to the Hebrews, clearly shows that in that age it was not attributed to Paul. But the same Tertullian, in Book On Modesty, chapter xx, assigns the Epistle to Barnabas, Paul's companion. Hence Jerome, in On Paul: but it is believed to be either Barnabas's, according to Tertullian, etc.

units.la: V. Caius, Presbyter Romanæ Ecclesiue[?], sub Victore & Zephyrino Episcopis, Antonino Romanis imperante; Disputatione adversus Proclum Montani studiosum, Epistolas Pauli tredecim tantùm enumerans, decimamquartam quae fertur ad Hebraeos, dicit non ejus esse. Ita Hieronymus Catal. script. Ecclesiast. in Caio. Idem, Eusebius de Cajo Hist. Eccles. L. VI. C. XIV. τῶν ἱερῶν Ἀποστόλων δεκατριῶν μόνον ἐπιστολῶν μνημονεύει, τὴν πρὸς Ἑβραίους μὴ συναριθμήσας τοῖς λοιποῖς. Idem etiam Photius, in Bibliotheca Codice XLVIII. de Caio Presbytero, Καὶ ἐν Πρόκλῳ δὲ σπουδαστὴν Μον-τανιστὴν, σπουδαίαν διάλεξιν συντεταγμένην, ἐν ᾗ τρισκαίδεκα μόνας ἐπιστολὰς διεξέρχεται Παύλου, οὐχ ὑγιαίνουσαν[?] τὴν πρὸς Ἑβραίους.
units.tr: V. Caius, a Presbyter of the Roman Church, under the bishops Victor and Zephyrinus, in the reign of the Roman emperor Antoninus, in a disputation against Proclus, a zealous Montanist, enumerating only thirteen Epistles of Paul, says that the fourteenth, which is said to be to the Hebrews, is not his. So Jerome in the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers under Caius. The same is reported by Eusebius about Caius, Church History, Book vi, chapter xiv: he mentions only thirteen Epistles of the holy Apostles, not counting the one to the Hebrews among the rest [τῶν ἱερῶν Ἀποστόλων δεκατριῶν μόνον ἐπιστολῶν μνημονεύει, τὴν πρὸς Ἑβραίους μὴ συναριθμήσας τοῖς λοιποῖς]. The same is also stated by Photius, in the Bibliotheca, Codex xlviii, about Caius the Presbyter, that in his well-written dialogue against Proclus, a zealous Montanist, he runs through only thirteen Epistles of Paul, and does not count the one to the Hebrews as sound.

units.la: VI. Hyppolitus Martyr, Clementis Alexandrini, vel juxtà Photium, Irenaei discipulus, primùm Arabiae Metropolitanus, Portuensis exinde Episcopus Ecclesiae, quanquam hic diversus Vossio: apud Photium Cod. CXXI. in Libello contrà haereses, dicitur Epistolam ad Hebraeos è Paulinis expunxisse. Λέγει δὲ ἀλλὰ πῶς ἀσεβείας λοιπόμενα[?], καὶ ὅτι ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίους Ἑβραίους[?] Ἑβραίας Ἐπιστολὴ, οὐκ τῆς Ἀποστόλου Παύλου[?]; Refert autem cum alia non omninò probatum Epistolam ad Hebræos non esse Pauli Apostoli. Idem de Hyppolito affirmat apud eundem Photium. Cod. ccxxxii. Stephanus haereticus, ὅτι ἐπ[?]ταῖς πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἐπιστολὴν Παύλου[?], οὐκ ἐκείνου εἶναι φησί.
units.tr: VI. Hippolytus, the martyr, a disciple of Clement of Alexandria or, according to Photius, of Irenaeus, first Metropolitan of Arabia and afterwards Bishop of the Church of Portus, though Vossius thinks him a different man: according to Photius, Codex cxxi, in a little book against heresies, he is said to have struck the Epistle to the Hebrews from the Pauline writings. Photius reports that he said, with other matters not wholly approved, that the Epistle to the Hebrews is not the Apostle Paul's. Photius also states the same about Hippolytus in Codex ccxxxii. Stephen the heretic says that the Epistle to the Hebrews is not Paul's but another's [ἐπιστολὴν Παύλου, οὐκ ἐκείνου εἶναι φησί].

units.la: VII. Cyprianus, ut ejusdem sententiae patronus objicitur. Ratio, quia nusquam, in scriptis sanè genuinis & confessis, Epistolam legitur usurpasse. Et eo nomine Arnobius & Lactantius Afri, in eundem à nonnullis censum referuntur. Ipse Clariss. Pareus, Proœmio in Epist.ad Hebr. Haec sententia videtur fuisse veterum Latinorum Africanorum, Tertulliani, Cypriani, Lactantij, Arnobij, qui nunquam citarunt ut Apostolicam. Forte ex Bellarmino Tom.1. Controv. de Verbo Dei, L.1. C.xvii. Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Lactantius, Arnobius, hanc Epistolam non videntur agnoscere, nec enim eam unquam citant.
units.tr: VII. Cyprian is cited as a patron of this opinion. The reason is that in his genuine and acknowledged writings he is nowhere read to have used the Epistle. For that reason Arnobius and Lactantius, Africans, are by some counted among those of the same view. The illustrious Pareus himself, in the Preface to the Epistle to the Hebrews: This opinion seems to have been that of the older Latin Africans, Tertullian, Cyprian, Lactantius, Arnobius, who never cited it as Apostolic. Perhaps from Bellarmine, Volume 1, Controversies on the Word of God, Book i, chapter xvii: Tertullian, Cyprian, Lactantius, Arnobius do not seem to acknowledge this Epistle, for they never cite it.

units.la: VIII. Sed & Hieronymi videtur nu-tasse sententia, & hujus etiam se ruetur[?] Erasmus authoritate. Sanè Comment. in Amosi Caput VIII, dubius de Authore pronunciat: Quod, quicunque est ille qui ad Hebraeos scripsit Epistolam, disse-rens ait. Alibi septem tantùm Pauli ad Ecclesias recensèt Epistolas, exclusi-vè ad Ecclesiam Hebraeorum. Catalog. script. in Paulo, scripsit autem novem ad septem Ecclesias Epistolas, ad Romanos unam, &c. Comment. in Zachar. C. VIII. circa finem; Quae igitur septem ibi mulieres appellantur, i.e. Ecclesiae, (quarum numerus & in Paulo Apostolo continetur, ad septem enim scribit Ecclesias, ad Romanos, ad Corinthios, ad Galatas, ad Ephesios, ad Philippenses, ad Colof-senses, ad Thessalonicenses) Epistola ad Paulinum, de libris divinae script. quae est ciii. Operum Tom.iii. Paulus Apostolus ad septem scribit Ecclesias, octava enim ad Hebraeos à plerisque extrà locum ponitur.
units.tr: VIII. But the opinion of Jerome also seems to have wavered, and Erasmus is said to have relied on his authority. Certainly in his Commentary on Amos, chapter viii, he pronounces doubtfully about the author: Whoever he was who wrote the Epistle to the Hebrews, he says... Elsewhere he lists only seven Epistles of Paul to churches, excluding the one to the Hebrew church: in the Catalogue under Paul: he wrote nine epistles to seven churches, one to the Romans, etc. In the Commentary on Zechariah, chapter viii, near the end: Those seven women, therefore, are called the churches (whose number is also contained in the Apostle Paul, for he writes to seven churches: to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians, to the Thessalonians). In the letter to Paulinus on the books of Holy Scripture, which is letter ciii, in Volume iii of his works: The Apostle Paul writes to seven churches, for the eighth, to the Hebrews, is by most placed outside its proper place.

units.la: IX. Cassiodorus Divin. Lect.
