C. viii, mentionem facit gemini in Paulum Commentarij, utriusque in tredecim tantum Epistolas, seclusa illa ad Hebraeos; Prior hodieque visitur in Operibus Hieronymi, Pelagio haeresiarchae adscriptus. Alter Hilario Diacono, coaetaneo Pictavensi, restitutus. De quo Blondellus Apol. pro sententia. Hieronymus Sect. u[?]. Germanum Romanae Ecclesiae alumnum arguit, quod enarratis praecedentibus omnibus Pauli Epistolis, ab ea quam ad Hebraeos Romae dedit Apostolus, adeo manum abstinuit, ut vix semel ejusdem meminisse dignatus sit. Imo quorundam assertio est, Latinorum neminem in hanc Epistolam scripsisse Commentarios, ante Anselmum Cantuariensem.
units.tr: IX. Cassiodorus, in On Divine Readings, chapter viii, mentions a twofold commentary on Paul, each on only thirteen Epistles, with that to the Hebrews set aside. The first is still read today in the works of Jerome, but is ascribed to the heresiarch Pelagius. The other was restored to Hilary the deacon, a contemporary from Poitiers. On this Blondel, in his Apology for his opinion, says that Jerome, in section ..., accuses the German, a pupil of the Roman Church, of having, after expounding all the preceding Epistles of Paul, so kept his hand off the one which the Apostle gave to the Hebrews at Rome, that he scarcely deigned to mention it once. Indeed, some affirm that no Latin wrote commentaries on this Epistle before Anselm of Canterbury.

units.la: X. Nodum hunc scriptor Annalium Ecclesiasticorum ut expediat, utque notam illam male definiti Canonis, & rejectae nobilissimae Epistolarum omnium, a Romana abstergat Ecclesia, hanc incedit ille via. Primo, subdole varia & testimo-nia[?] & documenta, de dubia Latinorum vete[?]veterum mente subterfugit, & sicco pe-de transiit, à solius Eusebij fide pendere hoc totum inuenns. Secundò simpliciter & compendio quodam, id omne negat de Latinis, sive Veteribus, sive recentioribus, fuisse inter eos qui in germanis Pauli Epistolis non habuerint illam quæ est ad Hebræos. Vixque eo delabitur ut Caium unum ex Catholica excipiat antiquitate, ad Annum C. LX. Num. LV. Tertiò in Eusebium, ut fraudis omnis authorem stomachatur, quique incauto impo-suerit Hieronymo: satis superque esse existimantes quæ diximus, ad repellendam de Epistola ad Hebræos ab Eusebio illatam calumniam in Romanam Ecclesiam, quam sanctus Hieronymus (rogatâ veniâ dixerim, invitus enim nolensque licet, pro veritate ad eã obnitendum adducor) facile animis[?], quod miramur, admisit.
units.tr: X. To untie this knot, and to wipe away from the Roman Church the mark of a wrongly defined Canon and of a rejection of the most noble of all the Epistles, the writer of the Ecclesiastical Annals takes this course. First, he craftily slips past the various testimonies and documents about the doubtful mind of the older Latins, and passes over them with dry feet, claiming that all this rests on the sole word of Eusebius. Second, he simply and summarily denies that any of the Latins, whether ancient or more recent, were among those who did not have the Epistle to the Hebrews among the genuine Epistles of Paul. He goes so far as to except only Caius from the Catholic antiquity, in the year 200, number 55. Third, he rails against Eusebius, the author of all the deceit, who imposed on the unwary Jerome: Thinking it enough and more than enough what we have said, to repel the calumny brought by Eusebius against the Roman Church concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews, which holy Jerome (I may say with his pardon, for I am led, though unwilling and reluctant, to resist it for the sake of truth) readily admitted in their minds, which we marvel at.

units.la: XI. In quo & fidem Cardinalis desiderâmus, & candorem & judicium. Quid? De controversiâ illâ Eusebius aliquoties ut sui temporis, ut notâ, ut in Romana tum etiam Ecclesia agitâtâ; idem sexcenctes[?] Hieronymus ipse Latinus; idem hoc [?]estinus, alij; præsto sunt exempla; rationes etiam adsunt & causæ motæ controversiæ: Et tamen, si Baronio credimus, Latinorum nemo, nec per somnium, Epistolæ vel authorem vel authoritatem traxit in dubium? Nec ante nec post Concilij Nicæni tempora? Constantissimè à Romanis & Catholicis omnibus Pauli habita? Calumnia fuerit Eusebÿ & error Hieronymi? Hæccine est fides purpurati hoccine nodum solvere, an implicare & ludibrium debere sententiæ adversæ patronis?
units.tr: XI. Here we miss the Cardinal's good faith, his candour and his judgement. What of it? Eusebius mentions that controversy several times, as something known in his own day and as something that was then being debated even in the Roman Church. Jerome himself, the Latin, does the same, and other writers too; examples are at hand, and the reasons and causes that stirred up the controversy are also there. And yet, if we believe Baronius, not one of the Latins, not even in a dream, called into doubt either the author or the authority of the Epistle? Not before or after the time of the Council of Nicaea? That Paul was held by all the Romans and Catholics with the utmost constancy? Was it the slander of Eusebius and the error of Jerome? Is this the faith of a purple-clad man? Is this how he unties a knot, or does he tie one and make a mockery of the opinion of his opponents' defenders?

units.la: XII. Nos vero & rem totam illustramus, & quid de Latinis in hac causâ sentiendum, quid de tempore motæ inter Latinos controversiæ, causis, authoribus, quid denique de vi exceptionis suprà positæ, declaramus paucis. Primò itaque negamus, de Epistolâ inter Latinos fuisse controversum primis duobus sæculis, vel certè ante inclinationem secundi. Imò vero Pauli creditam illâ ætate conjectaius[?], v. ex communi tum Græcorum & Ecclesiarum omnium per Orientem, de canonica Epistolæ authoritate, imo authore Paulo, consensu, supra fusius demonstrato. ii. Ex sententia & suffragio Clementis Romanorum Episcopi, quem & citasse Epistolam, & habuisse in Paulinis, & ejus creditum interpretem, ante quidem intelleximus. iii. Quia primum de Epistolæ authoritate, exinde authore inter Latinos dubium, videtur demum exortum, post Marcionis in Italiam adventum, & disseminatas hæreses, ac nefaria dogmata. Quanquam enim ante Marcionem Ebion, in Pauli scripta omnia, ut qui à Lege defecisset, in Oriente grassatus: Marcion sanè in Occidente primus, de Paulinis quibusdam, cautius & occultius dubia Latinis instillavit. Speciatim in Epistolam ad Hebræos, ut interpolatam & adulterinam, suis semper somniis adversam, impurissimum os calumnias evomuit. Testatur supra Cap. vi. Epiphanius Hær. xli. Etiam Hieronymus proœmio in Epist. ad Titum, Tomo VII Ut enim de cæteris Epistolis taceam de quibus quicquid contrarium suo dogmati viderant, eraserunt, nonnullas integras repudiandas crediderunt, ad Timotheum, videlicet utramque, ad Hebræos & ad Titum. Ita Tertullianus L. v. Contrà Marcionem, Pauli Epistolas dicit illi mutilatas etiam de numero, & interpolatas. Notum prætereà quantas secta Romæ, (in quâ egit Marcion,) & in Italia, postmodum in Oriente radices egerit, morienti Epiphanio, quæ sumpserit incrementa, ut etiâ martyres aluerit in sinu suo. Contigere hæc secundo labente & vergente sæculo. Atque ab hinc demùm natam sanè arbitramur, inter quosdam Latinorum, de Epistola illiusq; scriptore controversiam. Accedentibus argumentis cum à styli diversitate, tum ab occultatione nominis, [?]ἐν τῷ ἀνεπιγράφῳ τῆς Ἐπιστολῆς; Succedentibus postmodùm etiam aliis, ut videndum fuerit, dubitandi causis tertio & quarto sæculo. IV. Eo propiùs, conjectura ad verum accedit, quod ex Ecclesiasticis inter Romanos scriptoribus, primus ille Caius Romanæ Ecclesiæ Presbyter, tertiò ineunte sæculo, Epistolam à Paulinarum reliquis segregasse memoretur. Hinc id Eusebius, & ex eo cæteri, ut rem dignam observatu, quæque alios in eandem postmodum errorem induxerit, traditum posteris voluêre. Imò verò nova occasione Caium in eam putem sententiam pertractum. Res ipsi fuerat cum Proclo Montanista, Scripturarum numerum adaugente, συντάττων[?] καινὰς γραφάς. In eadem ergo illa cum Proclo διαλέξει, ex ἀπο-στρία, (ut videtur) τῆς ἀντιλογικῆς[?], accidit ut Canonicorum contra librorum numerum amputarit. Quod illa a occasione factum colligimus ex Eusebio Hist. L. vi. C.xiv. & Photio, loco ante citato §iv. v. Quæcunque & Eusebius, & Hieronymus, de ancipiti Latinorum mente testati, spectant illa ipsa quibus vixêre, aut proxima tempora. Sanè de Epistola jam inde à Latinæ Ecclesiæ incunabulis rejecta aut controversa, meminêre nulli, ut patebit loca collaturis. Quod si esset[?], non
units.tr: XII. We, for our part, will clear up the whole matter and briefly set out what must be thought about the Latins in this case, about the time when the controversy arose among the Latins, its causes and its originators, and finally about the force of the exception put forward above. First, then, we deny that the Epistle was disputed among the Latins during the first two centuries, or at least before the decline of the second. Indeed, in that age the Pauline authorship was believed, as is shown by the common agreement of the Greeks and of all the churches throughout the East, which, as was demonstrated more fully above, accepted the Epistle's canonical authority and even its authorship by Paul. Second, by the judgement and vote of Clement, bishop of Rome, who we have already seen cited the Epistle, counted it among the Pauline writings, and was believed to be its interpreter. Third, the doubt about the Epistle's authority, and afterwards about its author, seems to have arisen among the Latins only after Marcion came to Italy and the heresies and impious doctrines spread. For although Ebion, who had revolted from the Law, raged in the East against all the writings of Paul before Marcion, it was Marcion who, in the West, first sowed doubts among the Latins about certain of the Pauline writings, more cautiously and more secretly. In particular, against the Epistle to the Hebrews, which he called interpolated and spurious and always opposed to his dreams, he vomited forth his most filthy calumnies. Epiphanius bears witness to this, Heresy 41, as we noted above in chapter 6. Jerome too, in the preface to the Epistle to Titus, vol. VII: "For to say nothing of the other Epistles, about which they erased whatever they saw contrary to their dogma, they believed some should be rejected altogether, namely both to Timothy, and to the Hebrews and to Titus." Tertullian likewise, in book 5 against Marcion, says that the Pauline Epistles were mutilated and interpolated by him, even in their number. Moreover, it is well known how greatly this sect, in which Marcion was active, took root at Rome and in Italy, and afterwards in the East, and how it grew, while Epiphanius was still alive, so that it even nourished martyrs in its bosom. These things happened in the late second century, as it was sliding towards its close. And we think that it was from this point on that the controversy about the Epistle and its writer really arose among certain Latins. Arguments were added, both from the difference in style and from the concealment of the name, in the anonymity of the Epistle [ἐν τῷ ἀνεπιγράφῳ τῆς Ἐπιστολῆς]. Afterwards other grounds for doubt followed, so that in the third and fourth centuries the matter had to be considered. IV. Our conjecture comes closer to the truth because, among the ecclesiastical writers at Rome, Caius, the presbyter of the Roman Church at the beginning of the third century, is recorded as the first to separate the Epistle from the rest of the Pauline writings. From this, Eusebius, and after him the others, handed it down to posterity as a matter worth noting, and as something that afterwards led others into the same error. Indeed, I think Caius was drawn into that opinion by a new occasion. He had a dispute with Proclus the Montanist, who was increasing the number of Scriptures, composing new scriptures [συντάττων καινὰς γραφάς]. Thus in that very debate with Proclus, from a kind of turning away (as it seems) from the spirit of controversy, it happened that he cut down the number of canonical books. We gather that this happened on that occasion from Eusebius, Church History, book 6, chapter 14, and from Photius, in the passage cited above, §4–5. Whatever Eusebius and Jerome have reported about the wavering mind of the Latins refers to the very times in which they lived, or to the times immediately before. Certainly no one before, from the very beginnings of the Latin Church, mentions the Epistle as rejected or disputed, as will be clear to those who compare the passages. But if it were so, not

units.la: id jam in Caio Romano, ut quid in eo ho- mine cum singulare, idem Eusebius & Hieronymus subnotassent.
units.tr: that this would already be found in Caius of Rome, since Eusebius and Jerome would have noted it as something singular in that man.

units.la: XIII. Secundò, damus controversiam illam recruduisse inter Latinos, Novatiani temporibus, tertio sæculo media jam sui parte lapso. Atque hæc altera ista occasio, & periodus, spretæ aut adductæ in controversiam Epistolæ. Nec affirmasse tantùm sufficerit. 1. Constat Novatianæ hæreseos præsidium omne fuisse in hac Epistola repositum.
units.tr: XIII. Second, we grant that the controversy broke out again among the Latins in the time of Novatian, in the third century, now half over. This is the second occasion and period in which the Epistle was either neglected or drawn into dispute. Nor is it enough merely to assert it. 1. It is established that the whole support of the Novatian heresy was placed in this Epistle.

units.la: Quum enim Novatus & Novatianus (si tamen hi distinguendi, reclamante Scaligero, Animadv. Euseb. MMCCLXVIII, qui non Novatum dictum sed Novatianum, sectatores Novatianos appellandos censet) lapsis, sive libellatici ij essent, sive sacrificati, spem omnem σωτηρίας ἐξ ἀλλήλων, ut refert Epiphanius hær. LIX, sive, ut mollius Socrates Lib. 1. hist. C. X. τῆς νοσοῦσης τῶν θείων μυστηρίων, καὶ τῆς ἀφέσεως ἐκ τῶν ἱερῶν, contrà Romanæ praxin Ecclesiæ interdicerent, errori suo doctrinam Apostolicam obtenderunt. Occasione quidem dem Decianæ persecutionis, nonnullo-rumque apostasiæ, revera ex quodam in-Cornelium, pœnitentes Apostatas recipientem, invidiæ & indignationis sensu. Et quidem unam Epistolam ad Hebræos, in causæ suæ patrocinium adhibuerè, & geminum illum locum Hebr. vi. & x. Testis est Epiphanius Hæres. LIX. contrà Catharos, Σφίλλα δὲ αὐτὰς τὸ ῥῆμα τῆς Ἀποστολικῆς ἀδύνατον γὰρ τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας &c. Seducit autem ipsos dictum Apostoli: Fieri non potest &c. Monet idem Eulogius Alexandrinus, L. II. contrà Novatian. ἀποφέρονται οἱ ἐπὶ Ναυάτῳ, τὸ Ἀποστολικὸν ῥῆμα, τὸ φάσκειν τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας &c. Hebr. vi. 4. Eodem Libro, μὴ μετανοούντων ἀδύνατον γὰρ ἡμῶν ἀναστανρούντων &c. Hebr. x. 26. Sic quotquot ferè ex Veteribus sive Græcis sive Latinis, in hanc postmodùm Epistolam commentati, & cū Novatianis congressi, hæc semper verba ab hæresi Novatiana vindicarunt. Sic Ambrosius: Lib. II. de Pœnit. C. II. instituta contrà Novatianos disputarione, verba illa Hebr. vi. de non iterando baptismo, minimè sanè de via ad poenitentiam lapsis præclu- denda, interpretatur. Et res ipsa docet, nihil in speciem faventius dogmati Novatiano, nihil urgentius fuisse hoc argumento : Qui non possunt renovari per poenitentiam, illi non sunt in Ecclesiam recipiendi; sed tales, teste Apostolo, semel illuminati & postmodum lapsi &c. 11. Constat nodum hunc illico plerisque Latinorum visum fuisse Gordium & ἄλυτον[?]. Hinc qui solvere non valebant secuerunt, & cum de Epistolæ authoritate, tum authore litem excitarunt. Adstipulatur Philastrius, Hær. XLı, qui inter causas subtractæ Paulo Epistolæ, hanc refert, quod faveret Novatianis. Eo magis, quod nonnullis Latinorum, inde à Caio, aut Marcionis temporibus, fuisset jam ante suspecta. Accessit quod latè serperent contagia Novatiani dogmatis, & sub initia exortæ hæreseos, Græcorum illud glossema, dictum Apostoli ut plurimùm interpretantium de φωτισμῷ[?] & ἀνακαινώσει[?] sacramentali, & Baptismo non renovando, do, vel nondum scirent, vel ut jejunû nec rutum satis Schismaticorū telis excipiendis, repudiarent. Nam fuêre in Romana & Occidentali Ecclesia, post Novatianos illos fluctus excitatos, Hilarios ante & Ambrosios &c. oppidò pauci, alicujus nominis & eruditionis scriptores, qui exil-lis sese angustijs & difficultatibus vale-rent expedire. Post modùm verò, inde ab Hilario, & Ambrosio, & Augustino, do-ctissimi Latinorum, interpretamen-tum illud de Baptismo adoptare, quam Epistolæ repudium mittere malue-runt.
units.tr: For when Novatus and Novatian (if indeed these are to be distinguished, though Scaliger objects, in his Animadversions on Eusebius, col. 1268, who holds that the followers should be called Novatians and not Novatus) and their people, whether they were libellatici or sacrificati, forbade, contrary to the practice of the Roman Church, any hope of salvation from one another [σωτηρίας ἐξ ἀλλήλων], as Epiphanius reports in Heresy 59, or, to put it more gently as Socrates does in book 1, chapter 10 of his History, that the sick should be kept from the divine mysteries and from absolution by the priests, they put forward the Apostolic doctrine as a cover for their error. The occasion was indeed the Decian persecution and the apostasy of some, but in fact it arose from a feeling of envy and indignation against Cornelius, who received penitent apostates. And they used the Epistle to the Hebrews alone in defence of their cause, together with those two passages, Hebrews 6 and 10. Epiphanius bears witness, Heresy 59, against the Cathari: "The saying of the Apostle misled them: for it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, etc. [Σφίλλα δὲ αὐτὰς τὸ ῥῆμα τῆς Ἀποστολικῆς ἀδύνατον γὰρ τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας]." Eulogius of Alexandria also warns, in book 2 against the Novatians, that the Novatians twist the Apostolic saying, that those once enlightened, etc. [ἀποφέρονται οἱ ἐπὶ Ναυάτῳ, τὸ Ἀποστολικὸν ῥῆμα, τὸ φάσκειν τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας], Hebrews 6:4. In the same book: for those who do not repent, it is impossible, for if we sin willingly, etc. [μὴ μετανοούντων ἀδύνατον γὰρ ἡμῶν ἀναστανρούντων], Hebrews 10:26. Thus almost all the ancients, whether Greek or Latin, who afterwards commented on this Epistle and engaged the Novatians, always defended these words against the Novatian heresy. So Ambrose, in book 2 of On Repentance, chapter 2, in a disputation against the Novatians, interprets those words of Hebrews 6 about not repeating baptism, and by no means as shutting the way of repentance to the lapsed. And the matter itself shows that nothing was more favourable in appearance to the Novatian doctrine, and nothing more pressing, than this argument: those who cannot be renewed through repentance are not to be received into the Church; but such, as the Apostle witnesses, are those once enlightened and afterwards fallen, etc. 2. It is established that this knot seemed at once to most of the Latins a Gordian knot, and unsolvable [ἄλυτον]. Hence those who could not untie it cut it, and stirred up strife both about the authority of the Epistle and about its author. Philastrius agrees, Heresy 41, who among the reasons for withdrawing the Epistle from Paul gives this: that it favoured the Novatians. All the more so because it had already been suspected by some Latins from the time of Caius or of Marcion. Besides, the contagion of the Novatian doctrine spread widely, and at the beginning of the heresy the Latins either did not yet know, or, as they were unskilled and not sufficiently armed to meet the weapons of the schismatics, rejected that gloss of the Greeks, the saying of the Apostle, which most interpreters took to refer to sacramental enlightenment [φωτισμῷ] and renewal [ἀνακαινώσει], and to baptism not being repeated. For in the Roman and Western Church, after those Novatian waves were stirred up, there were very few writers of any name or learning before Hilary and Ambrose etc. who were able to extricate themselves from these narrow straits and difficulties. Afterwards, however, from Hilary, Ambrose and Augustine onwards, the most learned of the Latins preferred to adopt that interpretation about baptism rather than to send the Epistle away.

units.la: XIV. Tertio, damus pariter de Epistola inter Latinos controversum, quarto seculo, & Arrianis temporibus. Nova scilicet haesitandi occasione ab haereticis oblata. Urgebant Christi τὸ ὁμοούσιον καὶ ἀΐδιον [?] everti, non uno Epistolæ loco. V.g. Capite 1. versu 3, dum dicitur χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως· καὶ ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ. Hinc colligere Arriani, Filium esse quid participatum, & essentiatum, & patre minus; habere se ad Patrem, ut radius ad solem, ut imago ad rem expressam imaginem, ut originatum ad originans, adeoque essentia ipsa à Patre esse distinctum. Cumprimis urgere illi ex voce ποίημα Cap. 1.4, Christum factitium esse Deum, creatum, ὅτι ἦν ποτε, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν[?]. Idem inferre iidem ex loco Hebr. 111.2. [illegible, ~12 letters], teste Epiphanio hær. LXIX contrà Arrianomanitas; Nimirum ex eo quod dictum est, fidelem existentem ei qui fecit ipsum, creaturam falsò inferentes. Hac ergò occasione factum, & ad declinanda Arrianorum tela, & molestiam interpretationis, ut ex Latinis quidem, antecessorum moti exemplo, Epistolam obelo configerent, & Pauli esse inficiarentur. Atque haec etiam Philastrius hær. XLI. qui tribus potissimùm causis expositis, ob quas Epistolam non afferərent esse Pauli, alteram hanc innuit, quia Christum factum dicit; simulque confutans monet corpore non divinitate factum. Hinc Hilarius disertissimus Latinorum, vindicandam sibi esse duxit hanc phrasim A posoli Lib. iv. de Trinit. hinc præsidio[?] idem alij, cum primis Græci Patres, qui hæc plerique verba à fœdo purgarunt in-terpretamento. Et qua ratione Christus sit χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως, καὶ ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, ex professo Basilius, luculentâ ad Nyssenum Fratrem epistola, quæ est XLII[?]. Tom. ii. Ut non immerito tertia hæc con-stituatur nobis periodus, de novo & ex accidente quodam interpolatæ hujusce controversiæ.
units.tr: XIV. Thirdly, we likewise grant that the Epistle was disputed among the Latins in the fourth century, in the time of the Arians. The heretics offered a new occasion for doubt. They pressed that the homoousion and the eternity of Christ were overturned, and not in just one place in the Epistle. For example, in chapter 1, verse 3, where it is said: the character of his substance, and the brightness of his glory [χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως· καὶ ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ]. From this the Arians gathered that the Son is something participated and made essential, and less than the Father; that he stands to the Father as a ray to the sun, as an image to the thing it expresses, as the originated to the originator, and so that his essence itself is distinct from the Father's. Above all they pressed from the word poiēma in chapter 1, verse 4, that Christ is a made God, created, "there was when he was not" [ὅτι ἦν ποτε, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν]. The same people drew the same inference from Hebrews 3:2 [illegible, about twelve letters]. According to Epiphanius, heresy 69, against the Arian-maniacs, they falsely inferred a creature from what is said, that he is faithful to him who made him. On this occasion, therefore, it happened that, both to ward off the darts of the Arians and to escape the trouble of interpreting it, some Latins, following the example of their predecessors, marked the Epistle with an obelus and denied that it was Paul's. Philastrius also does this, heresy 41. After setting out three main reasons why they did not allow the Epistle to be Paul's, he hints at this other one: because it says that Christ was made. At the same time, in refuting it, he warns that he was made in body, not in divinity. Hence Hilary, the most eloquent of the Latins, thought he must vindicate this phrase in Book 4 of his work On the Trinity. Others did the same, and above all the Greek Fathers, who purged most of these words of the faulty interpretation. Basil, in his learned letter to his brother of Nyssa, which is Epistle 42 in volume 2, expressly explains in what sense Christ is the character of his substance and the brightness of his glory. So this third period is not unreasonably set before us: a controversy that was new, arose from a chance circumstance, and was interpolated.

units.la: XV. Quartò itaque, supponi dicimus gratis, factum Epistolæ vitio, quod im-portunitate hæreticorum. Non quod soli hi de epistola ejusque Authore, secùs sint opinati, ut putat Faber Stapulensis, in Cap. ii. epistolæ. Sed quod aliis secùs opi-nandi præbuerint ansam. Quod & Caio Presbytero hoc primùm in controversia accidisse, antè vidimus. Pari ratione, ut de Apocalypsi controversum in Græcorum Ecclesiâ, quod Chiliastarum in speciem erroris patrocinaretur. Ut de Epistolâ Ja-cobi, quod in Paulinam de Justificatione doctrinam impingere videretur. Planè ut eadem origine derivandi persæpè errores, Patribus & Catholicis occasione hæreseôn adoptati. Verbi gratia, dogma de rebaptizandis hæreticis, ex æmulatione Cataphrygum & Novatianorum, in Orientalibus & Africanis sancitum Ecclesijs. Dogma de absoluta Baptismi necessitate, Augustini tempore, ortum cum à Cinicis [?] tum à Pelagianis, negantibus in remissionem peccatorum baptizari infantes. Illud Veterum plerorumque, de sanctis in Paradisum post resurrectionem corporum reducendis, probatum imprimis ob Gnosticos, paradisum terrestrem in Archangelum, sacramque Historiam in fabulas transmutantes. Ut alia istiusmodi præterea, alibi observanda.
units.tr: XV. Fourthly, therefore, we say it is groundless to assume that the fault lay with the Epistle, when it was the fault of the heretics' importunity. It was not that these men alone thought differently about the Epistle and its author, as Faber Stapulensis thinks, on chapter 2 of the Epistle. Rather, they gave others occasion to think differently. We saw earlier that this same thing happened first in the controversy over Caius the presbyter. In the same way the Apocalypse was disputed in the Greek Church, because it seemed to lend support to the error of the Chiliasts. The Epistle of James was disputed too, because it seemed to clash with the Pauline doctrine of justification. So it is plain that errors are very often derived from this same origin: doctrines were adopted by the Fathers and by Catholics on account of heresies. For example, the doctrine of rebaptizing heretics was sanctioned in the Eastern and African Churches out of rivalry with the Cataphrygians and Novatians. The doctrine of the absolute necessity of baptism arose in Augustine's time, both from the Cynics [?] and from the Pelagians, who denied that infants are baptized for the remission of sins. The opinion of most of the ancients, that the saints are to be led back into Paradise after the resurrection of the bodies, was approved chiefly because of the Gnostics, who turned the earthly paradise into an Archangel and sacred history into fables. There are other examples of this kind, to be noted elsewhere.

units.la: XVI. Quintò, [illegible, ~10 letters] est, ante Hieronymum à nomine Latinorum eam Epistolam inter Paulinas & sacras receptam. Quod falsum esse constat 1. ex iis quæ de prima controversiæ origine, paulo ante à nobis disputata. 11. ex testimoniis supra ex Eusebio, Hieronymo, &c. quæ nunquam universaliter de Latinis omnibus, benè indefinitè de Latinis, & particulariter de quibusdam, aut multis, aut plerisque Latinorum agunt. iii. inductione exemplorum, puta Clementis Romani, postmodum Hilarÿ, Victorini, Optati, Gregorÿ Boetici, Damasi, Faustini, Ambrosij, Philastrÿ, Gaudentÿ, Ruffini, Paulini, Augustini &c. qui omnes & Latinorum primipili, & Hieronymo vel anteriores, vel certè æquales, quorumque constans de Epistola sententia suprà explorata. iv. etiam ex suffragio Concilij Nicæni, quod præter Latinorum omnium fuisse mentem, verisimile non fit. v. quia suprà memoratos Patres quarti quidem sæculi, primos hanc sententiam de scriptore Paulo fecisse suam, & recessisse à majorum omnium consuetudine, primosque Epistolam recepisse in Canonem, nullis eorum verbis colligimus. vi. quoniam Philastrius, dum secus sentientes hæreticis accenset, minimè sanè id de Latinis omnibus, indè ab Apostolorum ætate ad suam usque, intellexit. Florere autem ipse etiam nonnihil ante Hieronymum coepit. Quin ipse Hieronymus diserte Epist. ad res prolapsi. De quo judicia, apud Pamelium, Rhenanum, Erasmum, Baronium, alios. Scripta etiam illius duûm generum, approbata quaedam, reprobata alia. Haec inter de Pudicitiâ Liber, quo Barnabam Epistolæ authorem prodit. Rhenani vero illatio infirma: ex eo quod Libro contra Marcionem v. ceteris Epistolis excussis illius quæ est ad Hebræos nullus meminit, Tertullianus, sequi eâ ætate non tributam fuisse Paulo. Atqui constat Tertullianum ex solis argumentari Epistolis, quæ Marcioni probarentur, eodem etiam ordine collocatis. Imò Epistolam ad Ephesios, cum Marcione vocat ad Laodicenos. Ergone secutus consuetudinem totius Ecclesiæ? Nihilne etiam Tertullianus vel scripserit, vel senserit, nisi ex omnium ore atque consensu? Quando imprimis de Canonicis variis, non idem omnium fuisse judicium apud Veteres, in confesso est.
units.tr: XVI. Fifthly, [illegible, about ten letters] is that before Jerome that Epistle was received among the Paulines and the sacred books, not by the name of the Latins. That this is false is clear, first, from what we discussed just above about the first origin of the controversy. Secondly, from the testimonies cited above from Eusebius, Jerome, and others, which never speak universally of all the Latins, nor even indefinitely of the Latins in general, but particularly of some, or many, or most of the Latins. Thirdly, from the citing of examples: Clement of Rome, and afterwards Hilary, Victorinus, Optatus, Gregory of Bætica, Damasus, Faustinus, Ambrose, Philastrius, Gaudentius, Rufinus, Paulinus, Augustine, and others, all of whom were leading men among the Latins, and either earlier than Jerome or certainly his contemporaries, and whose consistent view of the Epistle has been examined above. Fourthly, from the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which it is not likely expressed the mind of all the Latins. Fifthly, because from the above-mentioned Fathers of the fourth century we gather from none of their words that they were the first to make this opinion, that Paul was the writer, their own, and to depart from the custom of all their elders, and that they were the first to receive the Epistle into the canon. Sixthly, because Philastrius, when he counts those who thought otherwise among the heretics, certainly did not mean this of all the Latins from the age of the Apostles down to his own. Moreover, he himself began to flourish a little before Jerome. Indeed Jerome himself, in his letter to the fallen, clearly says so. On these matters there are judgements in Pamelius, Rhenanus, Erasmus, Baronius, and others. There are also writings of his in two kinds, some approved and others rejected. Among the rejected is the book on Modesty, in which he names Barnabas as the author of the Epistle. But the inference of Rhenanus is weak: that Tertullian, in Book 5 against Marcion, when he has gone through the other Epistles, makes no mention of the one to the Hebrews, and so it was not then attributed to Paul. Yet it is established that Tertullian argues only from those Epistles which were approved by Marcion, and arranged in the same order. Indeed, he calls the Epistle to the Ephesians, which Marcion also had, the one to the Laodiceans. Did he therefore follow the custom of the whole Church? Did Tertullian write or think anything except by the mouth and consensus of all? It is agreed, above all, that on the canonical books there was not the same judgement among the ancients.

units.la: II. De Caio & Hippolyto, res caret difficultate. Privati fuêre, & privato nomine disjunxêre Epistolam. Imò verò quando id de utroque Veteres traditum voluêre, ostendunt à communi illos recessisse usu. Qua vero occasione Caius Pauli scripta mutilarit, diximus supra. De Hippolyto, Photius, habuisse ἄλλα τινὰ ἀκριβέστατα λεπτόμενα. Et historica quaedam illius παραμυθία, si modo idem est, observat Scaliger Animadv. Eusebi ad A. MCCCCXV. iii. De Cypriano res obscurior. A non citatione scrupulus omnis. Et hoc ipsum suspicionem injiciat, concessisse in Tertulliani Magistri ( ut saepe alias ) sententiam. Quam ob dogma Novatianum, deinceps facilius admiserit. Ob illam etiam suam de rebaptizandis hypothesim, quam Veteres omnes everti voluere, loco Hebr.vi.
units.tr: II. As for Caius and Hippolytus, the matter is not difficult. They were private persons, and as private persons they rejected the Epistle. Indeed, when the ancients handed down that this was true of both, they show that these men departed from common usage. On what occasion Caius mutilated the writings of Paul, we said above. Concerning Hippolytus, Photius says he had other very precise and subtle [ἄλλα τινὰ ἀκριβέστατα λεπτόμενα] things. And Scaliger, in his Animadversions on Eusebius, at the year 1915 [sic], notes a certain historical consolation [παραμυθία] of his, if indeed it is the same man. III. The case of Cyprian is more obscure. The absence of any citation of it is a cause for every doubt. And this very fact suggests that he, as he often does elsewhere, yielded to the opinion of his master, Tertullian. Because of this, he afterwards more readily admitted the Novatian dogma. He also held that hypothesis of his about rebaptizing, which all the ancients wished to overturn, citing Hebrews 6.

units.la: Tamen nec aperte uspiam rejicit Epistolam, nec citationes desunt, suspectae quanquam & ex dubiis Cypriani. iv. De Arnobio & Lactantio, judicii nonnullorum praeceps & praeposterus. Quod, uti de Augustino, & Ambrosio, & Origene & Eusebio, in antecessis demonstratum. v. De Hieronymo, in persona illum sua dubitasse, ut contendit Roterodamus, falsum. Sexcentis in locis Paulo tribuit, imo id assertum it ac vindicatum. Formulas dubias Hieronymi, Epistolam citaturi, qui expenderit, satis intelliget, ex Latinorum quorundam mente loqui non suâs concedendo verius quam affirmando, κατὰ [?] συγχώρησιν [?], non κατὰ δόξαν [?]; adeóque nonnisi ex nonnullorum tum hypothesi, & distinguere Epistolas Pauli non controversas, ab eâ, quæ quibusdam & prioris & illius etiam ætatis in Romanâ Ecclesiâ controversa. vi. De Commentatoribus in tredecim tantùm Epistolas non admodùm laboramus. Duplici potissimùm de causâ à commentatione illâ abstinuêre. Primò ob rei difficultatem, secundò ob aliorum dubia de Epistolæ αὐθεντία [?]. Illo autem ipsissimo loco, de prætermissâ ea queritur Cassiodorus Divin. Lect. C. viii. Neminem verò Latinorum ante Anselmum, in Epistolam esse commentatum pernegamus. Largiri quanquam possemus sine dispendio, modo aliunde nobis de Latinorum mente clarissimè constet. Sanè circumlati in eam Commentarij, sub nominibus Ambrosij, Primasij, Sedulij, Remigij, Isidori, Bedæ, Haimonis. Quos ut interpolatos variè, & sive insertiâ sive protervi quedam, confusos nonnunquam & permixtos damus, at confictos omnes neutiquam. Quo magis horum temporibus recepta fuit opinio de scriptore Paulo. Sic Haimonis, Remigij, altero & amplius seculo Anselmo vetustiorum, genuinos esse foetus, non diffitentur eruditi. De Ambrosio, Cassiodorus Divin. Lect. C. viii. codicem Epistolarum omnium S. Pauli, reliquisse suavissimâ expositione completum. Si vera Cassiodorus, ergò & Epistolae ad Hebraeos, quando eam in Paulinarum censum, & hic & Ambrosius constantissimè retulêre. Quamvis de hodierni codicis Ambrosiani origine meritò ambigatur.
units.tr: Yet nowhere does he openly reject the Epistle, and citations of it are not lacking, though they are suspect, as are some of the doubtful works of Cyprian. IV. As for Arnobius and Lactantius, the judgement of some about them is rash and back-to-front, as has been shown above for Augustine, Ambrose, Origen and Eusebius. V. That Jerome doubted in his own person, as Erasmus of Rotterdam contends, is false. In six hundred places he attributes the Epistle to Paul; indeed, he asserts and defends it as Paul's. Whoever weighs the doubtful formulas Jerome uses when he is about to cite the Epistle will understand well enough that he speaks in the mind of certain Latins, conceding rather than affirming, by concession [κατὰ συγχώρησιν], not by opinion [κατὰ δόξαν]. And so he distinguishes the Epistles of Paul that were not disputed from that one, which was disputed both in his own time and in an earlier one in the Roman Church, by some. VI. We do not labour much over the Commentators on only thirteen Epistles. They refrained from commenting on it for two main reasons: first, because of the difficulty of the matter, and second, because of others' doubts about the authority [αὐθεντία] of the Epistle. Cassiodorus complains of this very omission in the same passage, Divine Lections, chapter 8. Yet we deny outright that any Latin before Anselm wrote a commentary on the Epistle. We could concede this without loss, provided it is quite clear to us from elsewhere what the Latins thought. Certainly commentaries circulated under the names of Ambrose, Primasius, Sedulius, Remigius, Isidore, Bede, Haimo. We grant that these are variously interpolated, and in some places confused and mixed up through insertions or clumsy additions, but we do not grant that they are all wholly fabricated. So much the more was the opinion about Paul as the writer received in their times. Scholars do not deny that the works of Haimo and Remigius, which are older by a century and more than Anselm, are genuine. Concerning Ambrose, Cassiodorus, in Divine Lections, chapter 8, says he left a codex of all the Epistles of St Paul, completed with a most sweet exposition. If Cassiodorus is right, then the Epistle to the Hebrews was also included, since both he and Ambrose most consistently counted it among the Pauline Epistles. Although the origin of the present Ambrosian codex is rightly open to doubt.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Testimonia recentiorum. Qui Paulo tribuunt ex Scholasticis & Pontificijs. Qui ex Lutheranis. Qui ex Reformatis. Magna nomina citata. Qui secùs sentiant. De Calvino. De Confessione Gallicanâ. De Theologis quibusdam aliis. De Novatoribus, Socinianis, Anabaptistis.
units.tr: Testimonies of more recent writers. Those who ascribe it to Paul, from the Scholastics and Papists. Those from the Lutherans. Those from the Reformed. Great names cited. Those who think otherwise. Concerning Calvin. Concerning the Confession of Gaul. Concerning certain other theologians. Concerning the innovators, the Socinians, the Anabaptists.

units.la: 1. Οὐ καλὸν πάντα λόγον παρὰ τέχνην φωτινὴν, μηδὲν πάντ' ἄλλα χρὴ [?] ἰσχύν μέν. Scilicet non aliorum semper judicio atque authoritate pendendum. Et exploratâ diligentiùs Veterum Græcorum & Latinorum men-re, de recentiorum judicio liceret nobis esse securis. Imprimis quando post Vete-res hîc sensêre. Fuerit tamen pretium o-perae, & illorum hîc consensum annecte-re, & potiorum calculo, Paulo Epistolam denuò ire transcriptum. Molestiam inte-rim citationis declinaturi illorum omni-um, quorum obvia de hac re sententia. Nomina plerumque subnotasse, & suo quæque ordine locasse contenti.
units.tr: 1. Οὐ καλὸν πάντα λόγον παρὰ τέχνην φωτινὴν, μηδὲν πάντ' ἄλλα χρὴ [?] ἰσχύν μέν. [It is not good to accept every argument without a luminous art; nothing at all should be...]. Certainly one should not always depend on the judgment and authority of others. And if we examined more carefully the opinion of the ancient Greeks and Latins, we might be free from anxiety about the judgment of more recent writers, especially since they agreed with the ancients on this point. Still, it will be worth the effort to add their consensus here and, by the weight of the more important voices, to transcribe Paul's Epistle once more. Meanwhile, wishing to avoid the tedium of citing all who hold an opinion on this matter, I am content to have noted most of the names and to have placed each in its order.

units.la: II. Ex Scholasticis & Pontificijs ferè omnes, Pauli Epistolam credidêre. Jam inde à Gratiano, & Lombardo, & Thomâ Commentatore Epistolæ. Adeò ut Ba-ronius ad A.C. LX.Num.LIV. Atque (ut uno verbo dicam) quotquot postea exstitê-runt rerum Ecclesiasticarum Catholici tractatores, eadem de Epistolâ ad Hebræos pari consensione firmarunt: exceptis tamen quibusdam Novatoribus, quos vel ingens temeritas arguit, vel hæresis infa- mat atque condemnat. Ita Bellarminus, dubia de Authore Paulo, hæreticis potis- simùm impingit, sive Veteribus sive no- vis, quo nomine Protestantes imprimis notat, Lib.i.de Verb. Dei, C.xvii. Duos- que tantùm excipit è suis, Erasmum & Cajetanum: quorum illum Faber Stapu- lensis, in Cap.ii. Epistolæ, & Marianus, suis in Hieronymum notis;hunc ipse Bel- larminus eo nomine perstringunt. Addi debet magni ex Pontificiis nominis, Lu- dovicus Vives, qui incertum esse authorem putat, suis in Augustinum de Civit. Dei Commentarijs, L.x.C.v. & L.xvi. C.xxii. Estius Prolegomenis in Epist. subjectum totius Epistolæ, & ordinem, à Paulo submi-nistratum dicit, compositionem alterius esse, cujus operâ Paulus u- tendum putavit. Quæ hausit ex Eusebio, sententiam Origenis declaraturo, quæ- que scrupulosiùs distinguere nihil neces- se est. Reliqui nihil tergiversantur, & præ- ter suprà memoratos, pro Paulo faciunt, Lyranus, Carthusianus, Ribera, Catharinus, Lindanus, Sixtus, Possevinus, Alapide, Tostatus &c. quotquot denique sive Epistolam Commentariis illustrarunt, sive controversiam attigerunt. Sed præsto est canon Tridentinorum, qui Sess. IV. Decreto 1. in Catalogo librorum N.T. Quatuordecim Epistolæ beati Pauli Apostoli, scilicet ad Romanos &c. ad Hebræos.
units.tr: II. Almost all the Scholastics and Papists have believed that Paul wrote the Epistle. Already from Gratian, Lombard and Thomas, the commentator on the Epistle. So much so that Baronius, at A.D. 60, num. 54, says: And (to say it in one word) all the Catholic writers on ecclesiastical affairs who have arisen since have confirmed the same thing about the Epistle to the Hebrews with equal agreement: except for certain innovators, whom either great rashness convicts or heresy brands and condemns. Thus Bellarmine, Book 1 On the Word of God, chapter 17, charges doubt about Paul as author chiefly upon heretics, whether ancient or new, a name by which he especially marks the Protestants. He excepts only two of his own: Erasmus and Cajetan. The former is attacked by Faber Stapulensis, in his notes on chapter 2 of the Epistle, and by Marianus, in his notes on Jerome; the latter is attacked by Bellarmine himself on that account. Also to be added is the great Papist name Ludovicus Vives, who thinks the author uncertain, in his commentaries on Augustine's City of God, Book 10, chapter 5, and Book 16, chapter 22. Estius, in the Prolegomena to the Epistle, says that the subject matter of the whole Epistle and its order were supplied by Paul, but that the composition is another's, whose work Paul thought he could use. He drew this from Eusebius, in order to state the opinion of Origen; and there is no need to distinguish this more scrupulously. The rest do not hedge at all, and besides those mentioned above they favour Paul: Lyranus, Carthusianus, Ribera, Catharinus, Lindanus, Sixtus, Possevinus, Alapide, Tostatus, etc., in short, all who have either illustrated the Epistle with commentaries or touched on the controversy. But the canon of the Tridentines is at hand, which in Session IV, Decree 1, in the catalogue of the books of the New Testament, lists: Fourteen Epistles of the blessed Apostle Paul, namely to the Romans etc., to the Hebrews.

units.la: III. Ex Lutheranis, à Luthero ipso discessère, & Paulum statuêre authorem, præter Flaccium, Chytræum, Palladium, Gesnerum, Gerardum, Horneium, Calixtum, plerique hodie recentiorum. Chemnitius, Exam. Concil. Trident. Parte 1. de scriptis & Epistolis Apostol. hanc penultimam Paulinarum facit, dubius licet nonnihil. Confessio Saxonica, superiore sæculo, in Wittebergensi Synodo conscripta, Paulo eandem tribuit, Artic. xv. Cum dicit Paulus ad Hebræos, sese obtulit &c. Quod vero aliter senserint Lutheranorum varij; quod Augustana, quod Wirtembergica Confessio, Epistolam ad Hebræos, simpliciter nec authore defignato[?] citent ; sacrâ ipsis Lutheri ferè unius authoritate effectum. Quâ si stan-dum, de Epistolâ Jacobi, deque Apoca-lypsi, nec de authoribus tantùm, sed canonicâ authoritate controvertendû fue-rit. Ne refricem illud Lutheri, in sermon.[?] Convival. titulo de Vet. & Nov. Test. quodque objectum à Bellarmino, authorem Ecclesiastis, sibi videri ocreis & cal-caribus destitutum, equitare tantùm in-soccis. Sed sive Lutheri, sive Brentij, sive Hunnij, sive Magdeburgensium, sive Osiandri, communes cum aliis objectiones & instantiæ, suo loco expendendæ veniunt.
units.tr: III. Among the Lutherans, those who departed from Luther himself and held Paul to be the author include, besides Flacius, Chytraeus, Pallas, Gesner, Gerhard, Horneius, Calixtus, most of the recent writers today. Chemnitz, in the Examination of the Council of Trent, Part 1, on the writings and epistles of the Apostles, makes it the penultimate of the Pauline Epistles, though he is somewhat doubtful. The Saxon Confession, written in the Synod of Wittenberg in the last century, ascribes it to Paul, Article 15: When Paul says to the Hebrews, he offered himself etc. But that the various Lutherans thought otherwise, that the Augsburg and the Württemberg Confessions cite the Epistle to the Hebrews simply, without naming an author, was brought about almost by the sacred authority of Luther alone. If we were to stand by that, the controversy would concern not only the authors but the canonical authority of the Epistle of James and of the Apocalypse. I will not rehash that saying of Luther, in the sermon Convival. under the title On the Old and New Testament, which Bellarmine also objected to: that the author of Ecclesiastes seemed to him destitute of spurs and stirrups, riding only in slippers. But whether the objections and instances, common to others, come from Luther, Brenz, Hunnius, the Magdeburgers, or Osiander, they will be weighed in their proper place.

units.la: IV. Ex Reformatis, Paulo Epistolam adscribunt; Confessio Helvetica, quæ illam passim Pauli Apostoli nomine citat, Artic. xi, xvi. &c; Confessio Belgica, cujus Articulo iv. recensetur canon scripturarum, & in his quatuordecim Epistolæ S. Pauli, quæ sunt ad Romanos, &c. ad He-bræos; Confessio Polonica, sive Czengeri-na, perbrevis aliàs, Responsione ad ca-lumniam adversar. Spiritui quoque Sancto cum Patre & Filio, Apostolus Hebr. iii. & iv; Confessio Bohemica, Articul. iv. & sequentibus. Paulus etiam ad Hebræos; Paulus Hebraeis scribens; Genevenses, qui in certâ Bibliorum editione, juxtà Græcorum codicum fidem, præfixêre titulum, Epistre de S. Paul aux Hebrieux; Angli pariter, in sacro Codice, The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews; & Annotat. Biblicis, publicâ Anglicanæ Synodi authoritate adornatis, Annotations on the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews; Chamierus de Canone Fidei, Lib. iv. Cap. ii. sententiam Orthodoxorum enarraturus, Novi Testamenti Libros numeramus viginti septem, &c. quatuordecim Epistolas Pauli. Speciatim, pro Paulo Epistolæ scriptore pronunciarunt, ex Germanis Theologis, Bullingerus Musculus, Hyperius, Polanus, Zanchius, Ursinus, Tossanus, Piscator, Pareus, Keckermannus, &c. ex Gallis, Beza, Sadeel, Junius, Mercerus, Chamierus, Mornæus, Molinæus, Jac. Capellus, Rivetus, Diodati, Mestrezatius &c. &c. ex Anglis, Perkinsius, Rainoldus, Willetus, Rollocus, Forbesius &c. ex Belgis, Gomarus, Walæus, de Dieu, &, ut paucis, quotquot ferè per Belgium Theo-logi, quos inter novissimè Joh. Hoorn-beeck, Vir Clarissimus, Append. ad 1. Controvers. Socinian. Recentiores au-tem omnes per Europam Reformatam Theologos, consultò prætermitti-mus.
units.tr: IV. Among the Reformed, many ascribe the Epistle to Paul. The Helvetic Confession, which cites it throughout under the name of the Apostle Paul, Articles 11, 16, etc.; the Belgic Confession, in whose Article 4 the canon of Scripture is listed, and among these the fourteen Epistles of St Paul, which are to the Romans, etc., to the Hebrews; the Polish Confession, or Czengerina, otherwise very brief, in its response to the calumny of adversaries: the Holy Spirit also, with the Father and the Son, the Apostle in Hebrews 3 and 4; the Bohemian Confession, Article 4 and following. Paul also to the Hebrews; Paul writing to the Hebrews; the Genevans, who in a certain edition of the Bible, following the testimony of Greek manuscripts, prefixed the title Epistre de S. Paul aux Hebrieux; the English likewise, in their sacred code, The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews, and in the Biblical Annotations, prepared by public authority of the English Synod, Annotations on the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews; Chamier, On the Canon of Faith, Book 4, chapter 2, about to set out the opinion of the Orthodox: We number the books of the New Testament at twenty-seven, etc., fourteen Epistles of Paul. Specifically, they pronounced Paul the writer of the Epistle: from the German theologians, Bullinger, Musculus, Hyperius, Polanus, Zanchius, Ursinus, Tossanus, Piscator, Pareus, Keckermann, etc.; from the French, Beza, Sadeel, Junius, Mercerus, Chamier, Mornay, Molinaeus, Jacques Cappel, Rivet, Diodati, Mestrezat etc.; from the English, Perkins, Rainolds, Willet, Rollock, Forbes etc.; from the Belgians, Gomarus, Walaeus, de Dieu, and, to be brief, nearly all the theologians throughout Belgium, among whom most recently John Hoornbeeck, a most distinguished man, in the Appendix to his first Controversy against the Socinians. But we deliberately pass over all the more recent theologians throughout Reformed Europe.

units.la: V. Subscripsêre viri alij maximi, & eruditionis omnis principes. Isaacus Casaubonus Exercit. xvi, contrà Baron. Num. cxlvii. Sic enim & Paulum, qui tot locis Apostolum Gentium se appellat, etiam ergà Judæos, quoties data est occa-sio, vim muneris sui extendisse, & in eorum synagogis studiosè Christum prædicasse, & ad eosdem etiam illam divinam Episto-lam scripsisse. Claudius Salmasius, Commentar. de Hellenisticâ, Quæst.v. Eâ-dem de causâ Paulus, cū ad fideles Judæos scriberet, non inscripsit Epistolam suam πρὸς Ἰουδαίους, sed πρὸς Ἑβραίους. Idem Quæst. vi. Sic Epistola Pauli ad Hebræos &c. Idem, Funere Ling. Hellenist. p. 38, 39. κατ' ἄρσιν & κατὰ θέσιν agit de causis suppressi Paulini nominis. Daniel Heinsius, Exercitat. ad Epistolam Pauli ad Hebraeos, notatis de authore, & authoritate Veterum dissensionibus, huic diserte inscribit. Jacobus Usserius, Annal. Part. II. A.C. 64, Circa idem tempus Epistolam ad Hebraeos Paulus scripsit, Timotheo jam soluto &c. Petrus Cunaeus, de Republ. Hebraeor. L. III. C. III. Ex illis petitum est, quicquid sublimi oratione dissertavit Apostolus in eâ Epistolâ, quam ad Hebraeos scripsit. Item, Melchisedeci sacerdotium à Divo Paulo, perpetuum atque infinitum constitui. Addimus Ecclesiasticæ antiquitatis promicondum, Dav. Blondellum, Præfat. in Apolog. pro sententi. Hieronymi, quo anno LXI. Paulus Epistolas ad Philippenses & Hebraeos, in vinculis scripsit.
units.tr: V. Other very great men have subscribed to this, princes of all learning. Isaac Casaubon, Exercitation 16, against Baronius, num. 147: For thus Paul, who in so many places calls himself the Apostle of the Gentiles, also extended the force of his office towards the Jews, whenever occasion was given, and diligently preached Christ in their synagogues, and wrote that divine Epistle also to them. Claudius Salmasius, Commentary on the Hellenistic, Question 5: For the same reason Paul, when he wrote to the faithful Jews, did not inscribe his Epistle πρὸς Ἰουδαίους [to the Jews], but πρὸς Ἑβραίους [to the Hebrews]. The same, Question 6: So the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews etc. The same, Funeral of the Hellenistic Language, pp. 38, 39, treats of the causes of the suppressed Pauline name under κατ' ἄρσιν and κατὰ θέσιν. Daniel Heinsius, in his Exercitations on the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews, noting the disagreements of the ancients about the author and authority, expressly ascribes it to him. James Ussher, Annals, Part II, A.D. 64: About the same time Paul wrote the Epistle to the Hebrews, Timothy having already been released etc. Peter Cunaeus, On the Commonwealth of the Hebrews, Book 3, chapter 3: From those things was taken whatever the Apostle discussed in sublime speech in that Epistle which he wrote to the Hebrews. Likewise, the priesthood of Melchizedek was established by Divine Paul as perpetual and infinite. We add, as a witness from ecclesiastical antiquity, David Blondel, Preface to the Apology for the opinion of Jerome: In the year 61 Paul wrote his Epistles to the Philippians and to the Hebrews in chains.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Excipit ex nostris Bellarminus, primò Calvinum de Authore dubitantem, gemino Institutionum loco. Nec diffitemur, & expressius idem, argumento in Epist. Ego ut Paulum agnoscam authorem adducinequeo. Ipsa docendi ratio & stylus alium quàm Paulum esse satis testantur. Circa finem Commentarij, ad Caput xiiii, 23. Verisimile est Lucam, vel Clementem esse authorem Epistolae, &c. Per nos sanè ita senserit Theologorum maximus. Suo finit ille quemque judicio frui, nec in ipsius verba jurare quemquam voluit. Privatae sententia illius discretionis est, non publicae authoritatis. Aliud etiam loqui καταγορικῶς, & per modum assertionis, aliud δοξαστικῶς [?] ἢ συγχαστικῶς [?], ut hoc loco Calvinus, & per modum obscurae cujusdam conjecturae. Nec Calvini rationes stringere, & doctissimus pridem intellexit Beza, & nos suo loco intelligemus. Adeò allucinari quandoque licuit & sanctissimis viris, nec maculis carent splendidissima sidera. Quanquam nec haec in eminentissimo Theologo macula est, divinitatem aliàs Epistolae magnificè, ut solet, deprædicante: Ego verò eam inter Apostolicas sine controversiâ ampletior, nec dubito quin artificio Satanae fa[?]tum fuit, ut illi authoritatem quidam detraherent. Nullus enim ex sacris libris, de Christi sacerdotio, tam luculenter &c. Argum. in Epistol. Imò Authorem perpetuò vocat Apostolum, ἐξόχως κ̓ ἀντωνομαστικῶς[?]. Et affinitatem ipsum inter & Paulum prodit, Comment. in Caput xiii. v. 13. Et hunc similiter docendi ordine tenere Paulus solet, ut fidelibus ostendat, quibus in rebus Deus exerceri eos velit, dum à frivolis ceremoniis eos abducere studet.
units.tr: Bellarmine first takes up Calvin from our side, who doubted the author, in two passages of the Institutes. We do not deny this, and the same point is stated more expressly in the argument to the Epistle: "I cannot bring myself to acknowledge Paul as the author. The very method of teaching and the style sufficiently testify that it is someone other than Paul." Near the end of his Commentary, on chapter 13:23, he writes: "It is likely that Luke or Clement is the author of the Epistle," and so on. Among us, the greatest of theologians clearly thought this way. He left each person free to enjoy his own judgment, and he did not wish anyone to swear to his words. His view is a matter of private opinion, not of public authority. It is one thing to speak categorically [kataghorikōs] and by way of assertion, and another to speak conjecturally [doxastikōs] or by way of conjecture [synchastikōs], as Calvin does in this place, by way of some obscure guess. Nor is it necessary to press Calvin's arguments; the very learned Beza understood this long ago, and we shall consider it in its place. So it has been permitted at times even to the holiest men to go astray, and the most brilliant stars have spots. Yet this is no blemish in that most eminent theologian, who elsewhere praises the divinity of the Epistle magnificently, as is his way: "But I hold it, without controversy, to be among the more outstanding of the Apostolic writings, and I do not doubt that it came about by the craft of Satan that some people detracted from its authority. For no book of Sacred Scripture speaks so clearly about the priesthood of Christ..." (Argument on the Epistle). Indeed, he always calls the author "the Apostle," eminently and as if by name [exochōs kai antonomastikōs]. And he reveals the close kinship between him and Paul (Commentary on chapter 13, verse 13). Paul usually keeps this same order of teaching as well, in showing the faithful in what matters God wishes them to be exercised, while he takes care to draw them away from frivolous ceremonies.

units.la: VII. Secundò excipit Bellarminus, Confessionem Gallicanam, cujus Articulo iii. à Paulinis subjungitur Epistola ad Hebræos, ut authoris incerti. Ita sanè est. At causa minimè hæc fuit, quasi dubitarint, quotquot id scripti genus primùm probavêre. Operam in Confessione eâ concinnandâ egregiam navavit Antonius Sadeel, pro Paulo authore tamen sentiens. Primus omnium Beza, in colloquio Poissiacensi, Ecclesiarū nomine exhibuit Galliarum Regi; atqui fatetur idem ille, vix alium quam Paulum authorem esse potuispotuisse. Necalia plerorumque per Gal- liam Theologorum opinio. Quod ergò ad Confessionum aliarum exemplum, non pronunciarit de authore Gallicana, factum sive ob reverentiam Calvini, sive ob Veterum quorundam scrupulos, sive ob Paulini nominis in limine absen- tiam.
units.tr: VII. Secondly, Bellarmine takes up the Gallican Confession, in whose third article the Epistle to the Hebrews is appended to the Pauline epistles as being of uncertain author. That is indeed so. But this was by no means because they doubted, as many as first approved this kind of writing. Antoine de Sadeel labored outstandingly in drawing up that Confession, though he himself held Paul to be the author. Beza was the first of all, at the Colloquy of Poissy, to present a Confession on behalf of the churches of France to the King; yet he himself admits that hardly anyone other than Paul could have been the author. Nor was the opinion of most of the theologians of France otherwise. As for why the Gallican Confession did not declare the author, as the examples of other Confessions do, this was done either out of reverence for Calvin, or out of the scruples of certain of the Ancients, or because the name of Paul is absent from the threshold of the Epistle.

units.la: VIII. Atq; hoc accidit potissimùm no- mine, ut doctissimi alij ex nostris Viri, E- pistolâ, non designato Paulo, frequenter usurparint. Citare hoc modo soliti, Epi- stola ad Hebræos; scriptor Epist. ad He- bræos; Apostolus. Quod de Authore, non idè omnes statuisse animad verterent. Ex philologis video Drusium, Seldenum, Grotium, & si qui alij. Ex Theolo- gis, Aretium, Marloratum, Whi- takerum, Martyrem, & perpaucos ex Orthodoxis. Joh.Camero, pro Bar- nabâ authore palàm pugnat, Quaest. 11. in Epist. ad Hebr. Vir ut acutissi- mi ingenij, & diffusæ eruditionis, sic novitatis & opinionum, quæ à vulgo TheoTheologorum discederent, plus nimium studiosus. Exempla habet Clariss. Molinæus in vitâ Cameronis. Novissimus Cō-mentator Anglus, ἀνώνυμος[?], cæterà do-ctissimus: Moderni & quorum probabilior sententia adscribunt Epistolam alicui E-vangelistæ, aut viro Apostolico. Si de pau-cissimis modernorum, non repugnamus. Si de potissimis, gratis, nec explorata sa-tis illorum mente. An verò sententia illa probabilior, ipsum est τὸ κρινόμενον, καὶ τὸ ἀμ-φισβητούμενον.
units.tr: VIII. This has happened chiefly for the following reason: other most learned men among us have often used the Epistle without naming Paul. They were accustomed to cite it in this way: "the Epistle to the Hebrews," "the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews," "the Apostle." It should be noted that they did not all determine the author from this. Among the philologists I see Drusius, Selden, Grotius, and some others. Among the theologians, Aretius, Marlorat, Whitaker, Martyr, and very few of the orthodox. John Cameron openly contends for Barnabas as author (Question 11 on the Epistle to the Hebrews). He was a man of acute talent and wide learning, but too much given to novelty and to opinions that departed from the common view of theologians. The most distinguished Molinaeus gives examples of this in his Life of Cameron. The latest English commentator, who is anonymous but otherwise very learned, writes: "Moderns, and those whose more probable opinion ascribes the Epistle to some evangelist or apostolic man." If he means very few of the moderns, we do not dispute it. If he means the chief of them, the claim is gratuitous, and their mind is not sufficiently established. But whether that opinion is "more probable" is itself the very thing under judgment and in dispute [to krinomenon kai to amphisbētoumenon].

units.la: IX. Minimè verò hic audiendi, qui ex Socinianis & Novatoribus, Epistolæ sive authorem, sive authoritatem subinde sol-licitant. Adfuit & causæ compendium suæ, & novaturiendi libido. Sollicitarunt nonnunquam pari temeritate & Canoni-cos. alios. Æquior hic tamen Socinus, de Authorit. script. Cap. i. & iv. qui de Paulo authore pronunciat veluti dubius, & opinionem hanc vulgò receptam profite-tur. Hinc inter eos positus à Gerardo, Pro-leg. in Epist. qui Pauli esse agnoscunt. Sic Jonas Schlichtingius, Prol. in hanc Epist. ex Pauli officinâ, & saltem illius instinctu ac spiritu profectam dicit. Accedunt A-nabaptistæ, qui sæpè ex Paulo ad Hebræos, in controversiis de Veteris abrogatione Testamenti, de Enthusiasmo, de lapsis excommunicandis, de cœlo nō referendo ante extremum diem, argumentari so-lent. Sed illorum omnium, qui à nobis discedunt, authoritas quantùm infra au-thoritates suprà positas, sive numerum sive pondus attendimus, subsidat, facilè omnes assequuntur.
units.tr: IX. Those from the Socinians and the innovators are by no means to be heard, who from time to time trouble either the authorship or the authority of the Epistle. Both the shortcut to their cause and the lust for innovation were at work. On occasion, with equal rashness, they have also troubled other canonical books. Socinus is fairer here (On the Authority of Scripture, chapters 1 and 4), where he pronounces Paul's authorship doubtful, and professes the opinion commonly received. Hence Gerhard places him among those "who acknowledge it as Paul's," in his Prolegomena on the Epistle. So Jonas Schlichting, in his preface to this Epistle, says it came from Paul's workshop, and at least from his impulse and spirit. The Anabaptists also come in, who often argue from Paul to the Hebrews in controversies about the abrogation of the Old Testament, about enthusiasm, about excommunicating the lapsed, and about not returning to heaven before the last day. But the authority of all those who depart from us, however far it sinks below the authorities set above, whether we consider number or weight, everyone readily grasps.

units.la: DE AUTHORE EPISTOLÆ AD HEBRÆOS. PARS SECUNDA. CAPUT I.
units.tr: ON THE AUTHOR OF THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS. PART TWO. CHAPTER I.

units.la: A testimoniis transitur ad rationes. Futilis quædam ratio rejecta. Prima, ex parte materiarum. Confertur Epistola cum reliquis Paulinis. Affinitas demon-stratur. Eadem de Christo encomia. Eadem oracula V.T. applicandi ratio. Citationes eadem. Exempla eadem inculcata. Loca plane gemina. Congruentiæ aliæ variæ in dogmaticis, & paraeneticis. Cameronis exceptio eversa. Alia exceptio confutata.
units.tr: The argument passes from testimonies to reasons. A rather frivolous reason is rejected. The first reason, from the matter. The Epistle is compared with the other Pauline Epistles. Their affinity is shown: the same praises of Christ, the same way of applying the oracles of the Old Testament, the same citations, the same examples urged, passages that are plainly twins, and various other agreements in doctrinal and hortatory matter. The exception of Cameron is overturned. Another exception is refuted.

units.la: I. FEstivè Hilarius, Prologo in Psalmos, Tobiam & Judith reliquis iccircò Canonicis accensét, ut horum numerus, Græcorum & Latinorum literis, quæ viginti quatuor, respondeat. Liceret fortè ad sanctissimi viri exemplum, pro Paulo scriptore Epistolæ, ex bisseptenario Paulinarum numero, ut perfecto & mystico argumentari. Eaque sive ex sacris sive ex prophanis congerere, quæ argumentum illustrarent. Ut ex oppositio, extrà paulinarum locum posuère Epistolam alij, quod remaneant septem, ad quas scripsit Paulus, Ecclesiæ. Sed minimè vacat ludere in re maximè seria. Et ea nobis præstò sunt argumenta, quæ stringant, quæque τὸ ἐπέχειν procul esse jubeant. Insita quidem, neque jam ex aliorum fide, dubia sæpè aut non explorata, sed nativis ex notis, indiciisque utplurimùm sumpta.
units.tr: I. Hilary wittily, in his Prologue to the Psalms, counts Tobit and Judith among the remaining canonical books so that their number may match the number of letters in the Greek and Latin alphabets, which are twenty-four. Following that great man's example, one might perhaps reason on behalf of Paul as the writer of the Epistle from the number fourteen, the double seven of the Pauline Epistles, as a perfect and mystical number, and gather from sacred and profane sources whatever might illustrate the point. Others, in the opposite direction, have placed the Epistle outside the Pauline number, on the ground that seven remain, the Epistles Paul wrote to churches. But it is not at all fitting to play games in a matter of the greatest seriousness. We have arguments at hand that are decisive and that bid us keep far from suspending judgement (τὸ ἐπέχειν). They are drawn not from the faith of others, which is often doubtful or unexplored, but from native marks and indications, taken for the most part from the text itself.

units.la: II. Primum fuerit ex parte materiarum, sententiarumque, quas passim author inspersit, quæque Paulum primâ fronte referunt. Neque de generali illo consensu, & quoad doctrinæ substantiam, qualis inter omnes scriptores sacros, sed plane singulari, & quoad doctrinæ similem modum. Ut accidit, scriptorem eundem reponere subinde eadem, & suis se prodere notis. Quod Paulo cumprimis familiare, & authorem arguit pagina quæque suum. Oecumenius, αὐτῷ τυγχάνειν ἐπιξολὴν, ἡ ἀναγνωσις αὐτὴ διδάσκει. Nec quæremus nodum in scirpo, neque animus est anxius & scrupulosius singula ἐξουσχίζειν, & congruentiæ umbras omnes sectari. Sat fuerit, ex indicijs quibusdam magè perspicuis, dignoscere ὅπ τῆς πατρὸς τὸ παιδίον.
units.tr: II. The first argument shall be taken from the matters and opinions which the author scatters throughout, and which at first sight point to Paul. I mean not that general agreement in the substance of doctrine that exists among all the sacred writers, but a peculiar one, both in substance and in the manner of teaching. It happens that the same writer often repeats the same things and betrays himself by his own marks. This is especially familiar in Paul, and every page of his proclaims its author. Oecumenius says: "the reading itself teaches that it is his letter" (αὐτῷ τυγχάνειν ἐπιστολὴν, ἡ ἀνάγνωσις αὐτὴ διδάσκει). We shall not seek a knot in a bulrush, nor is it my purpose to be anxious and scrupulous, dissecting each detail (ἐξουσχίζειν) and chasing every shadow of agreement. It will be enough to recognise, from certain clearer indications, that the child is like the father (ὅπῃ τῆς πατρὸς τὸ παιδίον).

units.la: III. Quod licet vel ex fronte perspicere, & observari in limine possunt coacervata illa de Christo elogia Hebr. 1. verf. 2, 3. In quibus sigillatim animadvertere est, & phrasim Paulinam, & genium, & ordinem eundem omninò, quem alias
units.tr: III. This can be seen at the very outset, and can be observed at the threshold, in those accumulated praises of Christ in Hebrews 1, verses 2 and 3. In them one notes, item by item, both the Pauline phrasing and the same spirit and the same order that the Apostle observes elsewhere.

units.la: Hebr. 1. verf. 2, 3.
units.tr: Hebrews 1, verses 2, 3.

units.la: dem oracula V.T. applicandi ratio. Citationes eædem. Exempla eadem inculcata. Loca planè gemina. Congruentiæ aliæ variæ in dogmaticis, & parænETICIS. Camerónis exceptio eversa. Alia exceptio confutata.
units.tr: ...the way of applying the oracles of the Old Testament. The same citations. The same examples urged. Passages plainly twin. Various other agreements in dogmatic and hortatory matter. The exception of Cameron overturned. Another exception refuted.

units.la: III. Quod licet vel ex fronte perspicere, & observari in limine possunt coacervata illa de Christo elogia Hebr.1.verf.2,3. In quibus sigillatim animadvertere est, & phrasim Paulinam, & genium, & ordinem eundem omninò, quem aliàs servavit Apostolus. Primum omni-um elogium est, haereditas: ὃν[?] ἔθηκε κληρο-νόμον πάντων. Paulina sententia, Rom. viii. 17. Συγκληρονόμοι τῷ χριστῷ[?]; ut quod ille inde ab omni æternitate, jure proprio, & na-turæ quadam lege, nos jure alieno, εἰσποιή-σει, & gratiæ beneficio. Alterum est, crea-tionis opus: Δι' ὃν καὶ τὰς αἰῶνας ἐποίησεν. Pau-lus Coloss. i.16, τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἔκτι-σαι. Sive enim αἰῶνας, ex Hebræorum idio-tismo dixerit, sive τὰ πάντα, ὁρατὰ τε ἢ ἀόρατα, sive etiam τὸ ποιῆσαι, sive τὸ κτίσαι usurparit, obvius est vocum usus promiscuus. Ter-tium est, imago Patris: ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτῷ[?]. Pla-nè, tum priori illo ad Colossenses loco, tum 2. Corinth. iv. 4. ὃς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου. Nec aliud effulgere in Christo splendorem Patris ac majestatem, aliud imaginem. Æquipollent etiam hoc in lo-co χαρακτὴρ, εἰκὼν, ὁμοίωμα. Et quidem u-trobique usurpant substantivum ὤν, ἐστὶν ut Græci notârunt Patres ἐμφατικῶς καὶ ἀ-κριβῶς; ὅτι οὐ ἀπέστραπον ἔχει τὸ εἶναι ἀπαύγασ-μα, εἰκῶνα, ἀλλὰ ἐξ ἀϊδίως, ἀεὶ ὤν. Quartum est, Christi providentia : Φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ. Idem, eodem il-lo ad Colossenses loco ; Τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συ-νέστηκεν, Cap.1.v.17. Nec diversa, ἐν αὐτῷ συ-νισάναι, vel δι' αὐτῆς Φέρεσθαι. Alias συνέχεσθαι, περιέχεσθαι, πηδαλιοχεῖσθαι, κυβερνᾶσθαι, ut se-quiores Graeci. Quintum est, per Chri-stum redemptio : Δι' ἑαυτοῦ καθαρισμὸν ποιησά-μενος, τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. Eâdem serie Co-loss.I,14. Ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. Promiscua autem haec Paulo, & familiaria, ἐν ᾧ & δι' οὗ. item καθαρισμὸς, ἀπολύτρωσις, ἄφεσις. Oecumenius cum vetustioribus, locum ad Hebraeos, interpretatur, de purgatione factâ ἐν τῷ βαπτισματι. Et sic affinis est locus Pauli E-phes. v.26, ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν, καθαρίσας τῷ λουτρῷ ὕδατι. Ultimum, sessio Christi ad dextram : Ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς μεγαλωσύνης, ἐν ὑψηλοῖς. Totidem verbis Paulus, Ephes. 1.21, ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις. I-dem alibi encomium Rom. viii.34. Coloss. iii.1. Quis jam non ex ungue leonem in-telligat, & quis, nisi hospes, non audiat Pauli vocem?
units.tr: III. This can be seen at the very outset, and can be observed at the threshold, in those accumulated praises of Christ in Hebrews 1, verses 2 and 3. In them one notes, item by item, both the Pauline phrasing and the same spirit and the same order that the Apostle observes elsewhere. The first praise is that of heirship: he has appointed him heir of all things (ὃν ἔθηκε κληρονόμον πάντων). This is Paul's sentiment in Romans 8:17, "joint heirs with Christ" (συγκληρονόμοι τῷ Χριστῷ): that he possesses this by his own right and by a law of nature from all eternity, while we possess it by another's right, by adoption (εἰσποίησις) and the benefit of grace. The second is the work of creation: through whom also he made the worlds (δι' ὃν καὶ τοὺς αἰῶνας ἐποίησεν). Paul, in Colossians 1:16, says that all things were created through him and for him (τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἔκτισται). For whether the author used "worlds" by a Hebrew idiom, or "all things" (visible and invisible), or the verbs "make" and "create" (ποιῆσαι, κτίσαι), the promiscuous use of these words is plain. The third is the image of the Father: who, being the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person (ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ). Clearly this is so both in that earlier passage to the Colossians and in 2 Corinthians 4:4, "who is the image of the invisible God" (ὃς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου). Nor is the splendour and majesty of the Father shining in Christ one thing, and his image another. In this passage χαρακτήρ, εἰκών and ὁμοίωμα are equivalent. Indeed both passages use the substantive "being" (ὤν, ἐστίν) in the same way, as the Greek Fathers observed, emphatically and exactly: that he does not have being as a brightness or an image received from elsewhere, but being eternally, always existing (ἐξ ἀϊδίως, ἀεὶ ὤν). The fourth is the providence of Christ: upholding all things by the word of his power (Φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ). The same in that same passage to the Colossians: "in him all things consist" (τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκεν), 1:17. Nor is "to hold together in him" or "to be carried through him" different. Elsewhere the later Greeks say "to be held together," "to be enclosed," "to be steered," "to be governed." The fifth is redemption through Christ: having by himself made purification of our sins (Δι' ἑαυτοῦ καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν). In the same sequence, Colossians 1:14: "in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" (Ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν). These expressions, "in whom" and "through whom," "purification," "redemption," "forgiveness," are used by Paul interchangeably and as familiar terms. Oecumenius, with the older writers, interprets the passage in Hebrews as referring to a purging accomplished in baptism (ἐν τῷ βαπτίσματι). So too Paul's words in Ephesians 5:26 are akin: he gave himself, cleansing her with the washing of water (καθαρίσας τῷ λουτρῷ ὕδατι). The last is the session at the right hand: he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν ὑψηλοῖς). Paul says the same words, Ephesians 1:21: he sat at his right hand in the heavenly places (ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις). The same praise recurs at Romans 8:34 and Colossians 3:1. Who now would not know the lion by its claw, and who, unless a stranger, would not hear the voice of Paul?

units.la: IV. Secundò loco ostendit Paulus [?] illegitimus [?], in oraculorum Prophetico[?]rum applicatione, quàdam ad Christum mystica & singularis. Et quae in Authore nostro stupent alij religipsè, carpunt alij blasphemè, minùs appositè trahi ad rem Christianam; nonnulla Veteris effata Testamenti, idem alibi in Paulo ridem. Sic quaedo Davide dicta videri possint Psalmo 11. de Salomone, 11. Samuelis vii; de Jehovah, Psalmo xcvii; de humano genere universo, Psalmo viii; Author Epistolae ad Hebraeos, ad Christum transferens Capitibus 1. & 11. Atqui in speciem plane hoc à locorum mente, & à literâ videtur alienum. At vero id Paulo familiare, pro sublimi illâ quâ fuit instructus sapientiâ. Plura id genus exempla suppeditant Epistolae ad Romanos, Corinthios, Galatas. Verbi gratiâ, quando quod de Jacobi praerogativâ in speciem externâ, Genesis xxv.23, ad electionis & reprobationis mysterium refert Apostolus Roman. ix, quod de posteris Iacobi & Esavi, Malachi 1.3, ad personas ipsas Patriarcharum Rom. ix, 13; quod de bove triturante non capistrando, Deuter. xxv, 4. ad Pastores Evangelij, 1. Corinth. ix, 9; quod de manna, & Petra, & nube, & per mare transitu, sacra Mosis Historia, ad Christum ejusque perceptionem sacramentalem, 1. Corinth. x, 1,2,3,4; quod Moses individualiter de Isaaco, aut collectivè, ut videtur, de Abrahæ semine, Paulus antonomasticè ad Christum, Galat. iii. 16; quod idem de Sarâ & Agare, Paulus ad Fœdus utriusque Testamenti, Galat. iv, 14. Sexcenta ferè istiusmodi à Paulino illo spiritu profecta.
units.tr: IV. Secondly, Paul shows, in applying the prophetic oracles, certain things to Christ that are mystical and singular. What others marvel at in our author with religious wonder, and what others carp at blasphemously as applied less aptly to the Christian matter, namely some sayings of the Old Testament, is found elsewhere in Paul too. Thus, passages which seem to be spoken of David, Psalm 11 about Solomon (2 Samuel 7), Psalm 97 about Jehovah, Psalm 8 about the whole human race, the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews transfers to Christ in chapters 1 and 2. Yet this seems plainly, in appearance, alien to the mind of the passages and to the letter. But this is familiar to Paul, in keeping with the lofty wisdom with which he was endowed. The Epistles to the Romans, Corinthians and Galatians supply many examples of this kind. For instance: when the Apostle refers what was said of Jacob's external pre-eminence (Genesis 25:23) to the mystery of election and reprobation (Romans 9); when he refers what is said of the posterity of Jacob and Esau (Malachi 1:3) to the persons of the patriarchs themselves (Romans 9:13); when he applies what is said of the ox treading out the corn and not to be muzzled (Deuteronomy 25:4) to the ministers of the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:9); when he refers the sacred history of Moses concerning the manna, the rock, the cloud and the passage through the sea to Christ and to the sacramental partaking of him (1 Corinthians 10:1–4); when Moses speaks of Isaac individually, or, as it seems, of Abraham's seed collectively, Paul refers it by antonomasia to Christ (Galatians 3:16); when he refers the same to Sarah and Hagar, to the covenants of both Testaments (Galatians 4:24). About six hundred examples of this sort proceed from that Pauline spirit.

units.la: V. Tertiò, non in ἀναγωγῇ tantùm illâ, Paulum inter & scriptorem Epistolæ convenit, sed & in locorum eorundem atque oraculorum citatione frequenti. Sequens docebit ὑποτύπωσις Psaltis illum locum, Filius meus es, hodie genuite, bis hac in Epistolâ de Christo expositum, Capitibus i, & v, Paulus similiter de eodem Christo interpretatur, Actor. xiii. 32. Nec obstat hîc ad resurrectione Christi trahi, quod istic ad illius cum filiationem, tum sacerdotium. Sufficit eidem sub-jecto applicari, prout ex resurrectione il-lius, & honore sacerdotali, Christi filiatio æterna sequebatur. Veteres autem de [ἐνανθρωπήσει[?]] quando illis vox hodie, [χρον-χὴν ἀποφαντικόν[?]] denotabat. Ita locus ille Habacuci Cap. II. 4, [ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται[?]] ad fidem justificantem, ejusque fructum trahitur, ut scriptori ad Hebræos Cap. x, 38, sic Paulo ad Romanos Cap. i, 17. & Galatas Cap. iii. ii. Quanquam Pro-phetæ in speciem, non de Evangelicâ illa virtute, sed legali verius, integritate, constantia, nec de salute, sed liberatione ex Babylonis servitute. Sic Psaltis ille lo-cus, de sessione ad dextram, Psalm. cx,1. de glorioso Christi regno exponitur, cita-turque, ut Hebr. i. 13, & x, 13. sic etiam 1. Corinth. xv, 25. Pariter Jeremiæ vati-cinium, de peccatis sub novo Fœdere tollendis, citatum authori Epistolæ, Capitibus viii. & x, Paulo itidem allegatur, ad Romanos Cap. xi, 27. Sic, tentati Dei illud flagitium, Israëlitis pridem impa-ctum, in Christum admissum dicitur, quemquemadmodum Hebr. iii. 9, ita 1. Corinth. x,9. Addimus illud de vindicta Deo propria, Deuter. xxxii. 35; totidem prolatum verbis, in Epistola ad Hebræos, Cap. x; 30. & in ea quæ est ad Romanos, C. xii. 19. Etiam locus ille, ἐ[?]ν' Ἰσαὰκ κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα[?]. Genes. xxii[?].9. legitur allegatus, cum ad Romanos C. ix, 7. tum Hebræos, C. xi,18. Exempla id genus alia, apposi-tissima sanè in rem nostram, sed cum lectoris tædio & nausea reponenda, con-scio studio prætermisimus.
