units.tr: V. Thirdly, Paul and the writer of the Epistle agree not only in that allegorical interpretation but also in their frequent citation of the same passages and oracles. The following will show this. The writer expounds the Psalmist's words, "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee," twice in this Epistle, in chapters 1 and 5, of Christ. Paul likewise interprets the same words of the same Christ, Acts 13:32. Nor does it matter that in Acts they are applied to Christ's resurrection, while here they are applied to both his sonship and his priesthood. It is enough that they are applied to the same subject, since Christ's eternal sonship followed from his resurrection and his priestly honour. The ancients, moreover, took the word "today" to denote the moment of his incarnation [ἐνανθρωπήσει] or of the declaration of his divinity. So too the passage of Habakkuk 2:4, "the just shall live by faith" [ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται], is applied to justifying faith and its fruit, as by the writer to the Hebrews, chapter 10:38, so by Paul, Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11. Yet the Prophet, in appearance, meant not the evangelical virtue but rather the legal virtue of integrity and constancy, and not salvation but deliverance from the Babylonian captivity. Likewise the Psalmist's passage about sitting at the right hand, Psalm 110:1, is expounded of Christ's glorious kingdom and cited as in Hebrews 1:13 and 10:13, and so also in 1 Corinthians 15:25. Similarly, the prophecy of Jeremiah about the taking away of sins under the new covenant, cited by the author of the Epistle in chapters 8 and 10, is alleged by Paul too, Romans 11:27. So too that crime of tempting God, long ago committed by the Israelites, is said to have been committed against Christ, in the same way as Hebrews 3:9 and 1 Corinthians 10:9. We add the saying about vengeance belonging to God, Deuteronomy 32:35, quoted in the same words in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10:30, and in the one to the Romans, chapter 12:19. Also the passage, "in Isaac shall thy seed be called" [ἐν Ἰσαὰκ κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα], Genesis 21:12, is cited both in Romans 9:7 and in Hebrews 11:18. Other examples of this kind, most apposite indeed to our purpose, we have deliberately passed over, lest they weary and nauseate the reader.

units.la: VI. Quartò, mirè author noster luxuriat, in urgendis Patriarcharum exemplis, Abrahami cum primis, hujus fi-de inculcanda, & promissione gratiæ fa-cta illius in semine. Patet Epistolæ Cap. vi, 13, 14, 15. Cap. xi. 8, 9, 10, &c. Quæ quàm apprimè quadrent, cum iis quæ habet Paulus, in sua ad Romanos, Cap. iv, 17. &c. haud prolixè opus est o-stendere. 1. Utrobique prædicatur fi-des Abrahami, digna omni admiratio-ne & omni præconio. ii. Fundamentum illius in promissione Dei certâ, & immoti, ὅτι πιστὸς, καὶ δυνατὸς ὁ ἐπαγγειλάμενος [?] Hebr. vi.13. xi.11. Roman.iv.21. iii. Objectum ejusdem fidei, Dei potentia in Sarae partu, & numerosissimo semine sese exerenda, & benedictio hinc exoritura, Rom.iv, 17, 18. Hebr.vi.14. xi,12. iv. Miraculum fidei à rei difficultate, quę præter veri speciem omnem; Abrahamo & Sarâ jam emortuis, & ad generationem, naturali lege ob ætatem, ineptis; utrobique usus author voce νενεκρωμένον, νέκρωσιν [?], Rom.iv. 19, Hebr. xi, 11, 12. v. Argumentatio Abrahami à majori, posse etiam Deum ἐγείρειν ἐκ νεκρῶν, vel ζωοποιεῖν τὰς νεκρὰς, Rom.iv. 17. Hebr.xi, 19. vi. Fructus fidei, & promissionis complementum, Rom.iv.22. Hebr.xi, 11, 12. &c. Ut non ovum ovo similius deprehendatur.
units.tr: VI. Fourthly, our author takes great delight in pressing the examples of the patriarchs, above all Abraham, urging his faith and the promise of grace made to him in his seed. This is evident in the Epistle, chapter 6:13, 14, 15, and chapter 11:8, 9, 10, and so on. It is hardly necessary to show at length how closely these agree with what Paul says in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter 4:17, and following. (1) In both places the faith of Abraham is proclaimed as worthy of all admiration and all praise. (2) Its foundation lies in the sure and unshaken promise of God, "that he is faithful who promised" [ὅτι πιστὸς καὶ δυνατὸς ὁ ἐπαγγειλάμενος], Hebrews 6:13, 11:11, Romans 4:21. (3) Its object is the power of God displayed in Sarah's giving birth and in a most numerous seed, and the blessing to arise from this, Romans 4:17, 18; Hebrews 6:14, 11:12. (4) The miracle of faith lies in the difficulty of the thing, which, beyond all appearance of truth, was impossible since Abraham and Sarah were now as good as dead and, by reason of their age, unfit for generation under the natural law. In both places the author uses the words "dead" [νενεκρωμένον] and "deadness" [νέκρωσιν], Romans 4:19, Hebrews 11:11, 12. (5) Abraham's argument from the greater to the less, that God can also raise from the dead [ἐγείρειν ἐκ νεκρῶν] or make the dead alive [ζωοποιεῖν τὰς νεκρὰς], Romans 4:17, Hebrews 11:19. (6) The fruit of faith and the fulfilment of the promise, Romans 4:22, Hebrews 11:11, 12, and so on. So closely do they correspond that one egg could not be more like another.

units.la: VII. Quintò, singularis quædam conformitas intercedit, inter geminum illum locum Hebr. ix, 15. ὅπως θανάτου γενομένου, εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων &c; & Roman. iii. 25. διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων &c. Utrimque 1. de Christi morte, & sanguine. II. De fine ejusdem fructúq; ἱλασμῷ , ἀπολυτρώσω. III. De latitudine ejusdé fructus, dũ se se extédit ad μεσιτεύοντος ἁμαρτίας, five τῆς ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεως. Ostèsurus peccata nulla, utroque sub Fœdere, præter quàm so'o intuitu mortis, sanguinis, redemptionis Christi, fuisse deleta. Nec ad præsentia tantùm restringendam, sed præterita, sed futura. Ubi denuò εἰκῶν πρὸς ἰδιωλικὸν Pauli.
units.tr: VII. Fifthly, there is a remarkable conformity between that twofold passage, Hebrews 9:15, "that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first covenant" [ὅπως θανάτου γενομένου εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων], and Romans 3:25, "for the remission of sins that are past" [διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων]. In both places: (1) the subject is the death and blood of Christ; (2) the end and fruit of it is propitiation [ἱλασμῷ] and redemption [ἀπολυτρώσει]; (3) the extent of this fruit is broad, since it reaches to the removal of sin [μεσιτεύοντος ἁμαρτίας], or of the transgression under the first covenant. The author intends to show that no sins were blotted out under either covenant except with regard to the death, blood and redemption of Christ alone. Nor is this to be restricted to present sins only, but extends to past and future sins as well. Here again is the characteristic manner of Paul.

units.la: VIII. Sextò, character itidem Pauli elucescit, Hebr. II. vers. 2. ἐν δὲ ὁ διάγγελων λαληθὲς λόγῳ, ἐγένετο βέβαιος. Hæc de Legę per Angelos promulgatâ, in Sinai monte. Parallelus omninò locus, Galat. III, 19. ὁ νόμῳ διαταγὲς διʼ ἀγγέλων. Lex ordinata, promulgata, per Angelos. Pauli hæc doctrina, causas instrumentales in traditione Legis, cùm Angelos, tum Mosem, commemorantis. Nec simile quid in scriptis Apostolicis, præterquàm Actor. VII. 53. Ἐλάβετε τὸν νόμον εἰς διαταγὰς ἀγγέλων, phrasi diversâ nonnihil. IX. Denique, congruentiæ istius generis innumeræ, sive in dogmaticis, sive in paraeneticis, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρό-[?] τὸν τῆς παιδείας[?]. Dijudicet æquus lector, quæ vel digito monstramus, horumque affinitatem expendat I. De Christo, supra Angelos, & creaturas omnes evecto, Hebr. 11. 7,8, collatione institutâ cum Ephes. 11. 21. Phil. 1. 19. II. De peccatis Christi sanguine purgandis, eluendis, Hebr. 1. 3, 1x,14. &c. factâ collatione cum locis Rom. 111. 25, Ephes. 1. 7. Coloss. 11. 17, III. De legalium ac ceremoniarum umbris, fuisse σκιὰν τῶν μελλόντων, totidem verbis Hebr. VIII. 5. X,1. & Coloss. 11. 17. IV. De promissionibus factis Abrahamo, quemadmodum Hebr. VII. 6, ita Epistolâ ad Gal. III. 16,18, V. De morte Christo victâ & triumphatâ, Hebr. 11.14, itaetiam 1. Cor. XV. 54. VI. De redemptionis objecto, quod τῶν μελλῶν, multorum nomine venit, universali syncategoremate limitato, Hebr. IX. 28, ita Rom. V. 19. VII. De fidei illâ πληροφορίᾳ[?], collatis locis cùm Hebr. VI, 11. X,22. tùm Roman. XIV, 5. 1. Thess. 1,5. VIII. De firmitate, ac constantiâ tiâ in fide inconcussâ, itidem locis expensis, Hebr 111.6,14. & Coloss.1.23. ix. De cavendis novitatibus, & ἐτεροδιδασκαλίαις[?], Hebr. xiii.9. conferendo cum Ephes: iv. 14. Coloss.ii.7. x. De habendis in pretio ductoribus,& imitandis, quod monitum ut Hebr. xiii. 7,17. sic Philipp.ii.29. 1. Thess.v,12,13. xi. De precibus pro iisdem Deo nuncupandis, Hebr. xiii.18, etiam Rom.xv,30. 2.Corinth.i,11. xii.De fiduciali & libero ad Deum accessu, μετὰ παῤ-ῥησίας, quod expressum Hebr.iv.16, & Ephef.ii.18, iii.12. xiii.De pace cum omnibus sectandâ, ut Hebr.xii.14, sic Roman. xiii.18. xiv. De sacrificio laudis, & spiritualibus victimis, iisque λατρείας[?], Deo faciendis offerendisq; Heb. xii,15.16. Rom. xiii.1,2. Atque hæc de materiæ affinitate, nobis observasse suffecerit. Quanquâ convenientiæ hæc ferè pars minima est, & affinia alia, subsequentium mox Capitum, ordinis ac distinctionis ergò, paginam utramq; sacient. Ex dictis tamen liquidò cóstat, haud immeritò ab affinitate argumenti,& doctrinæ quâdâ similitudine,pro Paulo scriptore, licere ratiocinari.
units.tr: VIII. Sixthly, the character of Paul also shines forth in Hebrews 2:2: "For if the word spoken through angels was steadfast" [ἐν δὲ ὁ δι' ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς λόγος ἐγένετο βέβαιος]. This refers to the Law promulgated through angels on Mount Sinai. The parallel passage is entirely the same, Galatians 3:19: "ordained through angels" [διαταγεὶς δι' ἀγγέλων], that is, the Law was ordained and promulgated through angels. This doctrine of Paul, which mentions both angels and Moses as instrumental causes in the transmission of the Law, is unlike anything else in the apostolic writings, except Acts 7:53, "who received the law as it was ordained by angels" [ἐλάβετε τὸν νόμον εἰς διαταγὰς ἀγγέλων], though in a somewhat different phrase. IX. Finally, there are countless agreements of this kind, both in doctrinal and in hortatory matters, arising from the same manner of teaching [κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον τῆς παιδείας]. Let the fair reader judge those which we can point out even with a finger, and weigh their affinity: (I) concerning Christ, raised above the angels and all creatures, Hebrews 1:7, 8, compared with Ephesians 1:21 and Philippians 2:9; (II) concerning sins to be purged and washed away by Christ's blood, Hebrews 1:3, 9:14, compared with Romans 3:25, Ephesians 1:7, Colossians 1:14; (III) concerning the shadows of the legal ceremonies, that they were "a shadow of the things to come," in just these words, Hebrews 8:5, 10:1, and Colossians 2:17; (IV) concerning the promises made to Abraham, which in Hebrews 6:17 are treated as in Galatians 3:16, 18; (V) concerning death conquered and triumphed over by Christ, Hebrews 2:14, and likewise 1 Corinthians 15:54; (VI) concerning the object of redemption, which is said of "many" [τῶν πολλῶν], a universal term restricted in meaning, Hebrews 9:28, and likewise Romans 5:19; (VII) concerning that full assurance of faith [πληροφορίᾳ], comparing Hebrews 6:11 and 10:22 with Romans 14:5 and 1 Thessalonians 1:5; (VIII) concerning firmness and constancy in an unshaken faith, likewise by comparing passages, Hebrews 3:6, 14 and Colossians 1:23; (IX) concerning avoiding novelties and strange teachings [ἐτεροδιδασκαλίαις], Hebrews 13:9, compared with Ephesians 4:14 and Colossians 2:7; (X) concerning honouring and imitating leaders, which is enjoined in Hebrews 13:7, 17 as in Philippians 2:29 and 1 Thessalonians 5:12, 13; (XI) concerning prayers to be offered to God for them, Hebrews 13:18, and also Romans 15:30, 2 Corinthians 1:11; (XII) concerning the confident and free approach to God, with boldness [μετὰ παῤῥησίας], which is expressed in Hebrews 4:16 and Ephesians 2:18, 3:12; (XIII) concerning the pursuit of peace with all, as in Hebrews 12:14, so Romans 12:18; (XIV) concerning the sacrifice of praise and spiritual victims, and the service [λατρείας] to be rendered and offered to God, Hebrews 12:15, 16 and Romans 12:1, 2. Let it suffice for us to have noted these affinities of subject matter. Yet this is scarcely the smallest part of the agreements, and other points of likeness in the chapters that follow will fill both pages, though we pass them over for the sake of order and distinction. From what has been said, it is nonetheless clear that it is not unreasonable to argue from the affinity of the subject matter and a certain similarity of doctrine that Paul was the writer.

units.la: X. Quod interim non placuit Came-roni, qui in hæc verba Quæst.11. in Epist. ad Hebræos. Ajunt ergò quædam reperiri in hac Epistolâ, quæ in aliÿs Pauli scri-ptis fere eadem habentur. Quid tum po-steà? Sanè in duobus Capitibus prioribus, Epistolæ Petri prioris, plura reperias quæ sunt eadem, quæ dixit Apostolus Pau-lus, quam in totâ hac Epistolâ. Ergone i-deò Paulina etiam est? Ego verò respon-deo, nostri vim argumenti, vel non per-spectam satis fuisse Cameroni, vel non fideliter expressam. Cruda sanè foret illa ratiocinatio, reperiuntur quædam in hac Epistolâ, quæ in aliÿs, ergò Pauli est. At non quædam, sed longè plurima, & planè singularia, nec eadem fere, sed omninò. Quod si fortè hactenus minùs demon-stratum, nos eâ quâ debuimus fide, & accu-ratione, ut in tabellâ quâdam exhiben-dum esse duximus. 11. Supponitur falsò, plura reperiri gemina cum Paulinis aliis, in duobus prioris Petri Capitibus, quàm in totâ ad Hebræos Epistolâ. Hîc verò opus non rationis, sed sensuum oculo-rum[?]. rūmque judicio. Et præter Cameronem, id vidit & observavit, nemo. Utut in ex-ordij formâ, & summâ rerum, consensum Petri cum Paulo non eamus inficias. Quàm verò illud sit jejunum, præter collationem antè institutam, docebunt sequentia. III Hoc etiam dato, laborat nihilo-minùs consequentia, & admittitur elen-chus parium. Priorem Petri, Pauli non esse constat vel ex inscriptione, sed Petri. Et quanquam hujus author latitaret, de-sunt rationes aliæ, præter affinitatem quandam argumenti, cur Pauli crederetur. Contrà, de Epistolæ ad Hebræos parente, res in obscuro est; rectè ergo ex fœtus illius lineamentis, patrem conjectamus. Imprimis, tot aliis conjectandi, imò certò pronunciandi rationibus ad-ducti, atque impulsi, prætermissis Cameroni ac dissimulatis.
units.tr: X. This, however, did not please Cameron, who in his Question 11 on the Epistle to the Hebrews says these words: "They say, therefore, that certain things are found in this Epistle which are almost the same as those held in the other writings of Paul. What then follows? Certainly in the two first chapters of the former Epistle of Peter you will find more things that are the same as those the Apostle Paul said than in this whole Epistle. Is it therefore Pauline too?" I reply, however, that either the force of our argument was not sufficiently grasped by Cameron, or it was not faithfully expressed. That would be a crude line of reasoning: certain things are found in this Epistle which are found in others, therefore it is Paul's. But the point is not "certain things" but very many, and quite distinctive ones, and not "almost the same" but altogether the same. If perhaps this has so far been less clearly shown, we have set it out in a kind of table, with the fidelity and care it required. (2) It is falsely assumed that more parallels with the other Pauline writings are found in the first two chapters of the former Epistle of Peter than in the whole Epistle to the Hebrews. Here the matter is to be decided not by reason but by the judgment of the eyes and senses. Apart from Cameron, nobody has seen or observed this. Although we do not deny the agreement of Peter with Paul in the form and general substance of the writing, the following will show how empty that claim is, beyond the comparison already made. (3) Even granting this, the consequence still fails, and the argument from equals is inadmissible. That the former Epistle of Peter is not Paul's is clear even from its inscription, which names Peter. And although its author is hidden, there are reasons other than a certain affinity of subject for believing it to be Paul's. On the other hand, the parent of the Epistle to the Hebrews is a matter of obscurity; we therefore rightly conjecture its father from the features of the offspring. Above all, we are led and impelled by so many other grounds for conjecture, or even for pronouncing with certainty, setting aside and concealing those of Cameron.

units.la: XI. Excipient fortassis alij, per retor-sionis quendam modum. Quæ Epistola continet talia, quorum vestigium in Paulinis nullum, minimè ea Pauli esse videatur. Atqui istiusmodi, quæ habet author de Melchisedeco, quæ de Christi sacerdo-tio, quæ de totali piorum defectione & apostasiâ, plane nova & singularia. Sed in promptu solutio est. i. Negando consequentiam: Neque enim necesse fuit ubique eadem repeti. Imò verò πολυμερῶς[?] καὶ πολυτρόπως promenda, illustranda, firmanda fuêre Evangelij mysteria. Sic multa in Epistolâ ad Romanos, (ut de solâ hac dicam ) Capitibus imprimis vii, ix, xi, quæ non alibi Paulus. ii. Falsum, quoad substantiam rei, nova plane exhiberi in illâ ad Hebræos. Imò eadem plane de Christi persona, officio, beneficijs,& modo ea nobis per fidem applicandi, quæ ubique Paulus. Diversus quamvis in non-nullis doctrinæ modus, conferendo diligentius typos cum antitypis, & legalem cum Evangelicâ œconomiam. Nihil etiâ novi temporarijs, & apostatis, & in spiritum sanctum blasphemis, interitum & exitium denunciari. iii. Si hîc quædam singularia, singulares etiam fuêre Apostolo, urgendi illa & illustrandi rationes. Res ipsi cum Hebræis Christianis, sectantibus adhucdum umbras, ἐνισχόμενοι τῷ νόμῳ καὶ τῆς σκιᾶς, (malè in meo Codice ναχι-αις [?]) ut est apud Athanasium, nec dedi-scentibus Ἰουδαΐζειν [?]. Quid ergo mirum, Legis in Evangelio complementum, & respectum illum mutuum, & obversam Legis ad Christum faciem, inductione quâdam, pressis nobilioribus quibusdam typis atque figuris, talibus ostendere Apostolum ac demonstrare? Quemadmodùm idem cum Gentilibus agens, non jam eos ex Veteri Testamento, sed ex propriis illorum principijs, arguit convincitque.
units.tr: XI. Others will perhaps object, by way of a certain counter-argument. This Epistle contains things of which no trace is found in the Pauline letters, and which therefore seem least of all to be Paul's. Yet the things the author says about Melchisedec, about Christ's priesthood, and about the total defection and apostasy of the godly are plainly new and singular. But the answer is at hand. (1) I deny the consequence, for it was not necessary that the same things be repeated everywhere. Indeed the mysteries of the Gospel had to be set forth, illustrated and confirmed in many parts and in many ways [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως]. So it is in the Epistle to the Romans, to speak of that one alone, especially in chapters 7, 9 and 11, which Paul treats nowhere else. (2) It is false that, as to the substance of the matter, new things are presented in that to the Hebrews. On the contrary, exactly the same things are set out about the person, office and benefits of Christ, and about the manner of applying them to ourselves through faith, as Paul sets out everywhere. The mode of teaching is different in some points, namely in comparing the types with the antitypes more carefully, and the legal with the evangelical economy. Nor is anything new announced there about temporary believers, apostates and those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, namely their ruin and destruction. (3) If certain things here are singular, the means of urging and illustrating them were also singular to the Apostle. He was dealing with Hebrew Christians, who still clung to shadows, held fast to the law and the shadow [ἐνισχόμενοι τῷ νόμῳ καὶ τῆς σκιᾶς] (wrongly read in my copy as ναχι-αις), as Athanasius has it, and who had not unlearned to Judaize [Ἰουδαΐζειν]. What wonder, then, that the Apostle should show and demonstrate, by a certain line of induction, the fulfilment of the Law in the Gospel, the mutual relation between them, and the face of the Law turned towards Christ, by means of certain more notable types and figures of this kind? In the same way, when dealing with the Gentiles, he argues and convinces them not from the Old Testament but from their own principles.

units.la: Non ignorari etiam debet, Melchisedecum, ejusque sacerdotium, celebratissimum fuisse inter Judæos, de quo Thalmudistæ varia, imo habitum Messiæ typum, ut in Bereschith Rabba, ad Cap. xiv. Genes. ut Isaac ben Arama, ad Cap. xlvii, Genes. ut Moses Hadarson, ad Cap. xvi. Numer. & si qui plures. Ut nihil mirum in eo urgendo iisdem & declarando, accuratiorem fuisse Apostolum.
units.tr: It must also not be overlooked that Melchisedec and his priesthood were very famous among the Jews, about whom the Talmudists say various things, and indeed regard him as a type of the Messiah, as in Bereschith Rabba on Genesis chapter 14; as Isaac ben Arama on Genesis chapter 47; as Moses Hadarson on Numbers chapter 16; and several others. So it is no wonder that the Apostle was more exact in urging and explaining these matters with the same people in view.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Ratio altera pro Paulo scriptore. Conformitas phraseôs cum Paulinâ. Illustratur exemplis variis. Propria saepissimè uni Paulo. Camerônis instantia notata. De stylo Epistolæ plura, in Parte ἀνασκευαστικῇ[?].
units.tr: A second argument for Paul as the writer. The phraseology agrees with Paul's. This is illustrated by various examples. Expressions peculiar to Paul are very often found in him alone. Cameron's objection is noted. More on the style of the Epistle in the refutative part [ἀνασκευαστικῇ].

units.la: I. Ex plumis avem, ex voce psittacum, habet verbum vetus. Ita ex phrasi, dictio-ne, expressionibus variis, Epistolæ authorem. Et quemadmodum ante, materiam ipsam ac doctrinam, ita jam formam, τὸν τρόπον τῆς λέξεως, attendendum esse judi-camus. Occurrent sanè phrases, & familiares Paulo, & singulares ferè, ac veluti χαρακτηριστικὰ ἰδιώματα. Neque una fortè aut altera, anxiùs conquisita, sed ἔλω τῶν ἰλλάχῳ[?], & pleno modo. Præter eas, quæ vel superiori Capite observari jam potuê-re, vel sequentibus reservamus.
units.tr: I. The old saying runs, "from the feathers one knows the bird, from the voice the parrot." So from the phrasing, the wording and the various expressions, we must judge the author of the Epistle. And just as before we considered the matter itself and the doctrine, so now we must consider the form, the manner of expression [τὸν τρόπον τῆς λέξεως]. There will certainly occur phrases both familiar to Paul and almost unique to him, and as it were characteristic idioms [χαρακτηριστικὰ ἰδιώματα]. These are not one or two, sought out anxiously, but occur in full measure. I reserve them, apart from those which could already be noted in the preceding chapter, for the chapters that follow.

units.la: II. Principio, notanda nobis videtur phrasis, Hebr.1.1. Quâ dicitur Deus, λαλήσας ἐν τοῖς προφήταις; item ἐλαλήσεν ἐν υἱῷ. Similis illa II.Corinth.xiii.3. ἐν ἐμοὶ λαλοῦντος Χριστοῦ. Utrobique τὸ λαλεῖν ἐν, pro λαλεῖν διὰ, ex usu Hebræorum. Nequicquam Cl. Gerardo, propriam significationem particulæ ἐν hoc loco retinente.
units.tr: II. First, the phrase in Heb. 1:1 seems worth noting, where God is said to have spoken [λαλήσας ἐν τοῖς προφήταις] "in the prophets," and likewise [ἐλάλησεν ἐν υἱῷ] "in the Son." Similar is 2 Cor. 13:3, [ἐν ἐμοὶ λαλοῦντος Χριστοῦ] "Christ speaking in me." In both places the expression "to speak in" stands for "to speak through," in the usage of the Hebrews. Cl. Gerhard is wrong to retain the proper meaning of the particle ἐν in this place.

units.la: III. Capite 1, versu 2, τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως, & si quibus alijs in locis Epistolæ, Hebraismus idem occurrit. Usitatissimus Paulo; σῶμα τῆς δόξης, σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως, πνεῦμα τῆς ἁγιοσύνης, λόγῳ τῆς σοφίας &c.
units.tr: III. In Chapter 1, verse 2, [τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως] "the word of his power," and in some other places of the Epistle, the same Hebraism occurs. It is very common in Paul: [σῶμα τῆς δόξης] "body of glory," [σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως] "body of humiliation," [πνεῦμα τῆς ἁγιοσύνης] "spirit of holiness," [λόγῳ τῆς σοφίας] "by the word of wisdom," and so on.

units.la: IV. Capite 11. versu 14, κεκοινώνηκε σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος; carnis & sanguinis, i.e. naturæ cum infirmitatibus colluctantis. Phrasis Paulina, Galat. 1. 16. οὐ προσανεθέμην σαρκὶ καὶ αἵματι[?]. Ephes. vi. 12. ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα.
units.tr: IV. In Chapter 2, verse 14, [κεκοινώνηκε σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος] "he shared in flesh and blood," that is, in a nature struggling with infirmities. It is a Pauline phrase: Gal. 1:16, [οὐ προσανεθέμην σαρκὶ καὶ αἵματι] "I did not confer with flesh and blood"; Eph. 6:12, [ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα] "our wrestling is against flesh and blood."

units.la: V. Capite 11. versu 11. τὸ ἁγιάζειν, de justificationis & redemptionis beneficio; ὁ πᾶς ὁ ἁγιάζων, καὶ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι, ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντες. Similis locus, Ephes. v. 26. ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς, ἵνα αὐτὴν ἁγιάζῃ.
units.tr: V. In Chapter 2, verse 11, [τὸ ἁγιάζειν] "to sanctify" is used of the benefit of justification and redemption: [ὁ πᾶς ὁ ἁγιάζων, καὶ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι, ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντες] "both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one." A similar passage is Eph. 5:26, [ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς, ἵνα αὐτὴν ἁγιάζῃ] "he gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her."

units.la: VI. Capite 111, versu 1. κλήσεως ἐπουρανίου μέτοχοι: Phrasis Apostoli, Philip. 111.14. τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ. 11. Timoth. 1.9. καλέσαντος κλήσει ἁγίᾳ[?].
units.tr: VI. In Chapter 3, verse 1, [κλήσεως ἐπουρανίου μέτοχοι] "partakers of the heavenly calling." This is the Apostle's phrase: Phil. 3:14, [τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ] "the upward calling of God"; 2 Tim. 1:9, [καλέσαντος κλήσει ἁγίᾳ] "who called us with a holy calling."

units.la: VII. Capite 111 versu 6, τὸ καύχημα
units.tr: VII. In Chapter 3, verse 6, [τὸ καύχημα] "the boasting"

units.la: XVII. Capite x, versu 36 [?], vocat εὐαγγέλιον [?], objectivè & terminativè, vitam æternam, statum gloriæ. Plane Galat. iii. 22. ἵνα ἡ ἐπαγγελία [illegible, ~10 letters] τοῖς πιστεύουσι [?].
units.tr: XVII. In Chapter 10, verse 36 [?], he calls [εὐαγγέλιον] "the promise," objectively and terminatively, eternal life, the state of glory. Plainly so in Gal. 3:22, [ἵνα ἡ ἐπαγγελία] "that the promise" [illegible, about ten letters] [τοῖς πιστεύουσι] "to those who believe" [?].

units.la: XVIII. Capite x, versu 39, εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς. Eodem sensu Paulus 1. Thess. v. 9. εἰς περιποίησιν σωτηρίας. II. Thess. ii. 14. εἰς περιποίησιν δόξης.
units.tr: XVIII. In Chapter 10, verse 39, [εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς] "for the saving of the soul." In the same sense Paul has, 1 Thess. 5:9, [εἰς περιποίησιν σωτηρίας] "for the obtaining of salvation," and 2 Thess. 2:14, [εἰς περιποίησιν δόξης] "for the obtaining of glory."

units.la: XIX. Capite xii. versu 1, vitam Christianam confert Apostolus, cum iis qui currunt in stadio; τρέχωμεν τὸν προκείμενον ἡμῖν ἀγῶνα [?]. Similitudo Paulina, 1. Corinth. ix, 24. & sequent. τρέχοντες μὲν πάντες [illegible, ~12 letters] εἷς λαμβάνει τὸ βραβεῖον [?]. Ibidem usus vocem ἀγωνίζεσθαι, quæ respondet voci ἀγὼν.
units.tr: XIX. In Chapter 12, verse 1, the Apostle compares the Christian life with those who run in a race: [τρέχωμεν τὸν προκείμενον ἡμῖν ἀγῶνα] "let us run the race set before us." Paul's comparison is similar in 1 Cor. 9:24 and following, [τρέχοντες μὲν πάντες ... εἷς λαμβάνει τὸ βραβεῖον] "all indeed run, but one receives the prize." In the same place he uses the verb [ἀγωνίζεσθαι] "to strive," which corresponds to the noun [ἀγὼν] "contest."

units.la: XX. Capite xiii. versu 9. διδαχαῖς παντοίαις μὴ παραφέρεσθε. Plane sic Apostolus Ephes. iv. 14. περιφερόμενοι παντὶ ἀνέμῳ τῆς διδασκαλίας.
units.tr: XX. In Chapter 13, verse 9, [διδαχαῖς παντοίαις μὴ παραφέρεσθε] "be not carried away by various teachings." The Apostle says just so in Eph. 4:14, [περιφερόμενοι παντὶ ἀνέμῳ τῆς διδασκαλίας] "tossed about by every wind of doctrine."

units.la: XXI. Capite xiii. versu 10, utitur phrasi ϑ [?], Φαγεῖν ἐκ θυσιαστηρίου [?], vesci altaris, i.e. victimâ. Idem omninò 1. Corinth. ix, 13. τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ συμμερίζεσθαι, eodem significatu. Item 1. Cor. x, 18. κοινωνοὶ τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ.
units.tr: XXI. In Chapter 13, verse 10, he uses the phrase [Φαγεῖν ἐκ θυσιαστηρίου] "to eat from the altar," that is, to eat of the victim. Exactly the same is 1 Cor. 9:13, [τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ συμμερίζεσθαι] "to share in the altar," in the same sense; likewise 1 Cor. 10:18, [κοινωνοὶ τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ] "partners of the altar."

units.la: XXII. Capite xiiii. versu 15,16. ibi preces confert cum sacrificio Deo offerendo, & quidem grato acceptoque; ἀναφέρωμεν θυσίαν; τοιαύταις γὰρ θυσίαις εὐαρεστεῖται ὁ Θεὸς. Nihil convenientius, Roman.XII.1 παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα, θυσίαν ζῶσαν, εὐάρεστον. Philipp.IV.18. δεξάμενος θυσίαν δεκτὴν, εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ.
units.tr: XXII. In Chapter 13, verses 15 and 16, he compares prayers with a sacrifice to be offered to God, and indeed a thankful and acceptable one: [ἀναφέρωμεν θυσίαν] "let us offer a sacrifice"; [τοιαύταις γὰρ θυσίαις εὐαρεστεῖται ὁ Θεὸς] "for with such sacrifices God is well pleased." Nothing is more fitting than Rom. 12:1, [παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα, θυσίαν ζῶσαν, εὐάρεστον] "to present your bodies a living sacrifice, acceptable," and Phil. 4:18, [δεξάμενος θυσίαν δεκτήν, εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ] "a sacrifice acceptable, well pleasing to God."

units.la: XIII. Capite xiii, versu 20. observari potest illud de Deo epithetum, ὁ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης. Solenne Paulo, & proprium quidem. Rom,xv.33. ὁ δὲ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης. Ita Rom.xvi.20. 11.Corinth.xiii.11. Philipp. iv.9. 1.Thessal.v.23.
units.tr: XIII. In Chapter 13, verse 20, one may observe that epithet for God, [ὁ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης] "the God of peace." It is characteristic of Paul, and indeed peculiar to him: Rom. 15:33, [ὁ δὲ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης] "and the God of peace." So also Rom. 16:20; 2 Cor. 13:11; Phil. 4:9; 1 Thess. 5:23.

units.la: XXIV. Ex his sanè & istiusmodi plu-ribus, sive simplicibus, sive complexis vo-cibus, abunde patet styli quaedam, phra-siologiae, & genij singularis conformitas. Plura investiget, cui plus concessum otij. Et hoc rationis genus, magnum pondus habere debet, ipso teste Camerone. Neque id attendisse mihi videntur satis, qui ad ravim usque & nauseam styli diversitatem urgent. Quam ut palàm faceret Camero, geminum profert exemplum, loco aliquoties notato. 1. Nusquam in Epistolis Paulinis, vocem illam αἰῶνες, eo sensu reperiri. II. Nunquam dicturum fuisse Paulum, [illegible, ~8 letters] Bona verba! Unus aut altera vocula, forte alibi non expressa, praeponderabit superioribus omnibus documentis? Unde etiam habuit Cameron, abhorrere ab his vocibus Pauli genium! Sed de his, aliisque quae de stylo objiciuntur, fusius in [illegible, ~8 letters] suo loco instituendum.
units.tr: XXIV. From these and many similar examples, whether simple or compound words, it is abundantly clear that there is a certain conformity of style, phraseology and singular genius. Whoever has more leisure may investigate more. This kind of argument ought to have great weight, as Cameron himself testifies. Those who press the difference of style to the point of weariness and disgust, it seems to me, have not paid sufficient attention to this. To make the difference plain, Cameron offers two examples, noted in several places. First, nowhere in the Pauline Epistles is that word αἰῶνες found in that sense. Second, Paul would never have said [illegible, about eight letters]. Good words! Will one or two little words, perhaps not expressed elsewhere, outweigh all the preceding evidence? Whence Cameron also had the notion that Paul's genius shrinks from these words! But concerning these and the other objections raised about style, the matter must be taken up more fully in its own place [illegible, about eight letters].

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Ratio tertia pro Paulo. Clausa Epistolae eadem cum Paulinis. Votum idem. Salutatio eadem. Signaculum idem. Cameronis exceptiones diluuntur. Ἐπιστολῶν διαφορὰ[?] Paulinarum, quale.
units.tr: Third argument for Paul. The closing of the Epistle is the same as in the Pauline Epistles. The wish is the same. The greeting is the same. The seal is the same. Cameron's exceptions are refuted. The character of the Pauline Epistles.

units.la: I. Succedit ab Epistolæ ultimis, scilicet claudendi modo, pro Paulo scriptore argumentatio. Seorsim urgenda, quando ponderosa est, & apodicticaferè. Tribus, ut plurimùm, Paulus clausam Epistolarum absolvit, voto, salutatione, signaculo. Quàm belle quadret nostræ clausa Epistolæ, quivis ex sequentibus arbitretur.
units.tr: I. The argument for Paul as author now moves on to the endings of the Epistle, that is, to the manner of closing. It should be pressed separately, since it is weighty and nearly demonstrative. Paul usually completes the close of his Epistles in three parts: the wish, the greeting, and the seal. How well the close of our Epistle fits this pattern, anyone will judge from what follows.

units.la: II. Ad finem Author proparaturus, incipit à voto, cujus hæc forma: ὁ δὲ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης, καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ &c. subjuncta doxologiâ, διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, ἀμήν. Hebr. XIII.20,21. Simili, inquam, & voto & δοξολογία, Paulus colophonem imponere solet Epistolis. Sic priori ad Thessaloni-censes, Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης, ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς &c. 1. Thess. v.22. Sic posteriori Epistolâ, αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης δώη ὑμῖν &c. 2. Thess. iii.16. Similis clausa Epistolæ ad Romanos, cum voto de confirmandis iis per illius Evangelium &c. eâdem δοξο-λογία terminando, Rom. xvi.25,27. Idem in Epistolâ ad Philippenses, ubi præmisso voto de adimplendâ in Philippensibus gratiâ, simili δοξολογία claudit, Philipp. iv.19,20. Quibus, solus Petrus affine quid habet, Epistolâ priori.
units.tr: II. Near the end, the author, about to finish, begins with the wish, which takes this form: "Now the God of peace make you perfect in every good work" (ὁ δὲ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης, καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ), and so on, followed by the doxology: "through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever, Amen" (διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, ἀμήν). Heb. 13.20, 21. I say that Paul usually puts a similar wish and a similar doxology as the finishing touch on his Epistles. So in the earlier letter to the Thessalonians: "And the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly" (Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης, ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς), and so on. 1 Thess. 5.22. So in the later letter: "Now the God of peace himself give you" (αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης δώη ὑμῖν), and so on. 2 Thess. 3.16. A similar close belongs to the Epistle to the Romans, with a wish that they may be strengthened through his Gospel, and so on, ending in the same doxology. Rom. 16.25, 27. The same is true of the Epistle to the Philippians, where, after a wish that the grace in the Philippians may be fulfilled, he closes with a similar doxology. Phil. 4.19, 20. Of the Epistles, only the first of Peter has something related to this.

units.la: III. Subjungit Author salutationem, Paulo ubiq; ferè solitam usurpari. Ἀσπάζονται τοὺς ἡγουμένους ὑμῶν, καὶ πάντας τοὺς ἁ-γίους. Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας. Hebr. XIII.24. Hebr.XIII.24. Quo, & fratrum nomine salutat quos compellat, & suo salutem nunciari alijs jubet. Mutuum hoc salutationis officium, perpetuum in Paulinis. Conferantur Epistolæ ad Romanos, Corinthios, Philippenses, Colossenses, Thessalonicenses &c. Nec fuit, quod instaret Camero, alios etiam salutationibus Epistolas suas claudere. Neque hic salutationem simpliciter, sed formam spectamus ac modum. Fideles etiam quos salutat, Paulino more vocat τὰς ἁγίας.
units.tr: III. The author next adds the greeting, which Paul nearly always uses everywhere. "They greet your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy greet you." Heb. 13.24. Heb. 13.24. By this he both greets in the name of the brothers, whom he addresses, and bids that his own greeting be conveyed to others. This mutual office of greeting is constant in the Pauline Epistles. Let the Epistles to the Romans, Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, and so on, be compared. Nor is there any reason for Cameron to press that others also close their Epistles with greetings. Here we are not looking at the greeting simply, but at its form and manner. He also calls the faithful whom he greets, in the Pauline manner, "the saints" (τὰς ἁγίας).

units.la: IV. Tandem, signaculo apposito, terminatur Epistola. Quod si Pauli esse evicerimus, vix superest dubitationi locus. Pauli signaculum quale sit, ipse docet, II. Thess. III.17. Ὁ ἀσπασμὸς, τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλῳ, ὅ ἐστι σημεῖον ἐν πάσῃ ἐπιστολῇ· οὕτω γράφω· ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ἀμήν. Quibus duo monet 1. eâ formulâ claudere se Epistolas omnes. II. illarum hoc esse proprium, & distinctivum à reliquis, πρὸς τὸ μὴ μεταπιστεύειν[?]. Atqui ipsissima illa verba, eodem etiam ordine ac loco, Hebr.XIII.25, ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ἀμήν. Et reverà, nusquam alibi Canonicis in Epistolis, eadem omninò forma. Petrus & Johannes, ad morem Hebræorum, precantur pacem. Tertullianus, adversf. Marcion L.v. de primâ ad Corinth. Nam & hodie Judæi in pacis nomine appellant, & retrò in scripturis sic salutabant. Paulus vero gratiam, τοῦτ' ἐςι[?], τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρ-τιῶν, καὶ τὴν καθαρσιν. In omnibus ad unam Epistolis, signaculi loco, ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν, vel μεθὰ πάντων ὑμῶν.
units.tr: IV. Finally, with the seal added, the Epistle is ended. If we have shown that it is Paul's, there is hardly any room left for doubt. Paul himself tells us what his seal is like: "The greeting by my own hand, Paul, which is a sign in every epistle; so I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." 2 Thess. 3.17 (Ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου, ὅ ἐστι σημεῖον ἐν πάσῃ ἐπιστολῇ· οὕτω γράφω· ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ἀμήν). In these words he notes two things: first, that he closes all his Epistles with this formula; second, that this is peculiar to them and distinguishes them from the rest, so that they are not confused with others. Now these very words, in the same order and place, occur at Heb. 13.25: "The grace be with you all. Amen" (ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ἀμήν). Indeed, nowhere else in the Canonical Epistles is the form exactly the same. Peter and John, after the manner of the Hebrews, pray for peace. Tertullian, in his fifth book against Marcion, on the first Epistle to the Corinthians: "For even today the Jews greet one another with the name of peace, and in earlier times in the Scriptures they greeted in this way." But Paul prays for grace, that is (τοῦτ' ἐστι), the forgiveness of sins and the cleansing. In all his Epistles, without exception, in place of a signature stands "The grace be with you" (ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν) or "with you all" (μεθὰ πάντων ὑμῶν).

units.la: V. Instat doctissimus Camero, σημεῖον illud διακριτικὸν Paulinarum, consistere in eo, quod propriâ manu salutationes scribat. Et hoc demùm velle pro signo haberi, in omnibus suis Epistolis. Id autem non factum in hac ipsâ, adeoque nec Pauli esse Epistolam. Atqui 1. supponit gratis, signi omnem hanc fuisse rationem, quod salutationes suâ ipsius manu scriberet. Expen-denti locum illum ad Thessalonicenses, de Pauli signaculo occurrunt duo; primò ratione formæ ipsâ Pauli Apostoli manu scribi solitum; deinde ratione materiæ constitisse his verbis, sic, inquit, scribo, ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν[?]. Quod ipsum, ἀσπασμὸν[?] vocat, coronidis loco subjungi à se ubique consuetum. Male ergo Vir eruditus, sigilli rationem, in eo solo constituit, quod salutaret ἰδιοχείρως[?]. Non attendens salutationis illius modum, & ipsa illa verba subnecti Paulo solita. ii. Supponit etiam, non fecisse hoc Authorem, ut manu propria subscripserit. Quod non precario tantùm, sed & falsò dici arbitramur. Viditne αὐτόγραφον[?] Camero, ut tam audacter pronunciarit? Quidni Paulus consueta illa verba, ἰδίᾳ τῇ χειρὶ[?] exararit? Cur, si latitare voluit, non aliâ usus ille claudendi formâ? Cur meminit Timothei, cur sui adventus, cur aliarum quæ authorem circumstantiarum prodérent? Eò magis, quod quia nomen Epistolæ in fronte non expressum, hac saltem ratione constare de authore Hebræis debuit. iii. Sed dato, non fuisse αὐτόγραφον illud ἰδιόχειρον[?]: quo modo Paulus ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ[?] à communi usu, & consueta exordiendi ratione recesserat, eadem ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ[?] recessisse dici poterit. Fueritque hoc [illegible, ~16 letters], ita commune Pauli omnibus Epistolis, ordinarie à se missis ad Ecclesias, ut excipi posset Epistola plane singularis ,* & ad eos data, quibus nec quidem nomen, nec Apostolatum expresserat. Quanquam ne hoc quidem statuere necesse est.
units.tr: V. The very learned Cameron insists that the distinguishing mark of the Pauline Epistles consists in this: that Paul writes the greetings with his own hand, and that this alone is to be taken as the sign in all his Epistles. But this was not done in this Epistle, and so it is not Paul's Epistle. Yet, first, he assumes without warrant that the whole reason for the sign was that he wrote the greetings with his own hand. If we weigh the passage on the seal in the letter to the Thessalonians, two things present themselves: first, in respect of its form, that Paul was accustomed to write it with his own hand; second, in respect of its content, that it consisted of these words, "so I write, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all." This he himself calls the greeting (ἀσπασμὸν), which he everywhere customarily adds as a crown to the Epistle. So the learned man wrongly located the reason for the seal solely in his greeting being written with his own hand (ἰδιοχείρως). He does not notice the manner of the greeting, nor the very words which Paul was accustomed to append. Second, he also assumes that the author did not write this with his own hand. We judge that this is said not only without proof but falsely. Has Cameron seen the autograph, that he pronounces so boldly? Why should Paul not have written those customary words with his own hand (ἰδίᾳ τῇ χειρί)? Why, if he wished to stay hidden, did he not use some other form of closing? Why does he mention Timothy, why his own coming, and other circumstances that would reveal the author? All the more so because, since the name of the Epistle is not expressed at the head, the author ought at least to have been made known to the Hebrews in this way. Third, but granting that this autograph hand-writing was not present, still, if Paul in this Epistle departed from common usage and from his customary way of beginning, it could be said that he departed from it in this Epistle. And this practice being so common to Paul in all the Epistles he sent ordinarily to the churches, one might except a Epistle quite singular, and addressed to those to whom he had not even expressed his name or apostleship. Yet we do not even need to assert this.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Quarta ratio pro Paulo Scriptore. Coacervantur circumstantiæ variæ. Quod meminit Author vinculorum. Exceptio Cameronis. Quod meminit, afflictionum Hebræorum. Quod, conscientiæ suæ & conversationis. Quod, precum profundarum. Quod, ex Italia salutet. Quod, se venturum promittat. Singula declarantur. Tempus scriptæ Epistolæ accuratius notatum.
units.tr: The fourth argument, that Paul is the writer. Various circumstances are heaped together. That the author mentions chains. Cameron's objection. That he mentions the afflictions of the Hebrews. That he mentions his conscience and conduct. That he mentions deep prayers. That he greets from Italy. That he promises to come. Each is explained. The time of writing is noted more precisely.

units.la: I. Imprimis verò huc facit argumentum, à circumstantijs Epistolæ variis, quæ Paulum Scriptorem produnt. Quæque quò expenduntur magis, eò assensum pertinaciùs extorquent. Sunt autè illæ in hac Epistola non unius generis, quæ scriptionis aut horum, etiam tempus, & locum sic indigitant, ut serio dubitasse eruditos, vix adduci possim ut credam.
units.tr: I. Above all, the argument from the various circumstances of the Epistle supports this, since they reveal Paul as its writer. The more carefully these are weighed, the more stubbornly they force assent. They are not all of one kind in this Epistle. Some indicate the time and place of writing, and of these, I can hardly bring myself to believe that learned men have seriously doubted.

units.la: II. Prima esto circumstantia, vinculorum illa mentio, Capite x, versu 34. Καὶ γὰρ τοῖς δεσμοῖς μου συνεπαθήσατε[?]. Constat enim soli Paulo, & fere semper venisse hoc usu. Et quas omnes ex Italia transmisit Epistolas, vinculorum suorum mentione quasi distinxit. Sic in illa ad Ephesios, vocat se iterato τὸν δέσμιον, Eph.iii,1.iv,1.etiam πρεσβεύουσα ἐν ἁλύσει, Ephes.vi.20. Sic ad Philippenses, quater meminit τῶν δεσμῶν μου[?]. Sic ad Colossenses, μνημονεύετέ μου τῶν δεσμῶν Coloss.iv.18. Sic posteriori ad Timotheum, ἁλυσιτῷ μέχρι δεσμῶν, 2.Tim.ii.9. Pariter ad Philemonem, bis repetit, ὁ τῆς δεσμοῖς μου, versu 10, 13. Denique, in illa quæ est ad Galatas, si non δεσμῶν, saltem στιγμάτων mentionem ibidem facit, Gal.vi.17. Tantique hoc visum est Veteribus argumentum, ut veluti in arce colloca- rint. Oecumenius, ex aliis: μαρτυρεῖ δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἐξῆς ἡ ἐπιστολὴ ὑπάρχειν Παύλῳ, τῷ γεγράφθαι[?] ἐν ταῖς δεσμοῖς μου συνεπαθήσατε[?] Nec urgeri debent Syri, Arabis, & Vulgati versiones Interpretis, qui legerunt τοῖς δεσμίοις συνεπαθήσατε[?], vinctis compassi estis. Fit enim præter codicum Græcorum fidem; præter rationem constructionis, sequente particulâ; præter usum etiam Apostoli, vincula aliàs sæpè sua commemorantis.
units.tr: II. The first circumstance is that mention of chains, in chapter 10, verse 34: "For you had compassion on me in my chains" [Καὶ γὰρ τοῖς δεσμοῖς μου συνεπαθήσατε]. It is established that this usage belongs to Paul alone, and that it nearly always occurs with him. In all the Epistles he sent from Italy, he marks them, as it were, by a mention of his chains. Thus in the Epistle to the Ephesians he calls himself "the prisoner" [τὸν δέσμιον] again, Eph. 3.1 and 4.1, and "an ambassador in a chain" [πρεσβεύω ἐν ἁλύσει], Eph. 6.20. Thus to the Philippians he mentions "my chains" [τῶν δεσμῶν μου] four times. Thus to the Colossians: "Remember my chains" [μνημονεύετέ μου τῶν δεσμῶν], Col. 4.18. Thus in the later letter to Timothy: "chained even to bonds" [ἁλυσιτῷ μέχρι δεσμῶν], 2 Tim. 2.9. Likewise to Philemon he twice repeats "my chains" [τῶν δεσμῶν μου], verses 10 and 13. Finally, in the Epistle to the Galatians, if not of chains, he at least makes mention in the same place of "marks" [στιγμάτων], Gal. 6.17. The Ancients thought this argument so weighty that they set it, as it were, in a citadel. Oecumenius, drawing on others, says that the Epistle bears witness in what follows that it is Paul's, since it was written: "you had compassion on my chains" [ἐν τοῖς δεσμοῖς μου συνεπαθήσατε]. Nor should the Syriac, Arabic and Vulgate translators be pressed, who read "you had compassion on the prisoners," "you had compassion on those in chains" [τοῖς δεσμίοις συνεπαθήσατε]. For this reading goes against the faith of the Greek manuscripts, against the rules of construction, since a particle follows, and against the usage of the Apostle, who otherwise often mentions his own chains.

units.la: III. Excipit suo more doctissimus Camero: Nemone potuit esse in vinculis præter Apostolum Paulum? aut in vinculis per Epistolas Ecclesiam admonere, hortari, atque consolari? Primò à potuisse ad esse, infirma consequentia. Demonstrandum quisnam alius ille, & quibus hoc indiciis cóprobetur. Secundò, potuisse esse in vinculis, imò reapsè fuisse illis temporibus præter Paulum alios, equidem largimur. De Timotheo vincto, legimus has in Epistolâ; de Aristarcho, in illâ ad Colossi;de Petri & Jacobi vinculis, in Actorū libro &c. Hos verò transmisisse Epistolam, somniavit nemo. Tertiò, probandum id fuit Cameroni, de Barnabâ, qui Epistolæ suspicatur authorem. De cujus sivę. sive in Italiâ vinculis, sive Epistolâ, nihil quicquam constat. Ut neque de Lucâ, aut Clemente, aut Apollo, quorum esse Epistolam, assertum fuit aliis. Tandem, Paulo convenire omnium optimè, quivis videt. Cujus constant ex sacris vinculis; quorum perpetua ipsi & familiaris mentio, qui septem in vinculis Epistolas conscripsit; & ex Italiâ quidem, in quam trajecisse legimus Apostolum, Actor. xxvii. 1. 6. Nisi forte de vinculis Paulo Hierosolymis injectis sermo, Actor. xxi, quae Hebraeis maximè innotuerant. Non fuit ergo quod Venerabilis Beza affirmaret, argumento admodum infirmo niti, qui ex hoc loco Pauli esse Epistolam colligunt.
units.tr: III. The very learned Cameron, in his usual way, objects: "Could no one have been in chains besides the Apostle Paul? Or could no one in chains admonish, exhort and console the Church by letters?" First, the inference from "could have been" to "was" is weak. It must be shown who that other person was, and by what indications this is proved. Second, I readily grant that others could have been in chains, and indeed that in fact others besides Paul were in chains in those times. We read of Timothy in chains, and we read this in this Epistle; of Aristarchus, in the one to the Colossians; of the chains of Peter and James, in the Book of Acts, and so on. But no one has dreamed that these men sent this Epistle. Third, it was for Cameron to prove this of Barnabas, whom he suspects of being the author of the Epistle. Concerning him, whether he was in chains in Italy or wrote the Epistle, nothing whatever is established. Nor is anything established about Luke, Clement or Apollos, whose authorship of the Epistle others have asserted. Finally, anyone can see that it fits Paul best of all. His chains are attested in the sacred books. Mention of them is constant and familiar in him, who wrote Epistles while in chains, seven of them. And he was in Italy indeed, into which we read that the Apostle was taken, Acts 27.1, 6. Unless perhaps the talk is of the chains laid on Paul at Jerusalem, Acts 21, which had become especially well known to the Hebrews. There was therefore no reason for the venerable Beza to affirm that those who gather from this passage that the Epistle is Paul's rest on a very weak argument.

units.la: IV. Altera circumstantia peti potest, non jam à [?] illâ Hebraeorum, de Paulinis vinculis, sed à [?] eorundem, [?] [?], [?] τῶν ὑπαρχόντων, quae cum gaudio Hebraei sustinuerant, Capite x, versu, 32, 33, 34.
units.tr: IV. The second circumstance may be sought, not now from that Hebrew [...] concerning Paul's chains, but from the [...] of the same people, [...] of their possessions, which the Hebrews endured with joy, chapter 10, verses 32, 33 and 34.

units.la: Earundem enim in Hebraeis illis perpessionum, alibi meminit idem Paulus. Dum Thes-salonicenses, contribulium rabie,& motâ in ipsos persecutióne, imitatores factos dicit Ecclesiarum quæ sunt in Judæâ, 1. Thess. 11.14. Atque ita, Epistola ad He-bræos, ad Palæstinas tantùm data fuerit Ecclesias, vel serpserit eadem persecutio postmodùm latiùs,ad Judæos quaquaver-sùm. Vidit & hoc ipsum Theodoretus, qui Argumento in Epist. ad Hebræos, de iisdem afflictionibus, sermonem esse docet, citato loco illo ad Thessalonicenses. Idem, alij ex Interpretibus. Et quanquam sola hæc fortè circumstantia non sufficeret, at alijs juncta, contemnendam minimè esse censemus. Imprimis si Paulinum morem perpendimus, quo & afflictiones singulis suas revocare in memoriam solet, & suavissimo solatiorum lenire balsamo.
units.tr: For the same Paul mentions these sufferings of the Hebrews elsewhere. When he tells the Thessalonians, who were suffering from the rage of their own countrymen and the persecution stirred up against them, that they became imitators of "the churches in Judea," 1 Thess. 2.14. So the Epistle to the Hebrews may have been addressed only to the churches of Palestine, or the same persecution may afterwards have spread more widely, among the Jews everywhere. Theodoret also saw this. In his argument on the Epistle to the Hebrews he teaches that it treats of the same afflictions, citing that passage to the Thessalonians. So do other interpreters. And although this circumstance alone perhaps would not suffice, we judge that, joined with the others, it is by no means to be despised. This is especially so if we weigh Paul's custom, by which he is wont both to call the afflictions of each to mind and to soothe them with the sweetest balm of comfort.

units.la: V. Tertia circumstantia est, Authoris illa suæ συνειδήσεως [?] καὶ ἀναφο-φῆς [?], sanctæ quidem & inculpatæ, recordatio. Quâ verè se Paulum ostendit, Hebr. xiii. 18. πεποιθαμεν γὰρ ὅτι καλὴν συνείδησιν ἔχομεν· ἐν πᾶσι καλῶς θέλοντες ἀναστρέφεσθαι. Primò quidem, is mos est Pauli singularis. Ita 11. Corinth. i. 12. & συνειδήσεως ἐν ἁπλότητι καὶ εἰλικρινείᾳ, & ἀναστροφῆς suæ testimonium ostentat. Ita Actor. xxiii. 1. πάσῃ συνειδήσει ἀγαθῇ, πεπολίτευμαι τῷ Θεῷ. Prætereà, Paulo singularis quædam ratio, conscientiæ suæ hoc in loco in testem adhibendæ. Audiebat apud Judæos, quasi διὰ σχῶν ἀπολογίαν τῶν νόμων. Hinc Judæorum in illum invidia, exacerbatio, contumeliæ. Purgat se ergò hunc in modum, & ad conscientiam provocat, Oecumenio, paraphraste; ἐν ἀπολογίαν τῶν νόμων κηρύσσομεν, καθὼς ἔνεστι διαβάλλουσιν, ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ τῆς γενέμα-τῶν καὶ τῆς σχέσεως, ἀπὸ τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν μετέχομεν. Sic etiam Theodoretus Commentario ad locum. Malè audiebat apud eos, ut qui legi contraria prædicaret. Ergò docet se nullâ aliâ causâ id facere, quàm ut pareat verbo divino. Quapropter etiam conscientiam vocat in teSimoniam[?]. Videri & Chrysostomus potest, ad ipsum hunc locum.
units.tr: V. The third circumstance is the author's recollection of his conscience and conduct, holy and blameless. In this he truly shows himself to be Paul, Heb. 13.18: "For we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring to live honourably in all things" [πεποιθαμεν γὰρ ὅτι καλὴν συνείδησιν ἔχομεν· ἐν πᾶσι καλῶς θέλοντες ἀναστρέφεσθαι]. First, this is Paul's own peculiar habit. So in 2 Cor. 1.12 he displays the testimony of his conscience, "in simplicity and sincerity," and of his conduct [συνειδήσεως ἐν ἁπλότητι καὶ εἰλικρινείᾳ ... ἀναστροφῆς]. So in Acts 23.1: "I have lived before God in all good conscience" [πάσῃ συνειδήσει ἀγαθῇ, πεπολίτευμαι τῷ Θεῷ]. Moreover, Paul had a particular reason for calling his conscience to witness in this place. Among the Jews he was heard as one who seemed to be teaching the abolition of the Law. Hence the Jews' hatred of him, their exasperation and their insults. He therefore clears himself in this way and appeals to his conscience, as Oecumenius explains in his paraphrase: we do not preach the abolition of the Law, as they slander us, but we share in the Spirit and the truth. Theodoret does the same in his commentary on the passage: "He was ill spoken of among them, as one who preached against the Law. Therefore he teaches that he does this for no other cause than to obey the divine word. For this reason he also calls his conscience as witness." Chrysostom too may be consulted on this same passage.

units.la: VI. Quarta circumstantia nobis ea est, quâ Apostolus Hebræorum preces in subsidium vocat, Capite xiii, vers. 17. 19. προσεύχεσθε περὶ ἡμῶν, περισσοτέρως δὲ παρακα-λῶ τάχιον τοῦτο ποιῆσαι[?]. Paulo nihil usitatius, quàm implorare fidelium, ad quos scribit, preces, & calidiora ad Deum vota, iisdem etiam omninò verbis. Ad Romanos xv, 30, παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς συναγωνίσασθαί μοι ἐν ταῖς προσευχαῖς ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ[?]. Ad Colossenses, iv.3. προσευχόμενοι ἅμα καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν. Prima ad Thessalonicenses v,26. προσεύχεσθε περὶ ἡμῶν. Secunda ad Thessalonicenses iii,1. προσεύχε-σθε περὶ ἡμῶν. Ad Ephesios vi.18. προσευχόμε-νοι [illegible, ~2 words] ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. Quin spectari hoc loco debet, materia ex parte illarum precum, sc. ἵνα τάχιον ἀποκατασταθῶ ὑμῖν, Hebr. xiii. 19. Ita planè Paulus, ad Philemonem, ver. 22, ἐλπίζω γὰρ ὅτι διὰ τῶν προσευχῶν ὑμῶν χαρι-σθήσομαι ὑμῖν. Hinc etiam Græci patres, pro Paulo argumentati, ἐκ τῶν λόγων, ἀκρι-βέστερον εὔχεσθε ἵνα τάχιον[?] &c. Quinetiam eadem serie, & preces illorum efflagitat, & rationem à conscientiæ suæ integritate subnectit, quæque hoc officij genus meretur. Patet, [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐν καλὴν συνείδησιν ἔχομεν. Idem verborum ordo II.Corinth.1. 11,12. [illegible, ~25 letters] &c. ἡ γὰρ καύχησις ἡμῶν [illegible, ~12 letters] τὸ μαρτύριον τῆς συνειδήσεως &c.
units.tr: VI. The fourth circumstance for us is that in which the Apostle calls on the prayers of the Hebrews to help him, chapter 13, verses 17 and 19: "Pray for us ... and I beseech you the more earnestly to do this, that I may be restored to you the sooner" [προσεύχεσθε περὶ ἡμῶν, περισσοτέρως δὲ παρακαλῶ τάχιον τοῦτο ποιῆσαι]. Nothing is more usual with Paul than to ask the faithful to whom he writes for their prayers and their more fervent vows to God, often in exactly the same words. Romans 15.30: "I beseech you to strive together with me in your prayers for me" [παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς συναγωνίσασθαί μοι ἐν ταῖς προσευχαῖς ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ]. Colossians 4.3: "praying at the same time also for us" [προσευχόμενοι ἅμα καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν]. First to the Thessalonians 5.25: "pray for us" [προσεύχεσθε περὶ ἡμῶν]. Second to the Thessalonians 3.1: "pray for us" [προσεύχεσθε περὶ ἡμῶν]. Ephesians 6.18: "praying ... for us" [προσευχόμενοι ... ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν]. Indeed, the matter of those prayers must be considered in this place, namely "that I may be restored to you the sooner" [ἵνα τάχιον ἀποκατασταθῶ ὑμῖν], Heb. 13.19. Paul does exactly the same in his letter to Philemon, verse 22: "for I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you" [ἐλπίζω γὰρ ὅτι διὰ τῶν προσευχῶν ὑμῶν χαρισθήσομαι ὑμῖν]. Hence also the Greek Fathers, arguing for Paul, draw from these words: "pray more earnestly that he may come the sooner" [ἀκριβέστερον εὔχεσθε ἵνα τάχιον] and so on. Moreover, in the same sequence he both asks for their prayers and adds a reason drawn from the integrity of his conscience, which makes this kind of service deserved: "It is plain that we have a good conscience" [καλὴν συνείδησιν ἔχομεν]. The same order of words occurs in 2 Cor. 1.11, 12 ... for "our boast is ... the testimony of our conscience," and so on.

units.la: VII. Quinta circumstantia est, à loco unde data Epistola. Ἀσπάζονταί ὑμᾶς, οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας. Ergò ex Italiâ scripsit, unde salutat. Quid magis in Paulum quadret? In Italiam certè profectum docet Historia Lucæ, Act.xxvii. In Italiâ vinctum fuisse constat. Ex Italiâ plures dedisse literas, ad Philippenses, Colossenses, Ephesios, Philemonem, extrà aleam controversiæ. Similiter, data hæc sive Romæ in vinculis, sive ex alio quodam Italiæ loco. Sive nondum solutus esset Paulus, sed solutionem & [illegible, ~9 letters] sperans, quemadmodum & in illâ ad Philemonem. sive jam dimissus, & fractis prioribus vinculis, sui quodammodò factus juris. Quod post biennium illud liberâ in custodia Romæ exactum, videtur contigisse. Fuerit sanè & in Italiâ Lucas, fuerit & Clemens, etiam Marcus, etiam Barnabas, quem Mediolanensis fundatorem Ecclesiæ, tradiderunt. At fuisse istic in vinculis; scripsisse illinc ad Ecclesias, pari cum Paulo valuisse apud has authoritate; ut mittam alia, quorum certa de Paulo ex sacris fides, in obscuro est.
units.tr: VII. The fifth circumstance is taken from the place from which the Epistle was sent: "Those from Italy greet you" [Ἀσπάζονταί ὑμᾶς, οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας]. So he wrote from Italy, from where he sends greetings. What could fit Paul more closely? Luke's history certainly shows that he sailed for Italy, Acts 27. That he was in chains in Italy is established. That he sent several letters from Italy, to the Philippians, Colossians, Ephesians and Philemon, is beyond the reach of dispute. Similarly, this Epistle was written either at Rome in chains, or from some other place in Italy. Either Paul was not yet released, but hoped for release, as also in the letter to Philemon; or he had already been dismissed, and the earlier chains broken, so that he was in some measure his own master. This seems to have happened after the two years of free custody at Rome. Certainly Luke was also in Italy, and Clement, and Mark, and Barnabas too, whom they report as founder of the church at Milan. But that these men were there in chains, wrote from there to the churches, and had the same authority as Paul among them, I pass over, along with other matters, of which the certainty, as far as Paul is concerned, from the sacred sources is obscure.

units.la: VIII. Sexta nobis circumstantia est, quod fideles Hebræos in eam spem erigat fore Apostolus, ut brevi illius bearentur aspectu, Hebr. xiii.23. Μεθ' ἕ (Τιμοθέος) ἐὰν ταχέως ἔρχηται, ὄψομαι ὑμᾶς[?]. I. Solenne Paulo, id suis pollicitari, sive solandis iis, sive confirmandis, sive coërcendis. Oecumenius, τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτοῖς (ὡς ἐν Θ· πλαχῇ) παρουσίαν ἐπαγγέλλεται. II. Quadrat etiam sacra cum Historia, Actor. xxviii[?], 30. Biennio enim illo transacto in vinculis, redditus sibi suisque fuit Paulus, ut spem facere sui potuerit aspectus & adventus. Indeq; in Hispanias alij, alij in Asiâ, & Oriente migrasse eũ prodiderunt. III. Hinc etiâ patet scriptæ Epistolæ tempus. Certo cercertiùs, eodem ferè cum Epi[illegible, ~9 letters] ippenses & ad Philemonem tempore, exaratam. Ubi ipsissima illa restitutionis suæ, & [?]παρακλήσεως pollicitatio, Philip. 1,26. Philem. 22. prout, quæ Philippensium fuerat ergà Paulũ sollicitudo, constantiũ ἀναγκαίως τῇ αὐτῇ ἀλλήλων Phil. iv. 14. eadem fuerat & Hebræorum, probationiũ συμπαθείαν τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὁμοίοις[?], Hebr. x. 34. prout etiam, quem ad Philippenses ablegarat Timotheum, Phil. ii. 19, brevi reducem sibi fore pollicebatur, adeóque & comitem itineris ad Hebræos instituendi, Hebr. xiii. 23. Scripta ergò ad Hebræos Epistola, nonnihil post illam ad Philippenses, prioribus Pauli vinculis vel solutis, vel jam jam solvendis. Adeóque biennio illo, quo liberâ in custodiâ Romæ detentus, vel expleto, vel mox explendo. Ut de suo ad Philippenses, & Philemonem, & Hebræos adventu, certius jam quid pronunciare potuerit. Consentiunt Baronius, ad annum Christi LX. Blondellus, præfat. in Apolog. pro Hieron. Us-serius, Annalium parte ii. sub finem, & si qui ad hos accedunt, post Theodoretum & Chrysostomum. Præcisius quod annum attinet datæ Epistolæ, Baronio est Nativitatis Christi LX, Passionis XXVI, conversionis Pauli XXIV, ejusdem in Urbem adventus II, ante martyrium annis fere IX. Blondello rejicitur hujus & alterius ad Philippenses scriptio, in annum Christi LXI. Quanquam idé sibi contradicit, eâdé Apolog. pag. 30. Usserio refertur ad finé anni Ch. LXIV, vix annis ante Pauli necem III. Juxta Scaligeri calculum, eandem Epistolarum scriptio rejicienda, in annum Christi LVIII, Passionis XXV. Neronis IV, ante primam in Christianos persecutionem annis V, siquidem hic erat annus septimus adventus Pauli in urbem, ut idem Animadv. Eusseb. MMLXXXIII [?].
units.tr: VIII. The sixth circumstance for us is that the Apostle raises the faithful Hebrews to the hope that they will be blessed by his sight, Hebr. xiii.23: "With Timothy, if he comes quickly, I will see you" [Μεθ' ἕ (Τιμοθέος) ἐὰν ταχέως ἔρχηται, ὄψομαι ὑμᾶς]. I. It is characteristic of Paul to promise this to his people, whether to console them, to confirm them, or to restrain them. Oecumenius: he promises them his own presence [τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτοῖς (ὡς ἐν Θ· πλαχῇ) παρουσίαν ἐπαγγέλλεται]. II. Sacred history also agrees, Acts xxviii. 30. For after those two years in chains, Paul was restored to himself and to his people, so that he could hold out the hope of seeing them and of coming to them. From there, some have reported that he went to Spain, others that he went to Asia and the East. III. Hence the time of the written Epistle is also clear. With greater certainty, it was written at about the same time as the epistle to the Philippians and to Philemon. There is the very promise of his restoration and of a visit, Philip. 1.26, Philem. 22; just as the Philippians' concern for Paul was, so the constancy of the same [Phil. iv. 14, ἀναγκαίως τῇ αὐτῇ ἀλλήλων] was also that of the Hebrews, their sympathy for the prisoners, Hebr. x. 34 [συμπαθείαν τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὁμοίοις]. Likewise, he had sent Timothy to the Philippians, Phil. ii. 19, and promised that he would soon be returned to him, and so also would be his companion on the journey to the Hebrews, Hebr. xiii. 23. The Epistle to the Hebrews was therefore written somewhat after that to the Philippians, while Paul's earlier chains were either already loosed or about to be loosed. And so it was written in those two years in which he was held in free custody at Rome, either completed or about to be completed, so that he could say something more certain about his coming to the Philippians, to Philemon, and to the Hebrews. Baronius agrees, placing it in the year of Christ 60; Blondellus, in the preface to the Apology for Jerome; Usserius, at the end of part ii of the Annals; and those who follow these, after Theodoret and Chrysostom. More precisely as to the year of the Epistle's writing, Baronius gives the Nativity of Christ 60, the Passion 26, the conversion of Paul 24, and his second arrival in the City, about nine years before his martyrdom. Blondellus places the writing of this one and of the other to the Philippians in the year of Christ 61, although he contradicts himself in the same Apology, p. 30. Usserius refers it to the end of the year of Christ 64, barely three years before Paul's death. According to the calculation of Scaliger, the writing of the Epistles must be placed in the year of Christ 58, the Passion 25, the fourth year of Nero, five years before the first persecution of the Christians, since this was the seventh year of Paul's arrival in the city, as the same Animadversions on Eusebius [MMLXXXIII?] show.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Quinta ratio, à facta mentione Timothei. Rationis momentum. Sex inde pro Paulo conclusiones. Prima exceptio, probata Cameronii. Altera exceptio ipsius Calvini. Tertia quorundam exceptio. Baranius de pluribus Timotheis, notatus.
units.tr: Fifth argument, from the mention of Timothy. The weight of the argument. Six conclusions drawn from it for Paul. First exception, refuted by Cameron. Second exception, by Calvin himself. Third exception, of certain others. Baronius, on several Timothies, noted.

units.la: O I. Om-
units.tr: I. Om-

units.la: I. Omnium dignissima observatione est, Timothei facta mentio Authori Epistolæ. Γινώσκετε τὸν ἀδελφὸν Τιμόθεον ἀπολελυ-μένον, μεθ' ὧν ἐὰν τάχιον ἔρχηταί &c. Capite xiii, versu 23. Suadere alia possunt, hoc sanè persuadet. Vidit jam olim Athanasius, de Trinit. Dialogo i. Ὁ [?]τὶ δὲ αὐτῆς ἐστιν ἡ Ἐπιστολὴ, φανερόν ἐστι, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς τέλεσ τῆς Ἐπιστολῆς, μέμνηταί γὰρ ἡ Τιμοθέου, λέγων. Quod Pauli sit Epistola vel ex fine manifestum est, meminit enim Timothei, dicens &c. Et hoc postmodùm argumento, impulsi cordatissimi quique ad assensum. Atque de Epistolæ authore, vel ex hoc solo judicium faciendum esse censuêre.
units.tr: I. Of all the matters most worthy of notice is the mention of Timothy made by the author of the Epistle: "Know that our brother Timothy has been set free, with whom, if he comes sooner, I will see you" [Γινώσκετε τὸν ἀδελφὸν Τιμόθεον ἀπολελυμένον, μεθ' ὧν ἐὰν τάχιον ἔρχηται], chapter 13, verse 23. Other considerations may suggest this, but this one surely persuades. Athanasius saw it long ago, in the first Dialogue on the Trinity: "That the Epistle is Paul's is clear even from its end, for it mentions Timothy, saying" etc. Later, the most discerning men were moved by this argument to assent, and they have judged that the question of the author ought to be decided by this alone.

units.la: II. Variè id enim ex verbis illis colligitur i. Vel ex solâ Timothei recordatione, qualis Paulo Apostolo consueta. Meminit conjunctissimi sibi illius Pamphili, in Epistolis omnibus, solâ exceptâ ea quæ est ad Galatas, & ad Titum. Imò meminit solus Paulus, non Petrus, non Jacobus, non Johannes, non Judas. ii. Ex Fratris illa appellatione. Nonnunquam τέκνον, ut juniorem ac discipulum, Paulo dictum fatemur, imprimis ubi ipsi ad Timotheū ser-mo mb. At quotiescunque de Timotheo ad a-lios, toties ἀδελφὸν, & συνεργὸν vocat. ii. Corinth. 1,1. Τιμόθεος ὁ ἀδελφός. Coloss. 1,1. Τιμόθεος ὁ ἀδελφός. 1. Thessal. iii.2, Τιμόθεον τὸν ἀδελφὸν, Philem. 1. Τιμόθεος ὁ ἀδελφός. Romanos xvi.21, Τιμόθεος ὁ συνεργός μου. iii. Ex eo, quod Pauli hic comes ferè individuus, Paulo associatus & familiaris, cum Paulo itinera instituere solitus, (ut hoc etiam loco μετ' ἡμῶν ὑμᾶς[?]) pauli unius gratia hinc illinc sæpè digressus, & conjunctim cum paulo Ecclesias compellans varias, ut ex inscriptionibus Epistolæ ad Ephesios, Colossenses, Thessalonicenses, Philemoné, ad Corinthios posterioris, liquet. iv. Quod συναιχμάλωτον[?] eum, & solu-tum captivitate monet. Iisdem ergo cum paulo compedibus Romæ adstrictus antea. Ut qui pauli audiret sive discipulus, sive minister, sive socius. Hinc prædica-tum illud ὁ δέσμιος, de utroque & paulo & Timotheo conjunctim intelligi potest, Philem. 1. Παῦλος ὁ δέσμιος[?] Τιμόθεος. Hinc eodem etiam tempore in libertatem videntur asserti, dum paulus mox subsecuturum se & hic, & in illa ad Philippenses profitetur. v. Quod per Timotheum missa legatur Epistola, si fides subscriptioni. Πρὸς Ἐφεσίους γραφὴ ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥωμαίας διὰ Τυχικοῦ. Quanquam ideo haec suspecta est, quod praeter Syri silentium Interpretis, cum absens dicatur fuisse Timotheus, quodque hujus solutionem Hebraeis nunciat, C.xiii,23. Sed alio saltem missus à Paulo colligitur. Aberat enim, & expectabatur Paulo, ἐν Τάξει ἱερᾷ ἀπὸ ἐκ. Utique huic ablegatus, & uti par est, in Macedoniam ad Philippenses, ut non longè antè hac eosdem spe lactarat, Philipp. ii. 19. Atqui ἐν τῷ Paulo ministrare solitus Timotheus, ab uno Paulo mitti & ablegari frequentius. Sic missus ab eo in Macedoniam Act. xix. 22; Corinthum 1. Cor. iv. 17; Thessalonicam, 1. Thess. iii. 2. Nec aliis ministrasse legitur, ipse Apostolorum socius, Ephesiorum jam Episcopus, singulari ratione Paulo obnoxius, necii|sdem cum aliis necessitudinibus junctus.
units.tr: II. For these words yield several inferences. (i) From the bare recollection of Timothy, such as was customary with the Apostle Paul. He mentions his closest companion, Timothy, in all the Epistles except the one to the Galatians and the one to Titus. Indeed, only Paul mentions him, not Peter, not James, not John, not Jude. (ii) From the title brother. We admit that Paul sometimes calls him "my child," as a younger man and a disciple, especially when he is speaking to Timothy himself. But whenever he speaks of Timothy to others, he calls him "brother" and "fellow worker": 1 Corinthians 1:1, "Timothy the brother"; Colossians 1:1, "Timothy the brother"; 1 Thessalonians 3:2, "Timothy our brother"; Philemon 1, "Timothy the brother"; Romans 16:21, "Timothy my fellow worker." (iii) From the fact that this companion of Paul was almost inseparable from him, associated and familiar with Paul, accustomed to make journeys with Paul (as here also "with us [and] you"), often going off hither and thither for Paul's sake alone, and addressing various churches jointly with Paul, as is clear from the inscriptions of the Epistles to the Ephesians, Colossians, Thessalonians, Philemon, and the second to the Corinthians. (iv) From the fact that he reminds them of his having been a fellow prisoner and of his release. Therefore he had earlier been bound in Rome with the same chains as Paul, as one who heard Paul, whether as disciple, minister or companion. Hence that designation "the prisoner," applied to both Paul and Timothy together, can be understood: Philemon 1, "Paul the prisoner and Timothy." Hence they also seem to have been set free at the same time, since Paul here, and in the Epistle to the Philippians, professes that he will soon follow. (v) From the fact that the Epistle is read to have been sent through Timothy, if the subscription is to be trusted: "To the Ephesians, written from Rome by Tychicus" [Πρὸς Ἐφεσίους γραφὴ ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥωμαίας διὰ Τυχικοῦ]. Yet this subscription is suspect, because, apart from the silence of the Syriac translator, Timothy is said to have been absent, and because the Hebrews are told of his release, Hebrews 13:23. But at least it is gathered that he was sent by Paul elsewhere. For he was away, and was expected by Paul, in a sacred order [ἐν Τάξει ἱερᾷ]. Certainly he was sent away to this place, and, as is fitting, into Macedonia, to the Philippians, as a little earlier Paul had raised their hopes of this, Philippians 2:19. But Timothy, accustomed to minister to Paul alone, was more often sent and dispatched by Paul alone. Thus he was sent by him into Macedonia, Acts 19:22; to Corinth, 1 Corinthians 4:17; to Thessalonica, 1 Thessalonians 3:2. Nor is it read that he ministered to others, he who was a companion of the Apostles, already bishop of the Ephesians, bound to Paul by a unique relationship, and joined to him by the same other ties.

units.la: Author secundi in Epistol. argumenti, apud Oecumenium: οὐδεὶς γὰρ, ὅμως ἐπιλεγόμενον ἐν διακονίᾳ Τιμόθεον, εἰ μὴ ὁ Παῦλος. Nemo opinor. [?]lnor dimisit ad ministerium Timotheum nisi[?] Paulus. vi. Eò magis, quod si alius à Paulo Epistolam adornasse censeatur, factum id fuerit Paulo terris exempto. Calvinus circa finem Commentarij, Haec omnia vel Lucae vel Clementi post Pauli mortem accidere potuerunt. Atqui tum vinctum iterato in Italia fuisse Timotheum, huc illuc vel à Luca, vel à Clemente missiratum, post Paulum rediisse in Italiam, ex Italia ad Hebraeos, & si quae alia sequi necesse est, dici queunt, non probari.
units.tr: The author of the second argument, in Oecumenius: "For no one, although Timothy is named in the ministry, except Paul." No one, I think. Nobody but Paul sent Timothy into the ministry. (vi) All the more so, because if another is judged to have composed the Epistle for Paul, that would have happened after Paul had been removed from the earth. Calvin, near the end of his Commentary: "All these things could have happened to Luke or to Clement after Paul's death." But that Timothy was then imprisoned again in Italy, sent hither and thither by Luke or by Clement, returned to Italy after Paul, and from Italy to the Hebrews, and whatever else must follow, can be said, but not proved.

units.la: III. Ad quae, tria excipi posse videntur, Primò, potuisse esse Timotheum alijs praeter Paulum familiarem. Ita Camero Quaest. ii. in Epist. ad Hebraeos: verbi gratia, inquit, Barnabae, quem Paulus dixit comitem peregrinationum suarum. Nos vero i. ut Timotheo, omni cum alio familiaritate velimus fuisse interdictum, absit! Quod nec assertum nobis, nec controversum. ii. Dicimus, comparatè nemini tam fuisse quàm Paulo familiarem, tam addictum, ὁ μὴν ἀνομολογεῖται[?]. iii. Nos que hoc tantùm, sed paulo cumprimis so-litum memorari Timotheum; socium pe-regrinationum adjungi; ad varios mitti, fratrem nuncupari; & si quæ alia diximus expendenda. iv. Quod ille de Barnabâ suo, dilutum est, præterquàm falsa nixum hypothesi. paulo in itinere Antiocheno, & Hierosolymitano adscitum comitem, discimus ex sacris. At in Italiam cum eo navigasse, aut Romæ adfuisse paulo, aut có-traxisse in ea peregrinatione singularem cum Timotheo necessitudinem, ut unius Timothei, datis ex Italia ad Hebræos literis, voluerit recordari, quis præter Cameronem? Ne hæc quidem repererit in Actis Barnabæ, aut Recognitionibus Clementis, aut Alexandro Barnabæ encomiasta, scriptis fabulosis & apocryphis.
units.tr: III. To these arguments three replies seem possible. First, "Timothy could have been someone other than Paul's familiar companion." So Cameron, Question 2 on the Epistle to the Hebrews: "For example, he says, Barnabas, whom Paul called the companion of his journeys." But we reply: (i) That Timothy should have been forbidden all familiarity with any other person, God forbid! That is neither asserted by us nor in dispute. (ii) We say that, comparatively, no one was as familiar with Paul, or as devoted to him, as Timothy. (iii) We claim not merely that Timothy is mentioned, but that he is mentioned especially in connection with Paul; that he is joined as companion of his journeys, sent to various places, called brother; and that the other points we have made are to be weighed. (iv) As for what Cameron says of his Barnabas, it is refuted, apart from its being based on a false hypothesis. We learn from the sacred text that Barnabas was taken on as companion by Paul on the journey to Antioch and Jerusalem. But who besides Cameron would claim that he sailed with Paul into Italy, or was present with Paul at Rome, or contracted with Timothy, in that journey, such a singular relationship that, in writing to the Hebrews from Italy, he would wish to mention Timothy alone? Cameron could not find even this in the Acts of Barnabas, or in the Recognitions of Clement, or in Alexander, the panegyrist of Barnabas, writings that are fabulous and apocryphal.

units.la: IV. Instant alij, non hæc Pauli esse verba vel inde inferri, quod Timotheus fratris veniat appellatione. paulo quidem filium vocari consuetum. Calvinus in hunc locum: Caterum si hic est Timotheus, nobilis ille Pauli comes, (quod ego libenter recipio) verisimile est Lucam vel Clementem esse authorem. Paulus quidem Filium magis vocare solet. Frigidiuscule, pace tanti viri. Vanitatem effugij nemo non videt. 1. Filium. paulo vocitari, dicitur vel [?]καλῶς, vel ἐν μέρει. prius, falsum esse docuimus supra, aliquot exemplis. posterius, ut nempe aliquoties filius, licet saepe etiam frater, concludendi vim nullam habet. 11. Negamus, filium unquam Paulo nuncupatum, quoties injecta ipsi Timothei ad alios mentio. Ita perpetuo fratrem, aliquando συνεργὸν dixit. Constabit inductione quadam, ex Actis & Paulinis, nec fugere id Calvinum, aliosque potuit. 111. At filij nomine compellari, quoties ad Timotheum ipsum verba facit Apostolus, ultro largimur. Sic in utriusque inscriptione Epistolae, Τιμοθέῳ τῷ ἀ-γαπητῷ τέκνῳ. Quando jam Timotheum instruit, hortatur, agit cum discipulo, & juniore, & tot sibi nominibus obstricto, familiarius.
units.tr: IV. Others insist that these are not Paul's words, and that this may be inferred from the fact that Timothy is given the title brother; Paul is accustomed to call him son. Calvin on this passage: "But if this is Timothy, that noble companion of Paul (which I gladly accept), it is likely that Luke or Clement is the author. Paul indeed is accustomed to call him rather 'son.'" A rather feeble argument, with all respect to so great a man. Everyone sees the emptiness of this escape. (1) That Paul calls him "son" is said either absolutely or in a certain respect. The first we have shown above to be false, by several examples. The second, namely that he is sometimes called "son," though often also "brother," has no force in the conclusion. (2) We deny that Paul ever called him "son" whenever mention of Timothy is introduced in speaking to others. Thus he always called him "brother," and sometimes "fellow worker."
