This will be established by a certain induction from the Acts and the Pauline Epistles, and Calvin and others could not have missed it. (3) But that he is addressed by the name of son whenever the Apostle speaks to Timothy himself, we freely grant. Thus in the inscription of both Epistles: "To Timothy, my beloved child." Naturally, when he instructs, exhorts and deals with a disciple, and a younger one, and one bound to him by so many ties, he speaks more familiarly.

units.la: V. Denique urgent alij, nihil necesse esse, de priore Timotheo verba intelligi. plures potuisse esse illa aetate cognomines.
units.tr: V. Finally, others press that it is not necessary to understand these words of the earlier Timothy; there could have been several men of that name in that age.

units.la: i. Ita sanè est, Timotheos potuisse esse plures. At reipsa fuisse, coævos Apostolis, Apostolorum socios, nec ex sacris nec ex Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus discimus. Ut gratis affirmarit Baronius, ad A.C.cix[?]. num. lvi. conciliandæ Pseudo-Dionysii de Divinis Nominibus ad Timotheum, authoritati. Uniusque meminit ille Timo-thei, Pudentis Senatoris filij, ex Actis apocryphis Pudentianæ & Praxedis. ii. Adeóque de alio Timotheo sermonem esse Apostolo, dicitur quidem, probatur nequaquam. Imò puduit illius effugij Erasmum, Calvinum, Cameronem, pertinacissimos aliás sententiæ nobis oppositæ assertores. iii. Contrà verò, esse ipsissimum Timotheum Evangelistam, Ephesiorum præfectum Ecclesiæ, circumstantiæ omnes hactenus docuêre. Ut recalcitrare, & soli tenebras offundere cæteri videantur. Atque id tandem colligimus, coacervatas hasce circumstantias, si non apodicticas, [illegible, ~4 letters] certè esse proximas.
units.tr: (i) Indeed it is so: there could have been several Timothies. But that there actually were, contemporaries of the Apostles and companions of the Apostles, we learn neither from the sacred writings nor from the ecclesiastical writers. Baronius rashly asserted it, under the year 109, number 56, in order to reconcile the authority of the Pseudo-Dionysius, On the Divine Names, to Timothy. He mentions one Timothy, the son of the senator Pudens, from the apocryphal Acts of Pudentiana and Praxedes. (ii) And that the Apostle is speaking of another Timothy is said indeed, but by no means proved. Indeed, Erasmus, Calvin and Cameron, otherwise the most stubborn defenders of the opinion opposed to us, were ashamed of this escape. (iii) On the contrary, all the circumstances hitherto have taught that it is the very Timothy, the Evangelist, the overseer of the Ephesian church. So the others seem to kick against the goad and to pour darkness on the sun alone. And at last we conclude that these circumstances, heaped together, if not demonstrative, are certainly very close to it.

units.la: CAPUT VI
units.tr: CHAPTER VI

units.la: Sexta ratio, à scopo totius Epistolæ.
units.tr: Sixth argument, from the scope of the whole Epistle.

units.la: Qui est, docere abrogatam legem & ceremonias. Proprium Pauli. Demonstratur, Occurritur exceptioni. Scriptam Epistolam ante urbis excidium. Etiam Paulo su-perstite. Septima ratio, ab Epistolæ metho-do. Paulinam esse ostenditur. Eadem cum Epistolis ad Romanos, Ephesios, Galatas &c. Octava ratio, à Pauli erga Judæos sollicitudine. Confirmatur. Argumen-tũ fuit Athanasij, Chrysostomi, Ambrosij, Petusiotæ [?] &c. Obviatur exceptioni. Quo-modo Paulus Apostolus Gentium, Judæos etiam docuisse.
units.tr: That is, that it teaches the abrogation of the law and the ceremonies. Proper to Paul. Demonstrated; the objection is met. That the Epistle was written before the destruction of the city, and while Paul was still alive. Seventh argument, from the method of the Epistle. It is shown to be Pauline, the same as the Epistles to the Romans, Ephesians, Galatians, etc. Eighth argument, from Paul's concern for the Jews. Confirmed. It was the argument of Athanasius, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Pelusiota, etc. The objection is met: how the Apostle Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles, also taught the Jews.

units.la: I. Liceat & ab Epistolæ totius scopo & argumento ratiocinari. In quantùm id unum Authori constitutum sedit, ut legis [illegible, ~12 letters], ceremoniarum inanes umbras, figurarum complementum, Mosaici antiquationem cultus, καὶ [illegible, ~24 letters], palàm Hebræis faceret. Quod præclarè deducit Athanasius sua in Synopsi. Quo etiam nomine Cerinthiis & Ebionitis, cum Pauli[?]næ reliquis invisa fuit Epistola, ut colligimus ex Epiphanio Hær. xxx. contrà Ebionæos.
units.tr: I. Let me also reason from the scope and argument of the whole Epistle. For the one purpose the author evidently set himself was to make plain to the Hebrews the end of the law, the empty shadows of the ceremonies, the fulfilment of the figures, the abolition of the Mosaic worship, and [illegible]. Athanasius draws this out well in his Synopsis. For this reason too the Epistle was hated by the Cerinthians and the Ebionites, along with the rest of Paul's writings, as we gather from Epiphanius, Heresy xxx, against the Ebionites.

units.la: II. Jam sanè Paulo id quodammodò fuisse proprium, ut Synagogæ sepelien-dæ, & Judaizantibus in viam revocandis, acriùs incumberet, pro confesso est. Docent Pauli Epistolæ aliæ, maximè ad Galatas & Colossenses. Docet Actorum Historia, in quâ Paulo exprobratur idem aliquoties. Actor. XXI. 21. Κατηχήθησαν δὲ περὶ σοῦ ὅτι ἀποστασίαν διδάσκεις ἀπὸ Μωσέως, τὰς κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη πάντας Ἰουδαίους. Ibidem v. 28, οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ κατὰ τοῦ λαοῦ [?] καὶ τοῦ νόμου [?], καὶ τοῦ τόπου τούτου πάντας πανταχῇ διδάσκων. Unde Chrysostomus, Præfat. in Epist. ad Hebræos. πολλαὶ ζητήσεις αὐτῷ πολλάκις ἐγένοντο περὶ τούτου. Inde Judæi & Pseudo-Apostoli, vocare cum Tarsensem, & Græcum, & apostatam Legis, ut Irenæus L.1. adversus Hæres. C.xxvi. & Epiphanius Hær.xxx. Merito ergò, hoc se indicio prodidisse Apostolum, in hac nostrâ ad Hebræos, arbitramur. Et quoniam tradu-cebatur invidiosiùs, hinc etiam in pro-bando, diducendo, ratiocinando, fusior, vehementior, accuratior. In Argumento Epistolæ, quod est apud Oecumenium. Ἐπειδὴ καταηχηθέντες ὑπῆρχον οἱ ἐξ Ἰουδαίων, ὡς ἀποστασίαν διδάσκει Παῦλος, εἰκὸς τὰς γνωρίσαι [?] χάριν τὴν συμφωνίαν, Ἑβραίοις ἔγραψε. Quoniam audierant ex Judæis, quasi defectionem à Lege doceret Paulus, merito ut consensum prædicationis ostenderet, ad Hebræos scribit.
units.tr: II. Now it was certainly in some measure peculiar to Paul to press hard on burying the synagogue and calling back those inclined to Judaism; this is admitted. His other Epistles teach it, especially those to the Galatians and the Colossians. The history of Acts teaches it too, in which Paul is several times reproached with the same thing. Acts 21:21: "They have been informed about you that you teach apostasy from Moses to all the Jews who are among the Gentiles" [Κατηχήθησαν δὲ περὶ σοῦ ὅτι ἀποστασίαν διδάσκεις ἀπὸ Μωσέως, τὰς κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη πάντας Ἰουδαίους]. Verse 28: "This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people and the law and this place" [οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ κατὰ τοῦ λαοῦ καὶ τοῦ νόμου καὶ τοῦ τόπου τούτου πάντας πανταχῇ διδάσκων]. Hence Chrysostom, in his preface to the Epistle to the Hebrews: "Many questions often arose for him about this" [πολλαὶ ζητήσεις αὐτῷ πολλάκις ἐγένοντο περὶ τούτου]. Hence the Jews and false apostles called him "the Tarsian," "the Greek," and "apostate from the Law," as Irenaeus does in Book 1 Against Heresies, ch. 26, and Epiphanius in Heresy xxx. Rightly therefore, we think, the Apostle betrayed himself by this mark in our Epistle to the Hebrews. And since he was being maligned more bitterly, he is for that reason also fuller, more vehement and more careful in proving, unfolding and reasoning. In the Argument of the Epistle, which is found in Oecumenius: "Since those from among the Jews had been informed that Paul teaches apostasy, it is likely that he wrote to the Hebrews to show the agreement of his preaching" [Ἐπειδὴ καταηχηθέντες ὑπῆρχον οἱ ἐξ Ἰουδαίων, ὡς ἀποστασίαν διδάσκει Παῦλος, εἰκὸς τὰς γνωρίσαι χάριν τὴν συμφωνίαν, Ἑβραίοις ἔγραψε]. Since the men from the Jews had heard that Paul teaches a falling away from the Law, he rightly wrote to the Hebrews to show the harmony of his preaching.

units.la: III. Neque exceptioni locus est quasi Pauli ex Schola, & discipulorum aliquo proficisci potuerit Epistola. i. Quia affirmare, quàm demonstrare facilius. ii. Quia referre ingenium Pauli, sublimem illam sapientiam, docendi modum, dictionem, perpetuam methodum, ne dicam authoritatè, vehementiâ, orationis illud flumen; ne etiam reponam circumstantias omnes supra Capitibus iii. iv. v. in antecessis ostensum. iii. Quia nata hæc Epistola, stante Templo & Levitico Sacerdotio, ὄντων τῶν ἱερέων, τῶν προσφερόντων [?] τὸν νόμον τὰ δῶρα, Hebr. viii 1.4. Neq; alias necesse fuerat declamare in sacrificiorum usu, & praxim sacerdotij, penitus eo, Templi & Urbis & Reipub. eversione, sublato. Neq; maximè omnium prægnans argumentum, Judæis confundendis, & coërcendis Pseudo-Apostolis, ab ipsâ jactura cultus & Hierosolymitanæ sedis, restitutionis spe nullâ amplius affulgente, prætermisisset. Ut taceam quæ de scriptionis tempore; quæ de Epistolâ Petro Apostolo memoratâ, etiam Clementi, ad Ecclesiam Corinthiorum, intrà A.C.LXVIIJ[?].&LXXVI (ut Dav. Blondellus, pro sentent. Hieronymi sect. II. Testim. I. [?]) literas exaranti, superiùs disputata. Atqui nullus eo tempore ex Pauli discipulis, ejus fuisse videtur in Ecclesiâ authoritatis. Paulo ipso adhuc, uti par est, superstite, & scribendi hanc in se provinciam suscipiente. Nam & qui Paulum scriptorem negant, post hujus demùm facta scriptam, faceri necesse habent. Quomodo Clementis illa, itidem data, jam dudùm in cælum receptis Apostolorum principibus. Et quanquam superstitibus iis, historiam Lucas suam chartis commiserit, alia ratio Epistolæ, Apostolicâ authoritate, ad omnes Hebræorum Ecclesias, edocendis iis, confirmandis, reducendis in viam, conscriptæ. Paulum autem, nondum concessisse tum facis, constare potest, quod triennio ante eversas Hierosolymas, Neronis anno XIIII[?] demùm è medio sublatus. Quanquam Scaliger, cum quibusdam recentioribus, conjiciat in ipsissimum annum perfectionis primæ, qui Neronis fuit nonus, vel decimus, Christi LXIII[?], vel LXIV. Indè verò à Pauli excessu, res Judæorum labascere, in peius ruere, turbari, miscerique summis, imminensque exitium genti prænunciari.
units.tr: III. Nor is there room for the objection that the Epistle could have come from a school of Paul, or from one of his disciples. First, it is easier to assert than to prove. Second, the genius of Paul, that sublime wisdom, his manner of teaching, his style and his unvarying method, not to mention his authority, his vehemence and that flood of eloquence, all bear his mark; not to mention the circumstances already shown above in chapters III, IV and V. Third, this Epistle was written while the Temple and the Levitical priesthood still stood: "there being priests who offer gifts according to the law" [ὄντων τῶν ἱερέων, τῶν προσφερόντων κατὰ νόμον τὰ δῶρα], Heb. 8:1, 4. Otherwise there would have been no need to hold forth at such length on the use of sacrifices and the practice of the priesthood, now utterly abolished with the overthrow of the Temple, the City and the Commonwealth. Nor would he have passed over the most weighty argument of all, for confounding the Jews and restraining the false apostles, drawn from the very loss of the worship and of the seat at Jerusalem, when no hope of restoration any longer shone. To say nothing of what has been argued above about the time of writing, and about the Epistle mentioned by the Apostle Peter, which Clement too, when he wrote a letter to the Church of the Corinthians between AD 68 and 76 (as Dav. Blondel argues, in favour of Jerome's opinion, sect. II, testimony I), had in view. Yet no disciple of Paul seems to have had authority in the Church at that time, while Paul himself was still alive, as is fitting, and was taking up this task of writing. For those who deny that Paul is the writer must also make it written after his death. Clement's letter is not like that, since it was given after the chief apostles had long since been received into heaven. And although those men were still alive, Luke committed his history to writing; but this Epistle was written with apostolic authority, to teach, confirm and bring back to the right way the Hebrew Churches. That Paul had not yet departed at that time can be established, because he was taken out of the way only three years before Jerusalem was overthrown, in the fourteenth year of Nero. Although Scaliger, with some more recent writers, conjectures the very year of the first perfection, which was the ninth or tenth year of Nero, AD 63 or 64. Indeed, after Paul's departure the affairs of the Jews began to totter, to slide for the worse, to be thrown into turmoil and confusion among their leaders, and imminent ruin was foretold for the nation.

units.la: IV. Excipit notatum aliis argumentum, ex parte methodi & ordinis, in Epistola observati. Duabus siquidem partibus absolvitur, altera διδασκαλικὴ[?], sive doctrinalis & theoretica; altera παρακλητικὴ[?], sive moralis & practica. Prior, doctrinalis de Christi Persona, capitibus I, II, III, IV; de Christi sacerdotali Officio, & Beneficiis, capitibus V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, ex parte etiam X; de Fide & percipiendi modo, capitibus X, XI. Posterior, hortatoria ad Christianas virtutes, tolerantiam, constantiam in adversis, sanctimoniam, pacem, charitatem, [illegible, ~8 letters] &c. capitibus ultimis. Attexta familiari, & epistolari clausulâ, de quâ in antecessum fusius Cap. III.
units.tr: IV. There is an objection, noted by others, based on the method and order observed in the Epistle. For it is divided into two parts: the one didactic, or doctrinal and theoretical; the other paracletic, or moral and practical. The first, doctrinal part concerns the Person of Christ (chapters I–IV); Christ's priestly office and benefits (chapters V–IX, and in part X); and faith and the manner of receiving it (chapters X and XI). The second part is hortatory, concerning Christian virtues: endurance, constancy in adversity, holiness, peace, charity, etc., in the final chapters. Attached is the familiar, epistolary closing, which was discussed more fully earlier, in chapter III.

units.la: V. Usitatiorem fuisse hanc sanctissimo Apostolo methodum, haud prolixè demonstrandum. Ut nempe præmissis fidei dogmatis, munitis iis & illustratis, subjungat vitæ, morúmque præcepta. Illustre suppeditat exemplum, quæ habetur ad Romanos, iisdem omninò partibus distincta. Similiter illa ad Ephesios, quinetiam ad Galatas & Colossenses. Didacticis & dogmaticis, [illegible, ~6 letters] & moralia perpetuò attexuntur. Quando Canonicæ reliquæ Jacobi, Petri, Johannis, in genere parænetico[?], & hortatorio ferè consistunt. Vel promiscuè theoretica practicis, moralia doctrinalibus permiscent. De quo analytici Commentarores. Quanquam Pauli methodum, ad imitationem trahere potuisse alios, quis forte excipiat. At hoc ut statuamus, quæ ratio, quæ necessitas cogit? Et quamvis seorsim si expendatur, aut in prima collocetur acie hoc argumentum, videri possit fallax, nec nisi in genere probabilium: at superioribus junctum, attextum, collatumque, respondere ad amussim caeteris, pondusque habere suum, largiri necesse fuerit.
units.tr: V. That this method was more usual with the most holy Apostle need not be demonstrated at length: namely, that after setting out the doctrines of faith, and having fortified and illustrated them, he adds the precepts of life and morals. The Epistle to the Romans supplies a striking example, divided into exactly the same parts. So too the Epistle to the Ephesians, and indeed the Galatians and Colossians. Moral teachings are constantly woven into the didactic and dogmatic. Whereas the remaining canonical Epistles of James, Peter and John consist for the most part of a paraenetic and hortatory kind. Or else they mix theoretical with practical, and moral with doctrinal, indiscriminately. Analytic commentators have discussed this. Someone might perhaps object that others could have been led by Paul's method to imitate it. But if we are to affirm this, what reason or necessity compels it? And although, if this argument is weighed on its own, it may be placed in the front rank and may seem fallacious, and only to belong to the class of probable arguments, yet, joined to the above, woven in with them and compared, it must be granted that it corresponds exactly with the rest and carries its own weight.

units.la: VI. Denique, nec negligenda illa ratio, quae à Pauli zelo, & sollicitudine derivatur. Quo sane ille fuerit in Judaeorum gentem affectu, quas versarit ille sub pectore curas, saluti eorum promovendae passim edocemur. Nusquam apertius, quàm dum damno etiam suo, & exitio, & anathematis poenâ, redemptam conversionem eorundem voluit, Roman. ix. 3. In Gentis ergo suae scripsisse gratiam, quidni vel hinc colligamus? Qua fuit imprimis in scribendo ille diligentia & accuratione? Quando Ecclesias omnes alias tam studiose per literas salutavit. Quando etiam Pauli Apostoli temporibus, Hebraeorum Ecclesiae variè vel premerentur, 1. Thess. ii. 14, 15, vel ad defectionem ad ceremonias umbrásque, à zelotis sollicitarentur, Actor. xv. xxi. Ipse autem Romae abesset. Paulus in vinculis, multis terrarum spatiis, & tanta[?] locorum intercapedine disjunctus. Scri-psisse ergò dicamus, sive in conversorum jam gratiam, illis de Evangelij naturâ & Legis usu planius erudiendis, sive nō conversorum, arguendis iis, si quando in illo-rum manus scriptum incideret, ac con-vincendis.
units.tr: VI. Finally, that argument must not be neglected which derives from Paul's zeal and concern. We are taught everywhere what affection he had for the nation of the Jews, and what cares he bore in his heart for promoting their salvation. Nowhere more plainly than when he wished, even at cost to himself, and at the risk of destruction and the penalty of anathema, that their conversion should be bought (Rom. 9:3). Why should we not gather from this that he wrote out of grace toward his own nation? What diligence and accuracy did he show above all in writing, when he so carefully greeted all the other Churches by letter? Also, in the times of the Apostle Paul the Hebrew Churches were variously oppressed (1 Thess. 2:14, 15), or were solicited by zealots to defect to the ceremonies and shadows (Acts 15, 21). But Paul himself was at Rome, in chains, separated by wide tracts of land and so great an interval of places. Let us say, then, that he wrote either for the sake of those already converted, to instruct them more plainly about the nature of the Gospel and the use of the Law, or for those not converted, to refute and convince them, should the writing at any time fall into their hands.

units.la: VII. Atque hoc argumentum, plerique ex vetustissimis[?] Patribus urgentius visum fuit. Athanasius, Synopsi S. Script. Lib. VII. [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: VII. This argument was pressed more urgently by most of the very ancient Fathers. Athanasius, in the Synopsis of Sacred Scripture, Book VII, [illegible]

units.la: Postquam scripserat omnibus Gentibus, scribit de cetero etiam omnibus ex circumcisione credentibus &c. Chrysostomus, Præfat. in Ep. [illegible, ~30 letters], quomodo non ad illos scripsisset pro quibus & anathema fieri voluit. Isidorus Pelusiota, Epistolarum Lib. 1. Epist. ccccvii. [illegible, ~45 letters] Qui pro Israelitis anathema fieri voluit, quid ille non sustinuit, vel fecit, ut salutis fierent com-munes? Consenserunt Theodoretus, Oecu-menius, menius, Theophylactus, & qust[?] horum aravere vitulâ. Ambrosius (aut quisquis ille est) Proœmio in Epist. similiter Paulum scripsisse dicit, ex solicitudine quadâ singulari ergâ Hebræos, ne superati tentationibus ad infidelitatem relaberentur.
units.tr: After he had written to all the Gentiles, he writes further to all the believers from the circumcision, &c. Chrysostom, Preface to the Epistle [illegible]: how would he not have written to those for whom he wished himself to become anathema? Isidore of Pelusium, Epistles Book 1, Epist. ccccvii [illegible]. He who wished to become anathema for the Israelites, what did he not endure or do, so that they might become partakers of salvation? Theodoret, Oecumenius, Theophylact agreed, and whoever else of these ploughed with the heifer. Ambrose (or whoever he is) in his Preface to the Epistle likewise says that Paul wrote from a particular solicitude for the Hebrews, lest, overcome by temptations, they should fall back into unbelief.

units.la: VIII. Nec instari velim, Gentium non Hebræorum fuisse Apostolum. Ad illos scripsisse ex officio, ad hos nonnisi præter rationem muneris. Primò, Gentium quoties dicitur Apostolus, à potiori fit denominatio. Scilicet principaliter & ut plurimùm ministerio illius dicato Gentibus, minimè exclusivè ad Hebræos. Nam abjecisse omnem Judæorum curam, aut nefas fuisse Paulo, extendere ad eos sui exercitium muneris, allucinatur quicunque putat. Scrupulum eximit ipse Paulus, Rom. xi.14,15. Ἐγὼ ἐιθνῶν Ἀπόστολος[?] τὴν διακονίαν μου δοξάζω. Εἴπως παραζηλώσω μου[?] τὴν σάρκα, καὶ σώσω τινὰς ἐξ αὐτῶν. Alibi, curam vendicat sibi omnium Ecclesiarum, 11. Corinth. xi. 28. Alibi factum se Judæum Judæis, ut Judæos lucrifaceret, 1. Corinth. ix,20. Tertullianus, initio fere Libri iv. contrà Marcionem. Dexteras miscuêre, & exinde officia prædi-candi distinxêrunt, ut illi in Judæos, Paulus in Judæos & nationes. Deinde, quâ ratione vivâ voce & verbi præconio Judæos erudijt, atque in Synagogis prædicavit, eâdem scripsisse putandus est. Prius enim constat ex sacris, & indeà tractu Hierosolymitano ad Illyricum sese Pauli exporrexit prædicatio, Rom.xv.19. Tandem, quemadmodum non missus erat ad baptizandum, baptizabat tamen, 1.Cor.1. 17. ita Gentium quanquam non Hebræorum Apostolus, hos tamen sive voce sive scripto, sibi quoque excitandos esse censuit. Præclarè Theodoretus, Τὸν ἐνσχεν ἐθνῶν Ἀπόστολον ὁ Παῦλος, Ἑβραίοις ἐπέσταλκε. Φαμὲν ὥσπερ βαπτίζειν οὐκ ἐπιτεταγμένος, ἐκ ἐξουσίας ἐβάπτισεν, οὕτως Ἑβραίοις ἐπέστειλε, πρὸς τὰ ἐθνη Ἀπόστολος. Dicimus, quod ut non injunctum ipsi fuit baptizare, ex abundanti tamen baptizavit, ita & ad Hebræos scribit, Gentium alias Apostolus. Simile quid Chrysostomus, etiâ Theophylactus, sub initium Commentariorum. Ut rationum momentis, superpondium quoddâ à consensu antiquitatis accedat.
units.tr: VIII. I would not insist that the Apostle was of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews. He wrote to the Gentiles as a matter of his office, and to the Hebrews only beyond the scope of his office. First, whenever he is called Apostle of the Gentiles, the name is taken from the greater part. That is, his ministry was chiefly and for the most part devoted to the Gentiles, by no means exclusively to the Hebrews. For whoever thinks that Paul had abandoned all care for the Jews, or that it would have been wrong for him to extend the exercise of his office to them, is deceived. Paul himself removes the scruple, Rom. 11:14, 15: "I magnify my ministry as Apostle of the Gentiles, if somehow I may provoke to emulation my own flesh and save some of them." [Ἐγὼ ἐθνῶν ἀπόστολος τὴν διακονίαν μου δοξάζω· εἴ πως παραζηλώσω μου τὴν σάρκα καὶ σώσω τινὰς ἐξ αὐτῶν.] Elsewhere he claims for himself the care of all the Churches, 2 Cor. 11:28. Elsewhere he made himself a Jew to the Jews, that he might gain the Jews, 1 Cor. 9:20. Tertullian, near the beginning of Book 4 against Marcion: They joined right hands, and then divided the offices of preaching, so that the one went to the Jews, Paul to the Jews and the nations. Then, by the same reasoning by which he taught the Jews by living voice and the proclamation of the word, and preached in the synagogues, he must be thought to have written to them too. For it is established from Scripture that Paul's preaching stretched from Jerusalem round about to Illyricum, Rom. 15:19. Finally, just as he was not sent to baptize, yet did baptize, 1 Cor. 1:17, so although he was Apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews, he nonetheless judged that these too must be roused by him, whether by voice or by writing. Theodoret rightly says: "Paul, the Apostle of the Gentiles, wrote to the Hebrews." [Ὁ Παῦλος τῶν ἐθνῶν ἀπόστολος Ἑβραίοις ἐπέστειλε.] We say that as he was not commissioned to baptize, yet baptized out of abundance, so also he wrote to the Hebrews, though he was Apostle to the Gentiles. Chrysostom says something similar, and Theophylact too, at the beginning of his Commentaries. Let these be weighed as reasons, with some added weight from the consensus of antiquity.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Nona ratio ab inductione. Nulli quàm Paulo tributa verisimilius. Qui Lucæ esse voluerunt. Origo sententiæ. Incommoda varia. Rationes nullæ. Qui Clementi Romano adscripsère. Assertionis paritèr origo. Falsitas variè demonstrata. Erasmi rationes frivolæ. An Hieronymus subindicârit, Epistolam esse Clementis?
units.tr: The ninth argument, from induction. No one is more plausibly the author than Paul. Those who wanted Luke to be the author. The origin of this opinion. Its various drawbacks. No reasons for it. Those who ascribed the Epistle to Clement of Rome. The origin of this assertion is the same. Its falsity demonstrated in various ways. Erasmus's reasons are trivial. Did Jerome hint that the Epistle is Clement's?

units.la: I. Quod superest ad plenariam sententiæ nostræ assertionem, paucis exeque-mur. Jam enim & excrevit disputatio, & vix eorum quicquam intactum hactenus, quæ sive ex antiquitate, sive ex ipsis Epistolæ visceribus, pro Paulo scriptore adduci potuêre. Agmen claudet, in tertia quasi constitutum acie, hoc argumentum. Quod scilicet, nulli quàm Paulo verisimilius tributa hucusque Epistola. Si enim authoritas cum authoritate, ratio cum ratione ponderetur, quæcunque vel pro Clemente, vel pro Lucâ, vel pro Barnabâ &c. scriptoribus, ab aliis asserta, ad superiorum lucem evanescere necesse fuerit. Imò verò gravioribus illi longè premuntur incommodis, ne absurditati-bus dicam.
units.tr: I. What remains for the full confirmation of our view, we shall go through briefly. The dispute has by now grown long, and hardly anything has been left untouched of the things that could be brought forward for Paul as author, whether from antiquity or from the very substance of the Epistle. This argument, drawn up as if in a third line of battle, will close the column: namely, that no one has hitherto been more plausibly named as author of the Epistle than Paul. For if authority is weighed against authority and reason against reason, whatever has been asserted by others for Clement, or for Luke, or for Barnabas and other writers, must necessarily vanish in the light of the former. Indeed, those views are weighed down by far more serious difficulties, not to say absurdities.

units.la: II. Lucam scriptorem Epistolae creditum, author est apud Eusebium Origenes, Hist. L. vi. C. xix. ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν δὲ ὅτι Λουκᾶς[?] ὁ γεγράφας τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον καὶ τὰς Πράξεις[?]. Etiam Hieronymus Catalogo script. in Paulo, Creditur vel Lucæ Evangelistæ juxta quosdam. Nec abludere videtur Calvi-nus, Comment. in Caput xiii. Epist. qui verisimile arbitratur vel Lucam, vel Clementé Epistolae esse authore. Quàm verò hoc sit alienum, & commentitium, & ab omni veri specie abhorrens, paucis edocendum.
units.tr: II. Origen, in Eusebius, Hist. bk vi, ch. xix, is the authority for believing Luke to be the writer of the Epistle: "by them it is said that Luke, who wrote the Gospel and the Acts" [ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν δὲ ὅτι Λουκᾶς ὁ γεγράφας τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον καὶ τὰς Πράξεις]. Jerome too, in the Catalogue of Writers, under Paul: "It is believed, by some, to be the work of Luke the Evangelist." Calvin does not seem to differ, in his commentary on chapter xiii of the Epistle, where he thinks it likely that the author is either Luke or Clement. How far this is alien, fabricated, and remote from every appearance of truth must be shown briefly.

units.la: III. Primò, quia de Lucae Epistolâ aliquâ canonicâ, neque ex sacris neque Ec-clesiasticis constat monumentis. Unum Philastrius, transcriptam ei quae dicebatur ad Laodicenses, diversissimam ab hac nostra, Haer. xc. Nec Lucae meminit idem Philastrius, agens de hujus Epistolae, falsò creditis authoribus, Haeres. xli. Nec idaliunde Hieronymus, quàm ex Eusebio, in quodam id Origenis scripto traditum memorante. Secundò manifesta hujusce oriorigo traditionis. Jam antè Origenem, creditus Lucas Epistolæ interpres & translator. Clemens Alexandrinus diserte, τὸν Λουκᾶν αὐτὴν μεθερμηνευόμενον [?], ἐκδοῦναι τοῖς Ἕλλησι [?]. Ex translationis ergo fama, orta de scriptione ipsa suspicio. Nec nisi de scriptione secundaria, & per translationis modum, Origenis verba accipienda esse putem. Quomodo de Evangelio Marci Tertullianus, contrà Marcion. L. iv. Et Marcus quod edidit, Petri affirmatur, cujus interpres Marcus.
units.tr: III. First, because nothing is known from sacred or ecclesiastical records of any canonical Epistle of Luke. Only Philastrius mentions one, a copy of what was called the Epistle to the Laodiceans, very different from this one of ours (Haer. xc). Nor does the same Philastrius mention Luke when he treats of this Epistle, which is wrongly credited to certain authors (Haer. xli). Nor does Jerome have it from any source other than Eusebius, who reports it from a certain writing of Origen. Second, the origin of this tradition is plain. Even before Origen, Luke was believed to be the interpreter and translator of the Epistle. Clement of Alexandria clearly says that Luke, translating it, published it for the Greeks [τὸν Λουκᾶν αὐτὴν μεθερμηνευόμενον ἐκδοῦναι τοῖς Ἕλλησι]. So the report about the translation gave rise to the suspicion about the writing itself. Nor do I think Origen's words should be taken except of a secondary writing, and in the manner of a translation. Tertullian says the same of Mark's Gospel, against Marcion, bk iv: "And what Mark published is affirmed to be Peter's, whose interpreter Mark was."

units.la: IV. Tertiò, ne Lucæ quidem fuit, similli Epistola convenire Hebræorū Ecclesias. Apostolicæ id fuit authoritatis&prærogativæ. Et à solis Apostolis profectæ, quas canonicas habemus hodieque. Nec eadem, ut monebamus, conscribendæ Historiæ, quæ Epistolæ ratio fuit. Ad illam φιλοσοφίᾳ τῶν πραγμάτων [?], & internus spiritus S. ductus & afflatus, ad hanc etiā authoritas externa, & Apostolica, & Ecclesiæ universalis cura, requisita. Ubi jam plures immò omnes Ecclesiæ, de gravissimis ac sublimioribus mysteriis erudiri, redargui, instrui, excitari. At Lucas nónisi Apostolorū discidiscipulus, & tanto posterior, quanto pa-sterioris Apostoli sectator, ut Tertullianus, pro Lucâ etiâ scripturus, adversus Anti-thesies Marcionis, Lib.iv. Imo hujus Hi-storiam, idem nonnisi pauli authoritate receptam: Nam & Lucæ digestum Paulo adscribere solent, capita Magistrorum videri, quæ discipuli promulgarint. Quartò, saltem non eâ polluit Lucas authoritate apud Hebræos. Ipse non Hebræus Vete-ribus, sed proselytus, & Gentilis origine, cujusque adeò in legem & sacerdotium tulissent iniquius declamationes. Nec hunc inter & Hebræorum Ecclesias, fa-miliariorem intercessisse necessitudinem discimus ex Sacris. Imò Paulo extinto, inter Achaios & Thebanos[?] versatum Lu-cam, ibiq; martyrio consummatum,[?] com-munis traditio est.
units.tr: IV. Third, not even an Epistle of Luke would have suited the churches of the Hebrews. That was a matter of apostolic authority and prerogative, and those Epistles which we still hold as canonical came only from the apostles. Nor was the method of writing an Epistle the same as that of writing a History, as we have noted. For the latter, the philosophy of the matters and the inner guidance and inspiration of the Holy Spirit were needed; for the former, external authority, both apostolic and the care of the universal Church, were also required. Here, indeed, more or rather all the churches are to be taught the most weighty and sublime mysteries, refuted, instructed and roused. But Luke was only a disciple of the apostles, and as much later as he was a follower of the later apostle, as Tertullian says, when he intended to write for Luke as well, against the antitheses of Marcion, bk iv. Indeed, Luke's history itself was received on Paul's authority alone: "For they are accustomed to ascribe Luke's digest to Paul too, the chapters seeming to be the teachers' and the disciples' promulgation." Fourth, at least Luke did not have authority among the Hebrews. He was not a Hebrew by origin but a proselyte and a Gentile, and so they would have more unjustly declaimed against the Law and the priesthood. Nor do we learn from Scripture that there was any closer familiarity between him and the churches of the Hebrews. Indeed, it is common tradition that after Paul's death Luke lived among the Achaeans and the Thebans, and there was finished by martyrdom.

units.la: V. Præterea stylus Epistolæ, à dictio-ne & phrasi Lucæ magis Græcanicâ, longissimè recedit. Quum illa Hebraismis sive Syriasmis scateat longè pluribus. Et nescio quid sublimius subinde, & à Magistro ipso profectum spiret. Erasmus sub finem Annotation. Ne Lucas quidem ipse in Actis Apostolicis, parum abest ab hujus Epistolæ eloquentia. Quanquam Clem. Alexandr. apud Eusebium, L.vi. C.xi, vel xiv. τὸν αὐτὸν χρῶ[?]ζα εὑρίσκεσθαι κατὰ τὴν ἑρμη-νείαν, ταύτης τε τῆς ἐπιστολῆς καὶ τῶν πραξέων. Quin ratio nulla, ( nisi forte quia Pauli discipulus ) nulla in Epistolâ circumstantia, quæ vel in speciem pro Lucâ magis, quàm quovis alio illorum temporum, allegari possit. Ne dicam, contrarias plerasque esse circumstantias, antè memoratas. Quod Calvinus, loco antè citato, cum quiscribit, liberum fuisse ac suæ potestatis, etiamsi largiremur, non à Paulo, ut visum fuit, alienum, expirante biennio captivitatis. Neque id Lucæ magis, quàm Marco, aut cuivis alij cum libero & suæ potestatis, competit.
units.tr: V. Furthermore, the style of the Epistle is far removed from the diction and phrasing of Luke, which is more Greek, whereas that is full of many more Hebraisms or Syriasms. And it breathes something more sublime at times, proceeding from the Master himself. Erasmus, near the end of his annotations: "Not even Luke himself, in the Acts of the Apostles, is far from the eloquence of this Epistle." Although Clement of Alexandria, in Eusebius, bk vi, ch. xi or xiv, says that the same style is found in the translation of this Epistle and of the Acts [τὸν αὐτὸν χρῶ... εὑρίσκεσθαι κατὰ τὴν ἑρμηνείαν, ταύτης τε τῆς ἐπιστολῆς καὶ τῶν πραξέων]. Indeed there is no reason, unless perhaps that he was Paul's disciple, and no circumstance in the Epistle that could be alleged, even in appearance, more for Luke than for any other man of those times. Not to mention that most of the circumstances, as mentioned above, are contrary. What Calvin writes in the place cited above, "that he was free and in his own power," even if we granted it, is not foreign to Paul, as it seemed, since the two years of captivity were expiring. Nor does that suit Luke more than Mark or anyone else who was "free and in his own power."

units.la: VI. Nihilo felicius, ex Clementis Romani officinâ profectâ alij voluêre. Quod nonnullis creditum fuisse, testatur præter Origenem & Hieronymum iisdem locis, etiam Philastrius Hær.xli. Dicunt alij aut Barnabæ esse Apostoli, aut Clementis de urbe Româ Episcopi. Subscribit Erasmus, ad Caput xiii. Epist. Caeterum admodum probabile est, quod subindicavit divus Hieronymus, in Catalogo scriptor. Illustr. Clementem Romanum Pontificem à Petro quartum, authorem huius Epistolae fuisse.
units.tr: VI. Others wished the Epistle to come from the workshop of Clement of Rome, with no more success. That this was believed by some is attested, besides Origen and Jerome in the same places, also by Philastrius (Haer. xli): "Others say it is the work either of Barnabas the apostle or of Clement, bishop of the city of Rome." Erasmus agrees, on chapter xiii of the Epistle: "Moreover, it is quite probable, as divine Jerome hinted in the Catalogue of Illustrious Writers, that Clement, the Roman pontiff, fourth from Peter, was the author of this Epistle."

units.la: VII. Ago, & figmentum conficiamus invictis argumentis. Primò quia origo itidem omnis, haud obscurè ex translatione Epistolæ. Quam à Clemente factam, traditum inde ab antiquissimis temporibus fuit, ut constat ex Eusebio Lib.iii. C.xxxu.[?] De primaria autem scriptione Clementi adscripta, nihil Eusebius, quanquam monendi ibidem locus, ubi de scriptis Clementi suppositis. Etiam ex affinitate quadam dictionis cum EpistolaClementis ad Corinthiorum Ecclesiam, orta suspicio. Eusebius, τὸν ὅμοιον τῆς Φράσεως χαρακτῆρα, τὴν τῆς Κλήμεντ[?]ος [?]ἐπιστολὴν, καὶ τὴν πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἀποσώζειν[?]. Hinc, inquam, omnis illa de Clemente authore fama, huic uni innixa fundamento. Infirmum illud quidem à dictionis quadam si-militudine[?] militudine. Quasi vero Clemens, longè post datam ad Hebræos Epistolam Corinthios compellaturus, non potuerit sibi hanc proponere imitandam? Aut Epistolæ illius fuisse ipsemet Græcus interpres? In eo præterea omnis affinitas, quod suam Clemens, variis alterius Epistolæ sententijs & dictis, quæ ad institutum suum facerent, exornavit. De cætero, omninò discrepat stylus, & ut Græca magis est phrasis Clementis, sic illa Epistolæ ad Hebræos magis mixta, & Hebræam redolens sæpissimè eloquentiam.
units.tr: VII. I shall proceed, and refute this fiction with unconquerable arguments. First, because the whole origin likewise is plainly from the translation of the Epistle. That it was made by Clement has been handed down from the earliest times, as is clear from Eusebius, bk iii, ch. xxxii. But Eusebius says nothing about the original writing ascribed to Clement, although there was a place to warn about it there, where he discusses writings falsely attributed to Clement. The suspicion also arose from a certain affinity of style with Clement's Epistle to the Church of the Corinthians. Eusebius: "they preserve the similar character of the phrasing of Clement's Epistle and of that to the Hebrews" [τὸν ὅμοιον τῆς φράσεως χαρακτῆρα, τὴν τῆς Κλήμεντος ἐπιστολὴν, καὶ τὴν πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἀποσώζειν]. Hence, I say, that whole report about Clement as author rests on this single foundation. And that is weak, resting on a certain similarity of diction. As if Clement, writing to the Corinthians long after the Epistle to the Hebrews had been given, could not have set it before himself as a model for imitation? Or as if he himself were the Greek translator of that Epistle? Moreover, all the affinity lies in this: that Clement adorned his own letter with various sayings and statements from the other Epistle, which suited his purpose. Otherwise the style is entirely different: Clement's Greek is more pure, while the Epistle to the Hebrews is more mixed and very often smells of Hebrew eloquence.

units.la: VIII. Secundò, verba sunt Eusebij, Τῆς [?] πρὸς Ἑβραίους [?] πολλὰ νοήματα [?] ἤδη δὲ [illegible, ~10 letters]. Jugulum petit, quod hanc, Clemens suæ Epistolæ aliquoties intexat, usurpet, causas suæ obtendat. Planè, ut Polycarpus, & Ignatius, Scripturæ phrases, & enunciata, ad majorem sive elegantiam, sive ἐνέργειαν, intertexere suis Epistolis solent. Sed ille longè plura, testibus Eusebio & Hieronymo, ut Epistolæ ad Hebræos colligat uterque inde antiquitatem. Ipse Camero, pro vano haberi debere quod Clementi tribuatur, quoniā iste Clemens meminit istius Episto-læ, ut scripti quod a majoribus accepisset.
units.tr: VIII. Second, these are the words of Eusebius: "many thoughts of the Epistle to the Hebrews..." [illegible in the scan]. This strikes at the very heart of the matter: Clement, it is said, weaves the Epistle into his own letter several times, uses it and cites it in support of his case. Clearly, Polycarp and Ignatius were accustomed to weave scriptural phrases and sayings into their epistles, for greater elegance or vividness. But Clement does so far more often, according to Eusebius and Jerome, and both draw from this the antiquity of the Epistle to the Hebrews. Camero himself thought that what is attributed to Clement must be considered vain, since that Clement mentions this Epistle as a writing received from his elders.

units.la: IX. Deinde quid Clementi, Romano homini & alienigenæ, cum Hebræis? Un-de illi tanta apud Hebræos gratia, authoritas, etiam familiaritas, qualem Author ostendit? Illis jam temporibus, ante urbis excidium, quibus recens adhuc fuit Apostolorum discipulus, neq; dum Romanæ præfectus Ecclesiæ, nonnisi à Pe-tro tertius, vel secundum Hieronymum, quartus. Neque etiam Romanum, aut Gentilem, sed Hebræum fuisse authorem scripti, constare potest. Sive ex dictionis charactere, sive ex argumento, è penetra-libus Hebræorum ut plurimùm prompto, quodque fuit hominis legalibus innutri-ti. Tum etiam, ut haberet pondus disputatio, ejusque aliquis fructus extaret, in hominibus suæ gentis æmulis, nec laturis extraneum in eorum irrepere sacra, aut cultum omnem Legis ire antiquatum.
units.tr: IX. Next, what had Clement, a Roman and a foreigner, to do with the Hebrews? Whence did he have such great favour, authority and even familiarity among the Hebrews, as the author shows? In those times, before the destruction of the city, when he was still a recent disciple of the apostles, and not yet prefect of the Roman Church, third from Peter, or fourth according to Jerome. Nor can it be established that the author of the writing was a Roman or a Gentile, but rather a Hebrew, whether from the character of the diction or from the argument, which is for the most part drawn from the innermost parts of the Hebrews, and from a man brought up on the Law. Then too, so that the argument might carry weight and bear some fruit, it would be directed at men who were rivals of his own nation, who would not tolerate a foreigner creeping into their sacred rites, or all worship of the Law being made obsolete.

units.la: X. Præterea sperat author Epistolæ, restituendum se Hebræis, Cap.xiii.19. Ergo agebat in Italiâ captivus, aut ad breve tempus, & alio res illū suæ, ad Hebræos nepe, avocabant. Quin hos inter ante versatum fuisse necesse est, siquidem illis debuerit [illegible, ~12 letters]. Quod, qui de Clemente Romano, & inter Romanos ministrante, dici possit? alij viderint. Quo imprimis argumento Bellarminus, sententiam Erasmi traducit tanquam ineptam.
units.tr: X. Moreover, the author of the Epistle hopes to be restored to the Hebrews (Heb. 13:19). So he was then a captive in Italy, or for a short time, and his affairs were calling him elsewhere, namely to the Hebrews. Indeed he must have spent time among them earlier, since he owed them [illegible]. What could be said about Clement of Rome, who ministered among the Romans? Let others judge. It is chiefly on this argument that Bellarmine dismisses the opinion of Erasmus as absurd.

units.la: XI. Tandem Clemens, nonnisi Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus accensendus esse videtur. Ejusdem cum Ignatio Antiochenæ, Polycarpo Smyrnensis, Dionysio Atheniensis Ecclesiarum Episcopis, aliisque Apostolorum filijs, ordinis. Nam πρωτεῖον[?] fuisse præomnibus aliis, & ejus authoritatis, qui Canonem Epistolâ Apostolicâ & verè divinâ locupletaret, quamdiu non aliunde edocemur, pernegamus. Alias recipienda in Canonem fuerit pari ratione, quæ illius est ad Corinthios. Et jam verè Apostolus ille fuerit, cui præter Romanæ Ecclesiæ, etiam Corinthiorum, etiam Hebræorum omnium, adeóque universalis Ecclesiarum cura incumbebat. Quòd quàm absurdum, omnes intelligunt, licet Apostolum eũ vocet Clem. Alexandr. Strom. Lib. iv. Hac etiam ratione concidit divina, & canonica Epistolæ authoritas. Siquidem fuerit scriptoris Ecclesiastici tantùm, de cujus divina authoritate non constet. Cujus Epistolæ aliæ, referri non meruêre in canonem. Quæque ejusdem sanè generis, cum Ignatij ad Philadelphios, aut Ephesios, vel Polycarpi ad Philippenses Epistolis.
units.tr: XI. Finally, Clement seems to be reckoned only among the ecclesiastical writers, of the same order as Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp of Smyrna, and Dionysius of Athens, bishops of their churches, and the other sons of the Apostles. For we deny that he held a primacy [πρωτεῖον] over all the others, or had such authority that he could enrich the Canon with an apostolic and truly divine Epistle, unless we are taught otherwise from elsewhere. Otherwise, by the same reasoning, his letter to the Corinthians would be received into the Canon. And he would indeed have been a true Apostle, to whom, besides the care of the Roman Church, there also fell the care of the Corinthians, of all the Hebrews, and so of the universal churches. Everyone understands how absurd this is, although Clement of Alexandria calls him an Apostle (Stromata, book iv). By this reasoning too the divine and canonical authority of the Epistle falls. For if it were the work of an ecclesiastical writer only, whose divine authority is not established, then its other Epistles would not deserve to be counted in the Canon. These are certainly of the same kind as the Epistles of Ignatius to the Philadelphians or Ephesians, or of Polycarp to the Philippians.

units.la: XII. Pudet Erasmi rationes apponere, nedùm confutare. Prima ipsius est, quod Clementis meminit Paulus. Atqui meminit idem Caji, & Aristarchi, & Onesimi, & sexcentorum istiusmodi, ut in fide, aut ministerij labore constantium. Præterquam incertum de quo Clemente dixerit, in illa sua ad Philippenses. Nullusque Clementis istius meminerit, scribens ad Romanos, & salutem omnibus, qui alicujus essent in Romana Ecclesia nominominis, sigillatim impertiens. Altera Erasmi ratio, quod Clemens Timothei quo-que mentionem faciat. An ut recens soluti vinculis? ut comitis fui, & itinerum so-cij? Ut ministrantis, & alio à se amanda-ti? Et si quae alia in hac circumstantia obser-vanda esse diximus Capite v. Sed his etiam paribus, cur hinc Clementis potius quam Pauli, Epistolam esse colligamus? Nam & hic Timothei mentionem facit, nec semel, sed aliquoties, & huic quam Cle-menti addictiorem fuisse Timotheum, diffitebitur nemo. Denique Hieronymi venditat nobis Erasmus authoritatem, in Catalogo virorum Illustr. ubi de Clemen-te. Idipsum nempe subindicasse & suspicatum esse, sagacissimum illum Patrum. Itáne? quod ex innumeris penè locis, supra citatis ex Hieronymo, ne semel quidem subolfacere licuit. Ille qui in ipso illo Catalogo, Pau-li historiam texens, aliorum de Luca, & Barnaba & Clemente authoribus, sententia memorata, suam tandem sic subjungit. Vel certè quia Paulus scribebat ad Hebræos &c. Scripserat autem ut Hebræus Hebraïs Hebraicè, id est, suo eloquio disertissimè, & hanc causam esse quod à cæteris Pauli Epistolis discrepare videatur. Unde verò Erasmi hoc de Hieronymo judicium? Quod scilicet de Clementis ad Ecclesiam Corinthiorum agens Epistolâ, dixit grandem in eâ esse similitudinem cum Epistolâ ad Hebræos. Sed nihil aliud voluit Hieronymus, quàm vel hujus ad Hebræos fuisse Clementem interpretem, vel etiam multis (ut exponit) de eâdem Epistolâ sensibus, juxtâ verborum quoq; ordinem abusum. Quo ipso satis indicat, Clemente anteriorem esse Epistolam, & alius à Clemente authoris. Sed de his plus satis.
units.tr: XII. I am ashamed to set out Erasmus's arguments, let alone refute them. His first is that Paul mentions Clement. But Paul also mentions Caius, Aristarchus, Onesimus, and six hundred of that kind, who were steadfast in faith or in the labour of ministry. Besides, it is uncertain which Clement he meant in that letter to the Philippians, and no Clement at all is mentioned when he writes to the Romans and sends greetings individually to all who had any name in the Roman Church. Erasmus's second argument is that Clement also makes mention of Timothy. But what then? As one recently released from chains? As his companion and fellow traveller? As one ministering and sent by him elsewhere? And if there are other circumstances to be observed in this matter, we have said so in chapter v. But on these same equal grounds, why do we conclude that the Epistle is Clement's rather than Paul's? For Paul too mentions Timothy, not once but several times, and no one will deny that Timothy was more attached to Paul than to Clement. Finally, Erasmus holds up to us the authority of Jerome in the Catalogue of Illustrious Men, where he speaks of Clement: that the most shrewd of the Fathers merely hinted at and suspected the same. Really? Yet from almost countless places of Jerome cited above, he was not allowed to sniff out even once. Jerome himself, in that very Catalogue, weaving the history of Paul, records the opinions of other authors about Luke, Barnabas and Clement, and then adds his own in these words: "Or certainly because Paul wrote to the Hebrews... He had written as a Hebrew to Hebrews, in Hebrew, that is, in their own most eloquent language, and this is thought to be the cause why it seems to differ from the other Epistles of Paul." But whence does Erasmus get this judgment of Jerome? From the fact that, when treating of Clement's Epistle to the church of the Corinthians, Jerome said that there is a great similarity in it with the Epistle to the Hebrews. But Jerome meant nothing other than either that Clement was the translator of this Epistle to the Hebrews, or else that there was abuse of many senses of the same Epistle, also in the order of the words, as he explains it. By this very thing he sufficiently indicates that the Epistle is earlier than Clement and was written by another author. But enough on these points.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Qui Epistolam Barnabæ adscripsêrẽ [?]. Nulla rei esse vestigia. Non in sacris, non in antiquitate. Non meminit Clemens A-lex. nec Origenes. De Epistolâ Barnabæ. De aliys Barnabæ affectis, & fabulosis. De circumstantiys quibusdam Epistolæ, alienis à Barnabâ. De Barnaba Apo-stolo.
units.tr: Those who ascribed the Epistle to Barnabas [?]. There is no trace of the matter. Not in the sacred books, not in antiquity. Clement of Alexandria does not mention it, nor does Origen. On the Epistle of Barnabas. On other matters concerning Barnabas, both real and fabulous. On certain circumstances of the Epistle that are foreign to Barnabas. On Barnabas the Apostle.

units.la: stolo.[?] An verè de Apostolorum choro? De Barnaba judaizante. De Pauli præ Barnaba eloquentia. Ab uno Tertulliano omnis traditio. Cameronis instantiæ tres. An Tertullianus ex sententia Romanorum hoc tradiderit? An Barnabas creditus Jupiter, ob oris, adeoque & styli majestatem? An incitatione fuerit quam Paulus animo?
units.tr: On Barnabas the Apostle. Was he truly of the company of the Apostles? On Barnabas the Judaiser. On Paul's eloquence, surpassing Barnabas's. All the tradition comes from Tertullian alone. Three instances from Cameron. Did Tertullian hand this down in accordance with the opinion of the Romans? Was Barnabas taken for Jupiter because of his countenance and so the majesty of his style? Was it from a stimulus different from Paul's own spirit?

units.la: I. Progredimur in eodem ab inductione argumento. Et Clemente ac Lucâ eli-minatis, sequitur de Barnaba disquisitio. Scriptoré hunc esse Epistolæ ad Hebræos, primus fuit author Tertullianus, Lib. de Pudicitiâ, Cap. xx. Extat & Barnabæ titulus ad Hebræos, adeò satis authoritati viri, ut quem Paulus juxtà se constituerit in abstinentiæ tenore. An ego solus & Barnabas non habemus potestatem operandi & utique receptior apud Ecclesias Epistola Barnabæ, illo apocryphο pastore moechorum. Hinc de Tertulliano, hoc ipsum tradidit Hieronymus, Catal. script. in Paulo. Et Epistolâ ad Dardanum, quæ est cxxix: Licet plerique eam vel Barnabæ, vel Clementis esse arbitrentur, & nihil interesse cujus sit. Accedit Philastrius Hær. xli. Sed dicunt aut Barnabæ esse Apostoli, aut Clementis &c. Ex recentioribus, sententiam recoxit Joh. Camero, Quæst. ii. in Epist. ad Hebræos. Libenter mihi persuaserim eam Barnabæ adscribi debere.
units.tr: I. We proceed in the same line of argument from the induction. With Clement and Luke set aside, the discussion turns to Barnabas. The first author to say that this man wrote the Epistle to the Hebrews was Tertullian, in the book On Modesty, chapter 20. There is also the title "To the Hebrews" attached to Barnabas's name, and the authority of the man is great enough that Paul placed him beside himself in the strictness of abstinence: "Have not I alone and Barnabas the power not to work?" And indeed the Epistle of Barnabas, that apocryphal shepherd of adulterers, is more widely received among the churches. From Tertullian, Jerome handed down this same claim in Catalogue of Illustrious Men, under Paul. And in his Epistle to Dardanus, which is the 129th: "Although most people think it is by Barnabas or by Clement, and it makes no difference whose it is." Philastrius adds in Heresy 41: "But they say it is by either the Apostle Barnabas or Clement, etc." Among more recent writers, Johannes Cameron repeated the opinion in Question 2 on the Epistle to the Hebrews: I would gladly persuade myself that it ought to be ascribed to Barnabas.

units.la: II. Imò verò, nonnisi singularitatis quodam studio id probatum Cameroni, & quicquid hic de Barnabâ, inter apocrypha relegandum esse constabit. Pindarus, Καὶ πρὸς τὴν ... ἀλήθειαν λέγον, ἐξαπατῶν μύθοι. Principio, vestigia rei nulla sacrâ in Historiâ. Et Barnabam quicquam mandasse literis, nullo vel probabili indicio conjectare inde licet. Quum de Pauli Epistolis, etiam aliquâ ad Hebræos, vel ex Petro ante constiterit. Et quæ Ecclesiasticis nonnullis scriptoribus, credita fuit Barnabæ esse Epistola, fœtus vel genuinus fuit, vel suppositivius. Si posterius, manet assertio, nihil videri scripsisse Barnabam; si prius, cur inter apo-
units.tr: II. Indeed, this view was upheld by Cameron only out of a zeal for novelty, and whatever is said here about Barnabas will plainly have to be relegated to the apocrypha. Pindar: [Καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν λέγων, ἐξαπατῶν μύθοις] — "speaking against the truth, deceiving with fables." First, there is no trace of the matter in sacred history, and from it one cannot conjecture, even with some probable sign, that Barnabas committed anything to writing. Since the question of Paul's Epistles, including the one to the Hebrews, was settled earlier, even on Peter's testimony. And an Epistle that some ecclesiastical writers believed to be Barnabas's was either a genuine offspring or a forgery. If the latter, the assertion stands that Barnabas seems to have written nothing; if the former, why was it counted among the apo-

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] apocryphas Scripturas habita? teste Hieronymo Catal. script. in Barnaba. Cur non relata in Canonem, æque ac Epistola ad Hebræos? Imprimis quando & illa faceret ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ, ut idem Hieronymus.
units.tr: [illegible, about six letters] apocryphal Scriptures? Witness Jerome, Catalogue of Illustrious Men, under Barnabas. Why was it not received into the Canon, just as the Epistle to the Hebrews was? Above all, since it too was useful for the edification of the Church, as the same Jerome says.

units.la: III. Secundo, quæ Barnabæ tributa Veteribus, diversissimi fuit ab eâ quæ est ad Hebræos argumenti. Patet ex iis, quæ inde Veterum inserta monimentis, Clementis scilicet, Origenis, Hieronymi. Ille, verbi gratia, Lib. II. Stromatum, ex Latinâ editione, Merito ergo Barnabas Apostolus: ex quâ, inquit, parte, studui paulatim ad vos mittere, ut cum fide vestra perfectam etiam habeatis cognitionem &c. Alibi, eodem Libro. Mystice profecto Barnabas. Deus qui est universi mundi Dominus, inquit, dat etiam nobis sapientiam & intelligentiam, scientiam, cognitionem justificationum ejus, & tolerantiam. Quæ sane in Epistolâ ad Hebræos comparent nusquam. Imo ab hac ipsâ, ut quam Pauli crederet, perpetuo Clementi discriminatur. Similiter Hieronymus, Libro de locis & nominibus Hebraicis, di-stinguit Epistolam Pauli ad Hebræos, & quæ Barnabæ ; & in hac, nomina Adami, Evæ, Manasses &c. quæ in istâ ne-quaquam. Atqui, quod attendendum ante omnia, unius tantùm Epistolæ, authore Barnabâ, meminère Veteres. Duas pluresve scripsisse, dicitur præter ejusdem Clem. Alexandrini, Origenis, Eusebij, Hieronymi, & totius antiquitatis fidem. Quod tamen necesse fuerit, si alterius illius ad Hebræos author esse existimetur.
units.tr: III. Second, what the Ancients attributed to Barnabas was of a character quite different from the Epistle to the Hebrews. This is clear from the passages the Ancients inserted from it into their writings, namely those of Clement, Origen and Jerome. Clement, for example, in Book II of the Stromata, from the Latin edition: "Rightly, then, Barnabas the Apostle: from which part, he says, I have been eager to send to you little by little, so that with your faith you may also have perfect knowledge, etc." Elsewhere, in the same book: "Mystically indeed Barnabas: God, who is the Lord of the whole world, he says, gives us also wisdom and understanding, knowledge, and the knowledge of his justifications, and endurance." Such things certainly appear nowhere in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Indeed, Clement consistently distinguishes that very Epistle from the one he believed to be Paul's. Similarly Jerome, in his book on Hebrew places and names, distinguishes the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews from that of Barnabas, and names such as Adam, Eve, Manasses, etc., occur in the latter but by no means in the former. But, which must be noted above all, the Ancients mention only one Epistle written by Barnabas. That he wrote two or more is nowhere said, beyond the testimony of Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius and Jerome and the whole of antiquity. Yet that would have been necessary if he is thought to be the author of the other Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: IV. Tertiò, si Barnabæ nostra hæc fuit, saltem ejus fuisse credita est primæ antiquitati, miramur silentium Clementis Alexandrini, etiam Origenis. Quorum u-terque[?] (ut visum priori Parte) de Epistola ad Hebræos, deque creditis ejusdem vel Authoribus, vel Interpretibus, ex professo tradidêre. Lucæ quidem, & Clementis mentio, Barnabæ nulla. Primus Hieronymus, id ex Tertulliano illo loco scriptum reliquit, & Tertulliano forte paucissimi deinceps ex Latinis accessêre[?]. Adeóque conjectare licet, inauditum quid fuisse utrique Alexandrino scripto-ri, nequedum natam & eductam è causis suis, quo scriberent tempore, sententiam. Scripsit enim Clemens Alexandrinus, secunda adhuc ætate, aliquandiu ante Tertullianum. Origenes Adamantius scribere & inclaruisse, tertio statim in-eunte sæculo, natus A. C. CLXXXV. Istud autem, (in quo de Barnabâ ad Hebræos) Tertullianeum opus de Pudicitia, est ex posterioribus illius Afri, & in Montani dudum familiam receptí, decrepitâ jam ætate, quâ fuisse eum diserte Hieronymus, in vitâ Tertulliani. Saltem necesse fuerit, nulli Græcorum, aut nulli alicujus notæ in Christiana Ecclesiâ, fuisse id de Barnabâ, Clementis & Origenis illâ ætate, ad optatum. Similiter Eusebius, Libro III. Historiæ, agens aliquoties de Epistolâ ad Hebræos, ejusque scriptore, Barnabæ nihil quicquam meminit.
units.tr: IV. Third, if this Epistle of ours was Barnabas's, at least the earliest antiquity believed it to be his, and we are astonished at the silence of Clement of Alexandria and even of Origen. Both of them (as was seen in the earlier part) professedly discussed the Epistle to the Hebrews and the men believed to be its authors or translators. Clement and Luke are mentioned, but Barnabas not at all. The first to record the attribution, deriving it from that passage of Tertullian, was Jerome, and afterwards perhaps very few Latin writers followed Tertullian. So one may conjecture that the opinion was unheard of by both Alexandrian writers, not yet born and drawn out of its causes at the time they wrote. For Clement of Alexandria wrote in the second age, some time before Tertullian. Origen Adamantius began to write and became famous at the very start of the third century, having been born in 185. Moreover, that work of Tertullian's, On Modesty, in which he speaks of Barnabas and the Hebrews, belongs to the later writings of that African, who had long since gone over to the party of Montanus, and it was written in his decrepit old age, as Jerome expressly says in the Life of Tertullian. At the very least, it would have been necessary for none of the Greeks, and none of any note in the Christian Church, to have held this view about Barnabas in the time of Clement and Origen. Likewise Eusebius, in Book III of his History, discusses the Epistle to the Hebrews and its writer several times, yet makes no mention of Barnabas at all.

units.la: V. Quarto, de Barnabâ apocrypha innumera & fabulosa, quorumque nulla fides, tradita fuisse nescirinon debet. Ta-ceo illam Epistolam, magno iisdem Patribus in pretio habitam. Revera in eundem censum, cum Epistolis Abgari ad Christum, Christi ad Abgarum, Mariæ ad Ignatium, Pauli vel Lucæ ad Laodicenos, Senecæ ad Paulum, Pauli ad Senecam, Lentuli ad Tiberium de forma Christi, Pilati ad eundem de morte Domini, &c. referendam. Cuisum præterea Evangelium Barnabæ, aut si mavis, Acta Barnabæ, nugacissimæ & dudum explosæ paginæ. Memoratus idem Barnabas, venisse Romam, ibique ex primis jecisse Christianæ fidei fundamenta, & Clementem convertisse, secúmque inde abduxisse, &c. Nec quæ dicam alia, si non palàm confecta, dubia sanè & incerta, apud rerum Ecclesiasticarum Scriptores. Suntq; pervetustæ illæ fabulæ, pleræq; jam secundo sæculo nugarum istiusmodi & fraudium ferácissimo, verè hoc sensu μυθικῶς καὶ ἠρωϊκῶς, creditæ & pervulgatæ. Neque tamen, in illâ commentorum de Barnaba segete, quicquam de scriptione ad Hebræos. Et hinc saltem, certi nihil de eodem Barnaba, ba, præterquam ex Sacris, affirmari posse patet.
units.tr: V. Fourth, it should not be unknown that innumerable apocryphal and fabulous stories about Barnabas were handed down, of which there is no credibility. I pass over that Epistle, which was held in high esteem by the same Fathers. Indeed it must be counted in the same class as the Epistles of Abgarus to Christ, of Christ to Abgarus, of Mary to Ignatius, of Paul or Luke to the Laodiceans, of Seneca to Paul, of Paul to Seneca, of Lentulus to Tiberius concerning the form of Christ, of Pilate to the same concerning the death of the Lord, etc. Besides these there is the Gospel of Barnabas, or, if you prefer, the Acts of Barnabas, most trifling pages long since exploded. The same Barnabas is said to have come to Rome, there to have laid, among the first, the foundations of the Christian faith, and to have converted Clement and led him away with him from there, etc. Nor should I mention other things, which, if not openly invented, are certainly doubtful and uncertain, among the writers of ecclesiastical history. And those very ancient fables, most of them already in the second century, the most fruitful breeding ground of trifles and frauds of this kind, were truly, in the sense of [μυθικῶς καὶ ἠρωϊκῶς] "mythically and heroically," believed and widely spread. Yet in that crop of inventions about Barnabas there is nothing about the writing to the Hebrews. And from this alone it is clear that nothing certain can be affirmed about the same Barnabas, except from the Sacred books.

units.la: VI. Quintò; à Barnabâ circumstan-tiæ Epistolæ variæ, notatæ suprà, alienæ esse videntur. Nam in Italiâ fuisse, minùs ex Italiâ compellasse Hebræorum Ecclesias, minimè constat ex Sacris. Et quum in Epistolis Paulinis Româ transmissis, Timothei, Marci, Aristarchi, Lucæ, Epaphroditi, aliorumque injiciatur mentio, nunquam tamen Barnabæ. Quanquam in Liguria prædicasse, & Mediolanensem erexisse Ecclesiam, quorundam traditio fit. Sic de Barnabæ vinculis Italicis, quæ de Paulinis ratione, res in obscuro latet. Sic Marci idem Barnabas, verius quam Timothei, meminisset, qui Barnabæ ἀνψιὸς[?], familiaris cumprimis & itinerum comes, qui Barnabæ à Paulo divisò, & in Cyprum navigantì, adhæsit individuus, Actor. xv. 39. quique μῆλον ἔριδ[?] inter utrumque, ejusdem societatem nolente diserere Barnaba, fuit. Contrà quàm bellè, quàm appositè, quàm congruenter in Paulum circumstantiæ omnes quadrent, antè demonstratum.
units.tr: VI. Fifth, the various circumstances of the Epistle noted above seem foreign to Barnabas. That he was in Italy, or that he addressed the churches of the Hebrews from Italy, is by no means established from the sacred books. And although in the Pauline Epistles sent from Rome mention is made of Timothy, Mark, Aristarchus, Luke, Epaphroditus and others, Barnabas is never mentioned. Although a tradition of some holds that he preached in Liguria and founded the church at Milan. So too, concerning Barnabas's Italian imprisonments, which in relation to Paul's imprisonments are obscure. Likewise, Barnabas would more truly have mentioned Mark than Timothy: Mark, who was Barnabas's cousin [ἀνεψιός], especially close to him and his companion on journeys, who clung inseparably to Barnabas when he was parted from Paul and sailed to Cyprus (Acts 15:39), and who was an apple of discord [μῆλον ἔριδος] between the two, since Barnabas was unwilling to be separated from his company. On the contrary, how well, how aptly and how fittingly all the circumstances agree with Paul has been demonstrated above.

units.la: VII. Sextò, fuisse Apostolici muneris & potestatis, scribere ad plures Ecclesias Epistolam, eamque canonicæ, universalis, & perpetuæ authoritatis, suprà monebamus. Jam ergò de Barnabâ inquirendum, an Apostolus, ejusdemque cum Paulo reliquisque ordinis? Sanè ita nuncupatur Actor. xiv. 13. ἀκούσαντες οἱ Ἀπόστο-λοι Βαρνάβας καὶ Παῦλος. Hoc elogio, Clementi τῷ γραμματεῖ[?], etiam Hieronymo, etiam Philastrio, & plerisque ex antiquis in Paulum Commentatoribus, insignitur. Hinc Symbolum Apostolicum in xiv. aliquando articulos distributum, qui xiv. responderent Apostolis. Isaacus Casaubonus Exercit. xiv. Sect. iv. agens de Apostolorum dignitate & numero, Matthias, Paulus, Barnabas, postea in illum divi-[?]num chorum sunt cooptati. Nihilominus, ejusdem cum primariis & principibus Apostolis fuisse classis & ordinis Barnabam, putamus esse salsissimum. Nec immediata legitur illius ad Apostolatum, prima
units.tr: VII. Sixth, as we said above, it belonged to the apostolic office and power to write an Epistle to several churches, and one of canonical, universal and perpetual authority. It must therefore now be inquired whether Barnabas was an Apostle and of the same order as Paul and the rest. Certainly he is so named in Acts 14:14: "When the Apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it" [οἱ ἀπόστολοι Βαρνάβας καὶ Παῦλος]. With this title Clement the scholar, Jerome, Philastrius and most of the ancient commentators on Paul honour him. Hence the Apostles' Creed was at one time divided into fourteen articles, to correspond to the fourteen Apostles. Isaac Casaubon, in Exercitation 14, section 4, discussing the dignity and number of the Apostles, says: Matthias, Paul and Barnabas were afterwards co-opted into that divine college. Nevertheless, to think that Barnabas belonged to the same class and rank as the chief and principal Apostles seems to us most absurd. Nor is any immediate call of his to the apostolate read of, the first

units.la: Apostolici muneris prærogativa, vocatio. Quomodo de Paulo in Actis, Cap.ix. & ad Galatas Cap.i. Etiā de Matthiâ, sorte, id est divinâ voce, in augustum illud collegium cooptato. Non etiam universalitas muneris, ἐπισκοπὴ[?] πάσης τῆς οἰκουμένης, commissa Barnabæ. Benè divinitùs Gentium ministerio destinatus, Act.xiii.2. Paulo q; sed dudùm Apostolo, jā antè (ut Calvinus) Apostolatu per annos complures functo, adlectus ad Gentes socius. Nō etiā extraordinario se illi & oculari testimonio, ut Apostolis, probasse Christum legimus. Non, ut Apostoli, insignem fuisse miraculis, & soli Paulo, quanquam adesset Barnabas, tribuuntur illa Act.xiii.9,10.xiv.10,11. Præterea distinguitur non semel ab Apostolis v.g. quando pecunias ad pedes Apostolorum depositisse, Act.iv.38, vel Saulo ad Apostolos dux fuisse perhibetur Act.ix,27. Nunquam ferè etiam Barnabas, semper Paulus fecisse legitur verba, unà cum essent. Sic Pauli ad Elymam, ad Antiochenos, ad Lystrenses, Barnabâ adstante, orationes Act.xiii.xiv. Quin etiam omnes Apostoli, paris interfesse[?] ἀξίας, ἐξουσίας, ἀλλήλοις ἰσόψυχοι[?]. Longè ta-men Paulo inferior Barnabas, ille autho-ritate, charismatis, functione, omnibus major. Quod verò attinet Veteres, dum Provincias inter Apostolos, ad orbis curam universi partiuntur, & Thomae Parthiam aut Indiam, Andreae Scytiam Eu-ropæam, Matthiae interiorem Æthio-piam, Judae Ægyptum &c. assignant, Barnabam in ea distributione praetereunt. Quin τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα[?], septuaginta discipu-lis, expresse Clemens Lib.11. Strom. Eu-sebius Hist.Eccles. Lib.i. Cap.xii. Epi-phanius Hæres.xx. contrà Herodianos, annumerant. Quod verò dicatur Aposto-lus, sit ratione suæ ad Gentes legationis, Paulo ipse associatus Apostolo. Voceque nonnihil laxiori, & nominis significatio-ne longius extensa, ut etiam Calvinus ad locum. Quomodo ἐπίσημοι ἐν Ἀποστόλοις[?], Junias & Andronicus, Rom.xvi.7. Quemadmodum Ἀπόστολοι Ἐκκλησιῶν[?], Titus aliique fratres & cooperarij Pauli, II. Co-rinth.viii.23. Prout etiam Veteres promiscuè miscuè Titum, Apollo, Sosthenem, LXX. discipulos, &c. Apostolos vocant. Quà de nomenclatione fusiùs, Salmasius, Casaubonus, Montacutius, Blondellus, Forbesius, & siqui alij de Ecclesiastica præclarè meriti antiquitate.
units.tr: The prerogative of the apostolic office was the call. This is shown for Paul in Acts chapter 9 and Galatians chapter 1, and for Matthias, who was chosen by lot, that is, by a divine voice, into that august college. Nor was the universal charge of the office, "oversight of the whole world" [ἐπισκοπὴ πάσης τῆς οἰκουμένης], committed to Barnabas. He was divinely destined for the ministry to the Gentiles (Acts 13:2), and was joined as companion to the Gentiles with Paul, who was already an apostle and, as Calvin says, had long performed the apostleship before then. We do not read that Barnabas proved Christ to people by an extraordinary, eyewitness testimony as the apostles did. Nor was he, as the apostles were, distinguished by miracles; those miracles are ascribed to Paul alone, although Barnabas was present (Acts 13:9, 10; 14:10, 11). Moreover, he is more than once set apart from the apostles, for example when he is said to have laid money at the feet of the apostles (Acts 4:38), or when Saul is said to have been brought to the apostles by Barnabas as his guide (Acts 9:27). Barnabas almost never, but Paul always, is read as having spoken when they were together. So Paul's addresses to Elymas, to the Antiochenes and to the Lystrans, with Barnabas standing by, are recorded (Acts 13, 14). Indeed, all the apostles were equal in dignity and authority, "equal in spirit to one another" [ἀλλήλοις ἰσόψυχοι]. Yet Barnabas was far inferior to Paul, who surpassed all in authority, gifts and function. As for the ancient writers, when they divide the provinces among the apostles for the care of the whole world, and assign Thomas Parthia or India, Andrew European Scythia, Matthias inner Ethiopia, Jude Egypt, and so on, they pass over Barnabas in that distribution. Indeed, Clement (Stromata, book 2), Eusebius (Church History, book 1, chapter 12) and Epiphanius (Heresy 20, against the Herodians) expressly count him among the seventy disciples [τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα]. That he is called "apostle" is due to his mission to the Gentiles, in which he was associated with the apostle Paul. The word is used somewhat loosely, and the meaning of the name is stretched further, as Calvin also says on the passage. So Junias and Andronicus are "notable among the apostles" [ἐπίσημοι ἐν Ἀποστόλοις] (Rom. 16:7), and Titus and the other brothers and fellow workers of Paul are "apostles of the churches" [Ἀπόστολοι Ἐκκλησιῶν] (2 Cor. 8:23). In the same way the ancients indiscriminately call Titus, Apollos, Sosthenes, the seventy disciples, and others "apostles." On this use of the name, more fully, see Salmasius, Casaubon, Montagu, Blondel, Forbes, and any others who have distinguished themselves in the antiquity of the Church.

units.la: VIII. Septimò, hinc constat Paulive-rius fuisse quàm Barnabæ, salutare hac E-pistola Hebræorum Ecclesias. Siquidem illi quà Apostolo, ac præconi universali, & harum cura fuit. Quas ille pro concione totiens, in Judæa, in Asia, in Europa, Hierosolymis, Antiochiæ, Iconij, Thes-salonicæ, Ephesi, &c. officij ratione do-cuerat. Quas in ore, quas in corde perpe-tuò gestabat. Quarum plurimas vel vel exerat[?], vel confirmarat. Apud quas ma-joris longe authoritatis, Pauli quàm Barnabæ nomen, ipso fatente Camerone. Imprimis quando: necesse fuerit, bar-nabam scripsisse vivo Paulo, si scripsit, & illum huic fuisse superstitem, juxtà cum obscurissimis ignoretur.
units.tr: VIII. Seventhly, from this it is clear that this Epistle to the Hebrews was written for the salvation of the churches by Paul rather than by Barnabas. For Paul, as apostle and universal herald, had the care of those churches. He had taught them so often in preaching, in Judea, Asia and Europe, at Jerusalem, Antioch, Iconium, Thessalonica, Ephesus and elsewhere, as his office required. He carried them constantly in his mouth and in his heart; he had planted many of them, or confirmed them. Among them the name of Paul carried far greater authority than that of Barnabas, as Cameron himself admits. Above all, if Barnabas wrote it at all, he must have written while Paul was alive, and whether he survived Paul is unknown, like many most obscure matters.

units.la: IX. Octavò, hoc etiam nomine Bar-nabæ adscribitur Epistola inconvenien-tiùs. Quòd ille à Judaizantium mollitie, minimè abhorruisse videatur. Qua & ipse de causa, taxatur Paulo, scribenti ad Galatas. Etiam postquàm divina voce fuisset ad Gentium ministerium ordinatus. Et post Hierosolymitanam illam Synodú quæ Actorum xv, ut doctissimi Interpretes. Adeóque non multis profectò annis, ante conscriptam Epistolam ad Hebræos. Aquâ sive mollitie, sive errore, Deus bone! quantum Scriptor noster abfuit? An verisimile fuerit eundem illum esse Barnabam, tanta jam vehementia, tanta dicendi copia & libertate, in cere-monias, & Judaizantes omnes invectum, qui paucos ante annos quadam ignavia, & præposterà simulatione, Christianam libertatem prodiderat? Contrà, quid accommodatius Paulo? jam inde à principio tam acriter tamque constanter, quà voce quà calamo, pro eadem libertate, adversus ceremoniarum usum decertauti.
units.tr: IX. Eighthly, this Epistle is also less fittingly ascribed to Barnabas on this account: that he seems not to have shrunk from the weakness of the Judaizers. For this very reason he is rebuked by Paul in writing to the Galatians, and that even after he had been ordained by a divine voice to the ministry to the Gentiles, and after the Jerusalem synod of Acts 15, as the most learned interpreters hold. So it was not many years before the Epistle to the Hebrews was written. Whether through weakness or through error, good God, how far was our author from that! Is it likely that the same Barnabas, who a few years earlier had betrayed Christian liberty through a certain cowardice and an inconsistent pretence, would now have attacked the ceremonies and all the Judaizers with such vehemence, and with such abundance and freedom of speech? On the contrary, what is more fitting to Paul, who from the beginning fought so fiercely and so constantly, by voice and by pen, for that same liberty against the use of ceremonies?

units.la: X. Nonò, neque hæc negligi ratio debet, ab Epistolæ singulari & eximia eloquentia. Cùm Barnabas in Actis, ferè χωφὸν πρόσωπον fuerit. Et dicendi partem Paulo perpetuò reliquerit, qui etiam ἡγούμενος τῷ λόγῳ[?], Actor. xiv.12. Ut Paulus verò Aaron fuerit, ipsis Lystrensibus Mercurius, interpres ille Deorum. Hinc nemo non colliget eloquij majestate, & roboro dictionis, & vi ratiocinio rum, Paulum longè superasse Barnabam. Atque ita illi quàm huic verius, tribui Epistolarum omnium, styli majestate ac sublimitate dictionis, maximè illustrem. Nam ut scripsere, sic verisimiliter, locuti viri Dei; ne dicatur forte de Barnaba quod de Pericle aliquo, aut Demosthene, etiam Augusto, scripsisse & dixisse præmeditatè, quàm extemporanee, longè disertius & elegantius.
units.tr: X. Ninthly, this consideration too should not be neglected: the singular and remarkable eloquence of the Epistle. In Acts, Barnabas was almost a silent person [χωφὸν πρόσωπον], and he always left the speaking to Paul, who was also "the leader of the speech" [ἡγούμενος τῷ λόγῳ] (Acts 14:12). Just as Paul was Aaron, so to the Lystrans themselves he was Mercury, the interpreter of the gods. Hence anyone will conclude, from the majesty of the discourse, the strength of the diction and the force of the reasoning, that Paul far surpassed Barnabas. And so the majesty of style and the sublimity of diction, which is most conspicuous in all the Epistles, is ascribed more truly to Paul than to Barnabas. For as they wrote, so the men of God probably spoke. Let it not be said, perhaps, of Barnabas what is said of certain men, Pericles, Demosthenes, even Augustus, that they wrote and spoke far more eloquently and elegantly when prepared than when speaking extempore.

units.la: XI. Denique, ut finem faciam, ab uno Tertulliano omnis traditio. Et quidem à vesano Montani spiritu, jam dementato. Ex obscuris etiam Afri illius verbis, quique dum per Epistolam Barnabæ, ἐξόχως[?] notat[?] illam ad Hebræos, recedit à tota, ut visum, antiquitate. Et si quæ huc aliæ conjecturæ faciunt, leviores eæ profectò, quàm ut tot invictis pro Paulo argumentis exæquari, nedum anteponi posse videantur. Ut pigeat congredi cum Came-rone ulterius, qui pro Barnaba sic disputat, ut causam prodat. Prima illius ratio est, ab ea, de qua diximus, Tertulliani authoritate. Non citaturum fuisse Epistolam sub nomine Barnabæ, nisi putasset Romanos in eadem sententia fuisse, quos ex eâ Epistolâ revincere conabatur.
units.tr: XI. Finally, to make an end: the whole tradition rests on the single authority of Tertullian, and indeed on the mad spirit of Montanus, which had already lost its wits. It rests also on the obscure words of that African, who, when through the "Epistle of Barnabas" he especially means that one to the Hebrews, departs, as it seems, from all antiquity. And if any other conjectures favour this view, they are surely too light to seem equal, let alone preferable, to so many unconquered arguments for Paul. It is tiresome to contend further with Cameron, who argues for Barnabas in such a way as to betray his own cause. His first reason is drawn from that authority of Tertullian which we have mentioned: that Tertullian would not have cited the Epistle under the name of Barnabas "unless he thought the Romans were of the same opinion, whom he was trying to convince from that Epistle."

units.la: XII. Sed infirma admodùm illatio Cameronis. 1. Quia hæreticorum jam partibus addictior Tertullianus, illorum potius quàm Ecclesiæ, placita & traditiones sectabatur. Hieronymus in Helvid. De Tertulliano quidem nihil am-plius dico, quam Ecclesiæ hominem non fuisse. 11. Quoniam communis hæc sententia Romanorum, aliis constaret sal-tem documentis. Meninissent, ut ditum[?] modò, Clemens, Origenes, postmodùm Eusebius. III. Sed & Hieronymus, opinionem illam de Barnaba scriptore, non Romanæ Ecclesiæ, sed unius Tertulliani facit, Catalog. in Paulo.
