Argumento sanè, singularem illam, non communem fuisse Ecclesiæ totius. IV. Quod si illo jam tempore fuerit inter Romanos de Authore controversum, verisimilius est Clementi Romano adhæsisse quam Barnabæ. Saltem divisas fuisse sententias, ut patet, nec idem sensisse omnes. Quo ipso, liberius Barnabam suum propinare potuit, Montanistæ satellites. V. Adeóque damus non illibentes, potuisse jam tum dubia de Authore, inter Romanos, sive à Marcione, sive ab illo Caio, esse disseminata. Nec omnes existimasse eam Pauli esse Apostoli. Et sic cadit instantia Cameronis; Si Romani, inquit, existimassent eam ab Apostolo Paulo fuisse conscriptam, ille qui ex Epistolâ conciliare voluit summam doctrinæ suæ authoritatem, titulum non immutasset. VI. Nos[?] attendens attendit Vir aliàs minimè obesse maris[?], Tertullianum opponere hoc loco Epistolam, Pastori moechorum, i.e. Hermæ,a-pocrypho scriptori. Scilicet illius Epistolæ prævalere authoritatem, receptiorem tamen esse apud Ecclesias, inter ipsos Romanos, (quocunque tandem authore,) libro illo, Pastoris nomine, trito & evulgato. Etiam receptiorem sub Barnabæ titulo, (sive jam ex sua, sive aliorum sui temporis loquatur hypothesi) qui utique esset Hermâ dignior. vii. Quicquid tandem largiamur Cameroni, nihil evincit. Supponamus, loqui Tertullianum ex receptâ Romanorum multis opinione, eönc Epistola Barnabæ est? Atqui ex Romanis, alij Lucæ, alij Clementis esse contendebant. Cur illorum, quàm horum authoritas potior? Atqui Græci omnes, & longè vetustiores, Paulo vindicarant. Atqui iidem Romani, errori renunciarunt, inde à Nicæno Oecumenico, certè inde ab Hilario, Ambrosio, Hieronymo. Et quorundam hæresin vocat Philastrius, circiter annis cl. post ætate Tertulliani. Nec ne-cesse cesse profecto est, vera fuisse omnia quæ-cunque tum Romani credidere.
units.tr: XII. But Cameron's inference is very weak. (1) Tertullian, already more inclined to the party of the heretics, followed their opinions and traditions rather than those of the Church. Jerome, in his book against Helvidius: "About Tertullian I say no more than that he was not a man of the Church." (2) This common opinion of the Romans would at least have been supported by other evidence. Clement, Origen and afterwards Eusebius would have remembered it, as has just been said. (3) Jerome, moreover, makes that opinion about Barnabas as author the view not of the Roman Church but of Tertullian alone (Catalogue, under Paul). This surely argues that it was a singular opinion, not one common to the whole Church. (4) If already at that time there was controversy among the Romans about the author, it is more likely that they adhered to Clement of Rome than to Barnabas. At least, opinions were divided, as is plain, and not everyone thought the same. By that very fact Tertullian could more freely put forward his Barnabas, as a satellite of the Montanists. (5) And so we grant, and not unwillingly, that doubts about the author could already then have been spread among the Romans, whether by Marcion or by that Gaius. Nor did everyone think it was written by the apostle Paul. Thus Cameron's instance falls to the ground. "If the Romans," he says, "had thought it was written by the apostle Paul, the man who wished to win over the supreme authority of his doctrine from the Epistle would not have changed the title." (6) The man, who is otherwise not inexperienced, has not noticed that Tertullian here sets against it the Epistle of the Shepherd of adulterers, that is, of Hermas, an apocryphal writer. Clearly the authority of that Epistle prevailed, yet among the churches, even among the Romans themselves (whoever its author was), it was more received than that book, trite and widely circulated under the name of "the Shepherd." It would be received even more under the title of Barnabas, whether he speaks from his own hypothesis or from that of others of his time, which surely was more worthy than Hermas. (7) Whatever we concede to Cameron, he proves nothing. Suppose Tertullian speaks from the opinion received among many Romans: is the Epistle therefore Barnabas's? But some of the Romans contended that it was by Luke, others that it was by Clement. Why is their authority greater than these? Yet all the Greeks, and they far more ancient, had claimed it for Paul. Yet the same Romans later renounced that error, from the Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, and certainly from Hilary, Ambrose and Jerome. And Philastrius calls it the heresy of some, about 150 years after Tertullian's time. Nor is it necessary, indeed, that everything the Romans then believed was true.

units.la: XIII. Ratio altera Cameronis, citius risum (detur venia verbo) quam assensum extorqueat. Barnabam, inquit, fuisse eo vultu & oris habitu, quem sublimitas illa styli maxime decere videatur. Probat antecedens, quod Lycaones, pro Mercurio Paulum, pro Jove vero Barnabam acceperunt. Non lepide minus, quam caeteroquin acute. Sed facile intellexit Vir doctus, ab externa quadam specie vultus ad stylum, fallacem nimis esse consequentiam, Ut de Tiberio Suetonius, fuisse adducto vultu & superbo, sermone mollo[?], aut rarissimo, eoque tardissimo. Praeterea, responderit oris majestati, oratio Barnabae, procedit ex mere particularibus argumentatio. Nec Pauli minus gravis, sublimis minus oratio. Quod vero de Jove & Mercurio subnectit, nititur fallacia non causae, adeoque Philosophoteste, ἀσυλλο-γιστον[?]. Causa enim omnis illius discrimini à Lystrensibus instituti, fuit Pauli oratio, silentium vero Barnabae. Hinc creditum ille nuncius alterius & interpres, Παυλ[?]ος ὁ ἡγούμεν[?]ος τῷ λόγῳ[?], Actor. xiv. 11, Atque ita Paulus Mercurius, Barnabas Jupiter, & hinc nascitur conclusio Cameronianæ oppositæ. Fuisse Paulum præ Barnaba, ea in dicendo majestate, eo eloquio, quod sublimitas illa styli maxime decere videatur.
units.tr: XIII. The second argument of Cameron would draw a laugh, pardon the word, more readily than assent. Barnabas, he says, had a countenance and bearing of face which that sublimity of style seems especially to suit. He proves the antecedent by the fact that the Lycaonians took Paul for Mercury and Barnabas for Jupiter. This is not as witty as it is otherwise acute. But the learned man easily saw that an inference from some outward appearance of the face to the style is far too fallacious. Suetonius says of Tiberius that he had a stern and haughty face, with soft, or very rare, and very slow speech. Moreover, Barnabas's speech, which matched the dignity of his face, proceeds by merely particular argumentation. Paul's speech was no less weighty and no less sublime. As for what he adds about Jupiter and Mercury, it rests on the fallacy of non-cause, and so, as the Philosopher bears witness, is unreasoned and invalid [ἀσυλλόγιστον]. The cause of that whole mistake made by the Lystrians was Paul's speech, and Barnabas's silence. Hence the messenger and interpreter believed that Paul was the chief speaker [Παῦλος ὁ ἡγούμενος τοῦ λόγου], Acts 14:11. And so Paul was Mercury and Barnabas Jupiter, and from this arises the conclusion opposite to Cameron's: that Paul surpassed Barnabas in that majesty of speech and that eloquence which that sublimity of style seems especially to suit.

units.la: XIV. Addit tandem, Barnabam videri paulò incitatiorem fuisse animo, quam Paulum. Hoc autem unde? Quia hinc natus ille paroxysmus, qui narratur Act. xv. 39. Quid si liberalius demus omnia Cameroni, eone conficietur Epistolam Barnabæ adscribi debere? Quia forte Barnabas ad iram & contentionem pronior? Quid commune hic, cum gravi illa Epistolæ, partim masculè docentis, partim suavissimè solantis & erigentis, majestate? Sed antecedens, quantum quidem ex Sacris assequimur, videtur esse falsum. Pauli animus ille concitatior, ubiq; conspicuus. Sic Petro in os resistit, Ananiam acriùs increpat, Corinthios, Galatas, vehementer redarguit. Pauli acta omnia, dicta, & scripta loquuntur, quæ alicubi Hieronymo sunt tonitrua, fulmina, rugitus leonis. Contrà describitur Barnabas, ut vir bonus, Act. xi. 24. ad solatia, & charitatis officia mirum in modum pronus. παροξυσμὸν[?] autem illū quod attinet, Paulum inter & Barnabam, primus ille, huic restitisse legitur. Nec exacerbatio aut excandescentia in Barnabam quam Paulo dicitur fuisse vehementior. Ut mirari subeat, non puduisse ingeniosissimum Cameronem istam vitilitigationem. Et pueriles conjecturas propinare ausum eruditis, gratas ei quia novas sordet quicquid spectavimus olim.
units.tr: XIV. Finally he adds that Barnabas seemed to be somewhat more excitable in spirit than Paul. But on what basis? Because from this arose that paroxysm which is related in Acts 15:39. What if we grant Cameron all of this more generously? Will it follow that the Epistle ought to be ascribed to Barnabas? Perhaps Barnabas was more prone to anger and contention? What has this to do with the grave majesty of the Epistle, which is partly manly in its teaching and partly most sweetly consoling and uplifting? But the antecedent, as far as we can gather from the Sacred writings, seems to be false. Paul's more excitable spirit is conspicuous everywhere. So he withstood Peter to his face, rebuked Ananias more sharply, and vigorously refuted the Corinthians and the Galatians. All of Paul's deeds, words, and writings speak of this, and which for Jerome are thunderings, lightnings, and roarings of a lion. On the contrary, Barnabas is described as a good man, Acts 11:24, remarkably inclined to comfort and to acts of charity. As for that paroxysm [παροξυσμόν] between Paul and Barnabas, it is read that the first resisted the second. Nor is the exasperation or heat said to have been greater against Barnabas than against Paul. So one is moved to wonder that the ingenious Cameron was not ashamed of this trifling quarrel, and dared to offer puerile conjectures to learned men, which please him because they are new: whatever we have seen before is distasteful to us.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Qui Apollo Epistolæ authorem conjectarunt. Propius ferè ad verum accedunt. Apollo illius descriptio. Falsum tamen esse authorem. Multis demonstratur. De Marco Evangelista. Ineptè author assertus. De Tertulliano fabula. Claudi-tur disputatio.
units.tr: Those who conjectured Apollos as the author of the Epistle come closer, roughly, to the truth. A description of Apollos. Yet he is shown to be not the author, by many arguments. On Mark the Evangelist. Wrongly asserted as author. The fable about Tertullian. The discussion is closed.

units.la: I. Sed morae pertaesi longioris, adstinem properamus. Eadem porrò indu-ctione, nec Apollo, nec quemquam alium, concinnasse hoc scripti genus, probaturi. Eò minus operosè, quod probabiliter minus, reliqui hi, scriptores asserti. Non opus hic Τυνδαρίδας πλημμελίζομεν[?]. Quanquam Lutherus, pro Apollo scriptore sensisse aliquando videatur. Ita enim ad Caput XLVIII. Geneseos, vers.20: Author Epistolæ ad Hebræos quisquis est, sive Paulus, sive, ut ego arbitror, Apollo, eruditissime &c. Sic Beza, comparate huic verius quàm reliquis, Epistolam adscribi posse censet: Nisi fortassis Apollos illam scripsisse existimari possit, cujus & eruditio & eloquentia cum maxima pietate conjuncta, tantopere commendatur. Et qui specialiter Judæos dicitur coarguisse.
units.tr: I. But weary of a longer delay, we hasten on to what is nearest. By the same method of induction, we shall prove that neither Apollos nor anyone else composed this kind of writing. We shall do so the more easily because the others named as authors are less probable. There is no need here to make Tyndarid blunders [Τυνδαρίδας πλημμελίζομεν]. Yet Luther seems at some time to have thought Apollos the writer. For thus, on Genesis chapter 48, verse 20: "The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, whoever he is, whether Paul or, as I think, Apollos, most learned &c." So Beza, comparing him with the others, thinks the Epistle could more truly be ascribed to him: "Unless perhaps it may be thought that Apollos wrote it, whose learning and eloquence, joined with the greatest piety, are so highly praised, and who is said to have refuted the Jews in particular."

units.la: II. Non est autem quod in hoc excutiendo immoremur. Revera, si præter Paulum quisquam alius scriptor existimandus foret, neque vestigia deessent apud Veteres, ille imprimis nobis Apollo probaretur. Hebræus fuit, magnæque in-ter conversos Judæorum existimationis. [illegible, ~9 letters] vir eloquens, & ad persuadendum natus, cuiq; eo potissimùm nomine Corinthij illi præ Paulo adhærerent, ut in primâ ad Corinthios. Etiam potens in scripturis, & ex Test. Veteris oraculis, revincens efficacissimè Judæorum pertinaciam. Deinde fervens spiritu, in docendo vehemens & masculus, in arguendo intrepidus, in omnibus sollicitus, & accuratus, cuiq; illius [illegible, ~12 letters] est, Act. xviii. Sed neq; hoc satis, nec indicia illa sufficiunt & lineamenta, ut illi hunc fœtũ adjudicemus.
units.tr: II. There is, however, no reason for us to linger over this question. Indeed, if any writer other than Paul were to be considered, and there were no traces among the ancients, Apollos would above all be approved by us. He was a Hebrew, and of great esteem among the Jewish converts; a man eloquent and born for persuading, and for whose sake especially the Corinthians clung to him rather than to Paul, as in the first Epistle to the Corinthians. He was also powerful in the Scriptures, and by the oracles of the Old Testament he very effectively overcame the obstinacy of the Jews. Then, "fervent in spirit," vehement and manly in teaching, fearless in refuting, careful and exact in all things, to whom ... belongs, Acts 18. But this is not enough, nor do those indications and outlines suffice for us to assign this offspring to him.

units.la: III. Vel hæ rationes obstant. 1. Quia talè scripsisse Epistolam, dicitur præter fidem utriusque historiæ, Sacræ & Ecclesiasticæ. Græcorum nemo, nemo Latinorum, id vel tradidisse posteritati, vel scripsisse legitur. Inaudiissent nonnihil vetustissimi illi Patrum, qui cæteroquin de Lucâ, de Clemente, de Barnabâ, meminêre. Neque Apollo inter Ecclesiasticos scriptores relatus fuit Hieronymo. II. Neque etiam universalis fuit & primarius Apostolus, illo quanquam nomine nonnunquam veniat Scriptoribus. Non immediatè sive vocatus, sive edoctus à Domino. Apostolorum, imò Priscillæ & Aquilæ discipulus. Act. xviii. 26. Non orbis etiam universi, non Hebræorum omnium præfectus Ecclesijs, sed Achajis & Corinthiis, ut Act. xviii. & 1. Cor. 1. 11. 111. Hinc Corinthum illi, veteres Provinciarum distributores assignarunt. Adeóq; non ea instructus authoritate, qui pari cum Apostolis passu Orbem universum edoceret. Nam, ut Tertullianus adversus Marcion. L. v. ad omnes Apostoli scripsêre, dum ad quosdam. 111. Sed neq; in eum quadrant circumstantiæ Epistolæ variæ, v. g. illo tempore Romæ fuisse; aut adstrictum vinculis; aut restituendum Hebræis, Hierosolymitanis imprimis; cum nonnisi inter Corinthios & Græcos legatur esse versatus. Et hos potius absens, ut discipulos suæque pridem institutioni suffectos, quàm Palæstinos, aut in communi Hebræos, compellasset. iv. Porrò quæcunque de illius sive facundia, sive eruditione, sive fervore, sive pietate memorantur, concludunt nihil. Sunt enim illa ἐκ τῶν ἐν μέρει neq; Apollo in his inferior fuit Paulus, si non major. Nec minus Paulo cum Judæis, imò Judaizantibus res fuit. Nec minus in Scripturis potens, & ex Mose & Prophetis, Judæos redarguens. Adeóque ex aliis primò circumstantiis& indiciis argumentandum foret, quæ Apollo quàm Paulo magis, aut alij cuivis convenirent. Et exinde demùm posset illius sive eloquétia, sive eximiæ aliæ dotes urgeri. v. Et ut paucis absolvamus, Lutheri ( nisi qui alij suffragantur ) hæc quædam sententia singularis. Nec tam sententia, quàm levis conjectura, quamque in Epist. Præfatione minimè reponendam duxit. Beza primas tribuit Paulo, nec nisi secundariò & comparatè ad Lucam, aut Clementem, pro Apollo eodem pronunciavit.
units.tr: III. Indeed, these reasons stand in the way. First, it is said that to have written the Epistle in this way is contrary to the testimony of both histories, sacred and ecclesiastical. No Greek, no Latin, is read to have handed down to posterity or written this. The most ancient Fathers, who elsewhere mention Luke, Clement and Barnabas, would have heard something of it. Nor is Apollos listed among the ecclesiastical writers by Jerome. Second, he was not a universal and chief apostle, though under that name he sometimes occurs in the writers. He was not called or taught immediately by the Lord. He was a disciple of the Apostles, indeed of Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18:26). He was not the prefect of the whole world, nor of all the Hebrews over the churches, but of Achaia and Corinth, as in Acts 18 and 1 Corinthians 1:11, 3. Hence the ancient distributors of the provinces assigned Corinth to him. Therefore he was not furnished with such authority as to teach the whole world on equal footing with the Apostles. For, as Tertullian says in Against Marcion, book 5: "The Apostles wrote to all, while [Apollos wrote] to some." Third, neither do the various circumstances of the Epistle fit him: for example, that he was at that time at Rome, or bound in chains, or to be restored to the Hebrews, especially those of Jerusalem; since he is read to have been active only among the Corinthians and the Greeks. He would have addressed these rather than the Palestinians, or the Hebrews in general, while absent, as disciples and as successors to his earlier instruction. Fourth, whatever is recorded of his eloquence, learning, fervour or piety proves nothing. For these are [ἐκ τῶν ἐν μέρει] things in part; and Apollos was not inferior to Paul in these, if not greater. Nor did he have less to do with the Jews, or rather with Judaizers, than Paul did. Nor was he less powerful in the Scriptures, refuting the Jews from Moses and the Prophets. Therefore one ought first to argue from other circumstances and indications, which would fit Apollos more than Paul or any other. Only then could his eloquence or other outstanding gifts be pressed. Fifth, to be brief, this opinion of Luther's (unless others support it) is peculiar to him. It is less an opinion than a slight conjecture, which he did not think should be given weight in the preface to the Epistle. Beza gave first place to Paul, and pronounced Apollos the author only secondarily and by comparison with Luke or Clement.

units.la: IV. Multo minùs, putandus est author Epistolæ Marcus, quod legere nos aliquando meminimus. Qua tamen authoritate, aut quo rationis fundamento, non legimus. Primò enim Marcus nonnisi Apostolorum filius & discipulus. Petri speciatim Apostoli, quum veriùs ex Pauli Schola, Epistolam intelligamus esse proprofectam. Ipsi deinde Petro Magistro, majorisque inter Hebræos authoritatis, potiùs adscribenda foret. Quo magis, ipsum Marci Evangelium, Petri creditum fuit. Quando etiam Petro adhuc superstite, scripsisse dicendus est Marcus, martyrio ante Apostolorum coryphæos sublatus, Neronis anno VIII, Christi LXII, juxtà Baronium LXIV. Imo hanc ad Hebræos misisset Epistolam, ante Pauli plerasque alias, ad quarum tamen, si non author ipse Paulus, scripta imitationem. Nam in Ægypto, & Alexandriæ, inde ab anno Claudij III. sedem fixisse Marcum; Eusebius, Chronic. Lib. II, in Claudio. Hinc eodem anno, antequam Roma mitteretur Alexandriam, scripsisse Evangelium, referunt. Postmodum autem Africa excessisse, concessisse in Italiam, ibidem fuisse vinctum, scripsisse inde ad Ecclesias Hebræorum &c. fabulæ sunt, & quæ nemo somniavit. Ut taceam styli illud & orationis, immensum, Marcum inter & scriptorem Epistolæ, discrimen.
units.tr: IV. Much less is the author of the Epistle to be thought Mark, which we remember reading at some time. By what authority, or on what foundation of reason, we do not read. For first, Mark was only a son and disciple of the Apostles, specifically of Peter; whereas we understand the Epistle to have gone out more truly from the school of Paul. Moreover, it should rather be ascribed to Peter himself, his teacher, who had greater authority among the Hebrews. The more so since the Gospel of Mark itself was believed to be Peter's. Also, Mark is said to have written while Peter was still alive, Mark having been taken away by martyrdom before the leaders of the Apostles, in the eighth year of Nero, the sixty-second year of Christ, or by Baronius's reckoning the sixty-fourth. Indeed he would have sent this Epistle to the Hebrews before most of Paul's other letters, though it imitates those, if not written by Paul himself. For they report that Mark fixed his seat in Egypt and at Alexandria from the third year of Claudius onward; Eusebius, Chronicle, book 2, under Claudius. Hence, in the same year, before he was sent from Rome to Alexandria, they report he wrote the Gospel. Afterwards, however, that he left Africa, went into Italy, was imprisoned there, and wrote from there to the churches of the Hebrews, etc., are fables, things which no one has dreamed. I say nothing of the immense difference of style and diction between Mark and the author of the Epistle.

units.la: V. Sed absurditatem longè omnem superat, quod tradidit Sixtus Senensis, Biblioth.Lib.vii.Cap.viii. tribuere quosdam Tertulliano. Quo commento post homines natos nullum insultius, impudentius nullum. Illos Epistolæ cothurnos aptari Tertulliano? Quem ante Justinus, Irenæus, Clemens uterque, Epistolam usurparunt totiens; qui Barnabæ ipsemet adscripsit; qui Timotheo, totâ ætate posterior; qui libro de Hæres. notat Theodotum, verba illa Epistolæ, apator, ametor, ageneologitus, cujus neque initium, neque finis, contorquentem; nec jam de phrasi Tertulliani diversâ toto coelo, ac Latinâ quidem eâ, & Africanâ, aliisque pro Epistolæ antiquitate dicam argumentis. Atque ita quod instituéramus primùm, plenissimè executos nos esse arbitramur. Omnibusque tandem æstimatis, authoritatibus omnibus expensis, rationibus libratis, instantiis excussis, exceptionibus eversis, id unum superesset, Pauli Epistolam ut esse credamus, credant quę nepotes.
units.tr: V. But the absurdity far surpasses all others, which Sixtus of Siena, Bibliotheca, book 7, chapter 8, handed down: that some ascribe it to Tertullian. By this invention, no more insolent or shameless thing has been produced since men were born. Are those lofty buskins of the Epistle to be fitted to Tertullian? Before him Justin, Irenaeus, and both Clements used the Epistle so often; Tertullian himself ascribed it to Barnabas; he is later by a whole age than Timothy; in his book on heresies he notes that Theodotus twisted those words of the Epistle, "without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life." And I say nothing now of Tertullian's phrasing, which is wholly different, and indeed Latin and African, nor of other arguments drawn from the antiquity of the Epistle. And so we believe we have very fully carried out what we first set out to do. And when everything has been weighed, all authorities examined, reasons balanced, objections shaken, and exceptions overturned, only one thing would remain: that we believe the Epistle to be Paul's, "as later generations will believe."

units.la: DE AUTHORE EPISTOLÆ AD HEBRÆOS, PARS TERTIA.
units.tr: On the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, Part Three.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Transitio ad Partem ἀναστρεπτικὴν. Objectiones multæ antè occupatæ. Aliæ authorem, aliæ etiam authoritatem feriunt. Aliæ Veterum, aliæ ferè recentiorum. De stylo Epistolæ ad Hebræos. Qui illius à Paulino ursêre discrimen. In quo discrimen constitutum. Vis objectionis qualis. De variatione styli. Exempla in Sacris. Speciatim in Paulo. Variandi quas habuerit causas. Pauli sermonem non fuisse ἰδιωτικὸν. Non solam phrasin in hac Epistolâ attendendam. Falsum etiam differre toto genere à reliquis. Occurritur instantiis cum aliorum, tum Cameronis. De voce [illegible, ~6 letters]. De phrasi μὴ [illegible, ~8 letters].
units.tr: Transition to the Part on Refutation. Many objections dealt with beforehand. Some strike at the author, others at the authority of the Epistle. Some come from the Ancients, others mostly from more recent writers. On the style of the Epistle to the Hebrews. Who have urged a difference from the Pauline style. In what the difference consists. The force of the objection. On variation of style. Examples in Scripture, especially in Paul. What causes of variation he had. That Paul's speech was not ἰδιωτικόν. That not only the phrasing of this Epistle should be considered. That it is also false that it differs in its whole character from the others. The instances are met, both those of others and those of Cameron. On the word [illegible, about 6 letters]. On the phrase μὴ [illegible, about 8 letters].

units.la: I. Potissimam viæ partem emensi, proximè dissertationis nostræ metam assequemur. Magnâ enim parte laboris de[?]functi sumus in antecessis. Dumque in [?]ἀντιλογίας[?], exceptiones ad nostra diluimus argumenta, & insistimus omnibus effugijs, accidit ut [illegible, ~9 letters] partem non contemnendam occupaverimus. Sic quicquid objicitur de Latinorum Veterum dissensu, de antiquioribus Graecis, de tardius receptâ Epistolâ, prolixè priori Parte, & quàm fieri potuit accuratè pertractatum. Pariter quod alij, de argumenti & methodi nonnullâ diversitate, quod de Paulo Gentium non Hebraeorum Apostolo, quod de clausâ Epistolæ, & sigillo ἰδιοχείρῳ[?] Paulinarum; quod de Lucâ authore; vel Clemente Romano; vel Barnabâ; vel Apollo &c. posteriori Parte, plenius exequebamur. De στύλῳ[?] etiam & charactere dictionis, annotavimus non pauca, Parte II. Cap. II. Et si quæ alia, quæ molestâ repetitione non egent. Nec solùm brevior, sed facilior tantò hæc Pars evasura est, quantò in adstruendo plus situm operis & molestiæ, quàm quidem in destruendo.
units.tr: I. Having traversed the greater part of the way, we shall shortly reach the goal of our dissertation. For we have largely laboured through in the earlier parts. While we answered the exceptions to our arguments in the [?]ἀντιλογίας[?], and pursued every means of escape, it happened that we occupied [illegible, about 9 letters] a not inconsiderable part. So whatever is objected about the disagreement of the Latin Ancients, about the earlier Greeks, about the Epistle being received more slowly, we treated at length and as carefully as possible in the former Part. Likewise, what others raised about some difference of subject and method, about Paul being the apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews, about the closing of the Epistle and the signature in Paul's own hand ἰδιοχείρῳ[?], about Luke as author, or Clement of Rome, or Barnabas, or Apollos, etc., we pursued more fully in the latter Part. About the style[?] and character of the diction we noted not a few things in Part II, Chapter II, and whatever other matters do not need tedious repetition. This Part will turn out not only shorter but also easier, in proportion as more of the labour and difficulty lies in building up than in tearing down.

units.la: II. Objectiones contrà Paulum authorem,
units.tr: II. Objections against Paul as author,

units.la: rem, non sunt unius generis. Aliæ enim authorem tantùm ⁊ aliæ etiam Epistolæ authoritatem sollicitant. Quædam præ-terea ipsâ se vetustate veluti commen-dant, aliæ à recentioribus contortæ magis, aut etiam excogitatæ. Quæ contrà scri-ptorem Paulum simpliciter, (illæsâ Epi-stolæ authoritate) à Veteribus objecta, tria potissimùm esse deprehendimus. Pri-mò enim styli maximam quandam urgent diversitatem: secundò inscriptionis, & Paulini nominis defectum: denique scriptorem semet discipulis accensere Apo-stolorum. Omnium instar esto, Author argumenti, prærixi Comment. Oecume-nij. Ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίους Ἐπιστολὴ, δοκεῖ μὲν οὐχ εἶναι Παύλου, διὰ τὸν χαρακτῆρα. καὶ τὸ μὴ [?]φέρειν ὡς ἐν ἀπιθάνοις τὰς ἄλλας Ἐπιστολάς. καὶ τὸ λέγειν, ὡς ἡμᾶς ἐκφευξώμεθα τηλικαύτης ἀμε-λήσαντες σωτηρίας, ἥτις ἀρχὴν λαβοῦσα λαλεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου, διὰ τῶν ἀκουσάντων εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐβεβαιώθη. Hisce tribus, recentiores præter ea quæ antè fusiùs attigimus, contrà Paulum authorem addunt, illud ex Capite v1.1,2. De Catechetica & initialis doctrinæ rudimentis, post Pauli (ut videtur) aetatem sic digestis.
units.tr: are not of one kind. For some trouble only the author, while others trouble also the authority of the Epistle. Moreover, some commend themselves by their very antiquity, while others are twisted or even invented by more recent writers. Those which the Ancients have raised against Paul as writer simply (the authority of the Epistle being left untouched), we find to be chiefly three. For first, they press a very great diversity of style; second, the lack of the inscription and of the Pauline name; and finally, that the writer reckons himself among the disciples of the Apostles. Let the author of the argument, Oecumenius, whom I cited before, stand for all: "The Epistle to the Hebrews seems not to be Paul's, because of its character, and because it does not bear, as the other Epistles do, the marks of an unpersuasive [sic] style, and because it says that we, having neglected so great a salvation, which having begun to be spoken by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard it." [Ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίους Ἐπιστολὴ, δοκεῖ μὲν οὐχ εἶναι Παύλου, διὰ τὸν χαρακτῆρα. καὶ τὸ μὴ φέρειν ὡς ἐν ἀπιθάνοις τὰς ἄλλας Ἐπιστολάς. καὶ τὸ λέγειν, ὡς ἡμᾶς ἐκφευξώμεθα τηλικαύτης ἀμελήσαντες σωτηρίας, ἥτις ἀρχὴν λαβοῦσα λαλεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου, διὰ τῶν ἀκουσάντων εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐβεβαιώθη.] To these three, the more recent writers, besides what we have discussed more fully before, add against Paul as author that objection taken from Chapter 6.1, 2, about the catechetical and elementary teaching of the rudiments of doctrine, thought to have been arranged after Paul's age (as it seems).

units.la: III. De hoc objectionum genere di-cendum impraesentiarum, primam illi ha-ftam jaciunt in Epistolae ftylum, quem a paulino mirum quantum recedere arbi-trantur. Fuitque jam olim inter dubitan-di caufas, prima. Nam Clemens Alexan-drinus, citato aliquoties loco, Lucae quàm paulo convenientiorem esse dictionem putat. Origenes, cùm alibi, tùm imprimis apud Eusebium, Hist. L. vi. C. xix, vel κὲ, hæc habet: Οὐ ὁ χαρακτὴρ τῆς λέξεως τῆς πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἀπηγεγραμμένης ἐπιστολῆς, ἂν ἔχει τὸ ἐν λόγῳ ἰδιωτικὸν ὁ Ἀπόστολος, ὁμολογήσαντ᾽ ἑαυτὸν ἰδιώτην εἶναι τῷ λόγῳ, τοῦτ᾽ ἔστι τῇ φράσει. Ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν ἡ Ἐπιστολὴ συνθέσει τῆς λέξεως ἑλληνικωτέρα, πᾶς ὁ ἀπισάμεν[?] κρίνειν φράσεων διαφορὰς, ὁμολογήσαι ἄν. Orationis characterem Epi-ftolae quae inscribitur ad Hebraeos, non ha-bere illam simplicitatem sermonis Pauli-ni. Quum fateatur se esse rudem indicen-do, i.e. formâ dictionis. Ipsam enim Epi-ftolam, dictionis compositione, magis acce-dere ad elegantiam Graeci sermonis ; fassurũ esse omnẽ, qui orationis differentias scit dignoscere. Sensit idem Eusebius, qui suprà Hist.L.iii.C.xxxii. phrasim, esse illi Clementis cumprimis affinem dixit. Hieronymus, hoc uno nomine non credi Epistolam esse Pauli, propter styli, sermo-nisque dissonantiam. Itidem Philastrius, nempe quia utitur sermone nimium plau-sibili. Unius fere illius difficultatis quæ Latinos priores ad dissensum induxerit meminere pariter, Isidorus de Eccles. Of-sic. L.i.C.ix. Rabanus, de Instit. Cler. L.ii. C. LIV. Hinc quotquot Veterum pro paulo pronunciarunt, sive ex Græcis, sive Latinis Patribus, fere obviarunt eidem difficultati. Ex posterioribus nodū hunc plusquàm Gordium facit Erasmus, sub finem Annotat. Restat jam argumentum illud quo non aliud certius, stylus ipse & orationis character, qui nihil habet assi-nitatis cum phrasi Paulinà. Accedit & ipse Calvinus, Argum. in Epist. Magde-burgenses Cent.i.L.ii.Cap.iv. quotquot denique (ne faciam longius) in hac de Authore controversia à nobis discesserè.
units.tr: III. Concerning this kind of objection, to be discussed now: they first hurl their spear at the style of the Epistle, which they think departs wonderfully far from Paul's. And this was already long ago the first of the reasons for doubt. For Clement of Alexandria, citing the passage several times, thinks the diction is more suited to Luke than to Paul. Origen, both elsewhere and especially in Eusebius, Hist. Bk. VI, ch. xxv, has these words: "The character of the diction of the Epistle written to the Hebrews does not have that simplicity of speech which the Apostle has in speaking, since he confesses himself to be rude in speech, that is, in the form of expression. But the Epistle itself, in the composition of its diction, is closer to the elegance of Greek; every one who knows how to judge differences of style would admit this." Origen says that the character of the Epistle entitled to the Hebrews does not have the simplicity of Paul's speech, since he confesses that he is rude in speech, that is, in the form of diction; the Epistle itself, by the composition of its diction, comes closer to the elegance of the Greek language; everyone who knows how to distinguish differences of style would confess this. Eusebius thought the same, who above, Hist. Bk. III, ch. xxxii, said that its phrasing was especially akin to that of Clement. Jerome says that by this single name the Epistle is not believed to be Paul's, because of the dissimilarity of style and speech. Likewise Philastrius, namely because it uses speech that is too plausible. Likewise the Latin writers before them mention the one difficulty which led them to disagree: Isidore, On the Ecclesiastical Offices, Bk. I, ch. ix, and Rabanus, On the Institution of Clergy, Bk. II, ch. liv. Hence all the Ancients, whether Greek or Latin Fathers, who pronounced against Paul, mostly met this same difficulty. Among the later writers, Erasmus makes this knot more than Gordian, near the end of his Annotations: "There remains that argument, than which none is more certain: the style itself and the character of the diction, which has nothing in common with Paul's phrasing." Calvin too joins in, in his Argument on the Epistle; the Magdeburg centuriators, Cent. I, Bk. II, ch. iv; and, to say no more, all who have departed from us in this controversy about the author.

units.la: IV. Summa est objectionis, Epistolam ad Hebræos, elegantiâ, ornatu, copiâ di-ctionis, aliquot parasangis superare om-nes Paulinas. Paulum magis ἑβραΐζειν[?]; contrà ἑλληνίζειν[?] magis, & ad Græcorum idiotismum nostrum accedere Authorem. Il-lum rudiorem fuisse sermone, & stylo ma-gis ad simplicitatem comparato; hunc jam induere cothurnos, & magis assurge-re. Paulum plus spirare lenitatis; Scripto-rem Epistolæ plus longè gravitatis, quique ferè ubique tonet atque fulguret. Denique hunc, iis nonnunquam usum esse vocibus atque phrasibus, quæ minimè sa-piunt τὸ ἡῆμα[?] Pauli: geminumque profert exemplum Camero, 1. à voce αἰῶνες[?], mun-dum significante; 11. ab illa phrasi μήποτε παραῤῥυῶμεν[?]. Ex his omnibus conflatur ar-gumentum. Qui stylus, qui dictionis character, toto genere ab eo diversus est, quem Paulus usurpare consuevit in omnibus Epistolis, alius cujusdam Scripto-ris is esse videtur: talis autem, qui sonat in tota ferè Epistola, talemque esse totā antiquitas agnovit.
units.tr: IV. The sum of the objection is that the Epistle to the Hebrews, in elegance, ornament and abundance of diction, surpasses all the Pauline Epistles by several parasangs. Paul is more Hebraizing [ἑβραΐζειν]; the author, on the contrary, is more Hellenizing [ἑλληνίζειν] and comes closer to the idiom of the Greeks. Paul was rougher in speech and his style was adjusted more to simplicity; this author now puts on the buskin and rises higher. Paul breathes more gentleness; the writer of the Epistle breathes far more gravity, and thunders and lightens almost everywhere. Finally, this writer sometimes used words and phrases that least of all savour of Paul's manner [ῥῆμα], and they bring forward a twofold example from Cameron: first, from the word αἰῶνες [aiōnes], meaning world; second, from the phrase μήποτε παραῤῥυῶμεν [lest we drift away]. From all this the argument is put together: the style and character of diction which differs in its whole kind from that which Paul is accustomed to use in all his Epistles, seems to be of some other writer; and such a writer as sounds through almost the whole Epistle, and such antiquity acknowledged to be wholly his.

units.la: V. Speciem habet argumentum, solidi-ditatis, si ad vivum resecetur, nihil. Cuique adeò plenissimè ut satisfiat, respondemus non uno modo. Primò quidem, in genere propositionem esse inconsequentem, nec necessariæ veritatis. Quâ ex styli nonnulla diversitate, scriptoris infertur diversitas. Si forte modò æquabilis modò magnifica, modò simplex modò ornatior, modò humilis modò sublimior, modò lenis modò gravior, modò pressa magis modò copiosior exurgat oratio. Variat enim ea multifariam, tum pro subjecti diversitate argumenti, quod vel tenue magis, vel gravius ab sublimius; tum pro variis scribentis affectibus, & animi motibus, modò demulcentis, modò indignantis; modò in lætis, modò tristibus constituti; modò vehementius, modò leviùs affecti; tum prout quis vel negligentius scribit, vel elaboratius, aut vel solutus curis vel implicitus; tum pro personis, quibus cum res est, quæque vel flecti faciles, vel tenaciores; vel pares, aut familiaritatis junctæ aliquo[?] vinculo, vel alius &c. & superioris à nostra sortis; vel propen-siùs in nos, vel iniquiùs affectæ. Sic alius longè character ἐπισολιμαῖος, alius ῥητορικὸς, alius διδασκαλικὸς, alius ἱστορικὸς, ab eodem sæpe etiam authore profectus. Et diver-sissimam hanc dictionis faciem, iidem Scriptores sacri, (ne de profanis jam aut Ecclesiasticis dicam) exhibent aliquo-ties. Quam dissimilis sui Moses? v. g. Gene-seos i. aut Deuteronomij xxxii, collatis cum reliquo passim contextu. Annon δὶς Ἀλ᾽ πατῶν distat Jeremias in Threnis, à semetipso in Vaticiniorum libro? An-non diversissimus Johannes, in Evange-lio, Epistolis, & Apocalypsi? quo hanc no-mine, alteri illi Johanni adscribebat Dio-nysius Alexandrinus.
units.tr: V. The argument has the appearance of solidity, but if it is cut down to its living core, it is nothing. To satisfy it fully, we reply in more than one way. First, in general, the proposition is inconsequential and not of necessary truth. From some diversity of style it is inferred that the writer is different. As if speech should sometimes rise evenly, sometimes magnificently; sometimes plainly, sometimes more ornately; sometimes lowly, sometimes more lofty; sometimes gently, sometimes more gravely; sometimes more compressed, sometimes more copious. For it varies in many ways: partly according to the diversity of the subject matter, which is sometimes slight, sometimes weightier, or more sublime; partly according to the various feelings and emotions of the writer, sometimes soothing, sometimes indignant; sometimes situated in joyful, sometimes in sad circumstances; sometimes more vehemently, sometimes more lightly affected; partly according as one writes more carelessly or more laboriously, or is free from cares or entangled in them; partly according to the persons with whom one has to do, who are either easily bent or more stubborn, or equals, or joined by some bond of familiarity, or otherwise, and superiors of a rank above ours, or more inclined toward us, or more unfairly disposed. So one character is [epistolary: ἐπιστολιμαῖος], another [rhetorical: ῥητορικὸς], another [didactic: διδασκαλικὸς], another [historical: ἱστορικὸς], often proceeding from the same author. And the very same sacred writers, not to speak now of profane or ecclesiastical writers, display this most diverse face of diction on many occasions. How unlike himself is Moses, for example, in Genesis 1 or Deuteronomy 32, compared with the rest of the text everywhere? Is not Jeremiah in the Lamentations far different from himself in the book of his prophecies? Is not John most diverse in the Gospel, the Epistles and the Apocalypse? For which reason Dionysius of Alexandria ascribed these to a different John.

units.la: VI. Secundò, de Paulo in specie, nec hunc semper sibi esse similem, reliquis in Epistolis.
units.tr: VI. Secondly, concerning Paul in particular: that he is not always like himself in his other Epistles.

units.la: Consentiunt enim omnes eru-diti, Epistolam ad Ephesios, sublimitate styli, & copiâ dictionis, supra cæteras as-surgere. Et tribus potissimùm de causis, ut sapientissimè, nostro judicio, Theodo-retus: primò, ὅτι πολλῇ σπουδῇ κέχρηταυ πρὸς αὐτὲς αὐτὸς γράφων; deinde, ὃν τὰ βαθύτερα τῶν νοη-μάτων αὐτοῖς ἐπιστέλλει; tandem, quod scribat κατηχουμένοις [?] τὰ ὑψηλά. Et has ipsas putamus esse causas, discrepantiæ illius omnis in Epistola ad Hebræos. 1. Quod Paulus majore jam studio & accuratiore iisdem scripserit. Ut sublimi illo eloquio, sapientiæ sublimitatem suæ, hominibus iniquiùs de se sentientibus, inter cætera exponeret. 11. Quod Epistolæ argumentum ferè diversum à reliquis esset. Magis etiam arduum ac sublime, ubi de Christi persona supra Angelos, suprà Mosem, suprà creaturas omnes evecta; ubi abstrusissima redemptionis nostræ mysteria, collata jam cum illis figurarum umbrarumque involucris: ubi historia Christi in cœlis agentis, sacerdotio æterno defungentis, solio majestatis insidentis, è cœlo opitulantis, suos Patri æterno sacrificio propitiantis &c. Qui sanè Paulus quasi intra velum consistebat, altissima cœlorum penetrabat, omnem illum terrestris sacerdotij, & sanctuarij mundani, & Mosaici cultus quantumvis splendidum deprimeprimebat apparatum, quid mirum, si so-lito jam gravius, s[?]disertius, si magnificentius dicit? 111. Quando etiam Paulo cum iis negotium, qui in Scripturis exer-citati, qui instructiores in iis, caeteris omnibus Paulo ante salutatis Gentibus, quibus inde eloquii illa majestas & sublimitas familiaris, qui ceremoniis etiam suis & traditivae majorum, pertinacius, & quasi mordicus adhaerescebant.
units.tr: All learned men agree that the Epistle to the Ephesians rises above the others in the sublimity of its style and the richness of its expression. Theodoret, in my judgment most wisely, gives three chief reasons: first, because Paul wrote it with great earnestness [ὅτι πολλῇ σπουδῇ κέχρηται πρὸς αὐτούς]; second, because he sets out for them the deeper things of thought [ὅτι τὰ βαθύτερα τῶν νοημάτων αὐτοῖς ἐπιστέλλει]; and third, because he writes sublime things to catechumens [κατηχουμένοις τὰ ὑψηλά]. I think these very causes account for all the difference in the Epistle to the Hebrews. (1) Paul had now written with greater zeal and more careful study, so that in that lofty eloquence he might set forth, among other things, the sublimity of his wisdom to men who judged him unfairly. (2) The argument of this Epistle was almost different from the others, and more difficult and sublime. It deals with the person of Christ, raised above the angels, above Moses, above all creatures; it treats the most abstruse mysteries of our redemption, now compared with the wrappings of figures and shadows; and it describes Christ's history as acting in heaven, discharging his eternal priesthood, sitting on the throne of majesty, helping from heaven, and propitiating the eternal Father for his own by his sacrifice, and so on. Paul, as it were, stood within the veil and penetrated the highest heights of heaven, and he cast down all that earthly priesthood, the worldly sanctuary, and the Mosaic worship with all its splendid apparatus. What wonder, then, if he speaks more weightily, more eloquently, and more magnificently than usual? (3) Paul also had to deal with men practised in the Scriptures, more learned in them than all the other Gentiles whom Paul had greeted before, to whom that majesty and sublimity of speech was familiar, and who clung to their ceremonies and the traditions of their fathers more stubbornly, as it were with their teeth.

units.la: VII. Tertiò, peccatur falsa hypothe-si, Paulum fuisse idiotam, aut sermonem ejus ubique ἰδιωτικόν. Quod ut de reliquis damus libentius Apostolis, de Paulo per-negamus. Testantur ejus passim scripta, & eximia eruditio, & probata totiens e-loquentia. Quàm ille saepè animosè, quam graviter, quam masculè dicit? Paulum quotiescunque lego, (inquit Hieronymus ad Pammachium Epist. L. Tom. II.) videor mihi non verba, sed audire tonitrua. Legite Epistolas ejus, sed maximè ad Romanos, ad Galatas, & ad Ephesios &c. Ipsi Pauli obtrectatores, Augustino teste de doctr. Christ. Lib. IV. C.VII. Epistolas illius graves & fortes esse confessi sunt. Unde hic nihil tam habuisset in votis, quàm, ut Romam in flore, Christum in carne, sic & cernere Paulum in ore. Quod autem de semetipso Paulus ad Corinthios, deque non affectatis verborum flosculis & veneribus, est ἀκαταδιόρθωτον[?]. Rudem suis-se se sermone dicit, συγκαταβατικῶς, non κατὰ φύσιν, ἐξουσίως non ἀναγκαίως, συγ-κριτικῶς non ἁπλῶς & comparatè ad fuca-tos illos & blandiloquos Philosophos ac Pseudo-Apostolos. Minimè ergo dubiū, quin potuerit etiam Apostolorum maxi-mus, magnum loqui, nitique cothurno. Atque, etiamsi ad id genium Apostoli & indolem minùs fuisse à natura compara-tam largiremur, ne sic quidem valeret consequentia. Non enim à se profecta, sed à Spiritu Sancto dictata, mandavere literis. Nec verba minùs, quam res san-ctissimis Dei hominibus inspiratæ. Nec authores fuêre, sed amanuenses. Et va-rius, pro occasionum & circumstantia-rum varietate, esse potuit Spiritus ille du-ctus & afflatus. Prout stylus & character ProProphetarum, non semper pro cujusque fuisse ingenio existimandus est.
units.tr: VII. Thirdly, one errs by the false hypothesis that Paul was an unlearned man, or that his speech was everywhere unlearned [ἰδιωτικόν]. We readily grant this of the other Apostles, but we deny it of Paul. His writings everywhere bear witness to his outstanding learning and to the eloquence so often proved. How often, how earnestly, how gravely and manfully does he speak? "Whenever I read Paul," says Jerome to Pammachius (Epistle 50, vol. II), "I seem to hear not words but thunderclaps. Read his Epistles, especially those to the Romans, the Galatians, and the Ephesians, etc." Augustine, in On Christian Doctrine Book IV, chapter 7, reports that even Paul's detractors have confessed that his Epistles are weighty and strong. Hence nothing would have been more in the hearts of those men than to see Paul face to face, as they would see Rome in its flower and Christ in the flesh. As for what Paul himself says to the Corinthians about his rough speech and his lack of affected flourishes and charms of words, it must be read with care. He says he is rude in speech condescendingly [συγκαταβατικῶς], not according to nature [κατὰ φύσιν]; with authority, not out of necessity [ἐξουσίως non ἀναγκαίως]; comparatively [συγκριτικῶς], not absolutely [ἁπλῶς], and in comparison with those painted and smooth-tongued philosophers and false apostles. There is therefore no doubt that the greatest of the Apostles could also speak greatly and strive after the buskin of tragedy. Even if we should grant that the Apostle's natural disposition was less suited to that kind of speech, the inference still would not follow. For they committed to writing not what came from themselves but what was dictated by the Holy Spirit. The words were no less inspired than the matter in these most holy men of God. They were not authors but amanuenses. And the guidance and inspiration of that Spirit could vary with the variety of occasions and circumstances, just as the style and character of the Prophets must not always be judged by the disposition of each one.

units.la: VIII. Quarto, perperam ex sola dictione de Authore judicatur. Quando sensus & materias Pauli esse constat. Quando ubique se prodit Paulinus ille genius, in ratiocinando, in citandis, applicandisque V.T. oraculis. Item in methodo, in docendi, claudendi, signandique modo. Illi etiam uni favent circumstantiae omnes loci, temporis, personarum, & si quae alia notanda esse diximus. Ut excepto nonnullo orationis discrimine, caetera omnia Pauli esse, jam olim luculenter professus sit Origenes, apud Eusebium L.vi.C.xix. Quidni illa omnia praeponderent, qualicunque styli diversitati? Quidni hinc colligamus, Apostolum data opera scribendi rationem immutasse nonnihil? Sic enim malim, quam (quod doctissimi alij viri) ut nomen, sic stylum arte dissimulasse. Imprimis tot gravissimis immutandi causis paulo ante expositis. Cum etiam assignetur nullus paulina illa aetate, cui convenientius forma dictionis adseribatur. Non Lucas, non Clemens, non Barnabas, ut prolixiùs oftensum.
units.tr: VIII. Fourthly, one judges the author wrongly from diction alone, when it is clear that the sense and the matters are Paul's. Everywhere that Pauline genius reveals itself: in reasoning, in citing and applying the oracles of the Old Testament, in method, and in the manner of teaching, concluding, and marking points. All the circumstances of place, time, and persons, and whatever else we have said should be noted, favour him alone. So Origen long ago clearly declared, in Eusebius Book VI, chapter 19, that, apart from some difference of expression, all the rest is Paul's. Why should all these things not outweigh any diversity of style? Why should we not infer from this that the Apostle deliberately changed his manner of writing somewhat? I would rather hold this than say, as some very learned men do, that he artfully disguised his style as he disguised his name. Especially since there were so many most weighty reasons for changing, set out a little earlier. And since no one of that Pauline age is named to whom this form of expression could more fittingly be ascribed, neither Luke, nor Clement, nor Barnabas, as has been shown at greater length.

units.la: IX. Quintò, τὸ πρῶτον τῷ ψευδῷ [?] est in assumptione, stylum toto genere esse diversum. Quod imprimis negandum esse arbitramur. Innumeris antè patuit exemplis, & voces, & phrases, & enunciationes integras, unius sæpissimè Pauli esse propriàs. Expendantur quæ suprà, Parte II. Capitibus I. II. III. IV. Nec deessent plura, apponere si vacaret. V. g. Cap. VI. 10. ἐπιλαθόμενοι τὸ ἔργον ὑμῶν, καὶ τὸν κόπον τῆς ἀγάπης. Planè sic 1. Thess. 1.3. μνημονεύοντες ὑμῶν τὸ ἔργον, καὶ τοῦ κόπου τῆς ἀγάπης. Iterum, eodem Capite VI. διακονοῦντες τοῖς ἁγίοις, καὶ διακονοῦντες. idem omninò Rom. XV. 25. διακονῶν τῆς ἁγίοις. 1. Cor. XVI, 15. εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς ἁγίοις. Præterea Epistolæ Cap. II.4. πνεύματι ἁγίῳ μερισμοῖς [?], nihil usitatius Paulo, quàm singulis τὸ Πνεῦμα μείζων, διαιρῶν, 1. Cor. XII.11. &c. Ita Capite XIV.1. τὴν ἀπερίαστον ἁμαρτίαν [?], vox Paulo usurpata, Tit. III,9. μάχας [?] Sed istiusmodi plenos modios jam antè exhibuimus. Itaq; hoc unum dici potest, gradu quodam gravitatis, & majestatis, distare ab Epistolis cæteris. Quæ discriminis ratio, præcipuè ab argumento, & majore jam studio Apostoli arcessenda. Unde etiam, ubi à sublimiori illâ materiâ, ad practica sub finem & moralia descendit, propiùs ad consuetam scribendi rationem accedit.
units.tr: IX. Fifthly, the first point of the false assumption is that the style is different in its whole kind. We think this must above all be denied. Countless examples have already been shown that words, phrases, and whole sentences are very often peculiar to Paul alone. Let those examples be weighed which were given above in Part II, chapters I, II, III, and IV, and more could be added if there were time. For instance, ch. VI.10: ἐπιλαθόμενοι τὸ ἔργον ὑμῶν καὶ τὸν κόπον τῆς ἀγάπης, just as in 1 Thess. 1.3: μνημονεύοντες ὑμῶν τὸ ἔργον καὶ τοῦ κόπου τῆς ἀγάπης. Again, in the same ch. VI: διακονοῦντες τοῖς ἁγίοις, and in Rom. XV.25 the very same: διακονῶν τοῖς ἁγίοις; 1 Cor. XVI.15: εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς ἁγίοις. Moreover, in ch. II.4 of this Epistle, πνεύματι ἁγίῳ μερισμοῖς: nothing is more usual with Paul than to distribute the Spirit to each, as in 1 Cor. XII.11, etc. So in ch. XIV.1: τὴν ἀπερίαστον ἁμαρτίαν, a word Paul uses in Titus III.9: μάχας. But we have already shown such full bushels before. So this one thing can be said: the Epistle differs from the others by a certain degree of gravity and majesty. The reason for this difference must be sought chiefly in the subject matter and in the Apostle's greater study. Hence also, where he descends from that loftier material to practical and moral matters near the end, he comes closer to his customary manner of writing.

units.la: X. Quod instant, phrasim nonnihil esse, quàm vulgò in Paulinis, ἑλληνικωτέραν[?], levissimum est. Paulum enim Græcè fuisse eloquentem, nec Græcæ venustatis nescium, quis negeat? Ipse in Græciâ natus, & inter Græcos toties conversatus. Imò Græcam linguam æquè aut magis familiarem habuisse, quàm Hebraicam vel Syriacam, non meis, sed magni Salmasij dicam verbis, de Hellenist. Part. 1. Quæst. vi. Quid ergò hîc insolens, de industriâ Paulum voluisse copiam & elegantiam Græci sermonis magis imitari? Et valeret demùm exceptio, si instar reliquorum ex Apostolis, nescivisset nisi Hebræorum aut Syrorum phrases verbis Græcis induere, aut Græca ad Hebræi sermonis formam inflectere. Præterea quot Hebraif-mi passim ubique dispersi? Plerique etiam
units.tr: X. As for their objection that the phrasing is somewhat more Hellenic [ἑλληνικωτέραν] than is common in the Pauline writings, it is very slight. For who would deny that Paul was eloquent in Greek, and not ignorant of Greek elegance? He was born in Greece and had so often lived among the Greeks. Indeed, to speak not in my own words but in those of the great Salmasius (On Hellenistic, part 1, question 6), he had the Greek language as familiar as, or more familiar than, Hebrew or Syriac. What is strange, then, in his deliberately wishing to imitate more closely the copiousness and elegance of the Greek language? The exception would hold only if, like the rest of the Apostles, he had not known how to clothe Hebrew or Syriac phrases in Greek words, or to bend Greek to the form of the Hebrew language. Moreover, how many Hebraisms are scattered everywhere? Many of them are

units.la: Paulo minime insolentes? Sive voces spe-ctamus, αἰῶνες, μεγαλωσύνη, συγκαλυμμὸς, ἁμαρτίαι, μάχαιρα, διχοτομῶν, &c. Sive constructionis modum, πρὸς τὰς ἀγγέλους. πρὸς τὸν ἡμῶν ὡς ἡμᾶς ἐκλέξατο. ἐν αὐτῇ νενομοθέτηται. παρῴκησεν εἰς τὴν γῆν. ὁμολογούντων τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ. εὐαρεστεῖ ὁ Θεὸς. ῥῆμα τῆς δυνάμεως. ὁ λόγος τῆς ἀκοῆς. καὶ ὁμοιότητα &c. Sive denique ellipses, enallagas, synechdochas, &c. He-bræis cum primis usitatas.
units.tr: not at all unusual in Paul. Whether we look at words, such as αἰῶνες, μεγαλωσύνη, συγκαλυμμός, ἁμαρτίαι, μάχαιρα, διχοτομῶν, and so on; or at the manner of construction, such as πρὸς τοὺς ἀγγέλους, πρὸς τὸν ἡμῶν, ὡς ἡμᾶς ἐξελέξατο, ἐν αὐτῇ νενομοθέτηται, παρῴκησεν εἰς τὴν γῆν, ὁμολογούντων τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ, εὐαρεστεῖ ὁ Θεός, ῥῆμα τῆς δυνάμεως, ὁ λόγος τῆς ἀκοῆς, καὶ ὁμοιότητα, and so on; or finally ellipses, enallages, synecdoches, and the like, which were especially common among the Hebrews.

units.la: XI. Instantia altera Cameronis, nul-lius omnino momenti est. Primò, de voce αἰῶνες, quæ occurrit Cap. 1. 3. xi. 3. Scilicet in Paulinis semper tempora, nunquam mundum, ut hoc in loco, denotare. Atqui 1. per συγχώρησιν dato, nos uni huic voci opponimus quamplures alias, Paulo soli usurpatas, atque frequentius nostro Au-thori adhibitas. 11. κατ' ἀρνησιν, negamus insuetam esse Paulo Apostolo, hoc etiam significatu, vocem. Vel uni huic loco in-sistimus, 1. Timoth. 1. 17. βασιλεῖ τῶν αἰώνων. Quid obstat, quo minùs mundi Regem, sive Dominû interpretemur? Quo magis hoc sensu Hebraei, רב העולמים, vel עולמים, רבון עולמים Dominus mundi. Arabes usitatiùs [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~5 letters] qui terras, ma- κύριος τῶν αἰώνων, re, sidera movet. Ne urgeam illud 1.Cor. 11.7. τῷ Τ αἰῶνων, quod minimè hanc si-gnificationem respuit, ut sit, πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. 111. Constat saltem vocis עולם & עולמים geminū esse usum apud Hebræos, ut & mundum notet & sæculum, & ipsa mundi corpora, & periodum corporum. Promiscuam acceptionem ne ipse Came-ro differetur. Quod cum ita sit, nihil mirum utroque sensu adhiberi Apostolo, ut alibi tempora, hic mundum designet. iv. Hinc etiam patet ἑβραΐζειν ipso in limine scriptorem, necadeo Graecam sectari e-loquentiam. Damus enim, non quidem in Paulinis, sed in Graecorum monumen-tis, nusquam eo sensu vocem illam reperi-ri, quo in hac Epistola. Etymologus αἰών, ἡ ζωὴ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὁ τῶν χιλίων ἐτῶν ἀριθμός. He-sychius, αἰών, ὁ βίος τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὁ τῆς ζωῆς χρόνος. Euripidi monente eodem, αἰών, ἡ ψυχή. Hyppocrati, αἰών, ὁ νωτιαῖος μυελός. Aliûs autem, πληθυντικῶς בלשון רבים, vix apud Græcos Scriptores. Vox in Chri-stianâ Ecclesiâ post Valentini portenta nimiũm nota. Nihilo opportunius alte-rum illud, quod Camero profert exem-plum, nunquam sc. dicturum fuisse Pau-lum, μήποτε [illegible, ~12 letters] μὲν, Hebr.ii.1. Egre-gie! An quia nova Scriptoribus sacris me-taphora est ? Atqui eadem illa perquàm familiaris. ii.Sam.xiv.14, futuri velut a-quæ diffluentes. Psalm.lviii.8, liquef-fiant sicut aqua. Christus in Evangelio, de utribus perruptis & vino effuso, sive diffluente, Matt.ix.17. An quia vox magis ad Græcam accedit elegantiam ? Sed & ipsi LXX. (notante etiã Camerone) eodem modo vertunt, Proverb.iii.21, ἐς μὴ πα-ῥῥησίᾳ[?]. An quia ab istiusmodi metaphoris abhorret Pauli genius? Imò in iis ferè to-tus est ; hinc Paulo doctrinæ vento agita-ri, currere, certare, stare, cadere, planta-re, rigare, parturire &c. Hinc similia illa à vasis testaceis, figulo, domo, fundamen-to, theatro, fermento, lacte, sigillo, arrhâ, aliisque pænè sine numero.
units.tr: XI. The second objection, that of Cameron, is of no weight at all. First, concerning the word αἰῶνες, which occurs in ch. 1.2 and 11.3. Clearly in the Pauline writings it always denotes times, never the world, as it does in this place. But (1) by way of concession, granting this, we set against this one word many others used by Paul alone, and used more often by our author. (2) By way of denial, we deny that the word is unusual for the Apostle Paul even in this sense. We rest on this one place, 1 Tim. 1.17: βασιλεῖ τῶν αἰώνων. What prevents us from interpreting it as "King of the world" or "Lord of the world"? All the more so because in this sense the Hebrews say rab ha'olamim, or olamim, ribbon olamim, "Lord of the world." The Arabs more commonly say, "who moves the lands, the sea, and the stars." Not to press that 1 Cor. 2.7, which by no means rejects this meaning, so that it means "before the foundation of the world" (πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου). (3) It is at least established that the word olam and olamim has a twofold use among the Hebrews: it denotes both the world and the age, both the bodies of the world themselves and the period of those bodies. Not even Cameron himself disputes this promiscuous meaning. Since this is so, it is no wonder that the word is applied to the Apostle in either sense: elsewhere it means times, here the world. (4) From this it also appears that the writer is Hebraizing from the very threshold, and is not pursuing Greek eloquence. For we grant that that word is found nowhere in that sense in which it is used in this Epistle, not in the Pauline writings, but in the monuments of the Greeks. The etymologist: aion is "the life of men," "the number of a thousand years." Hesychius: aion is "the life of men," "the time of life." Euripides, as the same source says, aion is "the soul." Hippocrates: aion is "the spinal marrow." Another use, in the plural in the manner of the Hebrew בלשון רבים, is hardly found among the Greek writers. The word, after the monstrosities of Valentinus, has become all too familiar in the Christian Church. Nothing more apt is the other example Cameron brings forward, that Paul would never have said μήποτε παραρρυῶμεν (Heb. 2.1). Excellent! Is it because the metaphor is new to the sacred writers? Yet that very metaphor is quite familiar: "fleeting like waters" (2 Sam. 14.14); "let them melt like water" (Ps. 58.8). Christ in the Gospel speaks of wineskins burst and wine poured out, or flowing away (Matt. 9.17). Is it because the word comes closer to Greek elegance? But the Seventy themselves, as Cameron also notes, translate in the same way at Prov. 3.21: μὴ παρρυῇ. Is it because Paul's genius shrinks from metaphors of this kind? On the contrary, it is almost wholly made of them. Hence Paul speaks of being tossed by the wind of doctrine, of running, striving, standing, falling, planting, watering, travailing, and so on. Hence come similar images drawn from earthen vessels, the potter, the house, the foundation, the theatre, leaven, milk, the seal, the earnest money, and almost countless others.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Aliorum ad objectionem eandem solutiones. Qui nonnisi materias Paulo tribuere. Stylum vero, Pauli amanuensi. Responsionis falsitas, & periculum. Qui phrasim volunt ex Hebraeo translatam. Ita Veterum & recentiorum pleriq;. Solutionis insufficientia. Non videri Epistola Hebraice esse scriptam. Salmasius notatus. Traditionis origo. Fundamenta illius eversa. Falsae Veterum hypotheses. Cur ad Hebraeos Graece scripserit? An Paulus Graece disertus? Argumentationes quaedam aliae. De Epistolae idiotismis Graecis. De voce διαθήκης [?]. Pareiatq; Erasmi exceptiones. De versione τῶν [?] LXX, usurpatâ. De aliis quibusdam. Bellarmini & aliorum instantiae diluuntur.
units.tr: Other solutions to the same objection. Some attribute only the matter to Paul. The style, however, belongs to Paul's amanuensis. The falsity and danger of the answer. Those who hold that the phrasing was translated from Hebrew. This is the view of most of the ancients and of many recent writers. The insufficiency of the solution. That the Epistle does not seem to have been written in Hebrew. Salmasius is noted. The origin of the tradition. Its foundations overturned. The false hypotheses of the ancients. Why did he write to the Hebrews in Greek? Was Paul eloquent in Greek? Certain other arguments. On the Greek idioms of the Epistle. On the word διαθήκη [?]. The exceptions of Erasmus are weighed. On the Septuagint version of τῶν [?], which is used. On certain other matters. The instances of Bellarmine and others are refuted.

units.la: I. His solutionibus, quae decisionem omnino faciunt neglectis, Veteres, plerique etiam recentiorum, respondendum aliter censuêre. Scilicet posse fieri, ut stylus non sit Pauli, Paulum tamen habeat Epistola authorem. Hi denuo in diversas classes abeunt. Voluntque alij, non ipsum Paulum scripsisse, sed materiam scribendi bendi alteri de suo sup peditasse. Atque ita verba, dictionem, stylum, notarij esse & amanuensis, doctrinam, sententias, argumentum ipsius Pauli. Alij vero & potissimi, paulum Hebraico & patrio sermone scripsisse Hebræis, quæ postmodùm Græco Interpres vestiverit. Hinc redolere magis Epistolam, stylum phrasimque Interpretis. Hi denùo de interpretationis modo diversum sentire videntur.
units.tr: I. These solutions, which entirely settle the question, have been neglected, and the ancients, and most of the more recent writers as well, have thought it right to answer otherwise. Namely, it may be that the style is not Paul's, and yet Paul is the author of the Epistle. These again divide into different classes. Some have wished that Paul did not himself write it, but that he supplied the matter of writing to another from his own store. And so the words, the diction and the style belong to the scribe and amanuensis, but the doctrine, the sentiments and the argument belong to Paul himself. Others, and the chief among them, hold that Paul wrote to the Hebrews in Hebrew, his native tongue, and that an interpreter afterwards clothed it in Greek. Hence the Epistle smells more of the style and phrasing of the interpreter. These again seem to differ among themselves on the manner of the translation.

units.la: Alijque, Interpretem diligenter ac fideliter in translatione fuisse versatum. Alij paulina expolivisse eum nonnihil, & proprio quasi ornasse, atque ordinasse sermone, ut loquitur Hieronymus.
units.tr: Others hold that the interpreter translated carefully and faithfully. Others that he polished it somewhat and, as it were, adorned it with his own style, and arranged it in his own language, as Jerome says.

units.la: II. Priorum antesignanus fuit Origenes, ipsissimo quem ante adduximus loco, parte 1. Cap. vi. Origeni accessere, nonnulli recentiorum. Estius in prologom. Cap. ii. Subjectum sive materia totius Epistolæ, simul & ordo, fuit à Paulo subministratus, sed compositio & ornatus est cujusdam alterius &c. Similiter Bellarminus, ex duabus jam solutionibus memoratis, hanc cum simpliciorem, tum expeditiorem esse putat, Lib. 1. C.xvii. Ex nostris placuisse eadem videtur Hyperio, doctissimo Commentatori, qui in prolo-gem.adEpistolam; quod Paulus uti solitus sit amanuensibus seu notariis, & sensum potius dictare, quàm orationem & verba contexere. Itaque, cùm non semper eodem amanuensi seu notario uti potuerit, nihil mirum si aliqua styli dissimilitudo in quibusdam Epistolis inveniatur. Hæc ille.
units.tr: II. The forerunner of the first group was Origen, in the very passage we quoted before, part 1, chap. vi. Several recent writers have joined Origen. Estius, in the prologue, chap. ii: The subject or matter of the whole Epistle, and also its order, was supplied by Paul, but the composition and ornament belong to someone else, etc. Similarly Bellarmine, who thinks that this solution is both simpler and more expeditious than the two already mentioned, Book 1, chap. xvii. Among our own people, Hyperius, a most learned commentator, seems to have agreed, who in the prologue to the Epistle says: that Paul was accustomed to use amanuenses or scribes, and to dictate the sense rather than to weave together the words. Therefore, since he could not always use the same amanuensis or scribe, it is no wonder if some dissimilarity of style is found in some Epistles. So he says.

units.la: III. Nodum verò tantùm abest ut expediant, ut contrà longè implicent magis imprudentes. 1. Peccant salsissimâ hypothesi, quasi Epistolæ ὁ χαρακτὴρ ἡ λέξις[?], à Paulo Apostolo abhorreat. Quod revicimus ita ac refiximus, ut vix sit exceptioni locus. 11. Affirmatur idem gratis, & nullo fundamento, nullâ sufficienti traditione. Hausit enim à se, non à majoribus Origenes, & privata quædam fuit audacissimi Patrum conjectura. Motâ enim rei difficultate, subjungit, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀποφαινόμενος[?] ἄπαξ ἄν, Ego verò declaraturus, dixero &c. Formula hominis in re dubia conjecturam suam aperientis. 111. Petitur τὴν λέξιν[?], Paulum suis in Epistolis, solitum dictare sensus, non verba. Quod Hyperio, præstantissimo Theologo, nobiscum aliàs de Authore sentienti, excidisse miramur. Sic enim vocibus sua authoritas, suum pondus, sua quædam perit ἐνέργεια[?]. Sic nullibi Pauli oratio est, sed quorundam forte amanuensium. Quum ne quidem ipse ille Tertus, Rom. xvi. 22, tam scripserit Epistolam, quàm juxtà Syrum Interpretem, descripserit. iv. Si Paulus dictavit, dubio procul etiam verba. Non enim res dictaverit sine verbis. Hæc ergò accuratissimè notarius exceperit, & credibilius Pauli expressisse voces, quàm novas de suo finxisse. v. Absurdum, & propè ad impietatem accedit quod habet Bellarminus, scribam hujusce Epistolæ, magis disertum fuisse, quàm ipse qui scribà Paulus utebatur. Cedo nobis illum amanuensem, tanto Apostolo, & inter omnes Scriptores Sacros, eloquentiæ laude conspicuo, disertiorem? vi. Vel γραμματεύς Scriba ille fuit, vel inferioris ordinis & authoritatis. Si posterius, quantum Epistolæ detrahitur? Quàm eloquij illa majestas deprimitur, infrà illa omnia quæ ipsimet Sacri amanuenses in chartas retulêre? Si prius, quis ille quæso? Lucam enim fuisse, nec probari ulla ratione potest, nec ipsa styli ratio suadet. De Clemen-te, fabula est suprà rejecta, nec ille unquam ἰόπνυως[?]. Et sic fingitur Spiritum Sanctum partitum esse operas, illi materias, huic voces suggerendo. vii. Multum omninò interereat, in tanti momenti Epistolâ, ut à primario ipso Apostolo, totius orationis contextus adornaretur. In verbis enim, & in scriptionis modo, quantùm efficaciæ? quantùm roboris? Unde & ipsemet scripsisse Author videri voluit, & in primâ de se persona, iisdem etiam quibus alias Paulus verbis, in Epistolâ loquitur a liquoties.
units.tr: III. But these knots are so far from being untied that, on the contrary, they entangle the unwary even more. 1. They err with a very insipid hypothesis, as if the character and style of the Epistle were unworthy of the Apostle Paul. We have refuted and overturned this so thoroughly that there is hardly room for objection. 2. The same thing is asserted without cause, on no foundation and with no sufficient tradition. For Origen drew it from himself, not from his predecessors, and it was a private conjecture of the most daring of the Fathers. For, the difficulty of the matter having been raised, he adds: "But I, declaring, would say once", and so on: the formula of a man revealing his conjecture in a doubtful matter. 3. It is assumed that Paul, in his Epistles, was accustomed to dictate the sense and not the words. We are surprised that Hyperius, a most outstanding theologian who otherwise agrees with us about the author, let this slip. For in this way the authority, the weight and a certain energy of the words perish. Thus Paul's discourse is nowhere his own, but perhaps that of some amanuenses. Not even that Tertius himself, Rom. xvi. 22, wrote the Epistle, but, according to the Syriac interpreter, he only copied it out. 4. If Paul dictated, then undoubtedly he dictated the words too. For he would not have dictated things without words. The most careful scribe would have taken these down, and it is more credible that he expressed Paul's own words than that he invented new ones of his own. 5. Absurd, and nearly bordering on impiety, is what Bellarmine says: that the scribe of this Epistle was more eloquent than the one Paul himself used. Let me have that amanuensis, more eloquent than so great an Apostle, who is conspicuous among all the sacred writers for the praise of eloquence! 6. That scribe was either a γραμματεύς, a scribe of the first rank, or of inferior order and authority. If the latter, how much is taken away from the Epistle? How is that majesty of eloquence lowered, beneath all those things which the sacred amanuenses themselves committed to paper? If the former, who, I ask, was he? For that it was Luke can be proved by no reason, and the style itself does not suggest it. As for Clement, it is a fable already rejected above, and he was never [the writer]. And so it is pretended that the Holy Spirit divided the work, supplying the matters to one and the words to another. 7. In an Epistle of such moment it matters greatly that the whole texture of the discourse should be fashioned by the chief Apostle himself. For how much efficacy, how much strength lies in the words and in the manner of writing! Whence the author himself wished to seem to have written it, and speaks in the Epistle in the first person, often with the very words with which Paul speaks of himself elsewhere.

units.la: IV. Atque hinc accidit, ut recentiorum pars maxima, Veteres imitata, discrimen omne ab interpretatione derivarit. Et ad istam, ut sacram anchoram, in hac controversiâ confugerit. Neminí debere esse mirum, si Paulus aliter Hebrai-cè, quàm Græce scripsit. Si etiam Inter-preti, (quisquis fuit ille Deorum) suus in ververtendo fuit genius singularis. propen[?]dit in hanc sententiam, tota ferè antiqui-tas. Clemens Alexandrinus Lucæ, Eu-sebius Clementi, interpretationis hasce tribuere partes. Hieronymus favet eidem Clementi, & de Paulo, eloquenter scrip-sisse in Hebraeo, ut eadem eloquentius ver-terentur in Græcum. Subscribit Theodo-retus, Argum. Epistolae, ἐρμηνείαν δὲ τῆς Ἑβραίων φωνῆς[?], ἣν φασὶ μεταχειρισάμενον τὸν Κλήμεν[?]ma. Accedunt, Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus, Ambrosius, Primasius, Haymo, & quotquot Veterum in Epistolas scripsêre, quorum longum foret reponere verba. Certatim huc confluunt neoterici scriptores. Baronius, solo hoc responso, egregiè se defunctum arbitra-tur, ad A.C.LX, Num.XLV. Nec improbat Bellarminus, citato loco de Verbo Dei L.1.C.XVII. prolixè Ribera proœm.in Epist. Et ne de plerisque pontificiorum dicam, suffragio solutionem suo muni-unt, Zanchius, Tract.de Script.S. Tomo VIII. Hyperius, prolegom.in Epist. Tossa-nus, similiter in proœmio, aliique bene multi, multi, quos vel consulere vel allegare pi-get. Sed minimè præteriri debet Illustris Salmasius, de Hellenisticâ, parte I. Sic Epistola Pauli ad Hebræos, Hebraico, id est sermone tunc in Syriâ usitato, scripta fuit, & ab alio versa, quem quidam Clementem fuisse volunt, alii alium.
units.tr: IV. And hence it happens that the greater part of the more recent writers, imitating the ancients, have derived the whole difference from the translation, and in this controversy have taken refuge in it as in a sacred anchor. No one should be surprised if Paul wrote differently in Hebrew than in Greek. Nor, if the translator (whoever that god-like man was) had his own unique genius in translating. Almost all antiquity inclines to this opinion. Clement of Alexandria assigns these parts of interpretation to Luke, Eusebius to Clement. Jerome favours the same Clement, and says of Paul that he wrote eloquently in Hebrew, so that the same things might be translated more eloquently into Greek. Theodoret agrees in the Argument of the Epistle: the translation of the Hebrew language, which they say Clement handled. Add Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Theophylact, Ambrose, Primasius, Haymo, and as many of the ancients as wrote on the Epistles, whose words it would be tedious to repeat. Recent writers flock here eagerly. Baronius, by this answer alone, thinks himself to have dealt with the matter excellently, at A.D. 60, no. 45. Bellarmine does not disapprove, in the place cited on the Word of God, Book 1, chap. xvii. Ribera at length, in the proem to the Epistle. And not to mention most of the Papists, they support this solution with their vote: Zanchius, Treatise on Holy Scripture, Vol. VIII; Hyperius, prolegomena to the Epistle; Tossanus, likewise in his preface; and many others, whom it would be tedious either to consult or to cite. But the illustrious Salmasius must by no means be passed over, in De Hellenistica, part I: Thus the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews was written in Hebrew, that is, in the language then used in Syria, and was translated by another, whom some wish to be Clement, others someone else.

units.la: V. Certum omninò est, si Veterum statuas authoritate, & antiquitatis referamus archiva, ut loquitur Tertullianus, scripsisse Hebraicè paulum. Modò, quod illi tradidêre, cœco quodam suscipiamus assensu. Et illorum fortè reverentiâ præstaret [illegible, ~6 letters], remque in medio relinquere. Licebit interim nobis, quod jam antè gravissimis viris, vertere idipsum modestius in controversiam. Et rationibus ostendere variis, iisque solidis, & invictis, minimè tollendo scrupulo appositam esse solutionem. Primò, quia certum & indubitatum, Græcâ nonnunquàm elegantiâ, & dictionis sæpè copiâ, recedere ab Hebræorum Syrorumque idiotismo Epistolâ. Non characterem esse [illegible, ~9 letters], quo de verbo ad verbum dicitur facta translatio. Neque in eo aberrabat Origenes, esse Epistolam συνθέσιν τῆς λέξεως ἑλληνικωτάτην. Exempla proferre nihil attinet, contextus quando loquitur universus. Jam autem, docente alibi ipso Salmasio, hoc interest discrimi-nis inter libros sacros Græcè scriptos, & translatos, quod in Græcè scriptis purior Græcus, in translatis ubique τῇ ἑρμηνείᾳ ἰδιάζων. Quod varie idem probat, atque illustrat. Et ante Salmasium, observavit jam olim Hieronymus, & res ipsa loquitur. Fatetur idé ille solo translationis nomine, Matthæi Evangelium, Epistolas Petri, Jacobi, Johannis, longè frequentioribus scatere Syriasmis, quam Epistolas Pauli. Quo ipso suo se gladio confodit Vir Illustris, illamque ad Hebræos, ex translatarum numero vult exemptam. Siquidem hæc non solùm non frequentiores admittit Syriasmos, quàm Pauli reliquæ, sed rariores, parcioresque. Stylusq; nihil minùs sit quàm ἰδιωτισμὸς, sive ubique τῇ ἑρμηνείᾳ ἰδιάζων.
units.tr: V. It is certain beyond doubt, if we set up the authority of the ancients and appeal to the archives of antiquity, as Tertullian says, that Paul wrote in Hebrew. Only, we should not accept with blind assent what they handed down. Perhaps out of reverence for them it would be better [illegible] and to leave the matter open. Meanwhile it will be permitted us, as weightier men have done before us, to turn this very question into a more modest controversy, and to show by various reasons, solid and unconquerable, that the solution is by no means free of difficulty. First, because it is certain and undoubted that the Epistle sometimes departs, with Greek elegance and often with abundance of expression, from the idiom of the Hebrews and Syrians. It is not the mark of a translation made word for word. Nor was Origen wrong in saying that the Epistle is of a most purely Greek composition. It is pointless to bring examples when the whole context speaks. Now, as Salmasius himself teaches elsewhere, this is the difference between sacred books written in Greek and those translated: in books written in Greek the Greek is purer, in translated ones it is everywhere peculiar to the translation [τῇ ἑρμηνείᾳ ἰδιάζων]. He proves and illustrates this in various ways. And before Salmasius, Jerome had long ago observed it, and the thing itself speaks. Jerome himself admits, by the name of translation alone, that the Gospel of Matthew and the Epistles of Peter, James and John abound with Syriasms far more frequent than the Epistles of Paul. By this very sword the Illustrious Man stabs himself, wishing this Epistle to the Hebrews to be removed from the number of translations. For this Epistle not only does not admit more frequent Syriasms than Paul's other letters, but fewer and sparser ones. And its style is anything but idiom [ἰδιωτισμὸς], or everywhere peculiar to the translation.

units.la: VI. Secundò, observandum ab uno ferè Clemente Alexandr. omnem illam manare traditionem. Nam quod illè do Lucâ interprete, postmodum alij de Clemente dixêre. Et ut illius fundamentum omne, erat affinitas quædam phraseos cum Actis Apostolorum; ita horum, cum Epistolâ Clementis. Hinc quod ἑρμηνευτὴς[?] ille, de translatione, à quo non admodùm aberat sententia Origenis, postmodùm Eusebius; quod Eusebius, deinceps, ut ferè consuevit, Hieronymus; quod Clemens, Origenes, Eusebius, Hieronymus, reliqui Græcorum Latinorumque. Imprimis, quum urgerent alij illam styli diversitatem, neque solutio compendiosior occurreret. Unde, quotquot postmodùm, Epistolam ex Hebræo versam esse contenderunt, soliti nonnisi à Clemente Alexandrino, vel, Eusebio, vel Origene, ut Baronius inter cæteros & Bellarminus, sententiam arcessere suam.
units.tr: VI. Secondly, it should be observed that almost the whole of this tradition flows from one author, Clement of Alexandria. What Clement said about Luke as translator was afterwards repeated by others about Clement himself. Just as the whole basis of that view was a certain affinity of phrasing with the Acts of the Apostles, so the basis of this one was the affinity with the Epistle of Clement. Hence the view of that interpreter about translation, from which the opinion of Origen was not far removed, was afterwards held by Eusebius; what Eusebius held was then, as he usually did, followed by Jerome; and what Clement, Origen, Eusebius and Jerome held was accepted by the rest of the Greeks and Latins.
