This happened especially because others pressed the difference of style, and no shorter answer came to mind. So whoever afterwards contended that the Epistle was translated from Hebrew was accustomed to draw their opinion from no one but Clement of Alexandria, or Eusebius, or Origen, as Baronius among others and Bellarmine did.

units.la: VII. Tertiò, ne reponam τῷ Στρωματέως nimiâ sæpè sive in fingendo, sive in affirmando, facilitatem, cujusque alibi dedimus exempla, ratio illius pro Lucâ interprete levissima fuit. Scilicet, eundem esse orationis filum, τὴν αὐτὴν χρῶτα [?] τῆς ἑρμηνείαν, Epistolæ, & Historiæ à Lucâ contextæ. Primò enim falsa hæc fuit hypothesis. Lucæ oratio longè facilior, simplicior, ἰδιωτικωτέρα, quanquam Hieronymo, sæcularem redolens eloquentiam, ad Cap. vi. Esaiæ. Diffusa minùs, minùs assurgens, nihilque illius habens sublimitatis. Locutionibus etiàm nonnunquam Romanis distincta, nec eádem ratione, qua sæpè nostra, Hebraizans. Prodet sese illicò magnitudo discriminis, initium Actorum, cum Epistolæ limine conferenti. Deinde, per concessionem dato, illa ipsa affinitas orationis, obstat interpretationi. Non potest enim non differre toto genere dictio Græca, Græcè docti hominis, ab ea dictione quæ ex Hebræo aut Syro fideliter expressa est. Quæ differentia cum nulla ratione intercedat, inter Græcum Lucæ & Epistolæ contextum, eo ipso translationis suspicio evanescit. Idem de Clementis translatione dici debet. Non enim alio vel Eusebius, vel Hieronymus, vel Oecumenius &c. nixi fundamento, nisi quod ad Hebræos Epistola, τότε σῴζειν τὸν χαρακτῆρα[?]. Atqui Clemens, sua Græcè conceperat, stylo etiam diffuso & eleganti, ut hodieque intelligimus. Cui si affinis & perquàm similis nostræ characterî Epistolæ, quî illa, ex Hebræo ad verbum translata esse possit?
units.tr: VII. Thirdly, not to charge the Stromateus with his excessive readiness, both in inventing and in asserting, of which I have given examples elsewhere, his reason for Luke as translator was very flimsy. Namely, that the thread of the speech, the same colour of the interpretation [τὴν αὐτὴν χρῶτα τῆς ἑρμηνείαν], is the same in the Epistle as in the History woven by Luke. For first, this hypothesis was false. The style of Luke is much easier, simpler and more plain [ἰδιωτικωτέρα], although Jerome, in his comment on Isaiah chapter 6, found in it a smell of secular eloquence. It is less diffuse, rises less high, and has nothing of that sublimity. It is also marked in places by Roman expressions, and not in the same way as our Epistle, which often Hebraizes. The size of the difference will be obvious at once to anyone who compares the opening of Acts with the threshold of the Epistle. Next, even granting the point, that very affinity of style stands in the way of translation. For Greek diction from a man learned in Greek cannot but differ in its whole character from diction faithfully rendered from Hebrew or Syriac. Since no such difference exists between the Greek of Luke and the text of the Epistle, the suspicion of translation vanishes on that very ground. The same must be said of Clement's translation. For Eusebius, or Jerome, or Oecumenius, and the rest, rested on no other foundation than that the Epistle to the Hebrews preserved the character [τότε σῴζειν τὸν χαρακτῆρα]. Yet Clement had composed his own works in Greek, in a style also diffuse and elegant, as we understand even today. If the Epistle is akin to, and very like, the character of our author, how could it have been translated word for word from Hebrew?

units.la: VIII. Quartò, fuit & alia Clementis Alex. Eusebÿ, Hieronymi, aliorumque ratio: quod data esset Epistola Hebræis, & quidem ab Hebræo. Ergò scripsisse Hebraicè, τῇ πατρίῳ γλώττῃ. Hanc enim perpetuò rationem annectunt, ut locis suprà ex iisdem allegatis. Sed fefellit illa sanctissimos viros. 1. Quia spectabat Epistola fideles omnes Hebræorum, non Hierosolymitanos, non Palæstinos solos. Saltem cum aliis fuisse à Palæstinis communican-dam, demonstratum. Data enim in communi ἐθνῶς Ἑβραίας[?], quo veniebat nomine dispersa illa natio, oppositè ad τὰ ἔθνη. Quemadmodum in religionis negotio Ἰουδαῖοι, oppositè ad Ἕλληνας, ut prolixè Hellenisticariorum nostri ævi flagellum. Jam verò agentibus extrà Palæstinæ limites Hebræis, nativa plerumque & usitatior lingua, fuit Græca. Qua, totus Oriens loquebatur, ut monet Hieronymus, Prooemio sui in Epist. ad Galatas Commentarij, Tomo vi. Id est ipsam extrà Græciam, Syri, Ægyptij, Asiæ minoris populi, imò Persæ & Indi. Ab eo tempore, quo Alexander Macedo, Seleucidæ, & Ptolomæi, latè fuerant in Oriente dominati. ii. Ne ipsi Palæstini, Græcè tum erant nescij, imprimis qui alicujus notæ. Quod patet tum ex Josepho Historico, Hierosolymorum sacerdote; tum ex iis Græcè qui scripserunt Apostolis; quin ex inscriptione ipsâ Pilati Græca. Etiā ex communiori usu linguæ, illis temporibus, & innumerâ Judæorū quotannis Hierosolymas ex Græciâ & Oriente frequentantium, turba. iii. Utut Hebræis inscripta, communis tamen esse debuit omnibus Gentibus, & illius usus ad Græcorum tum etiam Ecclesias extendi. Et in Canonem cum reliquis referendam esse intelligebat Apostolus.
units.tr: VIII. Fourthly, there was another reason, given by Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, Jerome and others: that the Epistle was sent to the Hebrews, and indeed by a Hebrew. Therefore he must have written in Hebrew, in the native tongue [τῇ πατρίῳ γλώττῃ]. For they always attach this reason, as in the passages cited above from the same authors. But that reason deceived those most holy men. First, because the Epistle was addressed to all the faithful Hebrews, not to the Jerusalemites or the Palestinians alone. At least it has been shown that it was to be shared with others beyond Palestine. For it was addressed in common to the Hebrew nation [ἔθνος Ἑβραίων], which was the name for that scattered people, set over against the Gentiles [τὰ ἔθνη]. Just as in matters of religion the Jews [Ἰουδαῖοι] are set over against the Greeks [Ἕλληνας], as the lengthy scourge of the Hellenists of our own age shows. Now, when Hebrews lived outside the borders of Palestine, their native and more customary language was mostly Greek. Of this language, the whole East spoke, as Jerome warns in the preface to his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, Volume vi. That is, outside Greece itself, the peoples of Syria, Egypt and Asia Minor, and even Persia and India. This was so from the time when Alexander of Macedon, and the Seleucids and Ptolemies, had widely ruled in the East. Second, the Palestinians themselves were not ignorant of Greek at that time, especially those of any standing. This is clear both from Josephus the historian, a priest of Jerusalem, and from those who wrote Greek to the Apostles; indeed from the Greek inscription of Pilate himself. It is also clear from the more common use of the language in those times, and from the countless crowd of Jews who visited Jerusalem every year from Greece and the East. Third, although it was addressed to the Hebrews, it ought nonetheless to have been common to all the Gentiles, and its use was extended to the Greek churches of that time as well. And the Apostle understood that it was to be counted in the canon together with the others.

units.la: iv. Ad Hebræos etiam Petrus, etiam Jacobus, etiam Johannes scripserunt. Græcè tamen, quando Hebraicè extitisse unquam quam Epistolas, minimè constat. Quic-quid Salmasius de versione sentiat, in Commentario de Hellenistica.v. Si ideò Hebraicè, quoniam ad Hebræos, pari ratione inferri debet, Latinè scripsisse alias Paulum, quia ad Romanos. Patrius enim hic non minùs sermo Romanis, quàm Hebraeis Hebraeus. Quum autem & istos & omnes alios Paulus Græco, id est, suo idiomate, eoq; notissimo, & communi orbi universo, convenerit, nihil mirum si & eodem, Hebræorum Ecclesias. Quod enim attinet illam ad Romanos, explodimus Glossatorem Gratiani, Dist. ix. Cap. Ut Veterum: Totum enim Novum Testamentum scriptum est Græcè, praeter Evangelium Matthæi, & Epistolam Pauli ad Romanos, quæ est Latinè scripta.
units.tr: iv. Peter, James and John also wrote to the Hebrews. Yet it is by no means certain that they wrote in Greek, if they ever wrote Hebrew epistles at all. Whatever Salmasius thinks about the version, in his Commentary on the Hellenistic dialect. v. If therefore it must be inferred that the Epistle was written in Hebrew because it was addressed to Hebrews, by the same reasoning it must be inferred that Paul wrote in Latin elsewhere, because he wrote to the Romans. For Latin is no less the native speech of the Romans than Hebrew is of the Hebrews. Since, however, Paul addressed both them and all others in Greek, that is, in his own idiom, which was very well known and common to the whole world, it is no wonder if he did the same for the churches of the Hebrews. As for the claim about the letter to the Romans, we reject the gloss of Gratian, Dist. ix, chapter Ut Veterum: "For the whole New Testament was written in Greek, except the Gospel of Matthew and the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, which was written in Latin."

units.la: IX. Quinto, peccarunt etiam illi Veteres falsa alia hypothesi, scilicet Paulum Hebraice, quàm Græce fuisse eloquentiorem. Quod patet ex Hieronymo in Paulo, Scripserat Hebræus Hebraicè, i.e. suo eloquio disertissimè. Alibi passim imperitiam Græci sermonis, & solœcismos, ipsi impinproficiscerentur hierosolymas , non stringit. Nam & multi non migrabant; alij etiam ad breve tempus , nec nisi solemnitatum gratiâ ; suo etiam inter sese quique idiomate, aut communi omnibus Græco, uti poterant.
units.tr: IX. Fifthly, those ancients also erred by another false hypothesis, namely that Paul was more eloquent in Hebrew than in Greek. This is clear from Jerome on Paul: the Hebrew had written in Hebrew, that is, most eloquently in his own speech. Elsewhere, throughout, he does not censure the lack of skill in Greek speech or the solecisms, which ... proceeded to Jerusalem. For many did not migrate; others went for only a short time, and only for the sake of the festivals; and each could use among themselves either his own idiom or the Greek common to all.

units.la: X. Septimò, qui fit ut Veterum nemo de textu hebræo, testatus sit? Ut nemini vel lectum, vel etiam oculis sciamus usurpatum? Ubi latitavit ille thesaurus, non visus toti antiquitati? An verisimile fide-les hebræorum, in sacris asservandis tam religiosos tamque sollicitos, facilè adeò hunc sibi excidere passos? Non plures descriptos fuisse codices? Non inter hebræos variè fuisse distractos? Aut jactura istius fuisse nullam in primitiva Ecclesia memoriam? Quæ enim hodie sive Syriacè feguntur, sive hebraicè, edente Munstero, ex Græco translata esse constat. Pro-babilius longè de Matthæo credebant Veteres, hebraicè Evangelium concinnasse suum. Prostabat enim, & usurpabatur jam antiquitus, nec ea plerorumque erat industria, & peritia linguæ, ut eo ad Grægræcos codices exacto, discrimen deprehenderent, vel fraudem, siquę esset, subolerent.
units.tr: X. Seventhly, how is it that none of the Ancients has testified to a Hebrew text? That no one, so far as we know, has read it or even used it with their eyes? Where did that treasure lie hidden, unseen by all of antiquity? Is it likely that the faithful Hebrews, so religious and so careful in preserving sacred writings, would so easily have let it slip from them? Were not many copies made? Were they not variously dispersed among the Hebrews? Or was there no memory of its loss in the primitive Church? For the texts that are today circulated, whether in Syriac or in Hebrew, in the edition of Münster, are known to have been translated from Greek. The Ancients believed far more probably that Matthew had composed his Gospel in Hebrew. For it was extant and in use already from antiquity, nor was the diligence and skill in languages of most people such that, by comparing it with Greek manuscripts, they could detect a difference or sniff out a fraud, if there were one.

units.la: XI. Octavo, de Matthæi Evangelio quod objicitur diversa res est. An verè, an falsò hebraice illum scripsisse putarit antiquitas, non disputamus. Sed posito, traditioni nihil subesse fraudis, aut nimiæ in credendo facilitatis, dispar Epistolæ nostræ ratio. Nam longe plures, etiam vetustiores, inde à Papiâ, & Irenæo, istud de Matthæo proditum reliquêre. Præterea in Judæâ, imò hierosolymis conscriptum Evangelium, referente in suâ Synopsi Athanasio, ibidemque Ecclesiæ commissum. De Matthæo etiam dici posset, nescivisse græca, saltem minùs fuisse in scribendo expeditum. Nec abhorret illius phrasis à charactere ἑρμηνευτικῷ & translato. horum nihil, nec de Paulo, nec de Epistola ad hebræos affirmari potest. Adeóque ex traditionis de Matthæi Evangelio veritate ( suppositá jam ea & concessa ) alterius illius, de hebraice scripta Epistola, certitudo inferri nequit.
units.tr: XI. Eighthly, the objection concerning the Gospel of Matthew is a different matter. Whether antiquity rightly or wrongly thought he wrote in Hebrew, we do not dispute. But granting that the tradition contains no fraud and no excessive readiness to believe, our Epistle's case is unlike. For far more writers, and even earlier ones, from Papias and Irenaeus onward, handed down that report about Matthew. Moreover, the Gospel was written in Judea, indeed in Jerusalem, as Athanasius reports in his Synopsis, and was there entrusted to the Church. One could also say of Matthew that he did not know Greek, or at least was less skilled in writing it. Nor does his style shrink from the character of an interpreter and a translation. None of these things can be affirmed of Paul, nor of the Epistle to the Hebrews. And so from the truth of the tradition about the Gospel of Matthew (now supposed and granted), the certainty of that other claim, that the Epistle was written in Hebrew, cannot be inferred.

units.la: XII. Nonò, decretorium ferè argumentum est, à Græcorum idiotismis, hac in Epistola passim conspicuis. Pauca hæc de multis. Author Capite v. versu 8. elegante adhibet μεταφονομασίαν[?]. Scil. ἔμαξε ἀφ' ὧν ἐπαξε[?], qualem Hebraismus non ferebat. Græci contrà mirè sibi in talibus placent, ἀμφίπολιν ὑμετέραν πόλιν. Μιμήσεταί μᾶλλον ἢ μιμήσονται &c. passim utitur metaphoris, & phrasiologiis à Græcis mutuatis. Sic ἐπιτρίζεσθαι[?]. ἔχειν τὸν ἀγῶνα. ὄγκον ἀπολαύειν[?], ἀληθῆς πεπληρωμάτων[?], &c. Sed ante omnia notanda vox διαθήκης, & διατίθεσθαι, testamenti, & testandi significatu, Capite ix, 16. 17. Calvinus, hæc una ratio sani judicij hominibus, sufficiet ad probandum quod dixi, Græco sermone scriptam fuisse Epistolam. Optimo sanè jure. Neque enim בְּרִית[?] Hebræorum, unquam ultrà pacti & fœderis extenditur significationem. Nó Onkelos, non Jonathan, nó Hebræi, de Testamento unquam interpretati. Quin Rabbini, animadverso idiotismo, ex Græcâ formarunt vocem דִּיתִיק[?]. Ex oppositio, διαθήκην, & διαθέσθαι, sensu Apostoli apud Græcos frefrequentius. Apud Suidam, διαθήκην διατίθεσθαι condere testamentum. Διαθέσθαι, pro διαθήκην γράφειν, scribere testamentum. Vel διαπίθεσθαι, διαθήκην ποιεῖν, facere testamentum. Sic διαθήκης τῆς τελευτηκότως, testamentum defuncti. Sic διαθήκης ἐπιθυμία, testandi cupiditas. Sic διαθέσθαι τὰ ἑαυτοῦ, testari, disponere de suis. Galli, disposer de ses biens. Hinc διαθήκη, ut pro testamento, sic pro hæreditate quæ ex testamento obvenit, apud Budæum. Glossaria omnia Græcorum revolvere non est nostri instituti. Et hinc saltem liquet vis argumenti, à Græcorum illo idiotismo.
units.tr: XII. Ninthly, the argument from the Greek idioms, which appear everywhere in this Epistle, is almost decisive. A few examples out of many. The author, in chapter 5, verse 8, uses an elegant metaphonymy [μεταφονομασία], ἔμαξε ἀφ' ὧν ἔπαξε, which Hebraism would not allow. The Greeks, on the other hand, take wonderful pleasure in such things, ἀμφίπολιν ὑμετέραν πόλιν, μιμήσεταί μᾶλλον ἢ μιμήσονται, and so on. He uses throughout metaphors and phraseology borrowed from the Greeks, such as ἐπιτρίζεσθαι, ἔχειν τὸν ἀγῶνα, ὄγκον ἀπολαύειν, ἀληθῆς πεπληρωμάτων, and so on. But above all the word διαθήκης, and διατίθεσθαι, in the sense of testament and to make a testament, must be noted, in chapter 9, verses 16 and 17. Calvin: "This one reason will be enough for men of sound judgement to prove what I have said, that the Epistle was written in Greek." Most rightly so. For the Hebrew בְּרִית never extends its meaning beyond pact and covenant. Neither Onkelos nor Jonathan nor the Hebrews ever interpreted it as a testament. Indeed the rabbis, noticing the idiom, formed the word דִּיתִיק from the Greek. On the contrary, διαθήκη and διατίθεσθαι in the Apostle's sense are very frequent among the Greeks. In Suidas: διαθήκην διατίθεσθαι, to make a will; διατίθεσθαι, for διαθήκην γράφειν, to write a will; or διαθήκην ποιεῖν, to make a will. So διαθήκης τῆς τελευτηκότως, the will of the deceased; so διαθήκης ἐπιθυμία, the desire to make a will; so διατίθεσθαι τὰ ἑαυτοῦ, to make a will, to dispose of one's own affairs. The French say disposer de ses biens. Hence διαθήκη, as well as meaning a testament, means an inheritance which comes by will, in Budaeus. It is not my purpose to go through all the Greek glossaries. From this at least the force of the argument from that Greek idiom is clear.

units.la: XII. Excipiunt, eos inter ex decessoribus nostris summus Theologus, D. Pa-ræus, Græcos interpretes similiter usos voce διαθήκης. Et tamen eâ expressisse ברית Hebraeorum. Adeoque non firmiter satis eâ voce colligi, non esse Epistolam ex Hebræo translatam. Imò verò infirma admodum ista consequentia est. Siquidem Græcis interpretibus διαθήκη, idem est quod συνθήκη, pactum, fœdus, conventio. Et voce utraque promiscuè, hebraHebræam ברית reddidêre. prout διαθήκη etiam Græcis pro pacto usurpatur, idem sæpe quod συνθήκη, ἐπαγγελία, συνωμοσία. Ergò Apostolus, ut ad hanc sæpius alludit significationem, sic speciatim ad priorem illam, quâ pollebat ipse in docendo authoritate. Ad quam non respexisse putem LXX Interpretes.
units.tr: XII. Among our predecessors, the most distinguished theologian, D. Pareus, makes an exception for them: the Greek translators likewise used the word διαθήκη [diathēkē], yet they rendered by it the Hebrew בְּרִית [berith]. Therefore, he says, it cannot be sufficiently firmly inferred from that word that the Epistle was not translated from Hebrew. But this inference is in fact very weak. For among the Greek translators διαθήκη means the same as συνθήκη [synthēkē], a pact, covenant, or agreement. They rendered the Hebrew בְּרִית [berith] by either word indiscriminately. Likewise, among the Greeks διαθήκη is also used for a pact, and often means the same as συνθήκη [synthēkē], ἐπαγγελία [epangelia], or συνωμοσία [synōmosia]. So the Apostle, as he often alludes to this meaning, alludes in particular to that earlier sense in which he himself held authority in teaching. I do not think the Seventy translators had this sense in view.

units.la: XIV. Nihilo gravior Erasmi excep-tio est, hinc non videri Epistolam esse Pauli. Siquidem Author temere transeat à pacto, de quo in Lege sermo, ad Testamentum. Hinc apparare Epistolam scriptam ab eo qui Hebraice nesciverit, Annot. ad locum. Sed 1. falsa est hypothesis, nus-quam hoc sensu vocem apud Paulum occurrere. Non observavit ille parallelum locum, Gal. III. 15, ἀνθρώπου κεκυρωμένην δια-θήκην οὐδεὶς ἀθετεῖ, ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεται. Scilicet, hominis confirmatum morte testamentum, neminem rescindere, aut illi super addere. Pactum, etiam confirmatum, consensu mutuo rescindi & mutari potest. Nec pactum unius dicitur hominis, sed plurium inter se pacisccentium. Unde & Syrus, animadversa Græcæ vocis proprietate, retinuit בְּרִית[?]. Et Græi omninò vocant διαθήκην κεκυρωμένην[?], vel etiam ἄκυρον, testamentum ratum, aut irritum. II. Re-torquemus ergo, & illa ipsa vocis acce-ptione, Paulus sese prodit. Nec ista ratio-cinatio alius quam Pauli esse potuit. In qua si erratum, non jam authorem sed authoritatem, Erasmus revocat in dubium. III. Absit etiam, ut linguæ sanctæ id fa-ctum fuerit ignorantiâ. Quum alibi idem Author, ubi reddit Hieremiæ vaticinium, & בְּרִית[?], pro fœdere & conventione usurpet vocem. Hoc ergo voluit, revera illud Dei fœdus, quod tale est ratione formæ fœderalis, & mediationis inter partes dissitas, etiam induere formam testamen-ti. Quatenus largitio est hæreditatis, ratâ morte & sanguine Christi largientis. Et jam alludit ad alterum illum vocis διαθήκης inter Græcos significatum, vocemque in omnem quasi partem versat & rapit. ut stet immotum nostrum hoc argumentum.
units.tr: XIV. Erasmus's objection is no less weak, that it does not seem that the Epistle is Paul's, because the author rashly passes from the "pact" spoken of in the Law to the "Testament." Hence, in his notes on the passage, he says the Epistle was written by someone who did not know Hebrew. But, first, the premise is false: the word never occurs in Paul in this sense. He did not notice the parallel passage in Gal. 3:15, where it says: ἀνθρώπου κεκυρωμένην διαθήκην οὐδεὶς ἀθετεῖ, ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεται [anthrōpou kekyrōmenēn diathēkēn oudeis athetei, ē epidiatassetai], that is, "no one sets aside or adds to a man's covenant once it has been ratified by death," that is, a testament. A pact, even one that has been ratified, can be annulled and changed by mutual consent. Nor is a pact called the pact of one man, but of several parties agreeing among themselves. Hence the Syriac also, noting the proper force of the Greek word, retained the word berith. And the Greeks in general call a διαθήκη κεκυρωμένη [diathēkē kekyrōmenē], or even ἄκυρος [akyros], a testament that is ratified or invalid. Second, we turn the objection back: in this very sense of the word, Paul betrays himself. Nor could this line of reasoning have been anyone's but Paul's. If there is an error in it, Erasmus calls into question not the author but the authority of the author. Third, it is also far from the case that the sacred tongue was used out of ignorance. For the same author, where he quotes the prophecy of Jeremiah, uses the word בְּרִית [berith] for a covenant and agreement. He therefore meant this: that God's covenant, which in its form as a covenant and as a mediation between parties who are far apart, is indeed of such a kind, also takes on the form of a testament, inasmuch as it is a bestowal of an inheritance, the bestower being Christ, whose death and blood ratify it. And so he now alludes to the other meaning of διαθήκη among the Greeks, turning the word about and seizing on it in every sense, so that our argument stands unshaken.

units.la: XV. Decimò, Græce scripsisse pau-lum, merito & inde colligunt eruditi, quod loca omnia Testamenti Veteris, Author non ex Hebræis fontibus, sed Græcis codicibus citet. Qua de causa, quidam olim Epistolæ contradicebant, quod ad Hebræos scribens Paulus, utatur testimoniis quæ in Hebræis voluminibus non habentur, ut Hieronymus, ad Cap. VI. Esaiæ, Tomo IV. Et quidem in locis momentosis, in quibus Interpretes à litera Hebræa, longissimè recedunt. Jam autem si Hebraicè scripsit Paulus ad Hebræos, an ille, relicto Hebraico textu, & originali quidem, Græcum & translatum usurparit? Quid absurdius dici potest & præposterè magis? Utrumque tamen tuetur aperte Baronius. An verò, quod contendit Bellarminus, Paulus quidem ex Hebræo fonte testimonia protulerit, sed Græcus interpres postmodùm verterit, prout LXX? Rectius jam & optimè Baronius, neminem puto talia præsumpsisse, ad A.C.LX. Num.XLVI. Ita sanè est. Quis credat Interpretem tantum sibi arrogasse licentiæ? In iis ubi Græca mire ab Hebraeis discrepabant? In tantâ locorum segete, quibus tota scatet Epistola? Et quod
units.tr: XV. Tenthly, learned men also rightly infer from this that Paul wrote in Greek, because the author quotes all the passages of the Old Testament not from Hebrew sources but from Greek copies. For this reason some once objected to the Epistle, "that Paul, writing to the Hebrews, uses testimonies which are not found in the Hebrew books," as Jerome says, on Isaiah chapter 6, Tome IV. And indeed this happens in weighty passages, where the translators depart very far from the Hebrew letter. Now, if Paul wrote to the Hebrews in Hebrew, did he, leaving aside the Hebrew text, which is the original, use the Greek translation? What could be said that is more absurd or more perverse? Yet Baronius openly defends both. But is it, as Bellarmine contends, that Paul indeed produced the testimonies from a Hebrew source, but a Greek interpreter translated them afterwards, as with the Seventy? Baronius rightly and very well says: "I think no one has presumed such things," at A.D. 60, no. 46. And so it truly is. Who would believe that an interpreter had allowed himself so much licence? In those places where the Greek differed remarkably from the Hebrews? In such a harvest of passages, with which the whole Epistle abounds? And what

units.la: factum alibi fatetur Salmasius, Quaest.VI. de Hellenist. ut, quae Apostoli ex hebraeo textu deprompserant, Graece ad verbum reddiderint Interpretes, & hinc oriatur nonnunquam illa discrepantia a translationibus Graecis, idem fieri ab Interprete hoc loco debuit & potuit. Sed exceptionem patitur nullam, quod aliquoties Author, versionem illam Graecam ad scopum suum accommodat. Adeoque & a primario authore illa ipsa versio adhibita fuit. V.g. Cap.XI.7. ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν βραχύ τι παρ' ἀγγέλους. Quas ex LXX. desumptas Interpretibus voces, Apostolus imprimis urget, de Christi humiliatione ad breve tempus, infrà Angelorum sortem. Alludit ad vocem ἠλαττώσας, ad particulam βραχύν, ad illud, παρ' ἀγγέλους. Sic Cap.IX. ad vocem διαθήκης, quâ LXX. apud Jeremiam reddiderant vocabulum בְּרִית[?]. Sic Cap.X.5, illa verba σῶμα κατηρτίσω μοι[?], quae in versione Graeca longius abeunt à verbis Psaltis, omnino appositissima erant ad institutum Apostoli. Quibus denotaretur, obedientia Messiae incarnati, adaptatio corporis ad obsequium crucis, & redemptionem humani generis. Adeò hæc perspicua & aperta, ut Bellarmini aliorumque stupo-rem, stupere satis non possimus. Nemini ergo accidat mirum, scribentem ad Hebræos Apostolum, Græcorum uti versio-ne. Siquidem 1. Græco scriberet idiomate. II. Græcæ versioni lucem sæpius inferret. III. Ad scopum illa suum esset quàm ac-commodata. IV. Res ipsi cum Hebræis ἁρμόζοι, maximâ ex parte esset. V. Magno apud hos translatio esset in pretio, atque etiam usu. VI. Ipsi Hebræi illorum tempo-rum scriptores, Josephus, Philo, pariter usurparint. VII. Verbis etiam illa transla-tio, minimè sensu ab Hebræis codicibus discederet. VIII. Mos etiam Pauli esset Apostoli, suis passim in Epistoliis eâdem uti. Patet vel ex Epistolis ad Romanos, Galatas, in quibus cum ipsis disputat sæ-pè Judæis.
units.tr: Salmasius openly admits this happened elsewhere, in Quaest. VI. de Hellenist.: that the translators rendered word for word in Greek the things which the Apostles had drawn from the Hebrew text, and hence sometimes arises that discrepancy from the Greek translations. The same thing must and could have been done by the translator in this place. But no objection holds, that the author on several occasions adapts that Greek version to his purpose. And so that very version was used by the primary author himself. For example, Chapter 11, verse 7: ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν βραχύ τι παρ' ἀγγέλους [ēlattōsas auton brachy ti par' angelous], "you made him a little lower than the angels." The Apostle especially presses the words taken from the Seventy, about Christ's humiliation for a short time, below the lot of the angels. He alludes to the word ἠλάττωσας [ēlattōsas], to the particle βραχύ [brachy], and to the phrase παρ' ἀγγέλους [par' angelous]. So in chapter 9 he alludes to the word διαθήκης [diathēkēs], by which the Seventy in Jeremiah had rendered the word בְּרִית [berith]. So in chapter 10, verse 5, the words σῶμα κατηρτίσω μοι [sōma katērtisō moi], which in the Greek version depart further from the words of the Psalm, were wholly suited to the Apostle's purpose: by them is signified the obedience of the incarnate Messiah, the fitting of a body to the obedience of the cross and the redemption of the human race. These points are so plain and clear that we cannot sufficiently marvel at the amazement of Bellarmine and others. Therefore let no one think it strange that the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, used the Greek version. For, first, he wrote in the Greek idiom. Second, he often brought light to the Greek version. Third, that version was very well adapted to his purpose. Fourth, the matter was for the most part fitting to the Hebrews. Fifth, the translation was held in high esteem among them and was also in common use. Sixth, the Hebrew writers of that time themselves, Josephus and Philo, likewise used it. Seventh, in its wording this translation also did not depart from the sense of the Hebrew copies. Eighth, it was also the custom of Paul the Apostle to use the same version throughout his Epistles. This is evident even from the Epistles to the Romans and Galatians, in which he often disputes with the Jews themselves.

units.la: XVI. Undecimò, nec inepta, ut videtur Bellarmino, illa ratio est, quæque imprimis fuit Cajetani, ex Capite VII. versu 2. Quod sc. Author hebræam vo-cem
units.tr: XVI. Eleventhly, this argument, which is especially Cajetan's, is not foolish as Bellarmine thinks. It is drawn from chapter 7, verse 2, where the author translates the Hebrew words that the author gives into Greek.

units.la: cem[?] Melchizedek, & Melech Salem interpretatur Græce. Πρῶτον μὲν ἑρμηνευόμενον βα-σιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης, ἔπειτα ϰ[?] βασιλεὺς Σαλὴμ, ὅ ἐστι βασιλεὺς εἰρήνης. Omnino sunt hæc verba ipsius Scriptoris, voces alterius linguæ, eâ qua scribebat, interpretantis. Quomodo alibi idem Paulus, ἀββὰ, ὁ πατήρ. Johannes, ῥαββὶ, ὁ ἐστι, διδάσκαλε. Matthæus, Ἐμμανουὴλ, ὅ ἐστι μεθερμηνευόμενον &c. ἠλὶ, ἠλὶ λαμὰ σαβαχθανὶ, τοῦτ᾽ ἐστι &c. Nisi enim hæc sint primarij scriptoris, laxanda jam fabula Interpreti, qui interpretationem illam sibi usurparit, & de suo, integras voces & sententias textui authentico infarserit. Et quid si ille ἐν τῇ ἑρμηνείᾳ forte esset allucinatus? Hic vero excipiunt Bellarmi-nus, Ribera, alij, hāc ipsam interpretationem extitisse in textu Hebraico. Apostolum nomen proprium מלכיצדק reddidisse per מלך צדק, sic מלך שלם interpretatum esse מלך שלום. Quemadmodum si quis græce dicat, Δωρόθε-ῳ[?], ὃ ἐστι δῶρον Θεοῦ, pari-ter Latine, homicidium quod est hominis cædes; aut legifer quod est legem ferens. Atque ita nihil de suo adjecisse Græcum Apostoli interpretem. Nos vero respon-demus, 1. supponi gratis, illas voces Mel-chisedek, & MelechSalem, tali indiguisse interpretatione. Sic enim vox per se ipsam reddebatur, nec id erat ἑρμηνευών, sed ταυτ[?]ν, καὶ ἀξιολογ[?]ν. Sunt eædem voces, est eadē vocū significatio, nec alia poterat vel excogitari. Et sat fuerat Apostolo dixisse, לראשונה מלך צדק, πρῶτον μὲν βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης, ומלך שלום, ὁ[?] βασιλεὺς εἰρήνης.
units.tr: The author translates the names Melchizedek and Melech Salem into Greek: "First, being interpreted, king of righteousness [Πρῶτον μὲν ἑρμηνευόμενον βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης], then king of Salem, that is, king of peace [ἔπειτα βασιλεὺς Σαλὴμ, ὅ ἐστι βασιλεὺς εἰρήνης]." These are wholly the words of the writer himself, an interpreter of words from another language, the one in which he was writing. In the same way Paul elsewhere says "Abba, which is, Father [ἀββὰ, ὁ πατήρ]", John says "Rabbi, which is, Teacher [ῥαββὶ, ὁ ἐστι, διδάσκαλε]", and Matthew says "Emmanuel, which being interpreted is [Ἐμμανουὴλ, ὅ ἐστι μεθερμηνευόμενον]", and "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani, that is [ἠλὶ, ἠλὶ λαμὰ σαβαχθανὶ, τοῦτ᾽ ἐστι]". For unless these glosses belong to the original writer, the fable must be abandoned, namely that an interpreter took this translation for himself and, from his own invention, inserted whole words and sentences into the authentic text. And what if he had perhaps been mistaken in his interpretation? Here, however, Bellarmine, Ribera and others object that this very interpretation existed in the Hebrew text: that the Apostle rendered the proper name מלכיצדק [Malkitsedeq] by מלך צדק [melek tsedeq], and that מלך שלם was likewise interpreted as מלך שלום [melek shalom]. It is as if someone should say in Greek, "Dorotheus, which is, gift of God [Δωρόθεος, ὃ ἐστι δῶρον Θεοῦ]", or in Latin, "homicide, which is, the slaying of a man", or "legifer, which is, law-bearing". And so, they say, the Greek interpreter of the Apostle added nothing of his own. We, however, reply: (1) it is groundless to assume that the names Melchisedek and Melech Salem needed such an interpretation. For the word was rendered by itself in that way, and this was not an interpretation but a plain transcription and a statement of the meaning. They are the same words, and the meaning of the words is the same; nor could any other be devised. And it would have been enough for the Apostle to have said, לראשונה מלך צדק [first, king of righteousness], πρῶτον μὲν βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης, and ומלך שלום [and king of peace], ὁ βασιλεὺς εἰρήνης.

units.la: 11. Similia illa sunt dissimilia, mutatio accidit in vocibus major, etymologia etiam nonnihil remotior, nec ita obvia.
units.tr: 2. Those cases are dissimilar: the change in the words is greater, and the etymology is also somewhat more remote and not so obvious.

units.la: Præterea & illas ipsas voces Græcas & Latinas, Δωρόθεος[?], Legifer &c. qui homini-bus Græcis & Latinis exponeret, næ ille sibilo excipieretur, & se propinaret deri-dendum. Denique pondus huic addunt argumento, quę jam superius illustrata.
units.tr: Moreover, those very Greek and Latin words, Dorotheus, legifer and the rest, would have to be explained to Greek and Latin readers; otherwise the author would be hissed at and would expose himself to ridicule. Finally, they add weight to this argument with what has already been illustrated above.

units.la: XVII. Duodecimò, siquidem Vete-rum potissimùm traditione hæc nititur o-pinio, neque negligi istud debet. Scilicet plerosque, non tam loqui opinativè aut assertivè, quam quidem narrativè & hi-storicè. Non tam quid ipsimet sentirent, quàm quod vetustiores scriptum reliquis-sent. Nam praeter Clementem, Eusebium, & Hieronymum, de quibus diximus supra, & paucissimos alios, caeteri ad ipsorum fidè haud obscurè provocant. Theodoretus, Φασὶ μεθερμηνευσαι τὴν Κλήμεντος, nempe dixerat Eusebius. Oecumenius, ὕστερον μεθερμηνευθῆναι λέγεται. Ambrosius (nisi quis alius sit) Sunt qui ajunt Paulum hanc Epistolam propriâ linguâ scripsisse & misisse. Stephanus apud Photium Cod. ccxxxii[?]. Εὐσέβιος καὶ πολὺς ἄλλ ὁ τῶν θεοφόρων πατέρων ὁμολ[?], &c. Φασὶν ἐκ τῆς Ἐβραΐδος μεταφέρσαι τὴν Κλήμεντα. Sic videmus plerosq; recètiores, fide quasi implicitâ, re non expensâ, non à difficultatibus suis liberatâ, assensum praebere suum. Imò & ipse ὁ πάνυ Salmasius, apertâ hic se contradictione superiùs implicabat. Et solitus in istiusmodi plus nimium tribuere Hieronymo, aliisque nonnullis Veterum. Imò quod magis est, sui saepè oblitus, modò affirmat, modò negat. E re nostrâ est, exemplum promere luculentum, & quod vix fidé apud Lectores impetrabit. Quum idem, Paulum Scriptorem Epistolæ asse-ruerit supra aliquoties, & cū Veteribus, à Clemente aut forte alio, non scripta con-tenderit, sed translatam; etiam de causis suppressi Paulini nominis, in alio quodam scripto, egerit fusius, in novissimo Opere, illorum quasi nescius, imprudenter om-nia revocavit. Nempe Apparatu ad li-bros de Primatu Papæ, paginâ 19. Paulus non ad Judæos sed ad Gentes, omnes suas Epistolas scripsit. Nam quæ ad Hebræos inscribitur, Pauli non est; & plerique Veterum in ea sententia. Nec in eam Theodoretus commentarios edidit, &c. Salmasij hæc esse quis credat? Ut duabus jam quasi insideat sellis, aut suo se stylo cō-fodiat. Sic omnia neget, quasi aliter neo sensisset nec scripsisset unquam. Veterum plerisq; affingat, quod Græci omnes, & si-ne controversia, omnes Latini post La-ctantium scriptores, rejecerunt. Theodo-retum affirmet nullos in eā dedisse Com-mentarios, quos dedit luculentos. Ipse Theodoretus, Græcorum omnium nostræ pro Paulo sententiæ acerrimus & judicio-fissimus vindex. Adeò, bonus quandoquē dormitat Homerus, adeò humanū est la-bi. Et hæc quidē de nobilissimo Problema-te paulo accuratiùs. Nā quo pugnant alij, Spiritum S. voluisse Libros omnes Græcè primùm exire, quando de nonnullis Libris potiori jure controvertunt principes eruditorum, leviculum nobis esse videtur.
units.tr: XVII. Twelfthly, since this opinion rests chiefly on the tradition of the ancients, it must not be neglected. Namely, most of them speak not so much by way of opinion or assertion as by way of narrative and history: not so much what they themselves thought, as what the earlier writers had left in writing. For apart from Clement, Eusebius and Jerome, of whom we have spoken above, and a very few others, the rest appeal openly to their authority. Theodoret: "They say it was translated from Clement's [Φασὶ μεθερμηνευσαι τὴν Κλήμεντος]", that is, Eusebius had said so. Oecumenius: "It is said to have been translated afterwards [ὕστερον μεθερμηνευθῆναι λέγεται]." Ambrose (unless it is someone else): "There are those who say that Paul wrote this Epistle in his own language and sent it." Stephanus, quoted by Photius, Codex 232: "Eusebius and many other of the God-bearing fathers agree, etc. They say that Clement translated it from the Hebrew [Φασὶν ἐκ τῆς Ἐβραΐδος μεταφέρσαι τὴν Κλήμεντα]." Thus we see that most of the more recent writers give their assent, as it were with an implicit faith, without weighing the matter, and without its difficulties having been removed. Even the very great Salmasius himself was entangled here in an open contradiction. He is accustomed to give far too much weight in such matters to Jerome and some other ancients. What is more, forgetful of himself, he sometimes affirms and sometimes denies. It is to our purpose to produce a striking example, which will scarcely win belief among the readers. Although he had several times above asserted that Paul was the writer of the Epistle, and had contended, with the ancients, that it was not written by Clement or perhaps someone else but translated, and although he had discussed at length, in another writing, the reasons for the suppression of Paul's name, in his latest work he recalled everything rashly, as if he were ignorant of those views. Namely, in the Apparatus to the books on the Primacy of the Pope, page 19: "Paul wrote all his Epistles not to the Jews but to the Gentiles. For the one inscribed to the Hebrews is not Paul's, and most of the ancients are of that opinion. Nor did Theodoret publish commentaries on it, etc." Who would believe these are Salmasius's words? He sits, as it were, on two chairs at once, or stabs himself with his own pen. So he denies everything, as if he had never thought or written otherwise. He attributes to most of the ancients what all the Greeks, and without dispute all the Latin writers after Lactantius, rejected. He asserts that Theodoret wrote no commentaries on it, though he wrote splendid ones. Theodoret himself is the most keen and most judicious defender of our view that Paul wrote it, among all the Greeks. So, good Homer sometimes nods; so human it is to slip. And let this suffice on this most noble problem, rather more carefully. For as to the claim of others that the Holy Spirit willed all the books to come forth first in Greek, when the leading scholars dispute it for some books with better right, it seems to us a rather slight matter.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Altera objectio, de Epistolâ ἀνεπιγράφῳ. Objectionis antiquitas. Levitas, multis fatentibus. Solutiones minus solidæ. An Pauli nomen prius fuerit adscriptum? An Paulus reticuerit nomen, reverentiâ Christi Apostoli? Aut quia non Epistola est, sed Liber? Aut quia Latinum Pauli nomen, invisum Hebræis? Solutiones quædam aliæ. Singularum patroni. Earundem infirmitas.
units.tr: The second objection, concerning the Epistle without a title (ἀνεπιγράφῳ). The antiquity of the objection. Its weakness, as many concede. Less solid answers: Was Paul's name added later? Did Paul withhold his name out of reverence for Christ the Apostle? Or because it is not an Epistle but a book? Or because the Latin name Paul was hateful to the Hebrews? Some other solutions. The supporters of each. The weakness of them all.

units.la: I. Excipit objectio altera, eaque omnium maximè decantata. Scilicet, ex inscriptionis defectu, & prætermissis τὰς[?] περὶ τῆς Ἐπιστολῆς. Quod nec Pauli nomen, nec dignitas Apostolatus, in proœmio legatur expressa. Contrà morem Pauli Apostoli perpetuum, & rationem Epistolarum omnium, in quibus præfigi vel alterutrum, vel utrumque solet. Sive quia fescriptis, aut in Christianâ Ecclesiâ distra-ctis. Siquidem universalis hic fuerit codicûm omnium defectus, antiquior etiam ætate Clementis Alexandrini. Nam hic causas prætermissi nominis enarraturus, non id suis, sed beati cujusdam presbyteri verbis præstitit. Deinde, factum vel dolo molo, vel optimo certè fine. Si prius, quod erat penes Ecclesias Hebræorum αὐτόγραφον, aut quæ fidelium manibus terebantur ἀπογραφα, recensque etiam rei memoria, reddebant tum irritam fraudem. Si posterius, recurrit difficultas, quâ de causâ viri pij & Christiani, sacratissimum illud nomen expunxerint? Imò sacrilegis manibus, & temerario incœpto, divinæ exordium Epistolæ mutilarint? Quando ipse Apostolus, quâ erat illę prudentiâ, apponere veritus non fuerat? Præterea, non quæstio est simpliciter, de nomine expuncto, sed toto illo proœmio, quo & dignitatem suam, & inscriptionem, & salutationem, ad ipsum priusquam descendat argumentum, complecti solet. Et cui bono eradere Pauli nomen, quando tot indiciis se manifestabat authorem? Quî etiam nec Clemens Alexandrinus, nec Veterum quisquam, id subodorati? Quod urgent de mutationibus, circa ti-tulum qui hodie visitur in limine, aut sub-scriptionem illam ad Epistolæ calcem, c-lumbe est. Quando non sunt illa de inte-gritate sacri contextus: & talia à librariis pleraque addita jam olim, ab aliis etiam, prout erant judicia, ultrò omissa.
units.tr: I. The second objection follows, and it is the most widely repeated of all. Namely, that from the lack of a superscription and from the omission of the words [τὰς ... περὶ τῆς Ἐπιστολῆς]. The name of Paul is not stated in the preface, nor is the dignity of the apostleship. This is contrary to the constant practice of the Apostle Paul and to the pattern of all his Epistles, in which either one or both of these are usually prefixed. Whether this is because the copies were scattered among the Christian churches, the objectors say, this defect is found in all the manuscripts, and it is older even than the time of Clement of Alexandria. For when Clement set out to explain the reasons for the omitted name, he did so not in his own words but in the words of a certain blessed elder. Next, the omission was made either by fraud or by a mistake, or certainly with the best intention. If earlier, then the autographs that were in the churches of the Hebrews, or the copies that were worn in the hands of the faithful, and the still-fresh memory of the matter, would have made such a fraud pointless. If later, the difficulty returns: for what reason would pious and Christian men have erased that most sacred name? Indeed, with sacrilegious hands and rash daring, would they have mutilated the opening of a divine Epistle? When the Apostle himself, with all his prudence, had not been afraid to put it there? Moreover, the question is not simply about a name erased, but about that whole preface in which he is accustomed to include both his dignity and his superscription and greeting, before he comes to the subject itself. And to what advantage would anyone erase the name of Paul, when so many indications showed him to be the author? Why also did neither Clement of Alexandria nor any of the ancients suspect this? As for what they press about changes in the title that is seen today at the head, or the subscription at the foot of the Epistle, that is nothing. For those are not matters of the integrity of the sacred text, and most such things were added by copyists long ago, and others were likewise omitted at will, as each man's judgment dictated.

units.la: IV. Hieronymus, hoc modo negavit consequentiam. Si non est Pauli, quia Pauli nomen non habet, Ergò nullius est, quia nullius habet nomen. Ita Primasius Præfat. in Epistolas Pauli, Tomo 1. Bibl. Patrum, Parte II. Si propterea Pauli non erit, quia ejus non habet nomen, nec alicujus est, quia nullius nomine titulatur. Quod si absurdum est, ipsius magis credenda est, quæ tanto doctrinæ suæ fulget eloquio. Probat hanc responsionem Venera-bilis Beza, etiam Bellarminus, etiam Zanchius, Gerardus, Gomarus, Pareus, iis quibus de Epistolâ differunt locis. Quanquam magis illa videtur subtilis, quàm sium, aut quisquis Primasij nomine, publicavit in Epistolam Commentarium. Nec displicet solutio Bellarmino, atque quàm plurimis recentiorum. Sed præsto sunt instantiæ non paucæ, & graviores jam difficultates. Nam Christum quod spectat, alio longè sensu vocandus erat Ἀ̓πόστολος. Neque id tantùm, sed Ἀ̓ρχιερεύς, sed distinctivis aliis appellationibus, atque attributis. Non etiam exorsurus Epistolam Paulus, videtur ad eam vocem, quam fortè in progressu erat inserturus, intendisse mentis aciem. Quidni etiam solum adscripsit nomen, tacito Apostolatu? Aut Apostolum se dixit simpliciter, non Hebræorum Apostolum? Aut servum Jesu Christi, quemadmodùm in illâ ad Philippenses? Nec profectò fastus fuisset & superbiæ, præscribere nomen, aut demandatum sibi à Christo munus; uti nec humilitatis, premere silentio. Sic debuisset Camero enervare vim argumenti, potiùs quàm reponere exemplum Petri, se inscribentis ad Judæos dispersos, Apostolum. Nam, (quod urgebant imprimis
units.tr: IV. Jerome denied the inference in this way: "If it is not Paul's because it does not bear Paul's name, then it belongs to no one, because it bears no one's name." So Primasius, in the preface to the Epistles of Paul, Tome 1 of the Bibliotheca Patrum, Part II: "If for that reason it will not be Paul's, because it does not have his name, then it is not anyone's either, since it is titled with no one's name. But if that is absurd, we should rather believe it to be his, since it shines with such eloquence of his teaching." Beza approves this answer, as do Bellarminus, and Zanchius, Gerardus, Gomarus, Pareus, on the passages where they differ concerning the Epistle. Yet that answer seems more subtle than sound, as does the one who published a commentary on the Epistle under the name of Primasius. Nor does the solution of Bellarmino displease me, or that of very many of the more recent writers. But there are not a few objections at hand, and more serious difficulties too. For as far as Christ is concerned, he ought to have been called Apostle in a quite different sense [Ἀπόστολος], and not only that, but also High Priest [Ἀρχιερεύς], and by other distinctive titles and attributes. Nor does it seem that Paul, about to begin the Epistle, had fixed his attention on the word he was perhaps going to insert later in the course of the letter. Why could he not have written only the name, leaving out the apostolate in silence? Or why did he call himself simply Apostle, not Apostle of the Hebrews? Or servant of Jesus Christ, as in the letter to the Philippians? Certainly it would not have been pride and arrogance to prescribe his name, or the office committed to him by Christ, just as it would not have been humility to suppress them in silence. So Cameron should have weakened the force of the argument, rather than offering the example of Peter, who addresses the scattered Jews as Apostle. For (as those old writers especially urged) Peter does not, in his Epistles, give this same name to Christ.

units.la: Ἀ̓πόστολος ... Ἀ̓ρχιερεύς: Greek words in the margin-free text; see notes. mis illi Veteres,) non dat Petrus, suisin Epistolis, hoc idem Christo nomen.
units.tr: Ἀ̓πόστολος ... Ἀ̓ρχιερεύς [Apostle … High Priest]. Peter, in his own Epistles, does not give this same name, Apostle, to Christ.

units.la: VI. Nec probatur nobis illa solutio, non tam Epistolam scripsisse Apostolum, quam Dissertationem quandam aut Librum. Atque ita nomen praefigi aliàs solitum Epistolis, praescribere hoc loco necesse non fuisse. Quod non displicuit Gerardo, & inter causas alias omissi nominis, recenset Clarissimus Hoornbeeck, Socinianismi Confutati Lib.1.Cap.1. Appo-sitissimum id sane foret, nisi in promptu exceptiones essent. Nam ipse Author sub finem usus voce ἐπιστέλλων[?]. Διὰ βραχέων ἐπι-στειλα ὑμῖν[?], Cap.xiii.22. Adhibet quoque Epistolarem clausam, & similem Paulinis omnibus aliis. Etiam Epistolarum in morem, alloquitur perpetuo fideles Hebręo-rum. Compellat passim familiarius, solitis [illegible, ~10 letters] ἀγαπητοί, ἀδελφοί &c. Quin ab ævo, Epistolæ titulum & locum, in sacro Codice obtinuit. Non alia etiam methodus, quam reliquarum Pauli, ut superius ostensum. Nec prolixitas major, imo prolixiores Epistolæ ad Romanos & ad Corinthios prima.
units.tr: VI. Nor do we accept that solution which holds that the Apostle wrote not so much an Epistle as a certain Dissertation or Book, and that therefore it was not necessary to prefix the name, which was otherwise customary for Epistles, in this place. This did not please Gerardus, and the most distinguished Hoornbeeck lists it among the other reasons for the omitted name, in Socinianismi Confutati, Book 1, Chapter 1. That would indeed be most suitable, were there not exceptions ready to hand. For the author himself, near the end, uses the verb ἐπιστέλλων [?]: "I have written to you briefly" (Διὰ βραχέων ἐπιστεῖλα ὑμῖν [?]), chapter 13, verse 22. He also adds an Epistolary closing, similar to all the other Pauline letters. And in the manner of Epistles, he addresses the faithful Hebrews throughout, speaking to them quite familiarly with the usual terms, ἀγαπητοί, ἀδελφοί, etc. Indeed, from the earliest times it has held the title and place of an Epistle in the sacred Codex. Its method is no different from that of Paul's other letters, as has been shown above. Nor is it much longer; indeed the Epistles to the Romans and to the Corinthians are longer than the first.

units.la: VII. Nec satisfacit, quod alij, ad certum nullum coetum, certam nullam Ecclesiam, dirigi Epistolam. Hinc pro more non fuisse opus τὴν ἀπογραφὴν[?]. Quicquid sit, Epistola fuit, & praefigi nihilominus potuit nomen Apostoli, tum ad conciliandam illi Apostolicam authoritatem, tum ad distinguendam à scriptis aliis anonymis. Praeterea, Jacobus indefinite scribit duodecim tribubus, non definite ad certum coetum, praefigit interim nomen. Sed antecedens simpliciter negari potest: Ut ut enim ad plures Ecclesias directa, ad certas tamen, ex Hebraeis videlicet collectas. Unde enim salutationes illae in conclusione Epistolae? Unde pollicitatio illa sui adventus? Unde alia illa, quod compassi essent suis vinculis; quod eorum quidam deserèrent τὴν ἐπισυναγωγὴν, &c. Ut credatur merito, sic ad Palaestinas data primò Ecclesias, ut communis etiam esset omnibus aliis, ex Hebraeis inter Gentes aggregatis.
units.tr: VII. Nor does it satisfy that others say the Epistle was not directed to any fixed assembly or any particular church. From this, they say, it was not necessary by custom to have a superscription. Whatever the case, it was an Epistle, and the name of the Apostle could nonetheless be prefixed, both to win for it apostolic authority and to distinguish it from other anonymous writings. Besides, James writes indefinitely to the twelve tribes, not to a particular assembly, and yet he prefixes his name. But the antecedent can simply be denied. For although it was addressed to many churches, they were nonetheless certain ones, namely those gathered from among the Hebrews. For whence come those greetings at the close of the Epistle? Whence the promise of his coming? Whence that other remark, that they had sympathized with his chains, and that some of them were abandoning the assembling of themselves together, and so on? So it is rightly believed that it was first given to the churches of Palestine, though it was meant to be common also to all others gathered from among the Hebrews among the Gentiles.

units.la: VIII: Est & alia quorundam ratio, non adscripti Paulini nominis, quamq; habet CorneCornelius à Lapide. Videlicet quod Paulus Romanum esset & Latinum nomen, atque ita Judæis minùs acceptum. Si etiam se inscripsisset Saulum, ex opposito suspicionem facile in Gentilium animis potuisse exoriri, ad Judaismum illum esse relapsum. Sanè, Paulum Romanum fuisse nomen, faciles damus; quod ob parvam staturam Æmiliorum hæsisse genti, author est Sigonius. Quanquam Græca alij contenderint esse originis, à voce πῦλα[?]. Alij cum Hieronymo, ab Hebraeorum [illegible, ~4 letters], unde Hesychius ναῦλον, θαυμαστός[?]. Sed Latinum esto, idcirco invisum fidelibus Hebræorum? Cohorruissent illi, ad nomen ipsis ante familiare, & ubi de gravissimis religionis mysteriis erat informandi? Idcirco Paulus, missum fecisset non nomen, sed inscriptionem totam? Aut Ecclesiæ Gentilium, si se dixisset Saulum, suspicati essent apostasiam in tanto Apostolo? Et quidem ad Judaismum, quem totâ Epistolâ, ex professo ibat subversum? His ergo missis, simpliciter & sine ambagibus, subjungimus objectionis solutionem.
units.tr: VIII. There is also another reason some give for the omission of the Pauline name, which Cornelius à Lapide holds. Namely, that Paul was a Roman and Latin name, and so less acceptable to the Jews. And if he had signed himself "Saul," the opposite suspicion could easily have arisen in the minds of the Gentiles, that he had relapsed into Judaism. Certainly we readily grant that Paul was a Roman name, which, as Sigonius records, clung to the Aemilii because of the small stature of that family. Yet others have contended that it is of Greek origin, from the word for gate [πῦλα]. Others, with Jerome, derive it from the Hebrew, whence Hesychius has [ναῦλον, θαυμαστός]. But granted that it is Latin, is it therefore hateful to the faithful Hebrews? Would they have shuddered at a name that had been familiar to them before, and where they were to be instructed in the most serious mysteries of religion? Would Paul therefore have dropped not just the name but the whole superscription? Or would the churches of the Gentiles, had he called himself "Saul," have suspected apostasy in so great an Apostle? And indeed of apostasy to Judaism, which throughout the whole Epistle he was expressly setting out to overthrow? Setting these aside, then, we add the solution to the objection, plainly and without circumlocution.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Solida confutatio præcedentis argu-menti. Epistolarum Johannis prima, similiter ἀνεπίγεγραφος[?]. Reliquas inscriptas, esse Johannis. Præfigendi nomen necessitas nulla Paulo. Non id κριτικὸν[?] Paulinarum. Non eadem Epistolæ ratio, quæ cæterarum. Paulus invisus multis Hebræorum. Declaratur. Consentit universa antiquitas. Tres instantiæ diluuntur. Paulus Gentium non Hebræorum Apostolus. Hinc etiam ratio non additæ inscriptionis. Confirmatur. Occurritur exceptioni. Beza, Camero notati. Ratio à metu periculi Hebræorum. Alia, ab exordiendi modo. Retorquetur in adversarios argumen-tum.
units.tr: A solid refutation of the preceding argument. The first Epistle of John is likewise without a superscription (anepigraphos). The rest are inscribed, and are John's. Paul had no necessity of prefixing his name. This is not a mark of the Pauline Epistles. The reason for this Epistle is not the same as for the others. Paul was hated by many of the Hebrews. This is explained. All antiquity agrees. Three instances are answered. Paul was the Apostle of the Gentiles, not of the Hebrews. Hence also the reason for the omission of the inscription. This is confirmed. An objection is met. Beza and Cameron are noted. The reason from fear of danger to the Hebrews. Another, from the manner of beginning. The argument is turned back against the opponents.

units.la: I. Nempe ita habet tritissimum argu-mentum. Quæ Epistola, Paulinarum in morem, non habet Pauli præfixum nomen, non videtur eadem esse Pauli. Sed talis est controversia illa ad Hebræos. Missâ assumptione, de qua, ut monuimus, dubitatum, sic enervamus propositionem. Primò, negari illius non immerito consequentiam, vel hoc nomine. Quod non desint haud absimilia exempla Epistolarum ejusdem Authoris, quarum aliæ admittunt ἀπογραφὴν[?], ἀνεπιγραφοι[?] aliæ. In Sacris, occurrunt tres Canonicæ Johannis Apostoli. Posterioribus, præscripta, οὖν τῇ ἀπογραφῇ[?], καὶ τῷ ἀσπασμῷ[?], ἡ ὑπογραφή[?]. In Priori desunt omnia, nomen, inscriptio, salutatio. Non tamen hinc quisquam Veterum, sive istam, sive reliquas, conclusit non esse Johannis. Quod enim de postremis, cum aliis quibusdam dubitare visus Eusebius, εἴτε τῆς Εὐαγγελίῳ τυγχάνουσαι[?], εἴτε τῆς ἑτέρᾳ ὁμωνύμῳ[?], dubitandi alia ratio fuit. Quod scilicet præferrent nomen πρεσβύτερος[?]: quodque Johanni Apostolo fuisset Ephesi cognominis alius, dictus itidem πρεσβύτερος[?], Papiâ referente apud Eusebium, L.iii.C.xxxix. Non attento, æquè aut magis convenienter tribui epitheton, Apostolorum omnium postremo, seni grandævo, verè πρεσβύτερῳ[?], sive ætatis ratione sive authoritatis. Quum de cætero, & stylus, & argumentum & omnia, Johanni faverent Apostolo. Igi-turid volumus, ut quâ Johannes ratione, in aliis nomen præfixit, in prima non præ-fixit, idem Paulo licuerit. Et quid in eo absurdi, alibi apposuisse nomen, hic non apponere? Et quomodo de Johanne, non sollicitè admodùm inquirimus, quæ fue-rit omissæ inscriptionis ratio, quidni i-dem jam observamus? Siquidem non le-viora hic pro Paulo authore, quàm istic pro Johanne, pugnant argumenta.
units.tr: I. Indeed the argument runs in this very familiar way: an Epistle which, after the manner of the Pauline Epistles, does not have Paul's name prefixed, does not seem to be Paul's. But such is the controversy over the Epistle to the Hebrews. Granting the minor premise, about which, as we have noted, there is doubt, we weaken the major premise in this way. First, its consequence is not unfairly denied, at least on this ground: there are not lacking quite similar examples in Epistles of the same author, some of which admit a superscription (apographē), others are without one (anepigraphoi). In the Sacred Books there are three Catholic Epistles of the Apostle John. In the latter two, the preface, the signature (hypographē), the greeting, are present: "ἐν τῇ ἀπογραφῇ" and "καὶ τῷ ἀσπασμῷ." In the first, all are lacking: name, inscription, salutation. Yet from this none of the ancients concluded that either this one or the others were not John's. For as to the last ones, Eusebius seemed to doubt them together with some others, "whether they belong to the Evangelist or to another of the same name" (εἴτε τῆς Εὐαγγελίῳ τυγχάνουσαι, εἴτε τῆς ἑτέρᾳ ὁμωνύμῳ); the ground for doubt was different. Namely, they bore the name "presbyter" (πρεσβύτερος), and there was at Ephesus another man of the same name as the Apostle John, also called "presbyter," as Papias reports in Eusebius, Book III, chapter xxxix. Without taking into account that the epithet, equally or more suitably, could be assigned to the last of all the Apostles, an aged old man, truly "presbyter," whether by reason of age or of authority. Moreover, both the style and the subject matter and everything else favoured the Apostle John. Therefore we want the following: whatever reason John had for prefixing his name in the others and not in the first, the same liberty may have been Paul's. And what is absurd in this, that he put his name in one place and does not put it here? And since we do not inquire very anxiously about John, why should we not observe the same here, for the arguments for Paul as author in this case contend no less than those for John in that case?

units.la: II. Deinde, peccatur falsâ hypothesi, quasi hanc sibi fixerit perpetuam legem Paulus, ut nomen præponeret. Quasi de necessitate quâdam debuerit hoc loco [?]προγεγράφθαι. Quod fecit alibi, factum ab eo liberrimè, & pro recepto ut plurimùm [?]ore. Præterea ut & authoritatem Epi-stolis conciliaret, & authorem ipsum esse intelligerent. Jam verò si Paulus, in ipso statim limine sui ad Hebræos scripti, pro authore se haberi necesse non judicarit: si aliunde certissimè de authore & authori-tate Epistolæ, constare poterat Hebræis: si in progressu Paulum se indicabat Apo-stolum, stolum[?], solito sigillo, mentione vinculo-rum, etiam Timothei, salutatione, particularibus nonnullis, ablegatione nuncij &c. cessat necessitas inscriptionis. Et sic alibi in more habuit, ut nunquam tamen hanc sibi legem fecerit. Ut nunquam Epistolarum suarum διαταξικὸν[?] τι esse monuerit. Ut admiserit facillime exceptionem, istiusmodi consuetudo. Denique, ut longè sit æquius & opportunius, attendere ad sigillum Pauli perpetuum & distinctivum, quod competit illi soli & semper, quàm ad inscriptionē quæ nec solus Pauli est, nec semper ejus fuisse necesse est.
units.tr: II. Next, the argument goes wrong from a false hypothesis, as if Paul had set for himself this constant law, to put his name first. As if by some necessity he ought to have written a superscription (proegraphthai) in this place. He did so elsewhere, and did it quite freely, and mostly by an accepted custom. Moreover, he did it both to lend authority to the Epistles and so that they would understand the author himself to be the writer. But indeed, if Paul, at the very threshold of what he wrote to the Hebrews, did not judge it necessary that he be taken for the author; if the Hebrews could otherwise be fully certain of the author and authority of the Epistle; if in its course Paul indicated himself as Apostle by his usual seal, by the mention of his bonds, also of Timothy, by the greeting, by certain particular details, by the dispatch of a messenger, and so on, then the necessity of an inscription ceases. And so he kept to custom elsewhere, yet never made this a law for himself. He never warned that any of his Epistles was a "rule of arrangement" (diataktikon ti). He allowed exceptions to such a custom very easily. Finally, it is far more fair and fitting to attend to Paul's constant and distinctive seal, which belongs to him alone and always, than to an inscription which is neither peculiar to Paul alone nor necessarily always his.

units.la: III. Præterea, laborat in eo potissimum consequentia, quod, si hic novum quid & singulare, non defuerint etiam rationes illius Paulo singulares. Nunquam antea res ipsi immediatè cum Hebræis. Hactenus scripserat ad Gentes, & ex Gentilibus maximâ ex parte constitutas Ecclesias. Quid ergò mirum, si jam ad diversissimum hominum genus & variè erga se affectum scripturus, à solita scribendi ratione paulùm abit? Quomodo in antecessis ostensum, variare sæpè hac in Epistola & argumentum, & stylum, iisdem etiam de causis. Licet jam præcisè, distinctè, & in particulari, non assignemus omissæ causam inscriptionis.
units.tr: III. Moreover, the inference is weakest on this point: if here something new and singular occurs, there are also not lacking reasons peculiar to Paul. Never before had he had dealings directly with the Hebrews. Up to then he had written to the Gentiles and to churches made up for the most part of Gentiles. What wonder, then, if now, about to write to a very different class of men who were variously disposed toward him, he departed somewhat from his customary manner of writing? As was shown above, in this Epistle both the subject matter and the style often vary, for the same reasons too. Although we do not now assign precisely, distinctly and in particular the cause of the omitted inscription.

units.la: IV. Sed & præsto sunt causæ, eæque admodum graves, & quas universa pro-bavit antiquitas. Et vel sola hæc, cordato cuivis & ingenuo satisfaciet. Nempe inoleverat inter Hebræos, personale quoddam in Paulum odium, ejusque nomen. Dudum transfuga multis erat, & apostata, & Judæorum hostis. Invisus aliis, ob illius in ceremonias, circumcisionem, legalia invectivas. Aliis, quod se totum Gentium ministerio mancipasset, earumque profiteretur se Apostolum, quas Judæi ut profanas & impias plerumque abominabantur, ut Commentator, qui Ambrosij præ-fert nomen. Ne ergo solità inscriptione, & ambitioso in speciem titulo, & nomine plus satis exoso, sive veterem quorundam acrimoniam excitaret, sive infirmiorum animos offenderet, sive attentæ & modestæ lectioni obicem poneret, sive odio nominominis fronte prælati, utilitatem exclu-deret lectionis, fructumque vel in totum vel ex parte interverteret, maluit ἀπέχειν. Id est, ἀνεπιγράφως, rem ipsam continuò, & Apostolicâ plane gravitate, aggredi. Quantum enim interfuit in limine, legen-tium vel audientium animos, sinistrâ nul-lâ dicentis vel scribentis opinione occu-pari, quamque prudenter sint tractandæ præjudicatæ mentes, docent rhetores.
units.tr: IV. But there are also causes at hand, and very weighty ones, which all antiquity has approved. And this alone will satisfy any sensible and candid person. Namely, among the Hebrews there had grown up a personal hatred of Paul, and of his name. For a long time he had been a deserter to many, and an apostate, and an enemy of the Jews. He was hateful to some because of his invectives against ceremonies, circumcision and the law. To others, because he had devoted himself wholly to the ministry of the Gentiles and professed himself their Apostle, whom the Jews for the most part abhorred as profane and impious, as the commentator who bears the name of Ambrose says. Therefore, lest by his customary inscription, by a title ambitious in appearance, and by a name more than enough hated, he should either stir up the old bitterness of some, or offend the minds of the weaker, or put an obstacle in the way of attentive and modest reading, or, by the hatefulness of the name placed at the head, shut out the usefulness of the reading and wholly or partly turn its fruit aside, he preferred to abstain (apechein), that is, to approach the matter itself at once, without inscription (anepigraphōs), and with a plainly Apostolic gravity. For how much it matters, at the threshold, that the minds of readers or hearers should not be occupied by any unfavourable opinion of the speaker or writer, and how prudently prejudiced minds ought to be handled, the rhetoricians teach.

units.la: V. Atque hic ferè scopus, hæc summa, illius quâ gravissimi & antiquissimi Scri-ptores dedêre, solutionis. Memoratu di-gna Clementis apud Eusebium verba, L. vi.
units.tr: V. And this is almost the aim and the sum of the solution which the most grave and most ancient writers have given. The words of Clement in Eusebius, Book VI, are worth recalling.

units.la: C.XI. Μὴ γεγράφθαι δὲ (Παύλῳ Ἀποστόλῳ) εἰκότως. Ἑβραίοις γὰρ ἀπεστέλλων, προ λήψιν ἐπληφῶσι κατ᾿ αὐτὰ, ᾗ ὑποπτεύουσιν αὐτὸν, συνετῶς πάνυ ὅσα ἐν ἐκχῇ ἀπέτρεψεν αὐτὰς, τὸ ὄνομα Θεός. Idem fuit responsum B. Athanasij, ad instantiam Anomœi, quod non præferret Pauli nomen Epistola; causam fuisse dicit, ἵνα μὴ σεισθῶσι ὄντες αὐτῆς τὸ ὄνομα, κλέ-σωσι τὴν ἀκοήν. Ne scil. ad invisum nomen accensi, & quasi perculsi, aures illi nega-rent. Probavit præ omnibus aliis, hanc missæ inscriptionis causam, Chrysostomus Præfat. in Epist. Probata eadem Hieronymo, Ambrosio, Primasio, Sedulio, Haimoni, Theophylacto, suis , aut illorum nonnunquam nomine inscriptis, Commentariis. Ne ad recentiores descendamus, quorum certè plerique ( Illustri Salmasio fere invito, Funere Ling. Hellen. p. 37. 38. ) rationis momentum intellexerunt.
units.tr: Chapter XI. It is reasonable that (the Apostle Paul) is not named as author. For writing to the Hebrews, who were prejudiced against him and were suspicious of him, he very wisely turned them away at the outset from the name (Μὴ γεγράφθαι δὲ (Παύλῳ Ἀποστόλῳ) εἰκότως. Ἑβραίοις γὰρ ἀπεστέλλων, προλήψει ἐπτοημένοις κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ, ἢ ὑποπτεύουσιν αὐτὸν, συνετῶς πάνυ ἐν ἀρχῇ ἀπέτρεψεν αὐτοὺς τὸ ὄνομα). The same was the answer of St. Athanasius to the objection of the Anomoean, that the Epistle does not bear Paul's name; he says the cause was "so that they should not be shaken by the name and shut their ears" (ἵνα μὴ σεισθῶσι ὄντες αὐτῆς τὸ ὄνομα, κλείσωσι τὴν ἀκοήν). That is, lest they, roused against the hated name and as if struck, should refuse to listen. Chrysostom, in his Preface to the Epistle, approved this reason for omitting the inscription above all others. The same was approved by Jerome, Ambrose, Primasius, Sedulius, Haimo, Theophylact, and by their commentaries, which are either inscribed with their own names or with theirs at times. Not to descend to more recent writers, most of whom (almost against the will of the illustrious Salmasius, in his Funus Linguae Hellenisticae, pp. 37, 38) have understood the weight of this reason.

units.la: VI. Frustrà instabunt, Paulum declarare se aliquot indiciis authorem;noluisse ergò latere , aut nomen ignorari suum. Quod nec volumus, nec asserimus. Verum enim verò, si non occultare nomen, dissimulare certè nonnihil. Si non latere, at latenter quasi & sensim irrepere , & opportunè se manifestare. Post disputationem gravem, dictione sublimem, densam argumentis, rationibus validissimam. Post calumnias tacitè discussas , & abster-sam quam, illius sive doctrinæ , sive innocentiæ , labem adspergebant alij. Ut e-tiam patefaceret, nolle se nominis sui authoritate, sed sanctitate doctrinæ , cum Mosè per omnia consentientis , illorum animos permovere. Unde nonnisi decimo, & ultimo Capitibus, productâ jam disputatione, clarissimis sese & apertis prodit ille documentis.
units.tr: VI. They will in vain press that Paul by several indications declares himself the author; he did not wish, therefore, to hide or have his name ignored. This we neither want nor assert. For indeed, if he did not conceal his name, he certainly dissembled something. If he did not hide, yet he crept in covertly, as it were gradually, and revealed himself at a fitting moment: after a weighty discussion, sublime in expression, dense with arguments, very powerful in reasons; after calumnies silently dismantled and wiped away, the stain that others were splashing upon his teaching or his innocence. So that he might also show that he wished to move their minds not by the authority of his name but by the sanctity of his doctrine, which agrees in all things with Moses. Hence it is only in the tenth and last chapters, with the discussion now advanced, that he reveals himself by the clearest and open evidences.

units.la: VII. Urgeri solet, scribere Apostolum non Judæis, sed Christianis, non con-vertendis, sed conversis Hebræorum. Quibus erat imprimis charus, & notissimus, ut ex variis Epistolæ circumstantiis, non ergò invisus, non exosus. Sed facilis solutio est. 1. Acceptissimum fuisse plurimis, nonnullis etiam minùs. In numerosissimâ illâ Hebræorum turbâ, qui sive intrà Palæstinam, sive alibi Christo nomen dederant. Quorumque multi pertinaciùs Judaizantes, & iniquiori jam olim erga ipsum animo, quiq; tales esse non desierant. 11. Multi inter eos in Christianâ fide vacillantes, & apostasiæ proximi, ut colligimus ex vi. & x. Capitibus. Multi infirmiores, nec Christianam satis edocti libertatem, adeóque & secùs de Paulo in illo capite sentientes. Theophylactus, οὐδὲ οὔπω πάνυ [?]προσεῖχον αὐτῷ, [?]ἅτε δὲ νόμως [?]ἀπάγοντα παντελῶς, [?]ἢ τὴν [?]ἀξιοῦμένην λύσιν. Et evidentissimè constat, ex Pauli historiâ, & Actor. III. Denique ita directè scribit ad fideles Hebræorum, ut indirectè ad omnes. Siquidem & convertendis, pro-cul omni dubio Epistolam hanc suam uti-lem esse voluit. Ut constat ex illo Pauli in Judæos omnes zelo, & operosâ illâ di-sputatione Apostoli, confirmandis aliis, aliis etiam convincendis omninò institu-ta. Jam autem, nomen hic suum obtende-re & Apostolatum, erat à lectione hos prorsus arcere. Subticere contrà, & dissi-mulare, prudentissimi erat artificis, & op-tima insinuandi sese ratio.
units.tr: VII. It is often urged that the Apostle wrote not to Jews but to Christians, not to those to be converted but to the converted among the Hebrews. Among these he was especially dear and well known, as appears from various circumstances of the Epistle, and therefore not disliked, not hated. But the solution is easy. 1. It was most acceptable to very many, and to some less so. In that very numerous crowd of Hebrews, who had given their name to Christ either within Palestine or elsewhere, many were stubbornly Judaizing, and had long been of a more hostile mind toward him, and such had not ceased to be so. 2. Many among them were wavering in the Christian faith and close to apostasy, as we gather from chapters vi and x. Many were weaker, not sufficiently taught in Christian liberty, and therefore thought otherwise of Paul in that chapter. Theophylact: "They did not yet pay him much heed, since he seemed wholly to lead them away from the law, or the solution demanded" (οὐδὲ οὔπω πάνυ προσεῖχον αὐτῷ, ἅτε δὲ νόμου ἀπάγοντα παντελῶς, ἢ τὴν ἀξιουμένην λύσιν). And this is most evidently established from Paul's history and Actor. III. Finally, he writes so directly to the faithful among the Hebrews that he writes indirectly to all. For, without doubt, he wished this Epistle of his to be useful also for converting. As is clear from that zeal of Paul against all the Jews, and from that laborious disputation of the Apostle, undertaken altogether to confirm some and also to convince others. But now, to put forward his name and his Apostleship would have been to shut these men off completely from reading. On the other hand, to keep silent and dissemble was the mark of a most prudent craftsman, and the best way of insinuating himself.

units.la: VIII. Est & alia instantia Cameronis, sed frigidior neque tanti. Scilicet Pau-lum præfixisse nomen Epistolæ ad Romanos, quum tamen ex Judæis (saltem ex parte) horum constaret Ecclesia. In qua etiam contrà Judæos disputat, eorum-que rejectionem aperit. Sed admittit Vir doctissimus elenchum parium. Quum Romanorum Ecclesiam constituerent, ma-ximam sanè partem Gentiles. Magisque sermo sit Apostolo in sua ad Romanos de Judæis Judæis, quàm quidem ad Iudæos. Neque etiam apud hos sic invisum esset Pauli nomen, ut inter Palæstinos, & Orientales, quibus innotuerat magis. Quibuscum directè jam congreditur, & immediatè; & cū Hebræis solis; & in odioso ex parte argumento; ac præter praxim hactenus suā.
units.tr: VIII. There is also another instance from Cameron, but a weaker one and of little weight. He says that Paul prefixed his name to the Epistle to the Romans, although the Church there consisted, at least in part, of Jews. In that letter too he disputes against the Jews and reveals their rejection. But the most learned man admits the argument from equals (elenchus parium). The Church at Rome was made up chiefly of Gentiles, and Paul's discourse in his letter to the Romans is more about Jews addressed to Jews than addressed to the Jews as such. Nor was Paul's name so hateful to them as it was among the Palestinians and the Orientals, to whom it had become better known. With the Romans he now engages directly and immediately, and with Hebrews only, and partly with an argument that is offensive, and beyond his practice up to that point.

units.la: IX. Verùm, non prætermittenda altera illa ratio Paulini istius instituti. Nempe, à functione sui Apostolatus inter Gentes; quodque Gentium non Hebræorum foret Apostolus. Partim ex composito & amicā sorte, provinciis sic inter Apostolos distributis, ut in Epist. Galatas: partim speciali vocatione Gentibus destinatus, Actor. IX, 15. XIII. 2. Quum circumcisionis ministerium, & Judæorum cura, Petro & Collegis incumberet. Quod præclarè deducit Theodoretus, in procœmio Comment. in Epist. ad Hebræos. Unde accidit ut se Gentiū Apostolum, inscribat aliquoties Paulus, attento speciali illo exercitio eoq; potissimo sui muneris, Rom. I. 5, XI. 13. Gal. II. 7. Quo etiā sensu dicit se ἀ Φωρισμένον εἰς Εὐαγγέλιον &c. Rom. I. I.
units.tr: IX. But the other reason for Paul's arrangement must not be passed over. Namely, it arises from the office of his apostleship among the Gentiles, and from the fact that he was the apostle of the Gentiles, not of the Hebrews. This was partly by mutual agreement and a friendly lot, with the provinces so divided among the apostles, as in the Epistle to the Galatians; and partly because he was destined for the Gentiles by a special calling (Acts 9:15; 13:2), since the ministry to the circumcision and the care of the Jews fell to Peter and his colleagues. Theodoret draws this out admirably in the preface to his commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Hence it happens that Paul several times styles himself "apostle of the Gentiles," having regard to that special exercise of his office, which was its chief part (Rom. 1:5; 11:13; Gal. 2:7). In this same sense he also says that he was set apart for the gospel of God [ἀφωρισμένος εἰς εὐαγγέλιον] (Rom. 1:1).

units.la: Unde etiam frequentiores ad Gentiles dedit literas, imò hac exceptâ, omnes. Ergò, (ut redeamus ad institutum) ne præter officij rationem, aut conventionis legem, scribere ad Hebræos videretur, omisit ultrò nomen. Ne etiam Apostolos circumcisionis offenderet, aut afficeret æmulationis quodam sensu, falcem immittere visus in illorum messem. Ne præsumptionis quisquam argueret, quasi jam supra reliquos sese efferret, & protenderet limites sui Apostolatus. Hinc quasi veniam scriptionis rogare videtur, quando illorum speciatim non erat Apostolus: ὡς ἀκαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοί, ἀνέχεσθε τοῦ λόγου τῆς παρακλήσεως, καὶ γὰρ διὰ βραχέων ἐπέστειλα ὑμῖν, Hebr.XIII,22. Duobus nempe se excusat, tum quod sit λόγος παρακλήσεως, non ἐντολῆς. Tum quod paucis tantum illos voluerit, quum alias potuisset pluribus.
units.tr: For this reason too he wrote more frequently to the Gentiles, indeed to all of them except this one. Therefore, to return to our point: lest he seem, beyond the rule of his office or the terms of the agreement, to be writing to the Hebrews, he deliberately left out his name. He also did so lest he offend or affect the apostles of the circumcision with a feeling of rivalry, as if he were thrusting his sickle into their harvest. And lest anyone should charge him with presumption, as if he were already raising himself above the rest and extending the limits of his apostleship. Hence he seems to ask pardon for writing, since he was not apostle to them in particular: "I beseech you, brethren, bear with the word of exhortation; for I have written to you in few words" (Heb. 13:22) [παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοί, ἀνέχεσθε τοῦ λόγου τῆς παρακλήσεως, καὶ γὰρ διὰ βραχέων ἐπέστειλα ὑμῖν]. He makes two excuses: first, that it is a word of exhortation, not of command; second, that he wished to write to them in only a few words, though he might have written at greater length.

units.la: X. Hæc certè ratio prægnans semper visa, & simplicissima olim hodieque. Clemens Alexandrinus, rationibus aliis attexit; οὐκ ἐγγεάφει ἑαυτὸν, διότι τὸ ἐκ πίστεως σίας διὰς καὶ τοῖς Ἑβραίοις ἐπιστέλλειν, ἐθνῶν κήρυκος ὄντος ὁ Ἀ᾿ποστολος. Sed imprimis celebrari solet ejusdem patronus Theodoretus. Nam Argumento, quod præmisit Epistolæ, hanc unam urget, & graviter admodum ac prolixè, cujus verba compendij causâ non adducimus. Idem voluit Primasius, non meminisse Paulum sui Apostolatus, ne videretur quod se vellet præferre Apostolo Petro &c.
