Idem Ambrosius, quia ad eos qui ex circumcisione crediderant, ipse Gentium Apostolus non Hebræorum. Eadem apud Oecumenium, αἴτιον ἡ ἀκολουθία. Ἀ᾿ποστόλῳ δὲ ἐθνῶν ὑπῆρχεν ὁ Παῦλος, ἀλλὰ οὐχὶ Ἰουδαίων. Adstipulatur Thomas, qui hanc cæteris rationem anteponit, Præfatione Commentarij. Et præter innumeros alios, Claudius Salmasius, qui ultrò citroque rationibus variis collatis & expensis, hanc tandem cum Theodoreto verissimam esse putat, taciti nominis & Apostolatus, Funere ling.Hellen.p.38.
units.tr: X. This reason has always seemed the most telling, and the simplest, both in former times and today. Clement of Alexandria added other reasons to it: he does not write his own name, because it was fitting that the Apostle, being herald of the Gentiles, should write to the Hebrews. But the chief advocate of this view is usually taken to be Theodoret. In the argument he prefixed to the Epistle he presses this one reason alone, and does so at considerable length and with great force; for the sake of brevity I do not quote his words. Primasius held the same view, that Paul did not mention his apostleship, lest he seem to want to set himself above the Apostle Peter, and so on. Ambrose too, because he wrote to those who had believed from circumcision, while he himself was apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews. Oecumenius says the same: the reason is the sequence, since Paul was apostle of the Gentiles, but not of the Jews [αἴτιον ἡ ἀκολουθία· ἀποστόλῳ δὲ ἐθνῶν ὑπῆρχεν ὁ Παῦλος, ἀλλὰ οὐχὶ Ἰουδαίων]. Thomas agrees, and in the preface to his commentary prefers this reason to the others. Besides countless others, Claudius Salmasius, after comparing and weighing various reasons back and forth, finally judges this one, with Theodoret, to be the truest: that the name and the title of apostle were silently passed over (Funere ling. Hellen. p. 38).

units.la: XI. Quod cum ita sit, miramur eandem doctissimo Bezæ, non ullo argumento, sed contemptu solo & supercilio rejerejectam. Miramur etiam præstantissi-mum Cameronem ne meminisse quidem, nec excipere hic quicquam esse dignatu. Quum anxius & sollicitus in rationibus aliis confutandis esse videatur. Et sanè hoc unum excipi in speciem posse arbitra-mur. Quod ipsa verius scriptione, quàm præscriptione nominis, transilierit hoc modo limites sui Apostolatus. Quando ergo scribere nihil veritus est, potuisse facilè & apponere nomen. Sed in promptu denuò solutio est. 1. Quod præscribendo nomen & dignitatem, videbatur id jam affectare ambitiosius. Et facere ex authoritate, quod jam quasi ex accidente quodam, & occasione afflictionum quibus Hebræi premebantur. 11. Si dixisset se Gentium Apostolum, mirum in modum exacerbasset animos Hebræorum. Si Hebræorum Apostolum, involabat in aliorum munus & dignitatem. Si Apostolum simpliciter, visus jam fuisset, vi sui Apostolatus, adeóque pro imperio & authoritate, has sibi arrogare scribendi partes. 111. Optima & judiciosissima ratio Theodoreti, reti, in Argumento Epistolæ. Paulum in suis adGentium fideles Epistolis,adjecisse nomen & Apostolicam dignitatē,ut Doctor & Magister scribens ad discipulos. Hinc non adjecisse in suâ ad Hebræos , quod speciatim nec illorum Doctor esset,nec hi disciplinæ ipsius traditi.
units.tr: XI. Since this is so, we are surprised that the same reason was rejected by the most learned Beza, not on any argument but from contempt and disdain alone. We are also surprised that the most excellent Cameron does not even mention it, nor think it worth any exception, although he seems anxious and careful in refuting other reasons. Indeed we think that this one can be made an exception in appearance: that Paul went beyond the limits of his apostleship in the writing itself, rather than in the prefixing of the name. Since he was not afraid to write, he could easily have added the name as well. But the answer is again ready to hand. 1. To prescribe the name and dignity would seem to be aiming at this more ambitiously, and to make by authority what was already, as it were, a matter of accident and of the occasion of the afflictions by which the Hebrews were oppressed. 2. If he had called himself apostle of the Gentiles, he would have wonderfully exasperated the minds of the Hebrews. If he had called himself apostle of the Hebrews, he would have trespassed into another's office and dignity. If he had simply called himself apostle, he would already have seemed, by virtue of his apostleship, and so by command and authority, to claim for himself this role of writing. 3. The best and most judicious reason is Theodoret's, given in the argument of the Epistle: that Paul, in his letters to the faithful among the Gentiles, added his name and apostolic dignity, as a teacher and master writing to his disciples. Hence he did not add it in his letter to the Hebrews, because he was not their teacher in particular, nor had they been entrusted to his discipline.

units.la: XII. Et sanè hæ rationes ita comparatæ, ut pluribus opus non sit. Magnus tamen Beza , post quosdam alios hanc in medium profert, quam unam probat.Scilicet silentio transmisisse nomen suum Apostolum,ne majorem invidiam Hebræis crearet , eosque in discrimen adduceret. Ne grassantes jam in Christianum nomè, & plus satis exacerbatos Hierosolymitanos , odioso adhuc Pauli nomine,magis accenderet ac proritaret. Quam causam non additi nominis, Clar. Gomarus, plerisque aliis verisimiliorem putat. Nisi fortè regerant alij[?] , potuisse Judæos magis exacerbari ipso Epistolæ argumento, quod cultum ceremonialem funditus evertebat. Adeoq; ne sic quidem cautum satis illorum fuisse securitati. Nec necesse tio, ejusque, cum iis quas habuit Paulus, ponderis? Ut non immeritò doctissimus Beza: Ego verò contra ex hoc ipso contenderim, Pauli potius esse quam alterius cujusquam. Cur enim quisquam alius nomen suum reliquisset? At Paulo justa causa fuit &c. Sed de his plus satis, & præter institutum ferè prolixius.
units.tr: XII. And indeed these reasons are so well framed that more is not needed. Yet the great Beza, after some others, brings forward this one, which alone he approves: namely, that Paul passed over his name in silence so that he would not create greater hatred among the Hebrews and put them in danger. He did not want to inflame and goad on the Jerusalemites, who were already raging against the Christian name and more than sufficiently exasperated, by the still hated name of Paul. The distinguished Gomarus thinks this reason for omitting the name more probable than most others. Unless perhaps others object that the Jews could have been exasperated even more by the argument of the Epistle itself, which utterly overturned the ceremonial worship; and so not even in this way was sufficient caution taken for their safety. Nor is it necessary to... and its weight, set against those which Paul had? As the most learned Beza rightly says: "I, on the contrary, would argue from this very fact that the letter is Paul's rather than anyone else's. For why would anyone else have left out his name? But Paul had a just cause, etc." But enough on these points, and this has run somewhat longer than the subject required.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Tertia objectio, ex verbis Apostoli Hebr. 11.3. Profiteri se discipulū Apostolorū. Objectionis patroni. Præteermissa quibus. Variè respondetur. Verba textus expenduntur. Phrasis ἐις ἡμᾶς. Quomodo Paulus ἐλεεαιώθη. Historia, quæ habetur in Epistolâ ad Galatas. Quinam οἱ ἀκούσαντες. Locutio Apostoli rhetorica. Illustratur. Instantia diluitur.
units.tr: The third objection, from the words of the Apostle, Heb. 11.3, that the author professes himself a disciple of the Apostles. The objectors' case. Those passed over. Various answers. The words of the text are weighed. The phrase εἰς ἡμᾶς. How Paul was "confirmed." The history found in the Epistle to the Galatians. Who "those who heard" are. The Apostle's rhetorical manner of speaking, illustrated. The instance is answered.

units.la: I. Defuncti non infeliciter sumus, nobilissimis objectionum omnium. Cæteræ, & nobis prolixæ tractationis, & tædiosæ aliis lectionis molestiam condonabunt. Nisi forte non indigna videatur examine, hæc quorundam objectio. Ex ipsiusmet verbis Apostoli, Capite 11, versu 3. Ἥτις[?] (σωτηρίας) ἀρχὴν λαβοῦσα λαλεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Κυ-[?] ρίου, ὑπὸ τῶν ἀκουσάντων εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐβεβαιώθη.[?] Quibus, referre se inter discipulos Apostolorum videtur Author. Profiteri ab iis se edoctum, atq; confirmatum. Non ipsummet vidisse se vel audivisse, sed ab iis qui viderunt & audiverunt, accepisse. Adeóque nec Paulum scriptorem esse, nec Apostolorum quemquam. Quorum fuit immediata revelatio; qui testes oculares & auriti simul; qui non ab hominibus, sed à Christo ipso, de omnibus plenissimè instructi; qui Magistri ipsi, non discipuli; aut discipuli Christi, non ullius Apostoli.
units.tr: I. We have not been unhappy in dealing with the most notable of all the objections. The rest will excuse both us, for the lengthy treatment, and others, for the tedium of reading. Unless perhaps this objection of certain people seems not unworthy of examination. It rests on the Apostle's own words, chapter 2, verse 3: "which, having begun to be spoken by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard" (ἥτις ἀρχὴν λαβοῦσα λαλεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου, ὑπὸ τῶν ἀκουσάντων εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐβεβαιώθη). By these words the author seems to count himself among the disciples of the Apostles. He professes to have been taught and confirmed by them, not to have seen or heard Christ himself, but to have received the message from those who saw and heard. Therefore Paul is not the writer, nor is any of the Apostles. They were the ones to whom immediate revelation came; they were eyewitnesses and earwitnesses at once; they were fully instructed in everything not by men but by Christ himself; they were teachers themselves, not disciples; or they were disciples of Christ, not of any Apostle.

units.la: II. Non meminère objectionis, quantùm constat, vetustissimi Patrum. Benè meminit Oecumenius, in Præfatione Commentarij, aliique ex posterioribus. Avidè arripuére in causæ suæ subsidium, recentiorum multi. Et torsit ex primis Calvinus, Commentario ad locum: Cæterùm hic locus indicio est, Epistolam non fuisse à Paulo compositam, neque enim tam
units.tr: II. As far as is known, the most ancient Fathers do not seem to have raised this objection. Oecumenius does mention it well, in the preface to his commentary, and so do some of the later writers. Many of the more recent writers have eagerly seized on it in support of their cause. Among the earlier ones, Calvinus wrested it in his commentary on the passage: "Moreover this place is an indication that the Epistle was not written by Paul, for he does not usually speak so humbly as to confess himself one of the disciples of the Apostles."

units.la: [The line "humi-" is the catchword, not text.] humiliter loqui solet, ut se unum fateatur ex Apostolorum discipulis. Videntur sibi hoc argumento bene tuti, Magdeburgen-ses, Centuriâ i, Libro ii. Cap. iv. Quibus adstipulati, Lutheranorum nonnulli Theologi. Recens admodum Commentator Anglus, anonymus, satis aliàs accuratus; Hinc non improbabiliter colligitur, Paulum non fuisse authorem hujus Epistolae. Nunquam enim eximit se e numero Apo-stolorum, aut accenset se auditoribus &c. Doctissimum Grotium, ut quo apud ip-sum sit objectio loco intelligeremus, u-surpare non licuit.
units.tr: [The line "humi-" is the catchword, not text.] He does not usually speak so humbly as to confess himself one of the disciples of the Apostles. The Magdeburgenses, Century 1, Book 2, Chapter 4, seem to themselves quite safe with this argument. Some Lutheran theologians agreed with them. Quite recently an English commentator, anonymous and otherwise accurate enough, wrote: "From this it is not improbably inferred that Paul was not the author of this Epistle. For he never removes himself from the number of the Apostles, nor counts himself among the hearers, etc." As for the most learned Grotius, I was not permitted to quote him, so that we could understand at what point the objection occurs in him.

units.la: III. Fuêre tamen, pertinacissimi e-jusdem sententiæ assertores, qui telum reliquêre intactum. Non torquet Erasmus, nec suis ad locum Notis, nec in Appendice, corrasis interim omnibus, quæ causæ in speciem suæ patrocinarentur. Non urget Camero, Quæst. 11. de authore Epistolæ, nec postmodum, ubi locum su-sius enarrat. Neq; tanti profecto esse debuit, ut tot aliis clarissimis argumentis, tot pro Paulo in ipsa Epistola circumstantiis, evidentioribus longè, prævaleret. Imò si propiùs expendimus, nulla est objectio, nec patronis iis digna. Et damus ambabus manibus, Paulum fuisse Apostolum, non Apostolum discipulum, edoctum salutis mysteria immediatè à Christo, non mediatè ab hominibus, nihilque in eo inferiorem Apostolis cæteris. Sed nequeid ullâ ratione sollicitat locus, nedum evertit. Manetque, quod alibi affirmat, Gal.1.11,12. prorsus immotum.
units.tr: III. There have been, however, most stubborn defenders of the same opinion, who left the weapon unused. Erasmus does not twist it, neither in his notes on the passage nor in the Appendix; he has passed over everything that might seem to support the cause. Camero does not press it, in Question 11 on the author of the Epistle, nor later where he explains the passage more fully. Surely it ought not to have such weight that it prevails over so many other very clear arguments and so many circumstances in the Epistle itself pointing to Paul, far more evident ones. Indeed, if we weigh it more closely, there is no real objection at all, nor one worthy of such advocates. And we grant with both hands that Paul was an Apostle, not an Apostle who was a disciple, taught the mysteries of salvation immediately by Christ and not mediately by men, and in nothing inferior to the other Apostles. But the passage does not in any way disturb the point, much less overturn it. What he asserts elsewhere, Gal. 1.11, 12, remains entirely unshaken.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Primò, non contemnenda illorum videtur esse solutio, qui phrasin εἰς ἡμᾶς, attendendam monent. Ut sit, ἕως εἰς ἡμᾶς, usque ad nos, ad nostra usque tempora. Usitatissima enim est apud Græcos acceptio, cujus exempla penes Grammaticos, & Franc. Vigerum de Idiotismis Græcis. Quanquam videtur aliis Hebraismus purus, ex Hebræorum לְ. Qui utut recurrat feré aliàs in hac Epistolâ, nihil obstat quo minùs possit hoc esse Hellenismus loco. Quando etiam de doctrinæ salutaris, inde à Christo à quo initium sumpserit, periodo, sermo esse videadeatur. Sed neque in illas conjecti sumus angustias, ut hæc sit ἱερὰ ἄγκυρα [?] & nostrum asylum.
units.tr: First, the solution of those is not to be despised who advise attention to the phrase εἰς ἡμᾶς [εἰς ἡμᾶς], so that it means ἕως εἰς ἡμᾶς [ἕως εἰς ἡμᾶς], usque ad nos, that is, down to our own times. For this is a very common usage among the Greeks, with examples in the grammarians and in Franc. Vigerus on Greek idioms. Yet to others it seems a pure Hebraism, from the Hebrew לְ. Although this idiom recurs almost everywhere else in this Epistle, nothing prevents it from being a Hellenism in this place. Since the discourse also seems to concern the period of saving doctrine, from the initium Christ himself gave it. But we are not driven into such narrow straits that this should be our sacred anchor [ἱερὰ ἄγκυρα] and our refuge.

units.la: V. Secundò itaque, dicimus opponi quæ componi omninò possunt, & divelli quæ conjungenda. Sicque Apostolus immediatè potuit à Christo Domino edoceri, & accipere ardua illa mysteria, ut etiam de illis confirmari, βεβαιωθῆναι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀκου-όντων. Nec tam ipsemet confirmari, quam doctrina salutis, ἥτις (sc. σωτηρία) ἐβεβαιώθη: Aliud ergò didicisse Paulum ab Apostolis, quod ad Galatas scribens negat, aliud eadem quæ à Christo acceperat, fuisse ab oculatis testibus confirmata. Nec Pauli ipsius in particulari, sed in communi totius Ecclesiæ gratiâ. Vel si Pauli etiam respectu, non id ex necessitate factum, sed instar auctarij cujusdam, & ut consensum illorum omnium intelligeret, quæ cælitùs & ex revelatione hauserat. Ne referam quod alii, attendi hic confirmationem factam Ananiæ ministerio.
units.tr: V. Secondly, then, we say that things which can altogether be reconciled are being set against each other, and things which ought to be joined are being torn apart. Thus the Apostle could be taught immediately by Christ the Lord, and receive those difficult mysteries, so that he was also confirmed about them, "to be confirmed by those who heard" (βεβαιωθῆναι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀκουσάντων). Nor was he himself confirmed so much as the doctrine of salvation, "which (namely salvation) was confirmed" (ἥτις, sc. σωτηρία, ἐβεβαιώθη). So it is one thing for Paul to have learned from the Apostles, which he denies in writing to the Galatians; it is another that the same things he had received from Christ were confirmed by eyewitnesses. And this was not for Paul's own sake in particular, but for the grace of the whole Church in general. Or, if it was also with respect to Paul, this was done not from necessity but as a sort of addition, and so that he might understand the agreement of all those things which he had drawn from heaven and by revelation. Not to mention what others say, that the confirmation here is to be understood as made through the ministry of Ananias.

units.la: VI. Tertiò, huc facit quod observarunt doctissimi Interpretes, quodq; non abhorabhorret à vero. Respicere Apostolum ad historiam quam de se ipse refert, Galat.1. 18, 19. imprimis Cap.ii.2. In quâ, aliquot post conversionem annis, memorat se ad Apostolos profectum, & apud eos aliquandiu versatum. Imò contulisse privatim, cum principibus Apostolorum, Petro, Jacobo, Johanne. Et quidem de doctrina Evangelij, quam hactenus prædicarat. Etiam ne frustrà cucurrisset, ne forte dissensum cum Apostolis urgere possent alij, & prædicationis ita suæ fructum tollerent. Hoc ergo sensu merito dixerit Apostolus, ἥτις ἰδὼν τῶν ἀκουσάντων εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐξ- ἐβεβαιώθη[?]. Nec ista confirmatio pugnabat cum dignitate Apostoli. Facta amicâ συμ-βιβάσει[?], imò etiam mutua & reciproca, ut ex iis quæ de Petro & Paulo narrantur. Nec tam de doctrinæ veritate, quàm de consensu, non tà περὶ τῆς ὀρθοδοξίας quàm ὁμοδοξίας, & concordantiâ per omnia cum Apostolis.
units.tr: VI. Thirdly, to this point is what the most learned interpreters have observed, and what is not far from the truth: the Apostle is looking back to the history he relates about himself, Galat. 1.18, 19, and especially chapter 2.2. In that passage, some years after his conversion, he records that he went up to the Apostles and stayed with them for some time. Indeed he conferred privately with the chief Apostles, Peter, James and John, about the doctrine of the Gospel which he had preached until then, even lest he should have run in vain, lest perhaps others might press a disagreement with the Apostles and so take away the fruit of his preaching. In this sense, then, the Apostle could rightly say, "which, having been heard by those who heard, was confirmed to us." Nor did this confirmation conflict with the dignity of an Apostle. It was done by friendly agreement, and indeed even mutual and reciprocal, as is told of Peter and Paul. And it concerned not so much the truth of the doctrine as the consensus: not orthodoxy (τῆς ὀρθοδοξίας) so much as agreement of opinion (ὁμοδοξίας), and concord in all things with the Apostles.

units.la: VII. Quartò, salsissima hypothesis, quasi Apostolus simpliciter se eximat è numero τῶν ἀκουσάντων. Vocem accipit non ἀπλῶς, sed κατὰ[?]. Scilicet de iis qui audiverunt in terris, & in statu exinanitio-nis, Christo nondùm ad Patrem assump-to. Ità Paulus verissimè se ab iis distingue-re potuit, illæsis suis prærogativis. Aliàs & ipse ἀκουόντας, ipse ἰδιώτας[?], sed miraculosè in cœlos raptus, sed cœlesti voce percul-sus, cœlesti lumine collustratus. Rectè ergò monet Apostolus, salutarem illam (cujus aliunde sibi ipse erat conscius) do-ctrinam, post Christum exaltatum, ab e-jus similiter discipulis, & comitibus, & auditoribus perpetuis, fuisse deinceps confirmatam.
units.tr: VII. Fourthly, the hypothesis is most absurd, as if the Apostle simply removed himself from the number of "those who heard" (τῶν ἀκουσάντων). The word is not taken absolutely (ἁπλῶς), but with reference to those who heard on earth, in the state of humiliation, Christ not yet taken up to the Father. So Paul could most truly distinguish himself from them, his own prerogatives left intact. Otherwise he himself was a hearer, himself untaught, yet snatched up miraculously into heaven, struck by a heavenly voice, illuminated by a heavenly light. Rightly, therefore, the Apostle notes that that saving doctrine (of which he was himself aware from another source), after Christ was exalted, was thereafter confirmed by his disciples, companions and constant hearers in the same way.

units.la: VIII. Quintò, demus τῶν ἀκουόντων appellatione, Apostolos simpliciter, & prærogativam illam Apostolicæ dignita-tis, atque ocularia illa testimonia, dignari. Ne sic quidem nos ferit objectio. Nec enim Paulus his necessariò vocis, vel se ab Apostolis distinguit, vel in eundem se cum Hebræis censum refert. Pergit in figurâ illâ dictionis, dictâ rhetori-bus, ἀνακοινωσις vel κοινωνία. Quâ suis se auditoribus accenset, eleganter quidem & energeticè. Ut quod ab illis, etiam à se-met exigat ; quod illis tribuit, etiam sibi; quod de illis vult dictum , de se pariter per συγκατάβασιν [?] quandam & συγκοινωνίαν efferat. Ergo nobis confirmata salus , id est parti nostrūm maximæ, vobis, fidelibus, Ecclesiæ. Quod evidentissimè,& luce clarius constat, 1. Quia hoc ipso versu, locutionis istius insigne exemplum ; πῶς ἡμεῖς ἐκφευξόμεθα, τηλικαύτης ἀμελήσαντες σωτηρίας. Quomodo nos effugiemus, scil. poenam tantæ salutis neglectæ? Sic initio Capitis, Δεῖ ἡμᾶς προσέχειν &c. Μήποτε παραρρυῶμεν. Atqui longissimè aberat Apostolus, (quisquis fuerit) ab istius poenæ, aut negligentiæ, aut diffluxionis periculo. De se tamen condescendenter juxtà cū reliquis dictum voluit. Pergit igitur & eâdē, quâ incæperat, ratione dicere debuit, εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐβεβαιώθη. 11. Quia frequentior est Authori nostro illius ἀνακοινωσεως [?] usus. Capite VI.1. εἰς τὴν τελειότητα φερώμεθα. Capite x,26, ἑκουσίως ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν. &c. Quæ dubio procul non sibi applicabat divinus Author. III. Quoniam id non Authori tantum tùm nostro, sed Paulo est imprimis fami-liare sic 1.Thess. iv. 17. ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες, quum illi sermo de novissimorum temporum hominibus. Sic 1.Cor. x. 8, 9; μὴ πορνεύωμεν[?], μὴ ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν χριστόν[?]. Sic durissima illa similis communicationis ratio, Tit. iii. 3. ἦ μὲν γάρ ποτε καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀνόητοι[?], δουλεύοντες ἐπιθυμίαις[?], καὶ ἡδοναῖς &c. Istiusmodi plena plau-stra. iv. Quando etiam parallelus ferè locus huic nostro, legitur apud Judam, verf. 17. Memores esse verborum, quae praedicta sunt, ἀπὸ[?] τῶν Ἀποστόλων. Pariter, ἀπὸ[?] τῶν ἀκουσάντων. Quemadmodum enim ita se Judas videtur distinguere ab Apostolis, ut illorum pars aliqua tamen esset. Ita & noster Author ab auditoribus Christi & discipulis, ut interim se inclusum, non exclusum velit. v. Quia revera fuit ipse ἐκ τῶν ἀκουσάντων, qui auditione ab ipso immediate Christo acceperant. Adeóque, ut non hic se excludit, sic ibi non se aliter, quàm rhetorum notissimo illo communicationis schemate, includit. vi. Quin causae erant graves istius loquendi formae, penes Apostolum. Rhetorica quidem alte-ra, ra, ut persuaderet efficaciùs, ut magis se suaque insinuaret Hebræis. Dum nequaquam se effert suprà illorum sortem, sed iisdem se legibus, eidem obnoxium conditioni testatur. Quo schemate quàm feliciter uti soleant oratores, & facturi ad populum verba, pueri norunt. Altera Theologica, ab arctissimâ illâ unione, & communione inter fideles. Ejusdé membra corporis, ejusdem Magistri discipulos, ejusdem professores fidei. Hinc quod plerisque competit, facilè omnibus in communi adscribitur.
units.tr: VIII. Fifthly, grant that by the term "those who heard" the Apostles simply are meant, and that it includes that prerogative of Apostolic dignity and those eyewitness testimonies. Even so the objection does not strike us. For Paul does not necessarily distinguish himself from the Apostles by this word, nor does he count himself among the Hebrews. He continues in that figure of speech which the rhetoricians call ἀνακοινωσις or κοινωνία [ἀνακοινωσις, κοινωνία]. By it he counts himself among his hearers, elegantly and vividly indeed: what he demands of them he demands of himself too; what he attributes to them he attributes to himself; what he wishes said of them he likewise expresses of himself, by a certain condescension and fellowship. Therefore "confirmed to us" means to the greater part of us, to you, the faithful, the Church. This is established most evidently, clearer than light, for these reasons. 1. In this very verse there is a notable example of that locution: "how shall we escape, having neglected so great salvation?" (πῶς ἡμεῖς ἐκφευξόμεθα, τηλικαύτης ἀμελήσαντες σωτηρίας). That is, how shall we escape the punishment of so great a salvation neglected? So at the beginning of the chapter: "we ought to give heed" (Δεῖ ἡμᾶς προσέχειν), "lest we drift away" (μήποτε παραρρυῶμεν). Yet the Apostle, whoever he was, was far from danger of that punishment, or of negligence, or of drifting away. Nevertheless he wished to speak of himself condescendingly, along with the rest. He therefore goes on, and in the same manner as he began, had to say "confirmed to us." 2. Because our author uses that figure of anakoinosis quite often: chapter 6.1, "let us be carried on to perfection" (εἰς τὴν τελειότητα φερώμεθα); chapter 10.26, "if we sin wilfully" (ἑκουσίως ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν), and so on, which the divine author doubtless did not exempt from applying to himself. 3. Because this is familiar not only to our author but especially to Paul. So in 1 Thess. 4.17, "we who are alive" (ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες), though the speech concerns the people of the last times. So in 1 Cor. 10.8, 9, "let us not commit fornication" (μὴ πορνεύωμεν), "let us not tempt Christ" (μὴ ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν χριστόν). So too that harsh form of the same sharing, Titus 3.3, "for we also were once foolish" (ἦμεν γάρ ποτε καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀνόητοι), "serving desires and pleasures" (δουλεύοντες ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἡδοναῖς), etc. Such instances in plenty. 4. Because a nearly parallel passage to this one is read in Jude, verse 17: "remember the words which were spoken" (μνήσθητε τῶν ῥημάτων) "by the Apostles" (ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων). Likewise here, "by those who heard" (ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκουσάντων). For just as Jude seems to distinguish himself from the Apostles and yet to be some part of them, so our author distinguishes himself from the hearers and disciples of Christ, while wishing himself included rather than excluded. 5. Because in truth he himself was one of "those who heard," who had received the message by hearing from Christ immediately. So, as here he does not exclude himself, so there he includes himself in no other way than by that most familiar figure of communication, which the rhetoricians know well. 6. Indeed there were weighty reasons for this form of speech on the Apostle's part. One was rhetorical: he wished to persuade more effectively, and to insinuate himself and his own into the favour of the Hebrews. For he does not raise himself above their lot, but testifies that he is subject to the same laws and bound by the same condition. How happily orators use this figure when about to address the people, even boys know. The other was theological, arising from the very close union and communion among the faithful: members of the same body, disciples of the same Master, professors of the same faith. Hence what belongs to most is easily ascribed to all in common.

units.la: IX. Sextò, quod instant, Paulum non ita locuturum fuisse de se humiliter, imprimis cum Hebræis, ejus satis vellicantibus authoritatem, dilutum est. Contrarium enim verum, & ex adverso argumentamur. Sic loqui Paulum, quia ipsi negotium cum Hebræis. 1. Ut frequentioribus istiusmodi ἀνακοινῶ' σήση[?], probaret se hominibus jam satis ab ipso alienis, ingenuû, & minimè fastuosum, & communi cum iis vinculo colligatum. ii. Ut hoc in loco, suum cum reliquis Apostolis, speciaciatim Petro, Iacobo, Iohanne, Apostolis Hebræorum, consensum innueret. Quos τ' ἀκουσαντων nomine, imprimis notat. III. Ut vitaret invidiam sui Apostolatus, nec de se multa in limine diceret. Huc faciunt illæ ipsæ rationes, ob quas dignitatem ante suam, nomenque profiteri noluit. Et si jam apertè, in ipso adhuc exordio, Apostolatum ostentasset suum, quid opus fuerat paulò ante, opportuno in loco, præterire silentio? Vidit hoc Beza noster, sed post Veteres. Hi enim ita; ἵνα δὲ μὴ σκανδαλίση, οὐ λέγει ἐχ ἑαυτοῦ ἀπἀστελλεσθαι τῷ Χριστῷ, καὶ τοι ἠκουσεν.
units.tr: IX. Sixth, as to their objection that Paul would not have spoken of himself so humbly, especially to the Hebrews, who were rather sharp in attacking his authority: this has been answered. I argue the contrary, and on the opposite side. Paul spoke in this way because he had business with the Hebrews. (1) As in his other, more frequent communications of this kind [ἀνακοινώσεις], he wished to show that he was a candid man, not at all haughty, and bound to them by a common tie, even though they were already fairly alienated from him. (2) In this place he wished to signal his agreement with the other apostles, particularly Peter, James and John, the apostles of the Hebrews, whom he especially marks by the phrase "those who heard" [τῶν ἀκουσάντων]. (3) He wished to avoid resentment at his apostleship and not to say much about himself at the threshold of the letter. Those very reasons, for which he was unwilling to profess his dignity and name before, favour this view. And if he had already openly displayed his apostleship at the very beginning, why was there any need to pass over it in silence a little earlier, at a suitable place? Our Beza saw this too, but only after the ancients. For they say: "But lest he should give offence, he does not say that he was sent from himself by Christ, although he had heard it" [ἵνα δὲ μὴ σκανδαλίσῃ, οὐ λέγει ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ ἀπεσταλθαι τῷ Χριστῷ, καίτοι ἤκουσεν].

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Quarta aliorum objectio. De doctrinâ Catechetica Hebr. vi. 1. An congruat ætati Pauli? Calvino objectio probata. Ejus infirmitas. Strictim confutatur. Variè retorquetur. Calvini contradictoria assertio. Aliæ objectionum classes. Sed quæ ipsam Epistolæ authoritatem feriunt. Cur in hac disquisitione prætermittantur. Non esse hujus loci. Conclusio Authoris. I. Ha-
units.tr: The fourth objection raised by others. On the catechetical teaching of Hebrews 6:1. Whether it agrees with the age of Paul. Calvin's objection approved. Its weakness. Briefly refuted. Turned back in various ways. Calvin's self-contradictory assertion. Other classes of objections. But those which strike at the very authority of the Epistle. Why these are passed over in this inquiry. That it does not belong to this place. The author's conclusion. I. Ha-

units.la: I. Hactenus quidem ea omnia , quae non hodie demùm, sed pridem ac Patrum ætate , contrà Paulum authorem fuère objecta. Præter hæc, difficultatem quandam aliam, adversus authorem eundem, à recentioribus videmus esse motâ. Quod hempe doctrinæ Catechetica mentionem injiciat Scriptor, Cap. vi.1.2. Illorumque ordine capitum, quæ catechumeni, & novitij edocebantur. Quæ quidem consuetudo, quæ praxis, videatur Pauli ætate fuisse posterior. Atque ita non tam divinum illum Apostolum, quam discipulorum quendam censeri debere Epistolæ scriptorem. Quæ quidem objectio, authorem tantùm petit, salvâ omninò & illibatâ scripti authoritate. Primipilus jam est Calvinus, cujus hæc sunt verba, Præfatione in Epistolam: Præterea quæ de Catechismi consuetudine adducit, Capite vi, Pauli ætati minùs congruerent. Idem disertiùs Commentario ad locum: Hic respexit ad usitatam Catechismi formulam. Unde probabilis conjectura sumi potest, Epistolam hanc non statim ad exordio pro[?]mulgati Evangelij scriptam esse, sed quum jam aliquam politiæ rationem in Ecclesijs constitutam habérent. Post eum, urserunt[?] alij forte quidam, sed pauciores. Nec illius meminêre sive Erasmus, sive Cajetanus, sive Magdeburgenses, sive Canero[?], sive alij qui cum illis in hac quæstione sentiunt.
units.tr: I. Thus far, indeed, all those objections have been considered which were raised against Paul as author, not only today but long ago, in the age of the Fathers. Besides these, we see that another difficulty against the same author has been stirred up by more recent writers. This is because the writer mentions catechetical teaching, in Chapter 6:1-2, and the order of those chapters which catechumens and novices were taught. Indeed, this custom or practice would seem to have been later than the age of Paul. And so the writer of the Epistle ought to be regarded not so much as that divine Apostle as some disciple of his. This objection, however, seeks only the author, while the authority of the writing remains wholly intact and unharmed. Calvin is the first in this line, whose words are these, in his Preface to the Epistle: Moreover, the things he brings forward about the custom of catechism, in chapter 6, would be less suited to the age of Paul. The same, more clearly, in his Commentary on the passage: Here he looked to the usual formula of the catechism. From which a probable conjecture can be drawn, that this Epistle was not written at the very beginning of the promulgated Gospel, but when they already had some established order of government in the Churches. After him, some others, perhaps, pressed the point, but fewer. Neither Erasmus, nor Cajetan, nor the Magdeburg writers, nor Camero, nor others who think along with them on this question, made any mention of it.

units.la: II. Omninò levissimam omnium esse difficultatem, doctissimi Viri intellexe-runt. Et quidem primò, ponitur quod in quæstione est, & affirmat Calvinus, quod minimè probat. Imò quod ipse dubium esse & anceps non diffitetur, si verba Præfationis attendimus. Scilicet, formam illam catecheticæ & elementaris doctrinæ, minus congruere ætati Pauli. Cedo rationem, & vel ex Sacris, vel ex Antiquitate argumentum. Deinde, manifestà se contradictione involvit Virorum maximus. Commentaturus enim ad illum locum Capite v i. hæc habet. Hic unus locus abundè testatur, hujus ceremoniæ originem fluxisse ab Apostolis. Nempe illius ceremoniæ, quà transactà infantiâ ad catechesisim pueri offerebantur. Postea, Sciamus ergò à primis authoribus institutum suis-se &c.
units.tr: II. The most learned men have understood that this is by far the slightest of all difficulties. And first, what is at issue is assumed, and Calvin asserts it without proving it at all. Indeed, if we attend to the words of the Preface, he does not deny that it is doubtful and uncertain: namely, that that form of catechetical and elementary teaching is less suited to the age of Paul. Let me have the reason, and an argument either from the Scriptures or from antiquity. Next, the greatest of men entangles himself in a manifest contradiction. For when he comments on that passage in chapter 6, he says this: This one passage sufficiently shows that the origin of this ceremony flowed from the Apostles. Namely, of that ceremony by which, once infancy was past, children were offered for catechesis. Afterwards: Let us know, then, that it was instituted by the first authors, etc.

units.la: III. Tertiò igitur, salsissima est hypo-thesis, quæq; contradicit ipsi Paulo. Nam alibi elementaris illius doctrinæ palàm meminit ; & planè ut in hac Epistola distinguit, inter lac infantum, & cibum adultorum, easdemque planè, quas Author noster, adhibet voces τελειότητος, γάλακτος, βρωμάτων [?], νηπίων, 1.Cor.11.111. Nihil ergo Author noster novi, quod non alibi Paulus, præterquam nonnulla capita sigillatim enarret. Quartò, sola ratio, initialem aliquam obtinuisse illa ætate doctrinam, suadet. Fuisse enim tum cate-chumenos, rudiores, novitios, sacris ini-tiandos, quis neget? Hi ergo præscripta quædam fuisse capita, quæ primùm addis-cerent, quæ rogati responderent, quæ ad ritus sacros admittendi profiterentur, ne Calvinus quidem inficiatur.
units.tr: III. Thirdly, then, the hypothesis is utterly absurd, and it contradicts Paul himself. For elsewhere he openly mentions that elementary teaching, and he clearly makes the same distinction as in this Epistle, between the milk of infants and the solid food of adults, using plainly the same words that our author uses: perfection [τελειότης], milk [γάλα], meats [βρώματα], infants [νήπιοι], 1 Cor. 11.111. Therefore our author says nothing new, except that he sets out a few chapters one by one, which Paul elsewhere does not do. Fourthly, the reason alone, that some initial teaching had been established in that age, persuades us. For who would deny that there were then catechumens, the less instructed, novices, to be initiated into the sacred rites? So these were given certain prescribed chapters, which they first learned, which they answered when questioned, and which they professed in order to be admitted to the sacred rites. Not even Calvin denies this.

units.la: IV. Quintò, nec desunt in Scripturis Apostolicis, ipsæ etiam voces καταηχεῖσθαι [?] & κατηχούμενος [?]. Non quidem eo plane quo Ecclesiasticis deinceps scriptoribus sen-su, at certè affini, & pro elementari institutione. Locus est Act. xviii.25. de Apollo nonnisi primis imbuto rudimentis, acuratius postmodùm informando ; ἦν κατηχημένον τὴν ὁδὸν Κυρίου, μόνον ἐπιστάμενον βάπτισμα Ἰωάννυς [?]. Proferunt Gomarus, Gerardus, plures alij, locum Gal. vi.6. κοινωνείτω ὁ κατηχούμενος τῷ κατηχοῦντι. Sed palàm est generalius vocem usurpari, ut sit, ὁ διδασκόμενος μεταδιδότω τῷ διδάσκοντι. In tali autem catechetica institutione, usos fuisse formulâ, quamvis fortè alia ab Ecclesiasticis formulis, res ipsa docet. Nec incommodè huc trahi posset locus 1.Corint.
units.tr: IV. Fifthly, the very words [καταηχεῖσθαι] and [κατηχούμενος] are not lacking in the Apostolic Scriptures. Not indeed in the precise sense they later had with the ecclesiastical writers, but certainly in a related sense, meaning elementary instruction. There is a passage at Acts 18:25, about Apollos, who had been imbued only with the first rudiments and was afterwards to be more accurately instructed: [ἦν κατηχημένος τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ Κυρίου, μόνον ἐπιστάμενος βάπτισμα Ἰωάννου]. Gomarus, Gerhard and many others cite Gal. 6:6: [κοινωνείτω ὁ κατηχούμενος τῷ κατηχοῦντι]. But it is plain that the word is used more generally, so that it means: [ὁ διδασκόμενος μεταδιδότω τῷ διδάσκοντι], let the one who is taught share with the one who teaches. That they used a formula in such catechetical instruction, though perhaps a different one from the ecclesiastical formulas, the matter itself shows. Nor could the passage of 1 Corinthians be inappropriately brought in here,

units.la: XIV. πέντε λόγους λαλῆσαι, ἵνα κατηχήσω.
units.tr: [πέντε λόγους λαλῆσαι, ἵνα κατηχήσω]. Five words to speak, that I might instruct. [1 Cor. 14]

units.la: V. Sexto, per βαπτισμῶν διδαχήν, eruditi interpretantur non malè, doctrinam tradi solitam baptizandis. Sic διδαχὴ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, doctrina quam profiteri tenerentur, sacro hoc ritu initiandi. Et sanè omnino ea fuit Apostolorum praxis. Baptizabant, imponebant manus, sed praevia fidei, pænitentiæ, resurrectionis, judicij (quæ nostro Authori capita recensentur) ἐξομολογήσεως. Etiam de natura horum rituum (Βαπτισμῶν, Ἐπιθέσεως χειρῶν) circa initiandos adhibiti tum solitorum, informari primo necesse erat. Nec alia origo praxeôs in Christiana Ecclesia perpetuæ, non aliunde derivant vetustissimi Patrum, non aliunde ipse Calvinus.
units.tr: V. Sixthly, the learned interpret [βαπτισμῶν διδαχήν] not badly as the teaching customarily given to those to be baptized. So [διδαχὴ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ] is the doctrine which they were bound to profess when being initiated by this sacred rite. And indeed this was entirely the practice of the Apostles. They baptized and laid on hands, but after a prior confession of faith, repentance, resurrection, judgment (which are the chapters listed by our author). Also, concerning the nature of these rites ([βαπτισμῶν, ἐπιθέσεως χειρῶν]) used on those to be initiated, they had first to be instructed. Nor do the most ancient Fathers derive any other origin for a practice that continued in the Christian Church, nor does Calvin himself.

units.la: VI. Septimo, ex adverso, singula quæ hîc enarrantur capita, Pauli ætati vel imprimis congruant. Et hinc Epistolæ etiā antiquitatem arcessimus. Rectè antè nos observavit eruditissimus Camero, esse eadem illa quæ Paulus, pro concione Atheniensibus expositi, Act. xvii. Distinctè ibi videmus enarrari πίστιν εἰς Θεόν, μετάνοιαν, ἀνά-στασιν, κρίμα αἰώνιον. Ut hinc apud maximè rudes exordiri solitos fuisse, minimè dubium sit. Quod addit scriptor, de doctrina baptismatum, vel notat illa ipsa capita, rogari à baptizandis solita; vel præviam instructionem illorum rituum, circa eos quibus ritus illi conferebantur. Præterea, ceremonia illa ἐπιθέσεως χειρῶν, propria fuit istius ætatis. Ea videlicet, qua dona spiritualia in recens initiatos effun-debandebantur Actor. VIII. XIX Quam desiisse cum Apostolis, & cum miraculosâ eorundem gratia, eleganter Calvinus Lib. IV. Instit. Tandem constat, post illam ætatem nonnihil aliter digestos fuisse fundamentales articulos. Quod docet hodieque Symbolum, Apostolorum (si formam spectamus) falsò creditum.
units.tr: VI. Seventhly, on the contrary, each of the chapters explained here agrees above all with the age of Paul. And from this we also draw the antiquity of the Epistle. Our very learned Camero rightly observed before us that these are the same things which Paul set forth in his address to the Athenians, Acts 17. There we clearly see enumerated faith toward God, repentance, resurrection, eternal judgment. Hence it is hardly doubtful that these were customarily used with the most untutored. What the writer adds about the doctrine of baptisms either refers to those same chapters, which were customarily asked of those to be baptized, or to the prior instruction in those rites, for those to whom they were administered. Moreover, that ceremony of laying on of hands was peculiar to that age: that is, the one by which spiritual gifts were poured out upon the newly initiated, Acts 8 and 19. That this ceremony ceased with the Apostles and with their miraculous grace, Calvin elegantly shows in Book IV of the Institutes. Finally, it is established that after that age the fundamental articles were arranged somewhat differently. The Apostles' Creed, even today, teaches this (if we look at its form), though it is falsely believed to be theirs.

units.la: VII. Octavò, etiam posito, ab alio quàm Paulo Epistolam esse exaratam, nihilominùs ejusdem esse ætatis concedendum fuerit. Quod invictis antè evicimus argumentis, Parte II. Cap. IV. & VI. Scriptam adeo esse ante excidium Hierosolymitanum, & stante Sacerdotio. Ex quo vicissim colligimus, elementaré illâ doctrinam, congruere optimè illis temporibus.
units.tr: VII. Eighthly, even granting that the Epistle was written by someone other than Paul, it must nevertheless be conceded that it is of the same age. This we have already proved by unconquered arguments, in Part II, Chapters IV and VI. That it was written before the destruction of Jerusalem, while the priesthood still stood. From which in turn we conclude that that elementary teaching agrees very well with those times.

units.la: Verùm hæc satis, ad retundendam vim argumenti. Plura fortè, ex capitum singulorum examine mutuari possent. Sed Commentatoribus id relictum volumus, quos inter dignissimum sanè, optimus quondam nobisque conjunctissimus Parens, sibi locum vendicasset, ni fata, & hiulcæ mutilæque paginæ, ut plurimi plurimùm (si characteres spectamus) αἰ-νιγματώδεας, ac fere hieroglyphicæ, thesaurum tot expetitum votis, hactenus Theo-logis invidissent.
units.tr: But these points are enough to blunt the force of the argument. Perhaps more could be drawn from an examination of the individual chapters. But we leave this to the Commentators, among whom my excellent father, once so dear to us and so closely joined to us, would certainly have claimed the most worthy place for himself, had not the fates, and the gaping and mutilated pages, which for the most part (if we look at the letters) are enigmatic [αἰνιγματώδεις] and almost hieroglyphic, envied Theologians until now a treasure so much desired by their prayers.

units.la: VIII. Sunt hæ quidem omnes, quas sive Veteres, sive recentiores, in authorem Paulum strinxêre objectiones. Nisi jam aliud objectionum genus attendi-mus, quod ipsam Epistolæ canonicam authoritatem & ἀναμάρτητοσίαν vexat. Quarũ aliæ denuò vetustiorum, aliæ recentioris ævi. Illæ binæ potissimùm fuêre, 1. quod faveret Novatianorum impuro dogmati, de lapsis non recipiendis, 11. quod nec ab Arrianorum hæresi videretur aliena, & Christum factum creatumque haud obscurè doceat, de quibus nos libro 1. Cap. VIII. Hæ jam longè plures, motæ à Cajetano, Erasmo, Eniedino, & qui liberiùs de Canonicis variis pronunciarũt. 1. Peccare authorem in sacram Historiam. Dum virgam & urnam in Arca repositas fuisse dicit; dum, Librum fœderis sanguine, simul cum populo, à Mose aspersum; dum, usum hunc in aspersione, lana coccinea, aqua, hyssopo; dum, in has eundem erupisse voces, ἐκφοβός ἡμῖ καὶ ἐντρομος, Capitibus ix. & xii. ii. Arrietare in doctrinam, ab ipsis traditam Apostolis. Quando negat reditum ad poenitentiam, aut sanctorum perseverantiam; quando Esavi exemplo ipsis etiam poenitentibus spem adimit veniae; quando de salvificae naturā fidei, aliter ac Paulus loquitur, Capitibus x.xi.xii. iii. Allucinari in citatione & applicatione textus sacri. Sive loci illius ex Psalmo ii; sive alterius ii Sam. vii; sive qui extat Psalmo viii; sive denique Exod. xxiv, de Foedere & pacto Dei. Capitibus Epistolae i.ii.ix.
units.tr: VIII. These, indeed, are all the objections which, whether ancient or recent, have been levelled against Paul as author. Now let us attend to another kind of objection, which attacks the canonical authority and the infallibility of the Epistle itself. Some of these belong to older times, others to a more recent age. The two chief ones were these: first, that it favoured the impure dogma of the Novatians, about not receiving the lapsed; second, that it did not seem alien to the heresy of the Arians, and clearly taught that Christ was made and created, concerning which we spoke in Book I, Chapter VIII. These are now far more numerous, raised by Cajetan, Erasmus, Enedinus, and others who have spoken more freely about various canonical books. First, that the author errs in the sacred History, when he says that the rod and the urn were laid up in the Ark; when he says that the book of the covenant was sprinkled by Moses with blood together with the people; when he says that this was done in the sprinkling with scarlet wool, water and hyssop; when he says that the same author broke out into these words, "I am exceedingly afraid and trembling," Chapters 9 and 12. Second, that he goes astray in doctrine handed down by the Apostles themselves: when he denies a return to repentance, or the perseverance of the saints; when, by the example of Esau, he takes away hope of pardon even from those who repent; when he speaks of the nature of saving faith differently from Paul, Chapters 10, 11 and 12. Third, that he is mistaken in the citation and application of sacred texts: whether that passage from Psalm 2; or the other from 2 Sam. 7; or that which is found in Psalm 8; or finally Exodus 24, about the covenant and pact of God. Chapters 1, 2 and 9 of the Epistle.

units.la: IX. Sed haec alterius loci & disquisitionis. In illum εὐαγγελοφανῶν campum nos diffundere, nec instituti nostri fert ratio, neq; etiā temporis. Rem nobis esse cū iis potissimum intelligimus, qui de authora nō bene sentientes, authoritate pari nobiscū veneratione suscipiunt. Quin, dū paulo restituitur Epistola ac vindicatur, nullis jam machinis expugnari illius ἀυθεντία potest. Prius autem sic praestitum à nobis bis esse confidimus, & disputationem ita institutam, ut negare assensum, sit caliga-re in luce, καὶ λαλεῖν ὡς[?] ἐς τὸν ἥλιον[?]. Denique, ne Lectores nesciant, reservamus nobis aliquid in hoc argumento, cū iis suo tempore & loco communicandum. Nempe in nostro, de gravioribus Testamenti utrius-que Contradictoriis (missis sive leviori-bus, sive quæ fusius alij pertractarunt) Commentario. Quem aliquousq; produ-ximus, & Auditoribus etiamnum nostris publicè prælegimus. Sed nec festinabi-mus facere publici juris, ne scripturien-di (qui nostrorum morbus est temporum, sed nostri nec genij nec ætatis) affricetur nobis cacoëthes. Claudimus, disparilicet ratione, magni quondam Hipponensis verbis: Videor mihi debitum adjuvante Domino reddidisse. Quibus parum est, vel quibas nimium est, mihi ignoscant. Quibus autem satis est, non mihi sed Do-mino, mecum gratias congratulantes agant.
units.tr: IX. But these matters belong to another passage and another inquiry. Neither the plan of my work nor the time available allows me to spread myself out on that field of 'evangelical appearances' [εὐαγγελοφανῶν]. I understand that I have to deal chiefly with those who think poorly of the author, yet receive the Epistle with the same reverence for its authority as we do. Indeed, once the Epistle has been restored a little and vindicated, its authority [ἀυθεντία] cannot be overthrown by any siege engines. I trust that I have already twice done this beforehand, and so arranged the discussion that to withhold assent would be to be blind in broad daylight, and to speak as if to the sun [καὶ λαλεῖν ὡς ἐς τὸν ἥλιον]. Finally, so that readers may not be left in ignorance, I reserve for myself something on this subject to share with them at the proper time and place: namely, in my commentary on the weightier contradictions of both Testaments (leaving aside the lighter ones, and those which others have treated at greater length). I have carried this commentary some distance and have already read parts of it publicly to my hearers. But I shall not hasten to make it public, lest an itch to write (a disease of our times, though not of my genius or my age) take hold of me. I close, in a different manner, with the words of the great Bishop of Hippo: "I think I have paid the debt with the Lord's help. Let those for whom it is too little, or too much, pardon me. But let those for whom it is enough give thanks together with me, not to me but to the Lord."
